France, Décret 2020-1718 from 1 Jan 2021: paintings over 50 years €300,000 (was €150,000); watercolours, gouaches, pastels €50,000; drawings €30,000; prints €20,000; sculpture €100,000; photographs €25,000; other antiques over 50 years €100,000; printed maps over 100 years €25,000; the EU licence is now needed for exits to the UK (Ministère de la Culture note, https://www.culture.gouv.fr/Media/Medias-creation-rapide/Certificats-et-AST_modifs-decret-seuils_13-01-2021.pdf; vf V). NAV_RULES.fr.exp.needs matches.

Germany, KGSG § 24: third-country exports need a licence where Regulation 116/2009 applies; intra-EU thresholds category 3 paintings 75 years/€300,000; categories 4 and 7 (watercolours, sculpture) 75/€100,000; categories 5, 6, 8, 9 (drawings, prints, photographs, incunabula) 75/€50,000; category 12 archives 50/€50,000; category 14 means of transport 150/€100,000; category 15 other antiques 100/€100,000; other Annex I categories at the Annex ages and double the values; decision within 10 working days; a stay of up to two years exempt; works owned by their creator exempt (gesetze-im-internet.de, https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/kgsg/__24.html; vf V). NAV_RULES.de.exp.needs matches.

Italy, D.Lgs. 42/2004 art. 65(3)(a) as amended by L. 17 Mar 2026 n. 40 (GU 30 Mar 2026): works by deceased authors executed over 70 years ago need the attestato above €50,000 (was €13,500); library goods keep €13,500 (art. 65(3)(a-bis)); below the threshold a self-declaration under DPR 445/2000 whose validity equals the attestato’s (art. 65(4-ter)); loan authorisations within 90 days (Brocardi, https://www.brocardi.it/codice-dei-beni-culturali-e-del-paesaggio/parte-seconda/titolo-i/capo-v/sezione-i-bis/art65.html; Canella Camaiora, https://canellacamaiora.it/?p=37033; vf S). NAV_RULES.it.exp matches.

Spain, Ley 16/1985 art. 30: tax on the grant of the export authorisation; bands 5% up to 1,000,000 pesetas, 10% to 10,000,000, 20% to 100,000,000, 30% above, on the declared value as verified; exempt: goods lawfully imported within 10 years, authorised temporary exports, works by living authors (Normatia, https://normatia.com/es/normativa/patrimonio-historico-espanol/2026/titulo-iii-de-los-bienes-muebles/; Papelea, https://papelea.com/es/leyes/ley-del-patrimonio-historico-espanol/titulo-iii; vf S). The code’s euro bands €6,010 / €60,101 / €601,012 are the peseta limits at 166.386 (own arithmetic) and the band is applied to the whole value, as the statute reads; living artists skipped (!i.living) matches the exemption.

EU Regulation 2019/880: applies since 28 June 2025; import licence for archaeological objects and parts of monuments over 250 years old whatever the value; importer statement for other listed goods over 200 years old and worth over €18,000; goods created or discovered in the EU customs territory excluded (Bundesamt für Kunstverwaltung, https://www.kunstverwaltung.bund.de/EN/CulturalProperty/EuImportRegulation/EuImportRegulation_node.html; vf V). Arithmetic of flowModel (harness, vf V): London home $1m hammer → premium $280,000, 20% VAT on the premium $56,000, resale right £9,393 → $12,405 (4/3/1/0.5/0.25% bands on £757,174, under the £12,500 cap), buyer $1,348,405; an imported London lot adds 5% of the hammer ($50,000); Paris home → 20% on the premium $56,000 and the resale right €9,735 → $10,890; a Paris imported lot → 5.5% on hammer plus premium ($70,400) in place of the premium’s VAT; Geneva home → 8.1% on hammer plus premium ($103,680), none into the freeport; New York home → 8.875% sales tax on hammer plus premium ($113,600); any room → Manhattan use tax 8.875% ($113,600) with no sales tax; London → Paris 5.5% ($70,400) and Paris → London 5% ($64,000) on the price; HK → Geneva 8.1% ($103,680). Export cancels the room’s VAT on the premium and an imported lot’s import VAT; the resale right survives export. The ledger’s lo/hi sums equal the sum of its lines (test).

Arithmetic of the Navigator (harness, vf V): London → Washington/New York, $2.5m at auction: premium $670,000; use tax $190,200 (DC 6%) to $281,338 (NYC 8.875%) on hammer plus premium; the UK licence bites at £180,000 (50 years); landed $3.37m–$3.48m, 8–26 weeks. Spain → London, 1880 painting $1.5m: 30% band → $450,000; 5% UK import VAT $75,000. UAE: 5% duty then 5% VAT on the duty-paid value ($40,000 and $42,000 on $800,000). India: 11% duty then IGST on $555,000. Freeport → Switzerland: 8.1% on $1m = $81,000. A loan carries a carnet and no use tax or import VAT; a consignment enters under temporary admission.

Logic confirmed (harness): the EU licence (Regulation 116/2009) is tested only when leaving the Union and never on a UK → EU route; Germany’s intra-EU thresholds and the EU thresholds are applied in the right order (de → us, 60-year €200,000 painting: no national licence, EU licence due); a bar closes the gate for a sale or a move and opens it for a loan (Kahlo, Sher-Gil, pre-1890 Brazil); Spain’s export tax is skipped for living artists and for loans; the freeport takes Swiss law (navKey → 'ch') and bond for the tax; the sanctions gate closes a shipment to Russia from every sanctioning jurisdiction whatever the buyer’s passport; a company owner only changes the screening text (the beneficial owner must be named).

Whether the Bank of Russia renewed the $1m-a-month cap for April–September 2026 and October 2026–March 2027 (last confirmed to 31 Mar 2026).
Switzerland’s CHF 300 luxury-goods threshold and the SECO page; the Swiss AMLA CHF 100,000 cash rule (art. 8a) and the KGTG CHF 5,000 due-diligence line (carried from the terminal, not opened).

The GCC 5% duty on works of art for the UAE, Qatar and Saudi Arabia, Saudi’s 15% VAT, Brazil’s 4% II and 18% ICMS, Mexico’s 16% IVA and 0% duty, Australia’s 10% GST, Japan’s 10% consumption tax, Singapore’s 9% GST, Hong Kong’s zero (all plausible and consistent with memory; not re-opened this session).

The EU VAT rates the Navigator carries (France 5.5%, Germany 7%, Italy 5% since 1 Jul 2025 — the brief’s ‘Italy 10%’ is the pre-July-2025 rate —, Netherlands 9%, Spain 10%) and the UK’s effective 5% import VAT and 20% on the premium: carried from the terminal’s own primary citations (BOFiP, BMF, Assolombarda/Withers, Stb. 2025/339, Ley 37/1992, gov.uk), not re-opened.

The UK Artist’s Resale Right in sterling since 1 Apr 2024 (£1,000 threshold, £12,500 cap, bands at £50,000/£200,000/£350,000/£500,000) and France’s €750 threshold and €12,500 cap: the arithmetic matches Directive 2001/84 and the gov.uk guidance the terminal cites, but gov.uk was not opened this session.

US EAR Supplement No. 5 to Part 746 ($300 per unit for chapter 97) and EU Regulation 833/2014 Art. 3h (€300) and Art. 5b (€100,000): read by the research on a mirror and on K&L Gates / gesetze.legal; not re-opened.
New York’s non-resident purchase exemption (Tax Law §1118(2), TSB-A-08(7)S) and the credit for sales tax paid elsewhere; the DC credit rule.
Mexico’s list of artists declared artistic monuments (the data’s eleven names) and India’s nine declared art treasures beyond the five named in the row.
Whether Spain levies the export tax on definitive exits to other EU member states in practice (the statute’s text has no EU exemption).

The Phillips French and Geneva VAT guides behind VENUES.paris (5.5% on hammer plus premium for imported lots) and VENUES.geneva (8.1% on hammer plus premium): cited by the terminal with dates, not re-opened; Christie’s and Sotheby’s Geneva practice may differ (margin-scheme lots taxed on the premium only).

terms.what: The fee the house adds to the hammer price and keeps, unless it has promised part of it to the consignor (enhanced hammer) or to a guarantor (financing fee). Sotheby's, effective 13 February 2026 (all salerooms except wine): 28% on the hammer up to and including US$2m (£1.5m), 22% from US$2m to US$8m (£1.5m–£6m), 15% above US$8m (£6m); the 15% top tier was unchanged, the lower band rose from 27% and its ceiling from US$1m (£800,000) to US$2m. Christie's, since September 2025: 27% up to US$1.5m (£1m), 22% from US$1.5m to US$8m, 15% above US$8m (before that 26% to US$1m, 21% to US$6m, 15% above); the Antiques Trade Gazette confirms the September 2025 date and that Christie's 'has no current plans to change rates'. Phillips, from its own schedule effective 12 April 2026: 29% to US$2m, 22% from US$2m to US$8m, 15% above (London £1.5m/£6m; Paris €1.75m/€7m; Hong Kong HK$15m/HK$60m), with Priority Bidding rates of 25% / 20% / 14% for a binding absentee bid at or above the low estimate lodged at least 48 hours before the sale and paid by the invoice date; watches 27/21/14.5%. Bonhams, for sales after 1 October 2026 (GBP): 30% on the first £25,000, 28% to £500,000, 25% to £1m, 21% to £5m, 14% above. Sotheby's 2024 experiment (a flat 20% to US$6m and 10% above, with a flat 10% vendor's commission) was reversed within a year; chief executive Charles Stewart said it 'proved less attractive to potential sellers'. The schedules reproduce the published results exactly: the Pollock Number 7A at Christie's (18 May 2026) hammered at US$157m and sold for US$181,185,000, a premium of US$24,185,000 = 27% × 1.5m + 22% × 6.5m + 15% × 149m; the Basquiat Museum Security at Sotheby's (14 May 2026) hammered at US$45.25m and sold for US$52,717,500, a premium of US$7,467,500 = 28% × 2m + 22% × 6m + 15% × 37.25m. Citi Private Bank's primer notes the top-bracket rate has risen by roughly ten points since 2000 and that the houses have shifted their cost base 'to the buyer's side'.
terms.who_earns: The buyer pays; the house earns it. At the top of the market part of it is given back to the consignor or to a third-party guarantor, so the house's realised margin on a trophy lot is well below the headline rate: Sotheby's reported an auction commission margin (all commission revenue over net auction sales) of 14.3% in 2015, down from 16.6% in 2011, and blamed 'commission sharing arrangements and auction guarantees'.
src: Phillips, Buyer's Premium schedule (PDF), effective 12 April 2026
ArtDependence, Bonhams increases buyer's premium, 2 Sept 2026
The Value, Sotheby's Now & Contemporary, May 2026
Citi Private Bank, The art of auction economics
terms.note: Phillips's figures are primary (its own PDF, V). Sotheby's and Christie's rest on three agreeing trade-press and legal reports (The Art Newspaper and the Antiques Trade Gazette, Feb 2026; Grossman LLP, spring 2026) plus the exact arithmetic of four 2026 results; Christie's own financial-information page returned a bot-check script twice and its help-library page gives no figures. Bonhams is from one trade report (GBP only).

terms.n: Seller's commission (vendor's commission) and its waiver
terms.what: The consignor's fee is the house's most negotiable number. Sotheby's published a flat 10% vendor's commission in its 2024 structure and withdrew it in February 2025 because it 'proved less attractive to potential sellers'. At the top the commission is waived outright, and beyond that the house pays the consignor part of its own buyer's premium, which Citi Private Bank calls 'a negative seller's commission' and the trade calls the enhanced hammer. No house publishes the point at which the waiver begins; the sources read describe it only as a feature of 'the top of the market'.
terms.who_earns: Below the top the consignor pays it and the house earns it; at the top the house forgoes it to win the consignment.
src: Citi Private Bank, The art of auction economics
terms.note: The threshold for a waived commission is unpublished.

terms.what: The house pays the consignor the hammer price plus a share of the buyer's premium. Citi Private Bank describes it as a share of buyer's-premium proceeds passed to consignors, 'a negative seller's commission'. The one published account with figures is Katya Kazakina's for Bloomberg (26 April 2016): the trade codes the deal as a percentage of hammer — 'A 105' means the seller keeps an extra 5% on top of the hammer price, 'A 109' a 9% premium — and the named deals were: Sotheby's handed Audrey Irmas 'most of its $7.8 million buyer fee' on Cy Twombly's Untitled (New York City), sold for US$62.75m on 11 November 2015, and let the buyer, Daniel Sundheim, 'largely pay for the Twombly with a pledge to consign seven other works' worth US$50m–75m with guaranteed minimums; Christie's handed Sheldon Solow 'much of its $15.3 million in fees' on the Giacometti that hammered at US$126m in May 2015; and Sotheby's would earn no commission on the A. Alfred Taubman collection until it had covered the US$515m guarantee it gave the estate. Sotheby's commission margin had fallen 'to about 14 percent from 21 percent' since 2009. Harry Smith of Gurr Johns explained in December 2023 that when a lot is guaranteed the guarantor takes 'a significant part of the upside' while the house 'gets back the enhanced hammer'. Quotes: Doug Woodham, Christie's Americas president 2012–14: 'Enhanced hammer deals have had a profoundly negative impact on the economics of the auction houses'; Thomas Danziger, lawyer for consignors: 'We'd ask for enhanced hammer for anything'; David Nash: the houses 'would do anything to get the deal away from the competition'; Tad Smith (Sotheby's, Feb 2016): deal-making remains 'fairly significant' for competitive collections. No source published since gives a percentage for any named 2024–26 deal.
terms.who_earns: The consignor gains (102–110% of hammer in the trade's coding); the house gives up part of its premium. Rates on current trophy consignments are unpublished.
src: Bloomberg via WealthManagement.com, Katya Kazakina, 26 April 2016
Citi Private Bank, The art of auction economics
terms.note: The coding and the named 2015 deals are from Bloomberg (2016); 'most of' and 'much of' are the only quantities given for them. Pages that should have carried a current figure and do not: the Macklowe reports (2021–22), the Lauder announcement (2025), the Art Newspaper guarantee explainers (2018, 2023).

terms.what: The house promises the consignor a minimum price. If the lot sells above it the house is 'generally entitled to a share of the excess proceeds (the overage)'; if it sells below, the house funds the shortfall; if it fails to sell the house pays the guarantee and takes the work into inventory to resell later (Sotheby's Form 10-K for 2015, which warned that unhedged guarantees expose it to 'auction guarantee losses and/or deterioration in auction commission margins'). Scale then: outstanding guarantees of US$62.1m at 31 December 2015, of which US$28.7m was laid off through irrevocable bids; the guarantee liability carried was US$1m (2015) and US$5.3m (2014); the Taubman collection guarantee produced 'a projected loss ... of approximately $3 million'. Boodle Hatfield records that Sotheby's 'reportedly lost $52 million in one season' on guarantees in autumn 2008. Scale now: whole collections are guaranteed. Sotheby's gave the Taubman estate a US$515m guarantee in 2015 and would earn no commission until it was covered (Bloomberg, 2016); it guaranteed all 35 Macklowe lots in November 2021 (22 also with irrevocable bids) and all 30 in May 2022 (19 with irrevocable bids); it 'offered a financial guarantee' on the Leonard Lauder collection in September 2025 and declined to say whether third parties would share the risk, and all 24 Lauder evening lots, the Klimt Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer among them, were 'backed by a guarantee'. Christie's guaranteed all of the Riggio collection (May 2025, 38 lots, aggregate low estimate US$252m); Sotheby's guaranteed all 31 Landau lots (Nov 2023, aggregate low estimate US$344.5m) and the Macklowe collection (estimate 'over $600m', 2021); all 60 Allen evening lots (Nov 2022) and all 16 Newhouse lots (May 2026) came with guarantees. Catalogues mark a house guarantee with the symbol º and a third-party one with º♦; the amount is never printed.
terms.who_earns: The consignor gets certainty and gives up part of the upside; the house takes price risk in exchange for the consignment and a share of the overage. When the hammer total comes in under the guaranteed level, as the Riggio hammer total (c. US$228.6m) did against its US$252m low estimate, the house funds the gap. Hugill & Ip's illustration of an overage split is 70% to the consignor and 30% to the house.
src: Boodle Hatfield, Auction house guarantees: friend or foe?
Hugill & Ip, Third-party guarantees in the art market, July 2019
The Art Newspaper, Landau report, 9 Nov 2023
The Art Newspaper, Allen sale, 10 Nov 2022
Bloomberg via WealthManagement.com, Katya Kazakina, 26 April 2016
The Value, Sotheby's secures the Lauder collection, 16 Sept 2025
terms.note: Mechanism and 2015 amounts read on the filing; the Riggio guarantee level is not published, so the shortfall inference assumes the guarantee sat at or near the low estimate.

terms.what: A counterparty 'commits to bid a predetermined price' on the lot. If the bid wins, the counterparty pays that price plus the buyer's premium. If it is outbid, 'the counterparty is generally entitled to receive a share of the auction commission earned on the sale' and/or a share of the overage. In a partner-sharing arrangement the counterparty instead funds a share of any shortfall and takes a proportionate share of unsold property, 'in exchange for accepting a share of the financial exposure under the auction guarantee'. Counterparties are 'typically major international art dealers or major art collectors' (Sotheby's 10-K for 2015). The numbers the trade press gives: the guarantor's share of the overage is typically 20–30%, within a range of 10% to 50% (The Art Newspaper, Nov 2018); an anonymous guarantor in 2023: 'All I care about is the 20%, 25% or 30% or whatever the amount we agree on'; the dealer Inigo Philbrick in 2018 wanted US$100,000–150,000 for risking US$1m and said that if the work sold on a single bid he made about US$5,000. A guarantor who ends up buying receives its financing fee from the house and so pays less than rival bidders (The Art Newspaper 2018; Boodle Hatfield: the work is acquired 'essentially at a discount due to the fee owed'). Returns (ArtTactic/Deloitte): 21.4–21.8% average at the 2021 peak, 11.1% in 2022, 9% in 2023. Volume: US$3.47bn of auction sales guaranteed worldwide in 2018, US$2.5bn of it laid off to third parties; third-party guarantees about US$3.4bn in 2022, a likely record; down almost 30% in 2023. How common on the night: at Sotheby's Modern evening sale of 19 May 2026, 30 of the 42 lots offered came guaranteed by third parties and the guarantees were called on in about ten cases, a third (Il Sole 24 Ore); the Kahlo El sueño (Nov 2025) was 'offered with an irrevocable bid' after being consigned without a guarantee in September; 26 of the sold lots at Sotheby's Modern sale of 13 May 2025 were guaranteed, 24 by third parties; 25 of 31 Landau lots (Nov 2023) had third-party backing, their low estimates US$297.3m or 86.3% of the aggregate; Christie's arranged irrevocable bids on two-thirds of the Riggio lots including the top three (May 2025); each of the top eight Newhouse lots (May 2026) was 'subject to third-party guarantee'; at Christie's 13 May 2015 contemporary sale 50 of 85 lots were guaranteed, 36 in-house and 14 by third parties, and Christie's said sellers are 'not usually' told who the third party is. Guarantees are now syndicated: guarantors sell fractions to anonymous partners 'usually in fours, sometimes threes', and Christie's agreement forbids it ('you shall not share any sums paid to you under this Agreement with any third party').
terms.who_earns: The guarantor earns the fee and/or 20–30% of the overage when outbid, and buys at a discount when not; the house lays off its risk and keeps the rest of the premium; the consignor's floor is secured but, as Harry Smith warns, a guarantee can be 'a bad deal' for the vendor when the hammer materially exceeds the guarantee.
src: Boodle Hatfield, Auction house guarantees: friend or foe?
The Art Newspaper, Landau report, 9 Nov 2023
terms.note: Structure is primary (10-K); the percentages are from the trade press quoting anonymous guarantors and one named dealer (Philbrick, 2018), not from any house.

terms.what: The house's payment to the irrevocable bidder for standing behind the lot. Christie's 'agrees a financing fee with the third party' and the third party also receives 'a percentage of any sum made above the guaranteed amount' (The Art Newspaper, 2015). When the guarantor is the buyer it still receives the fee and so pays less than its rivals (The Art Newspaper, 2018). The sources read give no published fee percentage; the only figures are the guarantor's own wishes (Philbrick: US$100,000–150,000 on US$1m at risk) and the upside shares (20–30% typical).
terms.who_earns: The guarantor earns it; the house pays it out of the buyer's premium, which is why guaranteed trophy lots show thin realised margins for the house.

terms.what: Sotheby's 10-K for 2015: for auctions, buyer payment is due 'no more than 30 days from the sale date' and 'payments to consignors are due 35 days from the sale date'; for private sales the buyer pays on the sale date and the consignor is paid shortly after. Extended payment terms are 'usually up to one year from sale', rarely longer.
terms.who_earns: The house holds the float between the buyer's payment and the consignor's settlement; an extended-payment buyer gets credit from the house, which carries the receivable and the risk that the consignor must still be paid.
terms.note: Current (2026) conditions of business not read in this session; the 10-K rule is the last published one.

terms.n: Loan against the work or the proceeds (Sotheby's Financial Services)
terms.what: Sotheby's Financial Services makes consignor advances (short-term, against property to be sold within about a year) and term loans (initial maturities up to two years, variable market rates). Management targets a 50% loan-to-value ratio, calculated as principal divided by the low auction estimate; 51–60% is permitted and above 60% rarely. Average loan portfolio in 2015 US$732.8m. In February 2026 SFS closed a US$900m asset-backed securitisation (Sotheby's ArtFi Master Trust, Series 2026-1) backed by art-secured loans and, for the first time, loans against collectible cars; SFS chief executive Ron Elimelekh said the deal 'was significantly oversubscribed'. The first securitisation (Sotheby's ArtFi Master Trust, Series 2024-1, US$700m, April–May 2024) was backed by 89 art-equity loans and consignor advances secured on more than 2,800 works worth about US$1.4bn; SFS's loan book was about US$1.6bn at 31 December 2023, loans run from US$1m to US$200m, loan-to-value averages about 50% of appraised value, art-equity loans run one to two years and consignor advances 12 to 15 months; investors are repaid the US$700m by 22 March 2027 (The Art Newspaper, 23 May 2024). Interest rates are not disclosed in either report.
terms.who_earns: The lender (the house's finance arm) earns interest; the borrower (a consignor wanting cash before the sale, or a buyer) pays it. A work estimated at US$50m supports a US$25m advance at the 50% target.
src: The Art Newspaper, Gray Market, 23 May 2024
terms.note: Interest rates are not disclosed in the filing excerpt read.

terms.n: Introductory commission, advisers and the business-getters
terms.what: Advisers who bring a buyer or a consignment are paid a percentage. The published baseline for a buying adviser is 10% of the purchase price: 'to the extent that there's an industry standard, it's 10%' (The Art Newspaper, 2007), with dealers saying consultants ask for 15% or even 20% and adviser Candace Worth calling 10% 'a no-brainer'. Ralph DeLuca (Cultured, Feb 2025) lists the three current models — a percentage of the purchase price invoiced separately at the time of purchase, a yearly retainer, or a project fee — and the rule that the adviser 'should be compensated from only one side of the transaction': 'whoever pays the advisor is that advisor's client'. Inside the houses the business-getters are paid by the house: the one published price is Sotheby's purchase of Art Agency Partners on 11 January 2016 'for initial cash consideration of $50 million' plus 'earn-out payments not to exceed $35 million in the aggregate' over four to five years, 'contingent on the achievement of a minimum level of financial performance'. The Rybolovlev court papers put a figure on one specialist's take: of about US$19m Sotheby's earned on roughly US$316m of private sales to Yves Bouvier, over US$979,000 went to Samuel Valette, whose business was 86–97% Bouvier from 2011 to 2014.
terms.who_earns: The adviser earns from the buyer (or, improperly, from both sides); the house's specialists earn salary and incentive pay 'a function of Sotheby's profitability'; no lot-specific bonus is published in the filing excerpts read.
terms.note: The brief's lower bound of 2% for large purchases is not in any page read; the 10% baseline dates from 2007.

terms.what: The house funds the campaign. The sources read record the practice but not the budgets: the Sydell Miller collection was 'marketed and toured worldwide by Sotheby's' before the November 2024 sale; the Lauder collection opened Sotheby's new Breuer Building headquarters (Nov 2025); the Allen collection had been shown as a travelling museum exhibition (Seeing Nature, 39 works, Portland 2015–16) years before the sale. No marketing contribution figure for any sale was found.
terms.who_earns: The house pays; the consignor gets the campaign free; the figure is negotiated and unpublished.

terms.n: Private-sale commission (the alternative to the rostrum)
terms.what: The Rybolovlev v Sotheby's trial (Manhattan federal court, 8–30 January 2024) put the house's private-sale economics on the record: Bouvier spent roughly US$316m on four works through Sotheby's private sales and Sotheby's earned around US$19m from them, about 6%. On the Salvator Mundi, Bouvier bought through Sotheby's for US$83m on 2 May 2013 and sold to Rybolovlev the next day for US$127.5m. A ten-member jury cleared Sotheby's of aiding and abetting fraud; Rybolovlev had sought US$377m.
terms.who_earns: The house earns a negotiated commission from the seller (and sometimes the buyer); the intermediary dealer earns the spread.
terms.note: The 6% is this researcher's division of the two figures reported from the court papers.

terms.n: Insuring, moving and storing the lot
terms.what: The only published figures are for insurance. On the Klimt Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (expected 'more than $150 million'), Insurance Business reported on 11 November 2025 that annual premiums for the new owner could be 'north of 0.3% to 0.5% of insured value, translating to $450,000–$750,000 per year', rising if the work travels or sits in a region of high political or environmental exposure; that Sotheby's 'may temporarily extend coverage approaching half the painting's value'; and that insurers 'often mandate bespoke crating, constant GPS tracking, and dual-custody logistics' (Celia Santana, Personal Risk Management Solutions). FreightWaves (Dec 2019) gives only generic examples: about US$75,000 to move an expensive work from Australia to the UK, and 'around $100,000 for a three-month period' of commercial insurance on famous artists' works in the UK; Momart and Artex are named as specialist shippers but no price is attributed to them. No storage figure for a trophy lot was found.
terms.who_earns: The insurer earns 0.3–0.5% of value a year; the shipper and the storage facility earn fees that no source quantifies for a lot of this size.
terms.note: Insurance rate is one broker's estimate reported in the trade press; shipping figure is a 2019 generic example; storage: nothing published.

economics.description: Worked economics of a US$50m hammer at a New York evening sale in 2026, as far as the sources support it. Premium arithmetic is done from the published tiers and cross-checked against published hammer/with-fee pairs; the guarantee and advisor lines use the ranges the trade press quotes; the enhanced hammer has no published figure and is stated as such.

lines.party: The house: buyer's premium (Sotheby's schedule from 13 Feb 2026)
lines.takes: US$8.18m premium; price with fees US$58.18m
lines.basis: 28% on the first US$2m (US$0.56m) + 22% on US$2m–US$8m (US$1.32m) + 15% on the US$42m above US$8m (US$6.3m). The same tiers reproduce the Basquiat Museum Security result of 14 May 2026 exactly (US$45.25m hammer, US$52,717,500 with fees).
src: The Value, Sotheby's Now & Contemporary, May 2026

lines.party: The house: buyer's premium (Christie's schedule since Sept 2025)
lines.takes: US$8.135m premium; price with fees US$58.135m
lines.basis: 27% on the first US$1.5m (US$0.405m) + 22% on US$1.5m–US$8m (US$1.43m) + 15% on the US$42m above US$8m (US$6.3m). The same tiers reproduce the Pollock Number 7A result of 18 May 2026 exactly (US$157m hammer, US$181,185,000 with fees).

lines.takes: Nil on a lot of this size
lines.basis: Waived at the top of the market; Sotheby's flat 10% vendor's commission of 2024 was withdrawn in February 2025 as 'less attractive to potential sellers'. The waiver threshold is unpublished.
src: Citi Private Bank, The art of auction economics

lines.takes: US$50m hammer plus a share of the US$8.18m premium: US$2.5m at 'A 105' or US$4.5m at 'A 109' in the trade's coding; the actual rate on a 2026 trophy is unpublished; paid 35 days after the sale
lines.basis: Bloomberg (2016): 'A 105' means the seller keeps an extra 5% on top of the hammer, 'A 109' 9%; in the named 2015 deals Sotheby's gave Audrey Irmas 'most of' its US$7.8m premium on the US$62.75m Twombly and Christie's gave Sheldon Solow 'much of' its US$15.3m on the US$126m-hammer Giacometti. Citi: 'a negative seller's commission'; Harry Smith (Gurr Johns): the house 'gets back the enhanced hammer' when a guarantor takes the upside.
src: Bloomberg via WealthManagement.com, Katya Kazakina, 26 April 2016
Citi Private Bank, The art of auction economics

lines.party: The third-party guarantor (irrevocable bid at US$45m, outbid)
lines.takes: US$1m–1.5m as its 20–30% share of the US$5m overage (range US$0.5m–2.5m at 10–50%), plus any financing fee, which is unpublished
lines.basis: Overage = US$50m hammer − US$45m guarantee = US$5m. Typical upside share 20–30%, range 10–50% (The Art Newspaper, Nov 2018); 'the 20%, 25% or 30% or whatever the amount we agree on' (anonymous guarantor, May 2023). For the fee itself the only figure is one dealer's 2018 wish of US$100,000–150,000 per US$1m at risk, which on US$45m would be US$4.5m–6.75m; no house confirms any such rate.

lines.party: The third-party guarantor (if it buys at US$50m)
lines.takes: Pays the hammer plus premium but receives its fee back, so buys 'essentially at a discount'
lines.basis: The Art Newspaper (2018) and Boodle Hatfield; the 10-K confirms the bidder pays 'the predetermined price plus the buyer's premium'. Three guaranteed Sotheby's lots of May 2026 show premiums far below schedule — Picasso Arlequin (Buste): US$40m hammer, US$42.6m with fees (schedule implies US$46.68m); de Kooning Untitled III: US$23.5m / US$26.0m (US$27.7m); Rothko Untitled: US$15m / US$16.465m (US$17.93m) — consistent with a guarantor purchase netted of the fee, but no source read says so for these lots. Il Sole 24 Ore reports that at Sotheby's 19 May 2026 sale the guarantees were 'called on' in about ten of the 30 third-party-guaranteed lots, i.e. the guarantor took the work, without naming which.
src: Boodle Hatfield, Auction house guarantees: friend or foe?
The Value, Sotheby's Now & Contemporary, May 2026

lines.party: The house: net of guarantee and give-backs
lines.takes: Far less than the US$8.18m headline; Sotheby's all-in commission margin was 14.3% of net auction sales in 2015 against a top tier then of 12%–25%
lines.basis: Sotheby's 10-K for 2015: 'commission sharing arrangements and auction guarantees' reduce the auction commission margin (16.6% in 2011, 16.3% in 2012, 15.9% in 2013, 14.7% in 2014, 14.3% in 2015). Bloomberg (2016): the margin fell 'to about 14 percent from 21 percent' since 2009 while sales more than doubled.
src: Bloomberg via WealthManagement.com, Katya Kazakina, 26 April 2016

lines.takes: Up to US$5.8m at the 10% published baseline on a US$58.18m purchase; large deals are negotiated lower, but no lower figure is published in the pages read
lines.basis: The Art Newspaper (2007): 'to the extent that there's an industry standard, it's 10%'; Cultured (2025): a percentage of the purchase price, a retainer or a project fee, paid by one side only.

lines.party: The state (New York, if the work is delivered in New York City)
lines.takes: 8.875% sales and use tax: about US$5.16m on US$58.18m
lines.basis: NYC Department of Finance: 'a total sales and use tax of 8.875 percent' = 4% New York State + 4.5% New York City + 0.375% Metropolitan Commuter Transportation District surcharge. The base (hammer plus premium) follows the houses' conditions of sale, which were not read in this session; a work shipped out of state is taxed where delivered. No artist's resale right applies in New York.
src: NYC Department of Finance, New York State sales and use tax
lines.note: Rate is primary; the tax base and the absence of a US resale royalty are from general knowledge, not a page read.

lines.party: The lender (Sotheby's Financial Services) if the consignor borrows ahead of the sale
lines.takes: Interest on an advance of up to about US$25m against a US$50m low estimate (50% LTV target; 60% ceiling)
About 6% to the house: Sotheby's earned about US$19m on US$316m of private sales to Bouvier (2011–14)
lines.basis: Court papers in Rybolovlev v Sotheby's as reported by The Value; over US$979,000 of it went to the specialist Samuel Valette.

lines.takes: Insurance about US$175,000–290,000 a year at 0.3–0.5% of a US$58.18m insured value (the published range, quoted for the US$150m Klimt as US$450,000–750,000); shipping and storage unpublished for a lot of this size
lines.basis: Insurance Business (11 Nov 2025) on the Klimt Lederer: premiums 'north of 0.3% to 0.5% of insured value'; FreightWaves (2019) gives only a generic US$75,000 intercontinental shipping example and 'around $100,000 for a three-month period' of cover. The US$175,000–290,000 is this researcher's application of the published rate.

cases.work: Gustav Klimt, Bildnis Elisabeth Lederer (Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer), 1914–16
cases.price: US$236.3m with fees (US$205m hammer), 18 November 2025, Sotheby's New York (first marquee sale in the Breuer Building); reported elsewhere as US$236.4m
cases.consignor: The estate of Leonard A. Lauder (d. June 2025, aged 92); Sotheby's announced the consignment on 16 September 2025 (55 works, valued at about US$400m); the 24-lot evening sale made US$456.2m hammer / US$527.4m with fees against HENI's stated estimates of US$379.2m–412.4m (The Art Newspaper: 'in excess of $400m'), white-glove
cases.terms: Estimate on request of US$150m ('over US$150 million' at announcement; Blumenwiese US$80m–100m, Waldabhang US$70m–90m, the Munch 'more than US$20 million'). Guaranteed: Sotheby's 'offered a financial guarantee' to win the consignment and declined to say whether it would share the risk with third parties; all 24 evening lots were 'backed by guarantees' and the Klimt itself was 'backed by a guarantee' (guarantor unspecified). No enhanced-hammer or fee terms are published. The premium implied by the two published figures (US$31.3m on US$205m) matches Sotheby's then schedule (27% to US$1m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above). Insuring it afterwards: premiums 'north of 0.3% to 0.5% of insured value', US$450,000–750,000 a year on the estimate, per Insurance Business.
cases.buyer: Not identified; the winning bidder was on the telephone with Julian Dawes, Sotheby's vice chairman and head of Impressionist and Modern art
cases.underbidders: Four other telephone bidders and one woman seated in the front row; bidding ran nearly 20 minutes, at times in US$5m steps
people: Phyllis Kao (auctioneer of the Now & Contemporary sale the same night)
Cassandra Hatton (Sotheby's, phone bid for the Cattelan America)
cases.aftermath: Second-most expensive work ever sold at auction after the Warhol Marilyn (US$195m, 2022) and Sotheby's most valuable lot ever; Sotheby's night totalled US$605.1m hammer / US$706m with fees, its highest ever. Other Lauder lots: Klimt Blumenwiese US$75m hammer / US$86m; Klimt Waldabhang bei Unterach US$61m / US$68.3m; Munch Sankthansnatt US$30m / US$35.1m; Matisse La Serpentine US$14.5m / US$16.7m; Agnes Martin The Garden US$14.8m / US$17.6m (record).
src: The Value, Sotheby's secures the Lauder collection, 16 Sept 2025
cases.note: Buyer not identified in any page read; whether a third party stood behind Sotheby's guarantee is not disclosed. Artnet's report of the night could not be opened (site error).

cases.work: The Macklowe collection (Rothko No. 7, 1951; Giacometti Le Nez; Warhol Nine Marilyns; Twombly Untitled, 2007; Richter Seestück)
cases.price: US$922.2m with fees over two sales: 15 November 2021, 35 lots, US$588.7m hammer / US$676.1m with fees (estimate US$439.4m–618.9m); 16 May 2022, 30 lots, US$208.7m hammer / US$246.1m with fees (estimate US$167.6m–236.4m); Sotheby's New York
cases.consignor: Harry and Linda Macklowe, by court order: in January 2020 New York State Supreme Court Justice Laura Drager appointed Michael Findlay of Acquavella Galleries as receiver to sell the 65 most valuable works within three years; he postponed the sale in spring 2020 for the pandemic
cases.terms: Sotheby's guaranteed the collection to win it — 'We have guaranteed the collection which speaks to the quality of the collection' (Mari-Claudia Jiménez) — and did not confirm the amount, presumed by The Art Newspaper to be at least the US$600m estimate; adviser Todd Levin: 'the upfront guarantee was most likely the breakpoint'. Christie's lost the consignment. Every lot in both sales was guaranteed; 22 of the 35 November lots and 19 of the 30 May lots also carried irrevocable bids. Both hammer totals fell inside their estimate ranges, so the guarantee was covered. No enhanced-hammer or fee term is published.
cases.buyer: Rothko No. 7 (1951): US$77.5m hammer / US$82.4m, to a bidder from Asia on the line with Patti Wong after an eight-minute contest; Giacometti Le Nez: US$68m / US$78.3m, to a client of Hong Kong specialist Yonnie Fu, later identified by Justin Sun as himself; Pollock Number 17, 1951: US$53m / US$61.1m, via Grégoire Billault after a nine-minute four-way contest; Richter Abstraktes Bild (1993): US$28.5m / US$33m; Agnes Martin Untitled #44: US$15.2m / US$17.7m via Patti Wong. May 2022: Rothko Untitled (1960) US$41.5m / US$48m via Billault; Richter Seestück US$26m / US$30.1m via David Galperin; Warhol Self-Portrait (1986) US$16m / US$18.7m via Yasuaki Ishizaka; Lichtenstein Mirror #9 US$5m / US$6m via Lisa Dennison
cases.underbidders: Not named beyond the Asia-based contest for the Rothko and the four-way Pollock battle
people: Yonnie Fu (Sotheby's Hong Kong, Giacometti phone)
Grégoire Billault (Sotheby's head of contemporary art, Pollock and Rothko phones)
Justin Sun (buyer of Le Nez, by his own account)
David Galperin, Yasuaki Ishizaka (Sotheby's phones, May 2022)
cases.aftermath: The most valuable collection ever sold at auction at the time (ahead of the Rockefeller sales at US$835.1m), overtaken by the Allen sale a year later; Sotheby's most valuable single sale (US$676.1m) until the Lauder night of November 2025.
cases.note: Totals and guarantee coverage now sourced; the guarantee amount and the receiver's terms remain unpublished; the court papers were not read directly.

Il Sole 24 Ore: 30 of the 42 lots offered came guaranteed by third parties, nine of the top ten were guaranteed, and the guarantees were called on in about ten cases (a third), 'in three cases' probably saving the lot. The Picasso's reported premium (US$2.6m on US$40m) is well below the schedule (US$6.68m), consistent with a guarantor purchase at a netted fee; no page read says so, and Sotheby's lot page shows results only after login.

guarantors.reported: Reportedly gave the largest third-party guarantee on record, US$150m, for Modigliani's Nu couché (sur le côté gauche), 1917, which sold at Sotheby's New York in May 2018 for US$157.2m; named again in 2023 among the active guarantors.

Reportedly among the few parties guaranteeing works at US$20m–30m or more (2018); 'understood to trade guarantees back and forth' with Larry Gagosian (2023). No specific lot is named in the pages read.
Named with the Mugrabis as a guarantor who trades guarantees (2023); no specific lot named.
Said in 2018 he offered about 20–25 third-party guarantees a year and wanted US$100,000–150,000 for each US$1m risked; later convicted of fraud (2022) in matters unrelated to those guarantees.
guarantors.note: The conviction is from memory, not from the page read.

guarantors.reported: 'Hundreds of millions of dollars in guarantees' to date (Dec 2023); the only firm named in that report, which otherwise describes guarantors as 'a handful of very big collectors and dealers'.

Sotheby's said about 65% of its guarantors in May 2018 were private collectors, 40% of them first-timers, against 75% in November 2017; one unnamed collector guarantees about four works a year 'in the tens of millions'; an unnamed New York private dealer has orchestrated 'at least 20 or more' syndicated guarantees in fours and threes (2023).

Christie's guaranteed the whole Riggio collection (May 2025) and the Magritte Ertegun (Nov 2024, with a third-party bid behind it); Sotheby's guaranteed the Macklowe (2021), Landau (2023) and Miller Monet (2024) consignments and backed them with irrevocable bids; neither house names its counterparties, and Christie's says sellers are 'not usually' told who they are.

Sotheby's 'offered a financial guarantee' to win the 55-work Leonard Lauder consignment (announced 16 Sept 2025) and declined to say whether third parties would share the risk; all 24 evening lots on 18 Nov 2025, the US$236.4m Klimt included, were 'backed by a guarantee'.

No source publishes a financing-fee percentage, a marketing contribution or any current lot-level guarantee amount. Pages that should have carried them and do not: Sotheby's 10-K (2015), The Art Newspaper's guarantee explainers (2015, 2018, 2023), Boodle Hatfield, Hugill & Ip, Bloomberg's enhanced-hammer report (2016), the Macklowe reports (2021–22), the Lauder announcement (2025), The Art Newspaper's 2024 piece on the Sotheby's securitisation. The enhanced hammer is now quantified only by the trade's 2015–16 coding ('A 105', 'A 109') and the Irmas/Solow deals ('most of', 'much of' the premium).
Basquiat In This Case (2021): guarantee status not stated in three reports (BNN Bloomberg, ArtfixDaily, Rehs).

May 2026: the buyers and underbidders of the Picasso Arlequin (Buste), the de Kooning Untitled III and the Rothko Untitled are not named in any page opened (The Art Newspaper, HENI, Il Sole 24 Ore; Sotheby's lot page hides results behind a login); the inference that their irrevocable bidders bought them with the fee netted rests on the arithmetic and on Il Sole's count of about ten guarantees 'called on'.
Christie's November 2026 line-up beyond the Tisch consignment: two searches returned only its November 2025 pages; the Galerie report on Tisch misattributes its Christie's quote to Sotheby's.
Shipping and storage costs for a trophy lot: no lot-specific figure found (insurance now sourced at 0.3–0.5% a year; FreightWaves's US$75,000 shipping example is generic, 2019).

The Salvator Mundi buyer's identity appears only in search-result headlines not opened; the Macklowe and Rybolovlev court papers were not read directly (figures come from The Art Newspaper's and The Value's reports of them).
The tax base for New York sales tax (hammer plus premium) and the absence of a US artist's resale right are from general knowledge; the rate (8.875%) is primary.

Specialists' lot-linked bonuses: nothing published beyond the AAP earn-out (10-K) and the Valette figure (Rybolovlev papers); the Sotheby's bond prospectus was not found within the search budget and The Art Newspaper's 2024 securitisation piece discloses nothing on guarantees.

workflows.method: Research done 12 November 2026 within a budget of 25 searches and 40 page fetches. vf = V read on a primary source (the vendor’s own price page, the employer’s own job board or PDF), S from a secondary source (a job-board mirror of a posting, the trade or general press, a vendor’s comparison of rivals), U not confirmed in this session and carried from memory with no source cited. Figures carry their currency and the date read.

day: Help evaluate potential consignments with the head of department and the international team.
Catalogue consigned items for auction and private sale, researching ‘authenticity, condition, quality, provenance, and compliance’.
Write catalogue essays in two languages to copy deadlines; run catalogue production (photography, image editing, colour correction, layout).
Help produce valuation documents.
Prepare business-getting materials: private-sale presentations, fact-sheets, price comparisons and market analysis.
Answer estimate requests and business enquiries by e-mail, phone and in person; coordinate accounting, shipping and logistics for clients.
Plan pre-sale exhibitions and client viewings; brief base-makers and conservators; move property, including occasional hand-carry.
Accompany senior colleagues on client visits for appraisals; attend market gatherings and evening events.
Follow compliance policies, governance rules and ethical standards at all times.
roles.decides: Whether to recommend a consignment, the estimate and the catalogue text, using comparables (‘price comparisons’), provenance research and condition reports. The reserve and the pitch deck are owned at head-of-department level; the posting names neither.
roles.pain: Comparables and market analysis are assembled by hand for each pitch; estimate requests arrive by e-mail and phone and are answered one by one; the posting asks for the ability to learn new digital tools ‘including artificial intelligence’.
pays_for: Auction price databases (Artnet, Artprice, MutualArt) for price comparisons

Lead tours and exhibitions of sale highlights.
Oversee pre- and post-auction checks with sale coordinators to meet AML standards.
Approve purchase orders, property movement and marketing costs; review client charges weekly; escalate over-budget spend; feed the finance partner for reporting.
With specialists and logistics, clear old inventory and act on property that breaches the inventory policy.
Oversee shipping and keep shipment reporting current; work with the art transport director on regulatory changes.
Train the whole team in telephone bidding.

roles.pain: Client charges reviewed weekly from reports; shipment reporting kept current by hand; inventory breaches chased manually; the role lives across SharePoint, Teams, TCC, JDE (ERP), Canvas and Workday.

day: Underwrite, price and manage a portfolio of fine-art risks within an individual underwriting authority and rating structure.
Review insured exposures, aggregations, protection, loss-prevention controls, loss history and financials.
Evaluate fine-art valuations and check the secondary market for variances in insured values.
Monitor aggregate exposure and premium income; keep new and renewal business profitable.
Policy issuance and review, endorsements, invoicing, file maintenance on complex accounts.
Build broker and client relationships; attend broker meetings and art-industry events.
Track market conditions, competitor offerings and emerging risks.
roles.decides: Whether to write a risk and at what rate, from valuations checked against the secondary market, loss history and aggregation.
roles.pain: Checking insured values against the secondary market is a manual task listed in the posting; valuation methods must be kept current by the underwriter.
src: Liberty Mutual posting mirrored on The Muse: Fine Art & Specie Underwriter, New York (no longer open)

roles.n: Shipper’s project manager / art-fair coordinator and gallery account manager

Manage external suppliers such as overseas agents; book transport, case-making and freight.
Keep clients informed of cost changes; track costs; invoice each job file on time and profitably; authorise supplier invoices; resolve credit-control queries.
Travel to global art fairs; meet clients, host agents and fair organisers on site.
Identify upselling: storage and insurance.
Keep projected turnover accurate; provide activity reports.
roles.decides: Routing, suppliers and price for each shipment, from the job file, the internal system and knowledge of UK and overseas customs and road, air and sea routes.
roles.pain: Multiple files handled at once; long hours at fairs; customs knowledge lives with the coordinator; quoting, ATA carnets and condition checks are not mentioned in the posting.

pricing.note: The trade already pays for data by the seat, but cheaply and in pieces: a price database costs US$450–1,175 a seat a year at Artnet (capped by searches) and US$369–2,499 at MutualArt; research costs £2,340 a year at ArtTactic’s list price; news costs US$80–399 a year. Workflow software is priced per user per month at US$95–325 (ARTERNAL), US$95–185 (Collector Systems) and £42–£90 (Artlogic modules), so a working seat already runs US$1,100–3,900 a year before any data. Everything above those tiers (Artlogic Expert, ARTERNAL Enterprise, Artsy, LiveAuctioneers, LiveArt Enterprise, Artnet bulk access) is ‘on request’. A terminal that bundles comparables, counterparty files, the guarantee book and landed cost into one seat can therefore be priced at roughly the sum of what a desk now splits across three or four vendors — about US$3,000–6,000 a seat a year for houses and galleries, with enterprise and API pricing on request — and still sit at a tenth of a Bloomberg seat (US$28,320–31,980). The buyers who can pay more are the lenders and family offices, where one banker costs US$400,000–500,000 a year and only 27% of wealth managers trust the data they have.

cities.summary: Geneva is the reference free port. Ports Francs et Entrepôts de Genève SA (genevafreeport), majority-owned by the canton, earned CHF 23.8m in 2025 and is building a 14,500 m² art-storage block for early 2028, already fully let for 15 years. Natural Le Coultre (naturallecoultre), founded 1859, says it has 35,000 m² of storage; Crozier has a site at Satigny (crozier_geneva). The regime is the Swiss Zollfreilager: import duties suspended while goods are 'in transit', cultural property declared on Form 11.95, BAZG supervision. The number that matters, the Federal Audit Office's count of works, was not opened in this session and is left unconfirmed.

Zurich's art storage sits north of the city by the airport: Crozier at Kloten (crozier_zurich), Welti-Furrer Fine Art AG at Dielsdorf (zurich_weltifurrer; register entry 1996, CHF 200,000 capital, board president Dr Thomas Knecht-Lanz, managing director Timon Schenk, with a board and management change notified in September 2026), and Zürcher Freilager AG's Embraport at Embrach (zurich_freilager), the company that turned 100 in 2023 while its Embrach hub turned 50. Whether Embraport still runs a Zollfreilager for art, and which firm Crozier bought in Zurich, were not confirmed. The regime is the Swiss Zollfreilager rule as in Geneva.

Basel's bonded past is the Dreispitz: the Zollfreilager on Christoph Merian Stiftung land fell redundant when the logistics firms left, and the site now holds the Schaulager (2003), HEK (2011), the HGK art academy (2014) and Kunsthaus Baselland (2024) (basel_dreispitz). Kraft E.L.S. AG, the art transport firm, is registered at Florenzstrasse 5 in Münchenstein on the Dreispitz (basel_kraft_els). For the June fair Swiss customs closes transit at the hall and takes a simplified temporary-use declaration or ATA carnet within 48 hours; about 1,400 dossiers and 300 galleries in 2023 (BAZG). The number that matters: 1,400 customs dossiers for one fair. No Natural Le Coultre Basel site was found; the 'Kunstfreilager Dreispitz' page refused.

The former Le Freeport Luxembourg, opened September 2014 beside Findel airport and renamed Luxembourg High Security Hub in 2021 (luxfreeport), is a Type 1 EU free zone with customs staff on site inspecting everything that enters and leaves. Bouvier sold his 100% to Olivier Thomas's Colombe Investment in late 2023. Cost about €50–55m; an auditor questioned its future in 2022; a defence-storage reorientation was reported in 2025 but not opened.

Le Freeport Singapore (sgfreeport), built 2010 at a cost put at US$70m, was sold by Yves Bouvier to Bitdeer's Jihan Wu for a reported US$28.4m in September 2022 after a failed 2019 sale. Crown Fine Art also stores in Singapore (crown_singapore). Helutrans's facility is unconfirmed (helutrans). The number that matters: the 2022 price, well below cost.

Monaco has no free port; it has a customs warehouse at Fontvieille run by S.E.G.E.M (monaco_segem), several hundred square metres in units of 20–90 m² leased to seven customs forwarding agents, with duty and tax suspended and no bond required while stored.

Delaware Freeport (delawarefreeport), founded 2015 by Fritz Dietl, over 100,000 sq ft across three Delaware sites, is described by its new owner as the only fine-art-dedicated Foreign Trade Zone warehouse in the US; DIETL (The Rock-It Company) bought it in January 2026. UOVO (uovo_delaware) and Crozier (crozier_delaware) also keep Delaware sites; the draw is the absence of a state sales tax.

New York is the deepest market: UOVO at Long Island City, Bushwick and Rockland County (uovo_lic, uovo_brooklyn, uovo_rockland); Crozier at Chelsea, Long Island City, Williamsburg and three Newark NJ buildings (crozier_ny, crozier_nj), owned by Iron Mountain since 2015; CFASS in Red Hook (cfass), whose Sandy flooding in 2012 produced US$23m of lawsuits; ARCIS in Harlem (arcis), the 110,000 sq ft 'Manhattan freeport' that cost over US$40m and closed in October 2020. The number that matters: Iron Mountain's 2015 estimate of a US$900m storage industry.

UOVO (uovo_la, 130 South Myers Street) and Crozier's four sites at Culver City, Inglewood, the Arts District and Vernon (crozier_la) anchor Los Angeles; Artex's LA site came with Crozier's 2018 purchase (artex). No bonded facility was confirmed.
UOVO at NW 29th Street and West Palm Beach (uovo_miami) and Crozier at Davie (crozier_florida). No bonded facility was confirmed.
UOVO at Irving (uovo_dallas) and Bellaire (uovo_houston); Crozier at Arlington, TX (crozier_dallas). Addresses only; no sizes published on the pages opened.

London storage is private and often bonded under UK customs-warehouse authorisation: Momart in East London (momart), Crozier's six sites including the 39,000 sq ft Tower Bridge building (crozier_london), Cadogan Tate at Acton Lane and Wimbledon with 250,000 sq ft across five UK sites (cadogantate), Crown's Art Central (crownfineart). Gander & White, Martinspeed and Constantine were not opened. The brief's premise that Christie's Fine Art Storage closed in London could not be confirmed.

Paris stores at the airport fringe: André Chenue's ARTS centre at Le Bourget, 23,900–24,913 m², built for hypoxic storage (chenue_lebourget); Crozier at Pantin (crozier_paris); Cadogan Tate at Saint-Ouen, 4,800 sq ft (cadogantate_paris). No Gennevilliers facility was confirmed. France's 5.5% import VAT and EU customs-warehouse rules apply; not opened in this session.

Hasenkamp (hasenkamp) opened a 12,000 m² depot at Mörfelden-Walldorf near Frankfurt Airport in October 2026, replacing Kelsterbach, and says it has invested over €100m in storage. No Munich vault was confirmed.
Kunsttrans's Port4Art depots in Simmering total about 30,000 m² after a fourth building in 2026 and can be run as a Zollfreilager on request (kunsttrans_vienna); Hasenkamp also lists Vienna.

Open Care at the Frigoriferi Milanesi, about 8,000 m² of vaults under Bastogi S.p.A. (opencare_milan); Crown Fine Art in Via Mecenate and 900 m² at Abbiategrasso (crown_milan). Italy's 5% art VAT (cited by Hoffman in the Abu Dhabi piece) is secondary.

Hong Kong has no free port for art but a free-port economy: Crozier's three Kwai Chung units (crozier_hk) and Crown (crown_hk); a government-backed art-storage facility at the airport's Skytopia was expected late 2025/early 2026 (hk_skytopia). The Christie's and Phillips arrangements and Helutrans were not confirmed. The number that matters: record art and antiques imports of US$30.7bn in 2022.

The Shanghai International Artworks Bonded Service Center at Waigaoqiao, 68,300 m², opened September 2019 as 'the world's largest' (shanghai_waigaoqiao); artworks moving through the FTZ bonded area rose from about 35bn yuan in 2013 to over 100bn yuan a year by 2023. The West Bund art bonded warehouse (Xuhui) was not opened and is unconfirmed.

Beijing's hub is the Tianzhu Free Trade Zone in Shunyi (beijing_tianzhu), where December 2023 municipal measures promote bonded storage with exhibition and guarantee-free bonded shows for accredited firms. The Gehua 'Beijing Freeport of Culture' itself was not opened.

Incheon Airport's 83,228 m² art storage by Arshexa PFV, 37.95bn won, was targeted for 2026 and re-licensed in 2024 as a general cargo warehouse rather than a security zone (incheon_arshexa); Spasys One's 4,488 m² FTZ store was due October 2024 (incheon_spasys). Opening of either not confirmed.
Warehouse TERRADA's Tennoz art storage includes a bonded warehouse and a Helutrans-Terrada venture (terrada); Yamato was not researched.

The Dubai Free Port announced by Mohammed Bin Rashid Aerospace Hub at Dubai South in 2021 (17,000 m² of plots; 6,500 m² and 600 m² facilities) sits in a custom-bonded area with an airside zone outside customs jurisdiction (dubai_freeport); Crown (crown_dubai) and DIETL (dietl) also store in Dubai. Operating status unconfirmed.
No vault was confirmed; the February 2026 DCT programme waives the 5% customs duty on works worth AED 10m+ that stay three years, while 5% import VAT remains (abudhabi_regime).
GWC and QC+ announced in November 2025 the Gulf's largest fine-art storage and logistics hub in a Doha free zone with customs-bonded areas (doha_gwc); size, cost and opening date not published.
No Riyadh vault was found. ATHR and Hasenkamp launched The Art Storage in Jeddah on 24 May 2025 (jeddah_athr).

Mumbai has two confirmed options: Saffronart's climate-controlled store at Worli, run by the auction house with a 24-hour fire and security command centre (mumbai_saffronart), and Crown Worldwide's 27,616 sq ft four-storey fine-art and records vault inaugurated on 26 September 2023, alongside Crown's customs-bonded warehouse opened in Mumbai in April 2025 for wines, luxury goods, jewellery and electronics — fine art is not named in that service (crown_mumbai). No Mtec facility and no SEEPZ art store were found. The number that matters: 27,616 sq ft.

Crown Fine Art describes a specialised fine-art facility in New Delhi with climate control, racking, CCTV and fire suppression (delhi_crown); its address and size are not published, and no customs-bonded art warehouse in Delhi was found. Saffronart's page mentions no Delhi store.

São Paulo's private reserve market is small and now led by Clé Chenue do Brasil (saopaulo_clechenue), the Grupo Horus arm formed by merging Clé Reserva Contemporânea (5,500 m², since 2014, full) with ArtQuality; a 2,000 m² unit in the Barueri region opened in May 2026 on a R$17m investment, with modules from R$500 a month and revenue of R$25m. The CEO says Brazil has no legal equivalent of a free port and the firm will not try to build one. The number that matters: the Brazilian art market was R$2.9bn in 2023, up 21%.

unconfirmed: Geneva: the Swiss Federal Audit Office's figure for works stored (often quoted as 1.2 million) and the press's US$100bn-type estimates were not opened; the canton's exact shareholding in PFEG and the free port's total built area are not in the 2025 report.
Geneva: the Swiss 2016 inventory rules (owner, value per lot; export-declaration time limits) were not read on the BAZG page opened; the R-10-50 regulation PDF was not opened.

Luxembourg: exact shareholdings after the 2023 Bouvier sale, floor area, the 2022 €210m Russian-asset freeze, and the 2025 reports of a defence-storage reorientation (Paperjam, Les Frontaliers) — not opened.
Singapore: size, tenants, management and current operations of Le Freeport under Bitdeer (SCMP 2026 feature refused); Helutrans's Artspace@Helutrans and Hong Kong facility (no page opened).

Zurich and Basel (narrowed in the second pass): whether Zürcher Freilager's Embraport still runs a Zollfreilager for art; Welti-Furrer Fine Art's storage size and owner; which company Crozier acquired in Zurich; the 'Kunstfreilager Dreispitz' art bonded store (page refused); any Natural Le Coultre Basel site (none found in search).

London: Gander & White, Martinspeed and Constantine (no page opened); whether Christie's Fine Art Storage Services closed in London and who took its clients; Cadogan Tate's per-site bonded status and the 2024 facilities reports (PDFs not opened).

players.n: Russian Ministry of Culture — export permits for cultural valuables
players.scale: Export from the EAEU runs under EEC Board Decision No. 30 of 21 April 2015 (Annex 8, the Regulation on export of cultural valuables; categories in Annex 2, section 2.20): either a Minpromtorg licence (companies exporting permanently) or a Ministry of Culture conclusion (заключение — temporary export, export by individuals, or the basis for the licence), in the unified form of EEC Decision No. 45 of 16 May 2012; a passenger customs declaration made at import can substitute for items being re-exported. The conclusion rests on an expert examination by museum, archive and restoration specialists the Ministry authorises; an expert opinion from about RUB 20,000. Annex 2 thresholds: printed editions and coins/banknotes created 100 years ago or more; manuscripts and archival documents 50 years or more; ‘artistic valuables’ without a stated age. Under Federal Law 435-FZ (28 Dec 2017) items ‘of special significance’ — art and vehicles created before 1917, instruments and bows before 1900, antique weapons, memorial and archaeological items — leave only with an obligation to return.
players.edge: The gate every Russian consignment abroad must pass; the conclusion is the document the terminal should ask a Russian seller for.
src: Eurasian Economic Commission, Decision No. 30 page
EAEU restrictions table for individuals (via Belarus customs)
Ministry of Culture information via Consultant.ru
players.note: The age threshold for paintings and sculpture themselves (the 50/100-year rule the brief cites) sits in the text of Annex 2, which no page opened reproduces; the categories above are those IFCG quotes from it. The EEC page’s latest listed amendment to Decision 30 is No. 128 of 13 Sep 2022 (precious metals); Annex 8 was amended in 2015 and 2017.

players.n: US tariffs on art — the 2026 position
players.scale: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA ‘reciprocal’ tariffs on 20 February 2026 (six justices); the same day new tariffs of up to 15% were imposed under another emergency law for 150 days unless Congress extends them; on 4 March 2026 a New York federal judge ruled importers who paid the struck-down tariffs are due refunds; 22 state attorneys general sued over the replacement tariffs.
players.edge: Both laws exempt ‘informational materials’, which covers most fine art, rare coins, stamps and antiques over 100 years old; decorative art, antique furniture and other collectables are not exempt, and dealers are absorbing or passing on the cost.
players.note: A TAN teaser dated 28 Jul 2026 says the new regime ‘largely exempts art and antiques’ with tariffs of 10% or more on about 80 countries; not opened. China’s own retaliatory tariffs on US-origin art (2025) and the truce were not confirmed in any page opened.

markets.role: Moscow is a rouble market cut off from the Western houses. MyReport Art counts the official 2025 revenue of 260 companies at RUB 4.1bn (+5.4%): auction houses the fastest-growing segment (RUB 597m, +23.4%), galleries shrinking (−11.1%), and nearly half of participants not filing, so the true market is larger. The rooms are Cosmoscow (97 galleries, 55,000 visitors, September 2025), the gallery-run |catalog|, the state-adjacent Art Russia at Gostiny Dvor, and the houses Vladey, Litfund, Sovcom and the new AukziON. Buyers are returnees from Riga, London and Paris, ‘patriotic’ corporate buyers and new money such as Timati, who paid EUR 575,000 for a Tselkov at Vladey in November 2024. What bites: the EU/UK/US luxury-goods bans on supplying art to Russia and the Bank of Russia’s cash-currency limits, extended to 9 March 2027. Sell-through at domestic sales is often about half.

St Petersburg is the second Russian room: the June fair 1703 in the Manege, the Marina Gisich gallery, Erarta and the Hermitage’s orbit. Galleries from the city take stands at Cosmoscow and |catalog| in Moscow. No separate turnover figure is published; the city’s share sits inside the RUB 4.1bn national count for 2025. The same sanctions and capital rules apply as in Moscow. Treat all 2025–26 detail for the city as unconfirmed: no primary page could be opened within budget.

Tbilisi is a refuge room rather than a market. Russian migrant artists cluster at Rubezh, a cultural centre founded in Bishkek in 2022 that moved to Tbilisi in 2024 and runs festivals every few months on thin finances; participation is limited to artists with migration experience. The Russian-run spaces sell little; the city’s own galleries and the Tbilisi Art Fair were not confirmed in the pages opened. No turnover figure exists. What changed in 2025–26 is attrition: the migrant spaces that survive are the grassroots ones, and the money that left Moscow for the Caucasus is small (works usually under EUR 10,000, per a Moscow–Dubai dealer).

Belgrade’s Russian rooms are shrinking. KP Radionica, founded in 2024 by Nu Simakina and Nadezhda Lopardina, held the group show ‘Ne Ti Rusi’ at KC Grad in spring 2026 and stays open without a permanent curator; Nordistica Gallery is closing and WOONDER Studio has closed, both for financial reasons. Serbia applies no sanctions on Russian persons and no EU luxury-goods ban, which is why the diaspora settled there, but there is little buying and no auction house of note. No market figure exists for the city; the only published number is the count of closures. What changed in 2025–26 is attrition: the grassroots spaces survive, the gallery-shaped ones do not.

London’s dedicated Russian Sales, a fixture since the late 1980s, stopped in 2022: Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Bonhams cancelled their June 2022 Russian Art Week sales after the invasion, and only MacDougall’s kept a Russian-focused calendar. Russian material now surfaces inside other sales: Sotheby’s ‘Fabergé, Imperial and Revolutionary Art’ (three Serebriakova portraits EUR 750,000, autumn 2024), Bonhams’ 19th-century sale (a Polenov cycle work GBP 1.4m, 2024), Bonhams’ non-conformist sales in Paris and Lempertz in Cologne (Pivovarov EUR 108,000, November 2024). UK sanctions bar supplying art to Russia and dealing with designated persons; London’s wealthy Russian community has diminished.

Uzbekistan has no auction market and a thin gallery scene; what it has is a state programme. The Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF), chaired by Gayane Umerova, staged the first Bukhara Biennial from 5 September 2025 (about 70 commissions, 200+ Uzbek artists, artists from 38 countries, a reported 1.8m visitors) and has booked the second for 3 September–21 November 2027 under Kulapat Yantrasast; the Centre for Contemporary Art Tashkent, directed by Sara Raza on the YARAT model, slipped from March to 6 September 2026; a Tadao Ando national museum follows. The money is state money — critics call it exorbitant against an average income under US$529 — and the aim is tourism and soft power, not sales. Collectors with Central Asian interests now route through Bukhara in September.

Kazakhstan got its institutions in 2025 and still has no market. The Almaty Museum of Arts, Nurlan Smagulov’s 10,000 sq m Chapman Taylor building with over 700 works, opened on 12 September 2025 to 14,000 visitors in three days and about 60,000 in its first 19 days, under artistic director Meruyert Kaliyeva; Kairat Boranbayev’s Tselinny Center, an Asif Khan conversion of a Soviet cinema, was due the same month. There is no auction house of note, no fair of weight and no published turnover. The money is private and oligarchic, and the politics matter: Boranbayev was convicted in 2023 and freed after ceding assets, and Kazakhstan ranked 142nd for press freedom in 2024. What changed in 2025–26: Almaty became the place where Central Asian art is shown, as Bukhara became the place where it is commissioned.

Baku’s art scene is built around one private institution, YARAT Contemporary Art Space, which trained Sara Raza, the curator now running Tashkent’s new centre, and is the stated model for it. There is no fair of weight, no auction market and no published turnover; collecting is private and state-adjacent, and the state’s cultural spending goes to heritage and the Heydar Aliyev Center rather than a market. Azerbaijan ranked 167th in the 2025 RSF press-freedom index, which bears on what can be shown. No sanctions bar Russian buyers. Everything beyond YARAT’s role as model for Tashkent is unconfirmed; nothing on Baku’s commercial galleries was opened this session.

Istanbul is a mid-sized market priced in euros and squeezed by a currency crisis that has run since 2018, inflation above 30% in 2025. Its one international fair, Contemporary Istanbul, grew from 51 galleries (16 countries, September 2025) to more than 70 from 24 countries at its 21st edition on 23–27 September 2026 at Tersane, with 17 newcomers, a bond agreement and a Turkish Airlines freight deal to cut exhibitor costs, and a founder planning a second fair on the Asian side. Prices run from EUR 1,000 to over EUR 2m. The dealers are Pilevneli, Dirimart, Zilberman, Pi Artworks, Anna Laudel, Galeri Nev, Pilot and Sevil Dolmacı; the collections are Koç/Arter, Eczacıbaşı/Istanbul Modern and Sabancı (memory). Tax breaks for cross-border cultural exchange are the one helpful rule; Istanbul stays open to Russian and Gulf buyers.

Beijing is the mainland’s auction capital and, for modern and contemporary art, a RMB 1.1bn-a-year room: ArtPro counts Guardian Beijing at RMB 686m in 2025, Yongle RMB 204.3m, Kaipai RMB 158.31m and Beijing Poly over RMB 51.86m, against HK$2.96bn for the six Hong Kong houses; 22 of the year’s 91 lots over RMB 10m sold on the mainland. The pattern was ‘strong spring, stable autumn’; Zhang Peili’s ‘X?’ at RMB 71.3m (Guardian, 10 November 2025) was the mainland’s top contemporary price. What bites: the cultural-relics auction permits and the export ban on older works (memory), capital controls on outbound payments, and since 2025 the US tariff overlay, which exempts fine art as ‘informational materials’ but not decorative art. What changed in 2025–26: ‘tightening policies and changes in leadership’ at the smaller houses, and a stronger pull from Hong Kong.

Hangzhou is the home of Xiling Yinshe Auction, the house of the Xiling Seal Engravers’ Society, which ArtPro places in the mid-sized tier of the Chinese modern and contemporary market with over RMB 149.83m in that segment in 2025 (down 7.9% autumn on spring) and a Guan Liang record of RMB 24.15m; its real weight is in classical painting, calligraphy and seals, where no segment figure was opened. The city’s gallery scene is thin next to Shanghai; the same national rules apply (cultural-relics export limits, auction licensing). Nothing specific to 2025–26 beyond the auction figures was confirmed.

The Pearl River Delta has two houses of note in the modern and contemporary segment: Huayi International (RMB 48.8m in 2025, up 10.3% autumn on spring, a Shenzhen spring sale 90% sold, a combined Guangzhou–Shenzhen autumn sale) and Holly’s International in Guangzhou (Shang Yang’s ‘Dong Qichang’s Plan – Monument’ RMB 8.28m on 25 December 2025). Shenzhen’s fairs and its Design Society were not confirmed this session. The region’s role is as a feeder to Hong Kong an hour away, where 69 of 2025’s 91 lots over RMB 10m sold; the same national rules on relics and capital apply as in Beijing, and the US tariff overlay reaches it only through Hong Kong consignments. No separate 2025–26 change was confirmed beyond the auction figures.

Seoul is correcting by volume and recovering by value. KAMS’s 2026 survey puts the 2025 market at KRW 638.2bn (+3.8%), 20.9% below the 2022 peak, with galleries KRW 352.8bn (+4.0%) and auctions KRW 144.9bn (+20.3%) on 13% fewer lots; the auction associations count KRW 140.5bn hammer (+22%) at 53.4% sell-through, led by Chagall’s KRW 9.4bn record at Seoul Auction (November 2025), and H1 2026 hammer doubled to KRW 110.8bn on two lots (Nara KRW 15.0bn, Kusama KRW 10.45bn). The rooms are Frieze Seoul (133 galleries, 70,000 visitors, September 2026; Yoo Youngkuk KRW 2.2–2.5bn) and Kiaf (175 galleries, 80,000); Frieze moves to DDP in 2027. What bites is sentiment — the June 2026 election disorder and chip-stock swings — and the new art-service-business reporting duty under the Art Promotion Act (2026); 56.1% of galleries expect a flat 2026.

Japan is a deep, slow market made cheap by the yen. Art Basel & UBS’s 2026 report has Japanese sales down 1% in 2025; the Bank of Japan sees 0.6% growth in FY2026 with inflation above 2%. The domestic room, Art Fair Tokyo, had its best year: JPY 3.65bn in sales (+28.1%), 56,938 visitors and 141 exhibitors in March 2026. The international room, Tokyo Gendai (fourth edition 11–13 September 2026, Pacifico Yokohama, 69 exhibitors, two Hiroshi Senju at US$410,000 and US$620,000), moves to Ariake GYM-EX in Tokyo on 4–7 November 2027. SBI Art Auction’s 2026 sales ran to about JPY 4.6bn by September, led by a Foujita at JPY 506m (14 March) and a Lee Ufan at JPY 138m. What bites: consumption tax at import and the bonded-warehouse route (memory).
