markets.role: Singapore is South-east Asia’s trading post rather than its source: the fifth-largest importer of art and antiques (imports up 74% to just under US$1.7bn in 2024, Art Basel & UBS), tax-free holding at Le Freeport and Helutrans, and one fair. ART SG’s fourth edition (22–25 January 2026) had 95 galleries, down from 160 in 2023, and 43,000 visitors, with S.E.A. Focus folded in on subsidised SGD 8,000 stands; the top reported sale was Johyun’s sold-out Lee Bae at US$2.76m, and Sotheby’s week sale made US$13.1m with records for Pacita Abad and Anthony Poon. GDP grew 5% in 2025 and 81% of surveyed Singapore collectors are optimistic. What bites regionally is Indonesian and Thai import duty, which keeps buyers storing in Singapore; what changed is the fair’s shrink to a regional footprint.

Jakarta is the region’s biggest collector base and smallest open market. Art Jakarta’s 2026 edition (2–4 October, three halls at JIExpo Kemayoran) had 75 galleries — 42 Indonesian, 33 international, 19 first-timers — and added AJScope, six regional independent art markets backed by the Culture Ministry, plus the AJX institutional platform; Art Jakarta Gardens runs in May–June. Jakarta galleries such as ISA Art (Deborah Iskandar) sell at US$3,600–19,500 on the Singapore circuit, and Indonesia’s collectors (Museum MACAN’s founders among them, memory) buy through Singapore and Hong Kong to avoid import duty and luxury tax. No sales or visitor totals are published; the fair’s growth against ART SG’s shrink is the 2025–26 change.

Bangkok gained a private museum in 2025–26 — Dib Bangkok, founded by Purat Osathanugrah in a WHY Architecture building — and its founder spoke at ART SG 2026; BANGKOK CITYCITY GALLERY showed at Tokyo Gendai 2026, which marks the city’s galleries’ reach. The Bangkok Art Biennale and the Bangkok Kunsthalle (memory) are the other rooms; there is no auction house of weight. Thai import duty and VAT keep bigger purchases offshore (memory). Everything beyond the two sourced facts is unconfirmed.

Manila’s room is Art Fair Philippines, held 6–8 February 2026 across several floors of Circuit Corporate Center One in Makati, with Silverlens, León Gallery, Ames Yavuz, Gajah, Archivo 1984 and Japanese and Taiwanese galleries among exhibitors; the fair publishes no sales or visitor totals. The domestic collector base is built on the old business families, and two houses, León Gallery and Salcedo Auctions, set Filipino modern prices (Amorsolo, Zóbel, Ocampo) — the houses’ totals are from memory and unconfirmed. The money is peso money and stays at home: import duty and VAT on art and no freeport mean Manila collectors who buy abroad hold in Singapore or Hong Kong. Pacita Abad’s auction record at Sotheby’s Singapore in January 2026 is the Filipino price signal of the year.

Kuala Lumpur is a ringgit market dominated by Malaysian modernists, with Art Expo Malaysia as its fair, Henry Butcher Art Auctioneers as its house and the Ilham Gallery as its private institution — all from memory. It sits in Singapore’s shadow: the serious Malaysian collectors buy and store across the causeway, and ART SG’s January 2026 co-presentation with S.E.A. Focus was built for them. There is no published 2025–26 market figure, no sales tax relief for art and no auction house of international reach. Nothing on Kuala Lumpur was opened this session; the paragraph is a placeholder for the terminal to verify, and should not be displayed as fact.

Vietnam’s modern market — Le Pho, Mai Trung Thu, Vu Cao Dam, Nguyen Phan Chanh, the Indochina school — trades mostly in Hong Kong and Paris rather than at home, with a growing domestic scene in Ho Chi Minh City (Galerie Quynh, the Nguyen Art Foundation) and Hanoi, and strict export rules on older works — all from memory. The money is new, private and increasingly repatriating: Vietnamese buyers now underbid in Hong Kong for the Paris-trained moderns. No house of weight exists in either city and no 2025–26 figure was opened this session; the paragraph is unconfirmed and should be verified against the Hong Kong houses’ modern Vietnamese sales before display.

India is the fastest-rising market east of Moscow. Saffronart’s New Delhi sale of 27 September 2025 made US$40.2m from 85 lots, the largest sale ever held in South Asia; Sotheby’s followed on 29 September with US$25.5m and a Souza record of US$7.5m; Christie’s and Sotheby’s New York made US$27m and US$22.1m on 24–25 March 2026; and on 1 April 2026 Saffronart sold Raja Ravi Varma’s ‘Yashoda and Krishna’ to Cyrus Poonawalla for US$17.9m (INR 1,672m), beating Husain’s ‘Gram Yatra’ (US$13.7m, March 2025) as the Indian record. What changed: GST on art fell from 12% to 5% on 22 September 2025. What bites: the 1972 act’s ‘national treasure’ list (Ravi Varma among them) bars export, so top lots stay in India. India Art Fair’s 17th edition (5–8 February 2026) had 135 exhibitors Husains at US$2–6m.

Australia traded A$148.49m at auction in 2025 (to 10 December), with Howard Arkley the most traded artist (A$10.5m) ahead of Whiteley (A$8.4m) and Boyd (A$8.2m); two Arkleys tied the year’s top price at A$2.5m, and Deutscher and Hackett, the leader with over A$40m for the year, closed with an A$11.2m November round and opened 2026 with an A$4.67m Indigenous sale (120% by value, five artist records). The rooms are D+H, Menzies and Smith & Singer in Melbourne and Sydney, and Sydney Contemporary each September (not opened); the rules that bite are the 5% resale royalty (reciprocal abroad since 2025, memory), GST on the premium, and the Protection of Movable Cultural Heritage Act permits for older and Indigenous works (memory). What changed in 2025–26: the Arkley boom and a strong Indigenous round with foreign bidders.

markets.role: New Zealand is a small dollar market with two Auckland houses, Webb’s and Art+Object, and one fair, the Aotearoa Art Fair, with prices led by McCahon, Hotere and the contemporary Māori and Pacific artists — all from memory. The rule that changed: the Resale Right for Visual Artists Act brought a 5% royalty into force in December 2024, reciprocal with Australia and the UK (memory). Cross-Tasman buying is routine, and New Zealand collectors appear in Deutscher and Hackett’s Indigenous and modern rounds. No 2025–26 figure was opened this session; the paragraph is unconfirmed and the royalty date in particular should be checked against the Ministry for Culture and Heritage before display.

Dubai is where Moscow’s dealers went when the Western rooms closed. Gary Tatintsian moved there in 2022; Veronika Berezina’s NIKA Project Space and Alisa Bagdonaite opened spaces; Syntax runs between Moscow and Dubai and reports that expatriate buyers take smaller pieces, usually under EUR 10,000. The UAE applies no sanctions on Russian persons, which is why buyers and art flow there, and Gulf galleries (Leila Heller, JD Malat, AWC Contemporary) are now courted by Contemporary Istanbul in turn. Art Dubai is the fair (not opened). The number that matters is The National’s: Abu Dhabi’s US$1bn investment in Sotheby’s shares (cited September 2025) puts a Gulf shareholder behind a house still closed to Russian buyers. What changed in 2025–26: the Dubai Russian scene consolidated, while Paris and London took the serious money.

Yerevan took a large share of the 2022 Russian exodus — programmers, artists and the galleries that followed them — but no gallery, fair or sale of weight could be opened this session. From memory the rooms are the Cafesjian Center for the Arts, the HayArt centre and a handful of émigré-run project spaces; the money is thin, and the dealers who tried Yerevan have since moved on to Tbilisi, Belgrade, Dubai or Paris, the pattern Art Focus Now documents for the other cities. Armenia applies no sanctions on Russian persons and its banks still open accounts for them, which keeps it a transit point for payments rather than a market. No figure exists; treat the paragraph as unconfirmed.

Limassol is the EU jurisdiction with the largest resident Russian money, but it is inside EU Regulation 833/2014, so the Article 3h ban on supplying art over EUR 300 to persons in Russia and the asset freezes on designated persons apply in full; the money that remains is held by EU-resident Russians and Cypriots who can buy freely. No dealer, fair or sale in Limassol could be opened this session; from memory the scene is private (collectors, a few galleries) rather than public. Unconfirmed beyond the legal frame.

Hong Kong is where mainland Chinese money clears: ArtPro counts the six Hong Kong houses at HK$2.957bn of modern and contemporary art in 2025 against RMB 1.361bn for seven mainland houses, and 69 of the year’s 91 lots over RMB 10m. Christie’s HK (HK$1.598bn) and Sotheby’s HK (HK$745m) with Guardian Beijing hold about 70% of the Chinese segment; Phillips HK nearly tripled autumn on spring. The year’s prices: Picasso ‘Bust of a Woman’ HK$196.75m (Christie’s, 26 September 2025), Basquiat ‘Saturday Night’ HK$112.6m (spring), Nara HK$79.9m (Sotheby’s, 28 September 2025). Hong Kong has no sales tax or import duty on art; the overlay since 2025 is the US tariff regime, which exempts fine art as ‘informational materials’. The terminal already carries the Hong Kong market; this paragraph adds the 2025 segment count.

Shanghai is the mainland’s gallery and fair city; Beijing is its auction city. The November art week — West Bund Art & Design (nearly 200 galleries, 65 countries, in a new SOM hall in 2025) and ART021 (record attendance in 2025; Mennour 60–70% sold) — runs 10–15 November 2026 with the boutique Hangover Shanghai alongside; no sales totals are published. The houses are second-tier for contemporary but strong in classical painting: Shanghai Jiahe sold the mainland’s only nine-figure old master of 2025 (Qiu Ying, RMB 124.2m, 13 December) and Jinghua’s December sale made RMB 166m. The international galleries that stay are Almine Rech, Perrotin, Lisson, Ota and Arario beside ShanghART and Antenna Space. What bites: the property crash and deflation — core galleries ‘largely survived’ and must ‘work twice as hard’ — plus the national relics-export and capital rules.

russia.state: As of November 2026 the Russian market is a rouble market walled off from the Western houses. Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Bonhams cancelled London’s Russian Art Week in 2022 and have not restored dedicated Russian sales; Sotheby’s also barred Russian buyers in March 2022 (search headline, not opened). Inside Russia the trade has grown on isolation: MyReport Art counts the official 2025 revenue of 260 companies at RUB 4.1bn (+5.4%), with auction houses up 23.4% to RUB 597m, fairs up 16.2% to RUB 1.75bn and galleries down 11.1% to RUB 1.53bn, and says nearly half of participants do not file accounts, so the real figure is larger; 38% of galleries are weighing art-backed digital financial assets. The rooms are Cosmoscow (97 galleries, 55,000 visitors in September 2025), blazar, |catalog|, Art Russia and 1703, and the houses Vladey (Tselkov EUR 575,000, November 2024; no 2025 total published), Litfund, Sovcom and AukziON. The buyers are returnees from Riga, London and Paris, corporate ‘patriotic’ buyers and new money (Timati); dealers report sell-through of about half and money that cannot leave. What moves out is small — diaspora dealers in Dubai, Paris, Berlin, Tbilisi and Belgrade sell works mostly under EUR 10,000 — and Russian material abroad trades inside general sales at Sotheby’s, Bonhams, Lempertz and MacDougall’s.
russia.law: Export from Russia is governed by Law 4804-1 of 15 April 1993 ‘On the export and import of cultural valuables’, rewritten by Federal Law 435-FZ of 28 December 2017 (in force March 2018), inside the EAEU regime of EEC Board Decision No. 30 of 21 April 2015: Annex 8 is the Regulation on export of cultural valuables and Annex 2, section 2.20, the list of categories. Export needs either a Minpromtorg licence (a company exporting permanently) or a Ministry of Culture conclusion (заключение: temporary export, export by an individual, or the basis for the licence), issued in the unified form of EEC Decision No. 45 of 16 May 2012 after an expert examination by Ministry-authorised museum, archive and restoration specialists; an import-time passenger customs declaration can substitute for re-export. The categories IFCG quotes from Annex 2 are printed editions and coins or banknotes created 100 years ago or more, manuscripts and archival documents 50 years or more, and ‘artistic valuables’ without a stated age; the age line for paintings and sculpture themselves was not reproduced on any page opened (U). Items ‘of special significance’ under 435-FZ — art and vehicles made before 1917, instruments and bows before 1900, antique weapons, memorial and archaeological items — leave only with an obligation to return; Museum Fund items leave only temporarily and insured. On the Western side, EU Regulation 833/2014 Article 3h (inserted by Regulation 2022/428 of 15 March 2022) bans the sale, supply, transfer or export to any person in Russia, or for use in Russia, of luxury goods over EUR 300 listed in Annex XVIII, which names works of art, collectors’ pieces and antiques (HS 97); France suspended export licences for Russia-bound cultural goods on 6 April 2022. The UK’s Russia Regulations Schedule 3A and the US EAR luxury-goods rule (15 CFR 746.10) carry equivalent bans (memory, U). Capital rules: the Bank of Russia on 1 September 2026 extended to 9 March 2027 the US$10,000 cap on cash withdrawals from pre-March-2022 foreign-currency accounts and the ban on cash dollars, euros, sterling and yen for non-resident companies. Russian counter-measures (Decree 81 of 1 March 2022 and the Government Commission’s approval for deals with ‘unfriendly’ persons) remain from memory and unconfirmed.

tides.what: The top of the market turned first. The Art Basel and UBS report (March 2026) found auction sales above US$10m rose 30% in 2025, lots above US$1m rose 21% in value and 15% in number, and US works above US$10m rose nearly 40%. The first half of 2026 then broke records: ArtTactic counted US$6.8bn across Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips, up 70%, the best first half since 2022; Christie’s public auctions made US$3.5bn (up 71%) and Sotheby’s US$3.4bn (up 59%). Pollock’s Number 7A made US$181.2m and Brancusi’s Danaïde US$107.6m in the Newhouse sale (Christie’s, May 2026). Artnet’s Margaret Carrigan called it ‘a masterworks recovery, not a market-wide recovery’.

tides.what: The middle slipped while the top soared. Art Basel and UBS (March 2026) found lots under US$50,000 fell 2% in both value and volume in 2025, and dealers with turnover of US$1m–10m saw sales fall 1%, while dealers under US$500,000 gained double digits and those above US$10m gained 3%. The report gives no single middle-market figure. ArtTactic’s first-half 2026 report then found ‘strong growth’ in the US$50,000–500,000 segment, without figures, and Anders Petterson said the recovery was ‘far broader than the headline-grabbing results at the very top end’. Artnet disagreed: Carrigan called Christie’s Zabludowicz online sale of contemporary works ‘rather disastrous’ and the rebound a masterworks one. The evidence for a turn is one half-year and partly unquantified.

tides.what: Sculpture is taking the trophy slots. Brancusi’s Danaïde made US$107.6m in Christie’s Newhouse sale (New York, May 2026), an artist record and the highest price of the season after the Pollock. Henry Moore’s King and Queen made £26.3m at Christie’s London in March 2026, beating his £24.7m record of 2016 after eight minutes of bidding from £6m; Chillida made four times his low estimate in the same sale. Six Matisse bronzes made US$49m combined in the Lauder sale (November 2025). A 19th-century bronze Laocoön made £13.6m at Sotheby’s in July 2026, the second-highest price for a pre-Modern sculpture. The tide has a wake: Giacometti’s Grande tête mince, estimated above US$70m, failed at Sotheby’s in May 2025 with bidding stalled near US$64m, and Rodin’s Penseur passed at US$7.5m in May 2026.

tides.what: Design has its own Picassos now. François-Xavier Lalanne’s copper Hippopotame Bar made US$31.4m at Sotheby’s New York Design Week in December 2025 after seven bidders fought for 26 minutes, an artist record. Four months later Claude Lalanne’s fifteen mirrors made for Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé made US$33.45m in the de Gunzburg sale (Sotheby’s New York, 22 April 2026), more than three times the low estimate; her previous record, set a week earlier at Christie’s Paris, was US$7.1m. The de Gunzburg design sale totalled US$96m. In May 2025 a Frank Lloyd Wright lamp made almost US$7.5m, a record, after an eleven-minute war. ArtTactic counts design within luxury collectibles, up 25% in the first half of 2026. Figures for Royère and Nakashima and the houses’ design totals were not found on any page opened.

tides.what: Old Masters grew faster than any sector but Impressionism. Art Basel and UBS put the wider Old Masters auction category just under US$1.2bn in 2025, up 30%, 11% of fine-art auction sales; Artprice counts a 28% rise. New York’s January 2026 week set the tone: Christie’s US$54.3m sale was its best in the category for more than a decade, a Michelangelo chalk study made US$27.2m against a US$2m high estimate, a Rembrandt lion drawing US$17.8m, a Canaletto US$30.5m, and Artemisia Gentileschi’s self-portrait US$5.7m, a record. London in July 2026 was uneven: Sotheby’s £37.8m rose 161%, Christie’s £38.9m fell 30% without a Canaletto, and a Rembrandt-attributed panel sold on a single guarantor bid. Christie’s said Asian buyers took 40% of its sale by value; Andrew Fletcher said private buyers have dominated for years.

tides.what: Prints are recovering unevenly and by image, not by signature. Warhol was split: records for Silverspot Butterfly and Marilyn (II.26) in April, three Campbell’s Soup Cans unsold. Carrington expects ‘sharper separation between accessible editions and prints presented as major works, rather than a broad rise in prints’, and the first test of Hockney’s market after his death in June 2026 at Phillips on 19 September.

tides.what: The youngest buyers are now the biggest. The Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 (3,100 HNW collectors in ten markets, first half of 2026) found average fine-art spending of US$124,265 in 2025, up 13%, with Gen Z averaging US$347,460, up 19% and more than twice any other generation; Gen Z were nearly half of the 1% who bought a work over US$1m and held 13% of over-US$1m spending in the first half of 2026. Family influence brought in 28% of collectors and 40% of Gen Z, and almost 90% kept inherited works. Deloitte estimates US$992bn of art and collectibles will pass to younger generations within a decade, and that 61% of collectors have never discussed their collections with heirs. The houses see it at the till: 47% of Christie’s new clients in 2026 are Millennial or Gen Z.

links.what: Designated by the UK on 10 March 2022 (asset freeze; one of seven, with Deripaska, Sechin, Kostin, Miller, Tokarev and Lebedev) — status: designated. ICIJ states the EU sanctioned him ‘soon after the war began’ (the EU listing of 15 March 2022 is carried from memory for the date) and that the US did not sanction him, which ICIJ attributes to a Wall Street Journal report of an intervention by President Zelensky. Status: designated (UK, EU).

ICIJ/The Guardian (Oligarch Files, 22 Sept 2023) reported that on 4 February 2022, weeks before the invasion, trustees made Zhukova ‘irrevocably entitled to 51%’ of Ermis Trust distributions by a deed of amendment, after she had become an additional beneficiary in January 2021 (50/50); a later deed that month barred Abramovich from increasing his stake. The amendments did not require her knowledge or consent. ICIJ says the collection is not subject to an asset-freezing order. Status: reported; no finding by any authority.

Dasha Zhukova is his former wife; ICIJ states she is a US citizen, ‘is not subject to sanctions in any jurisdiction’, has publicly condemned the war, and that there is ‘no suggestion’ she has taken steps to undermine sanctions via the trust or other means. Nothing more than the family relationship and the trust position reported above.

HM Treasury (17 December 2025): ‘more than £2.5 billion’ from the Chelsea FC sale has been ‘frozen in a UK bank account since the sale in 2022’; the government demanded he hand it over for victims of the invasion, said the OFSI licence requires the proceeds to go ‘to humanitarian causes in the country’ (Ukraine), with only future gains spendable on victims of conflict worldwide, and said it was ‘fully prepared to take him to court if necessary’. Insider Sport (17 March 2026) reported the government’s solicitors had warned his lawyers that court proceedings were being prepared after the deadline passed; the government pursues £2.35bn–£2.5bn with interest, while his side says the pledge was voluntary, ‘cannot now be treated as a binding obligation’, that his obligation is about £987m net of a £1.4bn loan repayment, and that any confiscation would be contested; a separate Jersey criminal investigation is being challenged by him, and he denies wrongdoing. Status as last confirmed (March 2026): proceedings threatened, not confirmed filed.

David Nahmad bought Picasso’s ‘Women of Algiers, version H’ at the 1997 Ganz sale (ICIJ).

houses_of_capital.n: Offshore companies with nominee directors and bearer shares (Panama, Niue, BVI)
houses_of_capital.what: The Panama Papers (ICIJ, 7 April 2016) showed how the trade’s largest holdings sit in shelf companies: the Nahmads’ International Art Center S.A. (Panama, 1995, via UBS and Mossack Fonseca’s Geneva office) held Modigliani’s ‘Seated Man with a Cane’ while the family told New York courts it did not possess the work; its shares began as bearer shares and signatures from nominee directors were needed for each court motion (one such document cost US$32.10). The Ganz collection passed through Simsbury International Corp. (Niue, bearer shares, Mossack Fonseca as registered agent) six months before its 1997 Christie’s sale, with Joe Lewis holding power of attorney. The Goulandris pictures were said to have been sold in 1985 to Wilton Trading S.A. (Panama), a company with no directors until 1995. What it hides: beneficial ownership, the seller’s identity at auction and the location of the asset; what it reveals, when leaked, is the whole chain. Cost: a few thousand dollars a year per company (from memory, U). Since 2016 Panama has moved to immobilise bearer shares and the EU and UK have required beneficial-ownership registers — from memory (U).
src: ICIJ, The Art of Secrecy, 7 April 2016

houses_of_capital.n: Trusts and trust companies (Cyprus, Jersey, Guernsey, Bahamas)
houses_of_capital.what: ICIJ (22 Sept 2023) described the Abramovich structure: the Ermis Trust Settlement (Cyprus, 2010) controls Seline-Invest (BVI, redomiciled to Jersey), which owns the c. US$1bn collection; trustees and protectors came from the Cypriot firm MeritServus (UK-sanctioned April 2023); a deed of amendment of 4 February 2022 moved 51% of distributions to Dasha Zhukova without her knowledge or consent. Under EU, UK and US rules assets more than 50% owned by a sanctioned person can be frozen, which experts told the Guardian may explain the restructuring; the collection ‘is not subject to an asset-freezing order’. The Paris court of appeal (5 March 2024, The Art Newspaper) found the Wildensteins had concealed ‘an enormous estate via trusts’ including paintings valued at €1bn. What a trust does: separates legal from beneficial ownership, so a museum loan, a sale or a sanctions test looks at the trustee, not the family. Costs run to trustee fees and, as ICIJ reported for Harmony Trust, a US$500,000 annual art-adviser retainer.

houses_of_capital.n: Shell companies and the ‘agent as principal’ at auction
houses_of_capital.what: The US Senate PSI staff report (29 July 2020) found that after their March 2014 OFAC designation the Rotenbergs bought over US$18m of art in the US through Moscow adviser Gregory Baltser and shell companies (Highland Ventures, Highland Business, Advantage Alliance, Steamort — a Belize company whose owner ‘remains unknown’), that ‘the auction houses treated an art agent or dealer as the principal purchaser of art’ and that ‘Rotenberg-linked shell companies transferred over $120 million through the United States to Russia’. The report’s point for the terminal: US auction houses were not then subject to the Bank Secrecy Act, so know-your-customer stopped at the agent. The 2021 AML Act extended BSA rules to antiquities dealers but not to art, a gap still open in 2026 as far as established here — from memory (U).
src: US Senate PSI staff report, 29 July 2020

houses_of_capital.what: ICIJ (2016) reported the Nahmads’ Modigliani ‘reportedly stored in the Geneva freeport’ and that Yves Bouvier’s Natural Le Coultre then rented almost a quarter of the Geneva freeport, with at least five companies linked to Bouvier and two to Rybolovlev in the Mossack Fonseca files. The Justin Sun–Geffen dispute (The Art Newspaper, 13 May 2025) turned on ‘Le Nez’ being moved to a Delaware art storage facility before its sale. What a free port offers: suspension of import VAT and duties while goods are in transit, discretion about ownership and location, and a place to close a sale without the work crossing a tax border; what it costs is storage and insurance, and since 2016–20 the Swiss and EU authorities have tightened inventory and beneficial-owner reporting (Switzerland’s 2016 customs ordinance, the EU’s 5th AML directive bringing free ports and art dealers into scope) — from memory (U). The terminal already lists Geneva, Luxembourg, Singapore and Delaware as players.
src: ICIJ, The Art of Secrecy, 7 April 2016

houses_of_capital.n: Private museums and operating foundations with tax status (US 501(c)(3), French fondation d’entreprise, Swiss Stiftung)
houses_of_capital.what: The model is Glenstone (Rales), The Broad, the Rubell Museum, the Brant Foundation, the Fondation Louis Vuitton (Arnault), the Bourse de Commerce (Pinault), the Fondation Beyeler, the Museum Barberini (Plattner), LUMA Arles (Hoffmann), the Long Museum (Liu and Wang), the Leiden Collection (Kaplan, which lends rather than houses) and the Al Thani Collection. A US private operating foundation lets a donor deduct the fair-market value of gifted works while the family keeps curatorial control; the Senate Finance Committee asked eleven US private museums about public access and donor benefit in 2015–16 — from memory (U). A French fondation d’entreprise gives the sponsoring company a 60% deduction of sponsorship costs, debated publicly over the Fondation Louis Vuitton in 2018 — from memory (U). What it reveals: the public programme and, in the US, Form 990 filings; what it hides: the works kept at home and the terms of loans. The Leiden Collection shows the lending-library alternative: some 220 works lent to over seventy museums with no permanent home (site). Korea shows the state alternative: the Lee Kun-hee family gave c. 23,000 pieces to national museums in April 2021 (MCST).
src: Korean Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, 27 April 2021

houses_of_capital.n: Estates, divorces and the court-ordered sale
houses_of_capital.what: The record single-owner sales of 2021–25 were estates or court orders: the Macklowe Collection, 65 works, US$922.2m at Sotheby’s (15 Nov 2021 and 16 May 2022) — a divorce sale under a court-appointed receiver (receiver detail from memory, U); Emily Fisher Landau, 111 works, US$424.7m at Sotheby’s (8–9 Nov 2023), with hundreds more works at the Whitney; Leonard and Louise Riggio, US$272m at Christie’s (12 May 2025) with irrevocable bids on more than half the lots across the evening sales; Leonard Lauder’s five Klimts, US$392m at Sotheby’s (18 Nov 2025). What the estate sale reveals: provenance, prices and the guarantor’s hand; what it hides: the buyers, whom the houses decline to name (‘Sotheby’s declined to share the identity of the portrait’s buyer’, Fortune). The alternative is the private estate sale through dealers (the Marron estate via Pace, Gagosian and Acquavella in 2020 — from memory, U).

houses_of_capital.n: Sovereign and royal collections (Qatar Museums, DCT Abu Dhabi, the Saudi Ministry of Culture)
houses_of_capital.what: Qatar Museums, chaired by Sheikha Al Mayassa, is a state body; the trade attributes to it or to ‘Qatar’s royal family’ the Cézanne ‘Card Players’ (2011, said to be US$250m), the Cézanne ‘Montagne Sainte-Victoire’ from the Ford House (2013, reported US$100m) and the Gauguin ‘Nafea’ (2015, close to US$300m per the NYT’s sources; Artnet itself called the identification a rumour). The ‘Salvator Mundi’ was bought at Christie’s on 15 Nov 2017 for US$450m by Prince Badr bin Abdullah, reported by the WSJ to be acting for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (The Art Newspaper). What the sovereign structure hides: there is no register, no Form 990, no shareholder; the works surface only when a museum opens or a loan is announced — the Louvre Abu Dhabi’s announced loan of the Leonardo never materialised publicly.

houses_of_capital.n: Delaware LLCs, Liechtenstein Anstalts and Swiss family offices
houses_of_capital.what: Not confirmed on any page opened in this session; carried from memory (U) for the terminal to verify: a Delaware LLC is the standard US title-holding vehicle (no public member register, formation in a day for a few hundred dollars, no state income tax on out-of-state activity), and the Delaware Freeport (listed as a player) sits beside it so that a work can be bought, stored and resold without entering a sales-tax state; the Liechtenstein Anstalt (establishment) is a hybrid foundation-company used by European dealers and families (Marlborough’s historic structures were Liechtenstein-based — U) because it can hold assets for a founder with no shareholders and minimal disclosure; Swiss and Monaco family offices hold art through Swiss AGs or Luxembourg SPFs and bank it with the private banks the terminal lists as lenders (Pictet, Julius Baer, Lombard Odier, UBS), which lend against it at 40–50% of appraised value — figures from memory (U).

cases.n: The Rotenberg brothers’ art purchases (US Senate PSI report, 2020)

route.what: US$39.5m (Highland Ventures) and US$82m (Culloden Properties) wired from Pictet Group through the US financial system to Gazprombank, 18 Mar 2014, two days before the Rotenbergs were designated

people.role: lawyer who set up the shells and was BALTZER’s chief AML officer
people.status: named in the Senate report, Jul 2020; no charge is recorded

works: Lyonel Feininger, ‘Brücke II’, bought through Baltser at Christie’s London, 4 Feb 2014; consigned to Sotheby’s Feb 2019 (est. £4–6m) and withdrawn
René Magritte, ‘La Poitrine’, US$7.5m, May 2014, private dealer; moved to Moscow Aug 2019

cases.sums: About US$120m moved through the US to Russia in the 16–20 Mar 2014 window; over US$18m of art bought May–Nov 2014; over US$91m of post-sanction transactions by Rotenberg-linked companies (Senate PSI, 2020)

cases.control: A sanctions designation (OFAC, Dec 2019), then a joint US–UK action on 18 Apr 2023 (52 designations) and a federal indictment with seizure warrants
cases.outcome: Designated by OFAC (13 Dec 2019; network of 52 on 18 Apr 2023); designated by HM Treasury on 18 Apr 2023 under the Counter-Terrorism (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 with a full asset freeze — the first use of that domestic regime, barring him from the UK art market and naming White Starr DMCC, Bexley Way General Trading, Best Diamond House DMCC, Sierra Gem Diamonds, Park Ventures SAL and the Artual Gallery; indicted (EDNY, unsealed 18 Apr 2023), pending as of Nov 2026; in the UK the dealer Oghenochuko Ojiri was jailed in 2025 for failing to report his sales to Ahmad (see ‘ojiri’); from May 2025 UK art-market participants must report suspected sanctions breaches to OFSI (CMS) — the closest documented step to the brief’s ‘OFSI 2025’

cases.note: No page could be opened within budget; every line here is from memory and search-result headlines.

Pyotr Aven (Alfa Bank chairman; Larionov, Goncharova, Kandinsky; Chadwick, Moore and Bourgeois sculptures in his Surrey garden; a planned private museum in Riga) and Alisher Usmanov (who halted a 2007 Sotheby’s sale to buy the Rostropovich collection for more than £25m and gave it to a state palace) added by the EU on 28 Feb 2022; Boris Rotenberg under UK sanctions; VTB and Alfa Bank restricted; Abramovich, owner of Freud’s ‘Benefits Supervisor Sleeping’ (US$33.6m, Jun 2008) and Bacon’s ‘Triptych’ (1976, US$86.3m the same week), not yet listed on 28 Feb

freeports.n: Geneva (Ports Francs et Entrepôts de Genève)
freeports.flows: Majority-owned by the canton of Geneva, with floor space ‘equivalent to 22 football pitches’, most of it rented, and paying the canton CHF 10–12m a year (swissinfo, Nov 2015). Connaissance des Arts estimated around 1.2 million artworks stored there in 2013, and the press cited a value of CHF 100bn which the Swiss Federal Audit Office quoted without verifying (SFAO 2014). The SFAO’s 2014 evaluation found goods ‘stored for long periods of time, sometimes several decades’, used for private asset management and tax optimisation rather than transit, poor inventories and no traceability; it counted 10 free ports (down from 18 in 2008) and 245 open customs warehouses holding over CHF 15bn of goods, with suspended duties above CHF 1bn, and warned of misuse for ‘cultural goods, war materials, medicines or the trade in raw diamonds’. The cases that ran through it: the Nahmad Modigliani sequestered in Apr 2016 after the Panama Papers; Bouvier’s Natural Le Coultre as a major tenant (from memory). Reforms: in Nov 2015 the free port announced systematic identity checks on new tenants and clients, biometric access cards and removal of clients in trouble with the law; the 2016 federal rules required inventories to name and address the owner of the goods, up-to-date tenant and sub-tenant lists, time-limited licences (ten years for free ports) and minimum annual movements (5,000 for a free port); by 2018 Switzerland had 7 free ports and 194 open customs warehouses, the customs administration ran 109 checks in the first two months of 2018 (30 found conditions unmet) and the SFAO still said the free-port conditions ‘do not go as far as the SFAO would like’ (SFAO follow-up, 8 Apr 2019).
src: Swiss Federal Audit Office, ‘Free ports and open customs warehouses’, summary (PA 12490, 2014)
Swiss Federal Audit Office follow-up CDF-17458, 8 Apr 2019
freeports.note: The six-month export deadline and the on-site archaeologist from 2016–17 press reports could not be confirmed in the pages opened.

freeports.flows: Opened in 2010 at Changi airport, built for about S$100m and designed by Bénédicte Montant and Carmelo Stendardo for Yves Bouvier. It was for sale for several years after the Bouvier affair and was sold in July 2022 to Bitdeer Technologies, linked to the crypto-mining entrepreneur Jihan Wu, for S$40m (US$28.4m), the proceeds going mainly to debts owed to DBS among others; Bouvier reported a loss of about 70 million on it (currency as in the Paperjam summary). Bouvier’s Singapore proceedings against Rybolovlev ran through the Singapore courts until the Dec 2023 settlement.
freeports.note: The Artnet report of the sale could not be opened (site refused); the Paperjam page was read in a summary. The sale year is taken as 2022 from the article’s position in the 2022 coverage; the page itself showed only today’s date.

freeports.n: Luxembourg (Le Freeport Luxembourg, since 2021 the Luxembourg High Security Hub)
freeports.flows: A €50m high-security warehouse beside Findel airport, opened in Sep 2014 and founded by Yves Bouvier; Olivier Thomas (a French dealer, former board president) and Jean-Marc Peretti (a former Paris gaming-club manager whom the article links to money-laundering investigations) were also shareholders, and David Arendt was managing director. In 2018 MEPs Ana Gomes and Evelyn Regner criticised its lack of transparency, their report saying free ports ‘offer offshore storage solutions that can promote money laundering and tax concealment’; a 2018 European Parliament study found demand rising and free ports ‘conducive to secrecy’; in Jan 2019 MEP Wolf Klinz wrote to Commission President Juncker about it and MEPs called for free ports to be banned in the EU. Management said the hub exceeds EU financial-control rules and that its main use is insurance-premium reduction, not tax evasion. It was renamed the Luxembourg High Security Hub in 2021; in late 2023 Bouvier sold 100% of his shares to Olivier Thomas through Colombe Investment (Wikipedia), having earlier held them through Fortuis (Paperjam). The case that shadows it is the Bouvier affair: Bouvier was arrested in Monaco in Feb 2015 on suspicion of fraud over art sold at inflated prices. No tenant list or financial results were found in the pages opened.
freeports.note: Wikipedia’s infobox and text disagree on the founding date (2012 v 2014); the going-concern doubts reported by the auditor (search headline) were not opened.

freeports.n: Delaware (the Delaware Freeport, Newark, and the New Castle County warehouses)
freeports.flows: Fritz Dietl, an Austrian-born New York art shipper, secured a Foreign-Trade Zone designation from US Customs and Border Protection in 2015 for a 36,000 sq ft warehouse in Newark, Delaware, charging ‘a few dollars per square foot a month’ and, by Nov 2017, at capacity and scouting a second site. The draw is Delaware’s absence of sales tax: a US$10m painting shipped from Manhattan avoids New York City’s 8.875% (US$887,500) for as long as it stays, on an honour-system reporting of any return. Delaware’s art warehouses together exceed 200,000 sq ft and hold ‘hundreds of millions of dollars’ of art (AP, 2017): Atelier Art Storage (40,000 sq ft), Crozier Fine Arts’ New Castle warehouse (41,000 sq ft, Iron Mountain), Bayshore (60,000 sq ft since 1991) and Hopkins & Sons. No laundering case has been reported against a Delaware facility; the critics quoted by AP (an accountant, a dealer, a lawyer) fault enforcement of the use-tax rule, not the warehouses.
src: AP via The Washington Times, 19 Nov 2017
freeports.note: UOVO’s later Delaware facility (search result) was not opened.

freeports.n: New York (Arcis, Harlem — the Foreign-Trade Zone that closed)
freeports.flows: A US$50m, 110,000 sq ft purpose-built store on West 146th Street, insured to hold up to US$3bn of art, inside the first Foreign-Trade Zone of its kind in New York; developed by Cayre Equities and run by former Crozier and Dietl executives (Tom Sapienza, Kevin Lay), with the Van Gogh Museum and Vidaris as partners; planned for Jul 2017, opened in 2018. Works were exempt from US duty and excise tax until they left, could move between units inside the zone without duties, had no storage time limit, and a sale inside the zone had to be viewed in one of five viewing rooms; New York sales tax could still apply, which Arcis left to the client’s lawyers. Demand ‘surged’ among middle-market dealers in Jan 2020 (The Art Newspaper), and the art lawyer Judd Grossman warned ‘I see the likelihood of more fraud, not less fraud’. A Sep 2020 report said Manhattan’s first and only free port was closing.
freeports.note: The Sep 2020 closure is from a related-article teaser on the pages opened, not the article itself.

freeports.n: Beijing (the Beijing Freeport of Culture, Tianzhu bonded zone) and Shanghai (the Free Trade Zone bonded art warehouses, West Bund)
freeports.flows: Not confirmed in this session: the China Daily page on the Beijing Freeport of Culture (2014) returned ‘page not found’ and the Shanghai bonded-warehouse page was not on the fetch allowlist. From memory (U): the Beijing Freeport of Culture at the Tianzhu comprehensive bonded zone near Capital Airport was launched in 2014 by Beijing Gehua Cultural Development Group with a Sotheby’s joint venture; Shanghai’s pilot Free Trade Zone has run bonded art storage and exhibition space at the West Bund since the mid-2010s, where overseas works can be shown and sold with import duty and VAT suspended until they clear customs. China taxes imported art with a customs duty cut to 1% (from 3% and before that 6%) plus 13% VAT, which is why the bonded zones exist. No case running through either zone was found.
freeports.note: All figures here are from memory; search-result headlines (China Daily 2014, 2015, 2021, 2022; Pudong government 2024) confirm the zones exist but were not opened.

freeports.n: Monaco (no free port; the Bouvier arrest and the Russian-art sales)
freeports.flows: No free port operates in Monaco; the principality enters the record otherwise. Yves Bouvier was arrested there in Feb 2015 on suspicion of fraud over art sold at inflated prices (Wikipedia on the Luxembourg hub; the Rybolovlev settlement of Dec 2023 closed the Monaco proceedings). Monaco announced asset freezes on certain Russians on 28 Feb 2022 (The Art Newspaper), and Hermitage Art Sales in Monaco continued to hold Russian art and Soviet memorabilia sales after Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Bonhams cancelled their London Russian sales in Mar 2022 (AFP).
src: AFP via Hürriyet Daily News, 22 Mar 2022

patterns.n: The invoice that is not the price: a work shipped at US$100, a bribe paid as a ‘sale’ at thirty times value, a painting over-priced to carry proceeds
patterns.control: A customs valuation check against appraisal and auction records; an independent valuation on any price out of line with the artist’s market; courts treating the gap as the bribe
src: FATF, ‘Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market’, Feb 2023 (copy on regjeringen.no)

patterns.n: The shell buyer and the agent treated as principal: a Panamanian company, a Belize shell with a nominee director, a Moscow auction agent whom four houses never asked ‘for whom?’
patterns.control: Beneficial-ownership identification of the buying entity and of the agent’s principal; the Senate’s recommendation to bring art dealers under the Bank Secrecy Act; the EU’s €10,000 AML threshold for art
src: US Senate PSI staff report, 29 Jul 2020 (PDF)

patterns.n: The free-port vault: a work kept for twenty years in a Geneva unit under a shell’s name, a free port holding looted antiquities, a free-port operator who was also the dealer
patterns.control: Inventories naming the owner (Swiss rules from 2016), tenant lists, identity checks on new clients (Geneva, 2015), a prosecutor’s search; Singapore’s AML duties on licensed storage (FATF)
src: Swiss Federal Audit Office follow-up CDF-17458, 8 Apr 2019
FATF, ‘Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market’, Feb 2023 (copy on regjeringen.no)

patterns.n: Selling more than 100%: the same work or the same share sold to several buyers, consigned works sold or pledged, proceeds kept
patterns.control: A title and lien check before any purchase or loan (the Art Loss Register and UCC filings, from memory), possession or escrow, consignors reconciling sales to statements
src: Artnet News, 2024 (magistrate’s recommendation on the Philbrick Basquiat)

patterns.n: The loan against the work: fraudulent collateral, forged collateral, a pledge by a borrower who did not own the work
patterns.control: A lender’s independent authentication and title search; the FATF’s indicators on art-collateralised loans (unwillingness to identify, early or cash repayment)
src: Artnet News, 2024 (magistrate’s recommendation on the Philbrick Basquiat)
FATF, ‘Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market’, Feb 2023 (copy on regjeringen.no)

patterns.n: The museum as the final wash: a looted object lent or given to a museum, a forgery exhibited, a dealer’s inventory ‘validated’ by a gallery wall
patterns.control: Museum due diligence on provenance before accepting loans or gifts; the Manhattan DA’s Antiquities Trafficking Unit and HSI; a curator’s own provenance research (the Gilgamesh tablet)

patterns.n: The invented provenance: a dead collector’s label, a ‘Spanish collector’, a backdated letter, ‘acquired before 1981 in San Francisco’
patterns.control: Materials analysis (titanium white, cadmium), documentary verification of every provenance link, the dealer’s ‘reasonable belief’ tested in court
src: QIPCO v John Eskenazi Ltd [2022] EWHC 3023 (Comm), 29 Nov 2022

patterns.n: The tax route: a resale certificate for a collector, an undeclared trust holding the estate, personal spending booked to the gallery, cash on a train, a national treasure on a yacht
patterns.control: Tax-authority audits of resale certificates and trusts; the False Claims Act; customs checks for cash; export-licence refusals that follow the work
src: New York Attorney General press release, 14 Nov 2024

patterns.n: The family transfer before the list: a 51% trust entitlement to an ex-wife four weeks before designation, a company moved to an unsanctioned son, a daughter and a son commissioning works for a designated father
patterns.control: The 50% ownership rule applied to the trust deed, not the headline name; the Senate’s recommendation to sanction immediate family routinely; screening of households and agents
src: US Senate PSI staff report, 29 Jul 2020 (PDF)

patterns.n: The warehouse door: a frozen work shipped out of storage, a ‘luxury good’ made available to a person connected with Russia, a Picasso offered to clean a stock fraud
patterns.control: KYC at the storage facility and the shipper (the NCA’s 2024 Amber Alert to art storage), the UK’s May 2025 OFSI reporting duty for art-market participants, the auction house asking who owns the work before it ships

patterns.n: The silence that is the crime: a dealer who sells to a sanctioned name and files no report
patterns.control: The UK regulated-sector disclosure duty (Terrorism Act 2000) on art-market participants since Jan 2020; registration with HMRC; the first prosecution in 2025

patterns.n: Cash over the counter: 36.5% of €3.3m in notes at a Paris gallery; the FATF’s €500-note indicator
patterns.control: Statutory cash caps, suspicious-transaction reports by galleries, customs cash declarations
src: FATF, ‘Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market’, Feb 2023 (copy on regjeringen.no)

patterns.n: The bribe as a painting (‘yahui’): an official’s calligraphy bought at auction, a Monet sold on a dictator’s household signature, a sovereign fund’s Basquiat
patterns.control: PEP screening of buyer and seller, price-to-market tests, kleptocracy asset-recovery forfeiture (DOJ) and state auctions of confiscated property

patterns.n: The security that was not registered: fractional shares without a register, an insider trading the homepage, a wash-traded NFT, a rug-pulled mint
patterns.control: SEC Regulation A qualification and a Cayman SPC holding title (Masterworks); blockchain analytics; the FATF’s call to add NFT marketplaces to national risk assessments
src: SEC EDGAR, Masterworks 184, LLC, Form 1-A offering circular (2022)
FATF, ‘Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market’, Feb 2023 (copy on regjeringen.no)

unconfirmed: Hong Kong art-money cases: no documented Hong Kong prosecution centred on art was found; the Hong Kong links in the record are Nazem Ahmad’s designated House of Art Ltd and Fadico HK Ltd (OFAC, 2023) and the Hong Kong buyer in the Gulbenkian case. The Hong Kong Customs cases returned by search are trade-based laundering without art.

Dutch/Belgian freeport cases: no free-port case was found; the Belgian–Dutch record here is the Flor Bressers cocaine case with the stolen Frans Hals and a Breda gallery (ARCA blog), and the FATF’s Box 21 (Italy–Spain–Netherlands drug network laundering through the art trade) and Box 23 (Belgium, an NPO buying art via offshore firms).

Nazem Ahmad ‘OFSI 2025’: the documented UK steps are the HM Treasury designation of 18 Apr 2023, the Ojiri conviction (2025) and the May 2025 OFSI reporting duty for art-market participants (CMS); The National’s report that works seized from Ahmad in the UK prompted the change (Nov 2024) redirected and was not opened.
Matthew Green ‘UK 2022’: no 2022 UK step was found; the last page opened (The Art Newspaper, 27 Nov 2019) says he had ‘yet to plead’ in the EDNY case.
‘Scheck/Fairlight’: Fairlight Art Ventures is not named in the Basquiat title ruling opened (Satfinance and Delahunty are); no ‘Scheck’ matter was identified.
The Beijing Freeport of Culture and Shanghai’s bonded art warehouses: both pages failed to open (404; not on the allowlist); the free-port entry is from memory.
Salander-O’Reilly: no page opened; the entry is from memory and headlines.

Graham Bonham-Carter’s later plea and sentence; Sundar Nagarajan’s extradition and plea (Ahmad case); any Wildenstein cassation appeal after the 5 Mar 2024 conviction; any appeal from the 2026 New York order on the Nahmad Modigliani; Athena’s appeal in the Philbrick Basquiat title case; the Hauser & Wirth trial outcome (charged Nov 2025).
1MDB art specifics: the 2016 and 2024 DOJ releases opened name only Van Gogh, Monet, Picasso, Basquiat and Arbus; titles and prices (Basquiat ‘Dustheads’ US$48.8m etc.) are from memory.
Bouvier: the Feb 2015 Monaco arrest is confirmed only through Wikipedia’s Luxembourg page; the Salvator Mundi resale and the Natural Le Coultre tenancy in Geneva are from memory.

Christie’s and Sotheby’s AML findings: no regulator’s fine against either house was found. The documented findings are the Senate’s (both treated the agent as the client, 2020), the Sotheby’s NYAG settlement (2024) and the UK figure of more than 90 art-market participants facing regulatory action since Jun 2021 (CMS, 2025).

The ‘Freud and Bacon consignments and the frozen sales’: the pages opened document Abramovich’s 2008 purchases (Freud US$33.6m, Bacon US$86.3m) as holdings and the Mar 2022 cancellation of the London Russian sales; no withdrawn Freud or Bacon consignment by a sanctioned seller was found.

The EU’s 2022 luxury-goods ban (Regulation 2022/428, Annex XVIII, works of art above €300): the EUR-Lex text was not opened; the only prosecution found under a luxury-goods ban is the UK’s Hauser & Wirth case.
Lebanese and Gulf cases: covered by Nazem Ahmad, Ojiri and the two QIPCO judgments; no Dubai or Riyadh art-laundering prosecution was found.
Beltracchi: only Wikipedia was opened; the trial court (Landgericht Köln) is from memory. Gurlitt: the counts of works (c. 1,280 Munich, 238 Salzburg) are from memory.
The Swiss Federal Audit Office: the 2014 summary and the Apr 2019 follow-up (CDF-17458) were opened; no separate 2018 report was found — the 2019 follow-up reports on 2018 inspections.

whispers.t: Puck’s Marion Maneker wrote on 22 July 2026 that art sales had a ‘remarkable rebound during the first half of 2026’, especially at the very top of the market.
whispers.detail: Semiannual market report. The houses had released first-half figures the week before. The readable part of the piece gives no totals; the rest is paywalled.
whispers.outcome: Artlyst (16 Jul 2026) carried the houses’ own figures: Christie’s auction sales up 71% and Sotheby’s up 59% in the first half of 2026.

whispers.t: Puck reported on 24 July 2026 that Sotheby’s sales rose 59% from the first half of 2025 to the first half of 2026, which Maneker called ‘the takeoff phase of a new auction cycle across the fine art and collectibles landscape’.
whispers.detail: Maneker wrote that Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart was ‘understandably chuffed’ when they spoke the week before. The 59% figure is Sotheby’s own, as relayed by Puck. The remainder of the piece is paywalled.
src: Puck, The Four Horsemen of the Art Market (24 Jul 2026)

whispers.t: The Baer Faxt’s No Reserve (11 Aug 2026), citing ArtTactic, put design, decorative art and furniture sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips at about US$285m for the first half of 2026, the category’s highest first-half total in 12 years and roughly US$12m more than the three houses took for Old Masters in the same period.
whispers.who: Tim Schneider (The Gray Market) in No Reserve from The Baer Faxt, citing ArtTactic
whispers.detail: Given as the issue’s ‘number to know’. ArtTactic’s own report was not opened in this session.
src: No Reserve from The Baer Faxt, issue 48 (11 Aug 2026)

whispers.t: Sotheby’s will offer ‘Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection’ in a dedicated evening auction in New York on 18 November 2026, with Monet’s Le Jardin des Tuileries (1876), Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90), Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and works by Renoir, Pissarro, Degas, Gauguin, Derain and Vlaminck, as Finestre sull’Arte reported on 30 September 2026.
whispers.who: Finestre sull’Arte (editorial desk), reporting Sotheby’s announcement
whispers.detail: The Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier began buying in the 1960s through Lefevre and Wildenstein; some works came from Albert Lasker, Norton Simon and Lord Rothschild. The article gives no estimates and no guarantee information. Sotheby’s own sale page was not opened in this session.
whispers.outcome: Sale scheduled for 18 November 2026; result not yet known as of 12 November 2026.

whispers.t: Pace Gallery announced in early June 2026 that it would cut about 50 artists and estates from its roster (from about 135 to 85) and about 50 staff (from roughly 250 to 200); CEO Marc Glimcher told the New York Times that ‘the gallery model is broken; the current commercial art world has become too big’.
whispers.who: Artlyst News Desk (4 Jun 2026), citing the New York Times; The Art Newspaper (31 Jul 2026) also cites the NYT
whispers.detail: Artlyst reports that no Pace spaces are closing, that the Chelsea flagship stays, and that Glimcher told the NYT of the building: ‘If I were making that decision today, by no means would this be my decision.’ Alexander Rower of the Calder Foundation is quoted: ‘All of the mega galleries have lost their way.’ The artists cut were ‘mostly not the big names’ and are not named by Artlyst. The NYT piece itself was not opened in this session.
whispers.outcome: The FT reported in June 2026 that Pace was looking for a smaller London space; its 5 Hanover Square home was back on the rental market by 10 June 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 31 Jul and 17 Sep 2026). Pace is among 35 galleries not returning to Art Basel Qatar in January 2027 (The Art Newspaper, 27 Oct 2026).
src: The Art Newspaper, Gagosian exits Basel and Burlington Arcade (31 Jul 2026)
The Art Newspaper, Art Basel Qatar 2027 exhibitor list (27 Oct 2026)

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 31 July 2026 that Gagosian had left its 28–29 Burlington Arcade space in London in July (16 shows since October 2023) and planned to leave its only Basel gallery, Rheinsprung 1, ‘in the months ahead’; a spokesperson said the gallery was ‘exploring other real estate opportunities’ in Basel.
whispers.detail: The gallery agreed to vacate the Arcade so the landlord could bring in a long-term commercial tenant; Gagosian keeps 20 Grosvenor Hill and 17–19 Davies Street in Mayfair. The piece says nothing about Larry Gagosian’s succession or the gallery’s finances.
whispers.outcome: Gagosian is on the Art Basel Qatar January 2027 exhibitor list, showing Maurizio Cattelan (The Art Newspaper, 27 Oct 2026).

whispers.t: Artnet News reported in July 2026 that David Zwirner was leaving its 34 East 69th Street townhouse in Manhattan, programmed since 2017; a spokesperson told Artnet it was ‘always our plan to leave’ the neighbourhood after the Chelsea overhaul was completed the previous year.
whispers.who: Artnet News, as cited by The Art Newspaper (31 Jul and 17 Sep 2026)
whispers.detail: The Artnet piece itself could not be opened in this session; the report is carried as The Art Newspaper relays it.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (17 Sep 2026) noted that Hauser & Wirth’s co-founders sold the 69th Street townhouse that housed the gallery from 2009 to April 2024, a sale Artnet News confirmed in May 2025 at a reported US$10.5m, and that the gallery opens a permanent space in Palo Alto on 3 October 2026.
whispers.who: Tim Schneider, The Art Newspaper, citing Artnet News
whispers.detail: Hauser & Wirth runs 17 galleries worldwide, per the piece. Hauser & Wirth is among the galleries not returning to Art Basel Qatar in January 2027 (The Art Newspaper, 27 Oct 2026).

whispers.t: By Tim Schneider’s own count in The Art Newspaper (17 Sep 2026), at least 26 dealers downgraded their real estate or closed between 1 January and 21 July 2026; collector Alain Servais is quoted expecting that ‘more dramatic rightsizing will be necessary, particularly to compete with more efficient auction houses’.
whispers.who: Tim Schneider, The Art Newspaper; Alain Servais quoted
whispers.detail: Schneider calls the mega-dealers’ moves a wake-up call but not a sector-wide death knell, and says Pace is the only mega-gallery to have significantly trimmed staff or its artist and estate network. Adviser Adam Green says the primary-market softening ‘has impacted every gallery, regardless of size’.

whispers.t: The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026 put 2025 global sales at US$59.6bn, up 4%, with dealers at US$34.8bn (+2%), public auctions at US$20.7bn (+9%) and private sales just under US$4.2bn (−5%); lots above US$10m rose 30% by value while lots under US$50,000 fell 2%.
whispers.who: Art Basel and UBS (Arts Economics, Clare McAndrew)
whispers.detail: US US$26.0bn (+5%, 44% share); UK US$10.5bn (+2%); China US$8.5bn (+1%); France US$4.5bn (+9%). Online sales US$9.2bn, the lowest since 2019. The report page does not carry a publication date; the report is the 2026 edition covering 2025. The date given here is approximate (spring 2026) and should be read as such.
src: Art Basel, The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026

whispers.t: In the Art Basel and UBS report 2026, 43% of dealers expected sales to improve in 2026, 38% expected stability and 19% a decline; nearly half of mid-tier auction houses expected improvement (up 33% on a year earlier) and 21% expected weaker results (down from 40%). Noah Horowitz said ‘sustained growth will depend on bringing exceptional works to market’.
whispers.who: Art Basel and UBS report; Noah Horowitz (Art Basel CEO) and Paul Donovan (UBS) quoted
whispers.detail: Clare McAndrew: ‘The market welcomed a shift in direction in 2025, from the contraction of previous years to modest growth.’ Donovan cited ‘more than USD 83 trillion set to pass between generations in the coming decades’. Date approximate (spring 2026).
whispers.outcome: The first half of 2026 brought Christie’s US$3.5bn of auction sales (+71%) and Sotheby’s US$3.4bn (+59%), per the houses as carried by Artlyst (16 Jul 2026); Puck (22 Jul 2026) called it a ‘remarkable rebound’. Exceptional works did drive it: Newhouse, Gund, Mnuchin, Lewis.
src: Art Basel, The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 11 May 2026 that the May New York sales carried a combined low estimate of about US$1.8bn (up to US$2.6bn): Sotheby’s US$690.4m–942.5m (its low figure 70% above its May 2025 hammer total), Christie’s US$1bn–1.5bn, Phillips US$108.7m–157m, Bonhams about US$30m.
whispers.detail: Headline: ‘This month’s blockbuster auctions in New York could bring upwards of $2.5bn’. The sales were expected to ‘test the trade’s recent buoyancy’ after a three-year slump. No guarantees were named in the preview.
whispers.outcome: Apollo (24 May 2026) put the week at more than US$2.5bn with fees: Christie’s US$1.45bn, Sotheby’s US$908.6m (up 82.5% on May 2025), Phillips US$145.7m. HENI (22 May 2026) graded Christie’s week B+, with 160 guaranteed works and nine artist records against a norm of about 25.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (11 May 2026) reported that Christie’s would offer 16 lots from the S.I. Newhouse collection in a dedicated sale on 18 May 2026, estimated at up to US$450m and led by Jackson Pollock’s Number 7A (1948) and Brâncuși’s Danaïde (c. 1913), each at about US$100m.
whispers.detail: Newhouse bought the Brâncuși in 2002 for US$18.1m, then a sculpture auction record. The same evening carried Agnes Gund works (Rothko, Twombly, Cornell, together about US$123m) and the Marilyn Arison collection (Manet’s Pivoines dans une bouteille, US$7m–10m).
whispers.outcome: Sold 18 May 2026 for US$630.8m, all 16 lots, all guaranteed (HENI, 20 May 2026; Apollo, 24 May 2026). Pollock’s Number 7A made US$181.2m with fees, three times his previous record of US$61.2m, to a phone bidder advised by Christie’s global president Alex Rotter; Brâncuși’s Danaïde made US$108m to a phone bidder advised by Maria Los. HENI graded the sale C−, noting 44% of lots sold near or below their low estimates against a usual 7%.

whispers.t: Apollo (24 May 2026) wrote that, according to The Baer Faxt, dealer Iwan Wirth bid in the room on Pollock’s Number 7A until about US$150m before it sold to a phone bidder advised by Alex Rotter for US$181.2m.
whispers.who: The Baer Faxt, as quoted by Anna Brady in Apollo
whispers.detail: The buyer was not named by either outlet. The Baer Faxt issue itself was not opened in this session.
whispers.outcome: The buyer remains unnamed in the sources opened.

whispers.t: Mark Rothko’s No. 15 (Two Greens and Red Stripe) (1964), from the Agnes Gund collection, sold at Christie’s New York in May 2026 for US$98.4m with fees, a new auction record for the artist; Gund had bought it directly from the artist after a studio visit.
whispers.detail: Beat a record that had stood since 2012 (HENI). Artlyst (16 Jul 2026) lists it among Christie’s top three lots of the half.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (11 May 2026) reported that Christie’s would sell the Marian Goodman collection on 20 May 2026, led by Gerhard Richter’s Kerze (Candle) (1982) at US$35m–50m.
whispers.detail: Goodman is said to have bought the Richter before she began representing him in 1985.
whispers.outcome: Apollo (24 May 2026): all eight Goodman Richters were guaranteed and made US$78.8m together, over half of Christie’s US$136.8m 21st-century evening sale; Kerze failed to meet its US$35m estimate, hammering at US$30m (US$35.1m with fees).

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (11 May 2026) reported that Sotheby’s would sell Robert Mnuchin’s holdings on 14 May 2026 at the Breuer building, about US$130m in total, led by Rothko’s Brown and Blacks in Reds (1957) at US$70m–100m; Lucius Elliott of Sotheby’s said ‘the ultimate endorsement is that these are the works he held back’.
whispers.who: Sarah Cascone, The Art Newspaper; Lucius Elliott (Sotheby’s) quoted
whispers.detail: The same week: the Enrico and Adele Donati collection (Picasso’s Arlequin (Buste), 1909, up to US$40m, 19 May), Basquiat’s Museum Security (Broadway Meltdown) (1983) at over US$45m, de Kooning’s Untitled III at US$25m–35m, Van Gogh’s La Moisson en Provence (1888) at US$25m–35m, and Warhol’s Brigitte Bardot (1974) from the Gunter Sachs collection at US$14m–18m.
whispers.outcome: Apollo (24 May 2026): the Mnuchin sale made US$166.3m for 11 lots, all guaranteed by Sotheby’s or a third party; the Rothko made US$85.7m, within estimate but short of the then record of US$86.8m. HENI (15 May 2026) gives US$85.8m and a white-glove result. Artlyst (16 Jul 2026), citing Sotheby’s, gives US$173m for the Mnuchin collection, presumably including further lots.

whispers.t: Matisse’s La Chaise lorraine, from the Barbier-Mueller collection, sold at Sotheby’s New York on 19 May 2026 for US$48.4m against a US$25m estimate, the second-highest auction price for a Matisse painting, Apollo reported on 24 May 2026.
whispers.detail: Sotheby’s Madeline Lissner said 24 countries took part in the bidding and that ‘what was needed was material worthy of it, and lately that material has been surfacing’.

whispers.t: Adviser Megan Fox Kelly told Apollo (24 May 2026) that ‘the very top of the market is unquestionably alive’ and that ‘we’re seeing the great wealth transfer happening in real time’, but that she ‘would resist naming this as a broader based bull run, at least not yet’, describing a ‘really bifurcated market’.
whispers.who: Megan Fox Kelly, quoted by Anna Brady in Apollo
whispers.detail: Her stated test is whether confidence at the top ‘starts to filter downward’. Apollo noted that Richter’s Kerze missed its estimate, that minimalism remained ‘trickier’ and that energy flagged late in Sotheby’s sale.
whispers.outcome: Open. First-half 2026 totals (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026) show the rebound concentrated in the top lots; Tim Schneider (The Art Newspaper, 17 Sep 2026) counted at least 26 dealers downsizing or closing in the first seven months of 2026.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (11 May 2026) reported that Phillips’s 19 May 2026 evening sale would be led by Warhol’s Sixteen Jackies (1964) at US$15m–20m, with a Lee Bontecou canvas at US$1.2m–1.8m and a Danish-art collection from the late ambassador John L. Loeb Jr.
whispers.who: Sarah Cascone, The Art Newspaper; Robert Manley (Phillips) quoted
whispers.detail: Bonhams (20 May) offered Yoshitomo Nara’s ...Words Mean Nothing at All (2012) at US$4m–6m and 21 Renoirs from the Gabrielle Renard family.
whispers.outcome: Apollo (24 May 2026) put Phillips’s week at US$145.7m with fees; the Warhol’s price was not in the pages opened.

whispers.t: Christie’s reported first-half 2026 sales of US$4.5bn, with public auctions at US$3.5bn (up 71% year on year), private sales just over US$1bn, Old Masters at US$183m (up 232%) and the Jim Irsay Americana collection at US$105.2m over five auctions, Artlyst reported on 16 July 2026.
whispers.detail: Sell-through by lot 91%; 20th/21st-century art US$2.3bn; luxury US$539m (+15%). Christie’s said 85% of bids came online and 47% of new clients were Millennials or Gen Z. Christie’s own release was not opened in this session.

whispers.t: Sotheby’s reported record first-half 2026 turnover of US$4.4bn, with public auctions at US$3.4bn (up 59%), record private sales of US$826m, a US$908.6m May marquee week and the Lewis collection sale in London in June at US$406.2m, described as the highest-value Impressionist, modern and contemporary sale ever staged in Europe, Artlyst reported on 16 July 2026.
whispers.detail: Sotheby’s also cited a US$900m securitisation in January 2026 and an US$825m bond issue in April 2026; Ron Elimelekh of Sotheby’s Financial spoke of the institutionalisation of art-backed lending. Watches: average spend per bidder up about 60% to US$129,000.

whispers.t: Christie’s CEO Bonnie Brennan, on the first-half 2026 results (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026), said ‘where estimates got pushed, bidding was thinner’ and ‘nobody has a crystal ball’; she expected several discretionary sellers who came to market in 2026 after the late-2025 recovery to keep doing so, but would not forecast beyond the next three to four months.
whispers.who: Bonnie Brennan (Christie’s CEO), as reported by Artlyst
whispers.detail: Cautious confidence rather than a forecast. The underlying press call or release was not opened.
whispers.outcome: Open. The Art Newspaper’s 12 Nov 2026 teaser says the New York houses hope single-owner collections will fuel a US$2.4bn November week.

whispers.t: In an interview published by The Value on 19 December 2025 (conducted September 2025), Christie’s CEO Bonnie Brennan said Christie’s had incorporated in Saudi Arabia and was ‘prioritizing expansion’ there, that 40% of new buyers the previous year came from Asia, and that ‘the biggest challenge is that instability lowers seller confidence, making sourcing more challenging’.
whispers.detail: Brennan said the market decline ‘has leveled off’ and gave no forecast for 2026 or 2027. First-half 2025 sales were US$2.1bn, ‘even with last year’. Rahul Kadakia leads Asia.
whispers.outcome: Christie’s first-half 2026 auction sales rose 71% (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026).

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 27 October 2026 that Art Basel Qatar’s second edition runs 28–30 January 2027 (VIP days 26–27 January) at M7 and the Doha Design District with 82 galleries, down from 87, and that 35 galleries (about 40%) are not returning, among them Hauser & Wirth, Pace, Almine Rech, Victoria Miro and Dubai’s Gallery Isabelle; 30 are new, including Pilar Corrias and Silverlens.
whispers.detail: Artistic director Wassan Al-Khudhairi (theme ‘between’) succeeds Wael Shawky. From 2027 the fair will cover 50% of outbound shipping for unsold works, up to US$20,000 per gallery. Vincenzo De Bellis of Art Basel: ‘it is natural for the exhibitor list to change from year to year.’ Art Basel declined to say why individual galleries withdrew.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper (27 Oct 2026) wrote that Art Basel Qatar’s 2027 list was released ‘as renewed threat of war looms over Gulf’: it cited attacks in Saudi Arabia in October 2026 and warnings that the US and Israel could resume war with Iran, and recalled that in late February 2026 Iran fired missiles into Qatar, injuring 16 people and disrupting airspace; it speculated, without confirming, that some galleries may have withdrawn over Gulf tensions.
whispers.detail: Exhibitors can take a refund or defer to January 2028 if the fair is postponed or significantly altered; last-minute withdrawals face a standard penalty. This is the paper’s own speculation, not a sourced report.
whispers.outcome: Open; the fair is scheduled for 28–30 January 2027.

whispers.t: Monet’s Iris (1924–25), from the collection of Jeanne Schlumberger, sold at Sotheby’s Paris on 22 October 2026 for €50m with fees (US$56m) against an estimate of €22m–30m, the highest price for any work of art sold in France before inflation and the most expensive Monet sold in France, The Art Newspaper reported on 23 October 2026.
whispers.detail: Six bidders over nearly 45 minutes; the buyer bid by phone through Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia, and was not named. The Schlumberger sale made €74.4m (US$83.7m) for 27 lots, all sold, three-quarters above high estimate, against a €40m estimate. The guarantee position is not stated.

whispers.t: Art Basel Paris closed its fifth edition early, at 7pm on Friday 23 October 2026, and stayed shut on 24–25 October, after violent demonstrations across France over the cost of living and school conditions; an e-mail to VIPs co-signed by fair director Karim Crippa said ‘the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority’, The Art Newspaper reported on 22 October 2026.
whispers.detail: The BBC counted at least 2,700 arrests across France; President Macron allowed only authorised union protests on the Saturday. White Cube tagged Julie Mehretu’s Rise of the New Suprematists (2001) at US$7.8m. A related Art Newspaper piece (not opened) reported ‘a flurry of seven- and eight-figure works’ sold on the opening days.

whispers.t: A comment piece in The Art Newspaper (22 Oct 2026) reported that Senator Jacques Grosperrin introduced a bill in the French Senate in March 2026 to ‘strengthen mechanisms for controlling French cultural property’, which would widen the trésor national definition to French artists’ works regardless of age and extend state pre-emption to private transactions outside auction; the author warned it could ‘poison the contemporary art ecosystem’.
whispers.who: Kaisse Sokrane, comment in The Art Newspaper
whispers.detail: The piece gives no bill number, no parliamentary stage beyond introduction and no timetable, and names no supporters or opposing bodies; its criticisms are the author’s own. It cites an Italian auctioneer’s estimate of 70–80% value loss for export-restricted works.
whispers.outcome: Open; no vote reported as of 12 November 2026 in the sources opened.

whispers.t: HENI News wrote on 5 November 2025 that ‘after a run of underwhelming New York sales, even a modest rebound would lift the HENI Auction Index this November’, with more than US$1bn of modern and contemporary art headed to the three houses against recent marquee weeks of roughly US$1.3bn–1.5bn.
whispers.detail: Index grades: May 2024 D, November 2024 C−, May 2025 C−. Lauder collection at Sotheby’s (18–19 Nov 2025), opening the Breuer HQ; Christie’s with Wynn, Edlis and Kawamura works.
whispers.outcome: Came true: the week brought the US$236.4m Lauder Klimt and a US$1.2bn Sotheby’s week (HENI, 1 Jan 2026), US$2.2bn across the houses per Citi Wealth (WealthBriefing, 7 May 2026), and HENI graded it B, then B+ for May 2026 (HENI, 22 May 2026).

whispers.t: Guido van Nispen (Cultureel Persbureau, 5 Jan 2026), summarising the Art Basel/UBS, Artprice, Artnet Intelligence and ArtTactic outlooks, wrote that ‘2026 will not be a spectacular recovery year, but it will be one in which new equilibria become visible’, that the top segment above US$10m ‘remains vulnerable’, and that the year would be ‘a quiet correction, not a revolution’.
whispers.detail: Also: The Art Newspaper’s unnamed insiders expected ‘less spectacle, more transactions’ at fairs rather than fewer fairs.
whispers.outcome: Largely wrong on the top end: Pollock US$181.2m, Brâncuși US$108m and Rothko US$98.4m in May 2026, Christie’s auctions up 71% in the first half (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026). Partly right on galleries: at least 26 dealers downsized or closed by July (The Art Newspaper, 17 Sep 2026).

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 30 September 2026 that Sotheby’s expects the 12-painting Blaquier-Arrieta collection to make ‘in the region of $450m’ in New York in November 2026 (‘Plus, maybe plus’, said Helena Newman, Sotheby’s chairman of Impressionist and Modern art), and that Sotheby’s has guaranteed the whole collection; Newman confirmed the guarantee but would not disclose its size.
whispers.who: Anny Shaw, The Art Newspaper; Helena Newman (Sotheby’s) quoted
whispers.detail: Van Gogh’s Châtaignier en fleurs roses et blanches (May 1890) is estimated at US$180m (the auction record is US$117m, Christie’s New York 2022); Newman believes it could reach US$200m or more. Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90) is estimated at around US$120m, a would-be auction record for the artist; Pissarro’s La Place du Théâtre-Français US$30m–40m; Renoir’s En Canot US$25m–35m; Monet’s Le Jardin des Tuileries US$15m–20m; Vlaminck US$2m–3m. The paper says houses were ‘vying’ for the collection and that Christie’s had previously handled works from it, including Van Gogh’s The Zouave, reportedly sold privately for around US$190m. Newman: ‘At public auction, there hasn’t been anything at this level’; the market is ‘almost like a return to order’. On the collectors, as the paper states it: Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier (died 2020) was reportedly the sole heir to the Ledesma sugar company; Carlos Pedro Blaquier (company president 1970–2013, died 2023) was, the paper reports, charged in 2012 with allegedly participating in kidnappings during the 1976 dictatorship, which he denied; he died without standing trial.
whispers.outcome: Sale set for 18 November 2026; result not known as of 12 November 2026.
src: The Art Newspaper, Anny Shaw (30 Sep 2026)

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper’s pick of the November 2026 auctions (2 Nov 2026) led with Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection since 1975 and not seen publicly since, at ‘in the region of $180m’ against the artist’s record of US$117.2m (Verger avec cyprès, Christie’s New York, November 2022), and Cézanne’s Arlequin at around US$120m, one of only four harlequin pictures, with a Vollard–Durand-Ruel–Rosenberg–Rothschild provenance.
whispers.detail: Both are in Sotheby’s ‘Legendary’ evening sale on 18 November 2026; no guarantee is mentioned in this piece (the 30 Sep 2026 report says Sotheby’s guaranteed the collection). The third pick is Man Ray’s Le Baiser (c. 1930) from the Roger Thérond collection at Christie’s Paris on 13 November 2026, €250,000–350,000.

whispers.t: Galerie reported on 13 October 2026 that Christie’s will sell property from the collection of Wilma (Billie) and Laurence Tisch across its New York marquee week of 17–20 November 2026 (20th Century Evening Sale and the Impressionist and Modern and Post-War and Contemporary day sales) and its Modern British evening sale in London, led by Henry Moore’s Seated Figure at US$5m–8m, with a Picasso Femme assise, a Léger, a Dubuffet, an Arp and Noguchi; some lots are slated for 2027.
whispers.detail: No total estimate or guarantee is given. Galerie attributes a quote (‘We are humbled to have been entrusted as stewards of their exceptional collection’) to Conor Jordan, whom it calls a Sotheby’s deputy chairman; that attribution conflicts with the Christie’s sale and is not relied on here. Moore’s record is US$34.9m for King and Queen at Christie’s London in March 2026, per Galerie.

whispers.t: Puck’s ‘November Rain’ preview of the November 2025 New York sales put the combined low estimate at US$1.67bn (ARTDAI data) against US$1.12bn a year earlier, with about 1,760 lots (up 35%), three Klimts from Leonard Lauder’s estate carrying a collective low estimate of US$300m, and Elaine Wynn’s Diebenkorn Ocean Park #40 (bought four years earlier for a then-record US$27m) estimated at US$15m without a third-party guarantee.
whispers.who: Puck (Wall Power), by its own account citing ARTDAI data and Christie’s Alex Rotter
whispers.detail: The piece explains Christie’s strategy of much lower estimates to draw bidders, as set out by Alex Rotter. The page carries no visible date; the content (Lauder estate, Wynn collection) places it in early-to-mid November 2025, so the date here is approximate. The remainder is paywalled.
whispers.outcome: The Lauder Klimt Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer made US$236.4m and Sotheby’s week US$1.2bn (HENI, 1 Jan 2026); Citi Wealth put the November 2025 New York sales at US$2.2bn, up 77% (WealthBriefing, 7 May 2026); HENI graded the week B, up from C− in May 2025.

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 29 September 2026 that Art Basel Miami Beach (4–6 December 2026, VIP days 2–3 December) will have 272 exhibitors with a Galleries sector cut from 226 to 204 and a footprint about 12% smaller, moving from five plazas to four; director Bridget Finn said ‘the smaller footprint is a deliberate choice’ in service of a more focused fair.
whispers.detail: Returning: Gagosian, White Cube, Pace, Hauser & Wirth. Not returning from 2025: Commonwealth and Council, Night Gallery, Gallery Hyundai, Gallery Wendi Norris, Kurimanzutto, Pippy Houldsworth, Richard Saltoun and Ellie Rines Gallery. More than 30 first-time exhibitors, many in Nova and Positions.

whispers.t: Senators Chuck Grassley (R-IA) and John Fetterman (D-PA) announced the Art Market Integrity Act on 23 July 2025, which would add ‘a person engaged in the trade in works of art’ to the Bank Secrecy Act’s definition of a financial institution and require dealers, galleries, advisers and auction houses to run anti-money-laundering programmes, with exemptions below US$10,000 per transaction or US$50,000 a year, DLA Piper reported on 21 August 2025; Sheppard Mullin (17 Feb 2026) still described it as a proposal, not law.
whispers.who: DLA Piper (21 Aug 2025); Sheppard Mullin Art Law Blog (17 Feb 2026)
whispers.detail: FinCEN would design an examination regime for the art market. Transparency International US supports the bill; an earlier bill (H.R. 5886, 115th Congress) died in committee.
