No bill number or timetable is given in the pages opened, and no vote is reported as of 12 November 2026 in the sources opened.
whispers.outcome: Not enacted as of the latest page opened (17 Feb 2026).
src: Sheppard Mullin Art Law Blog (17 Feb 2026)

whispers.t: Puck’s Marion Maneker wrote on 14 August 2026 that Artnet’s Katya Kazakina had reported Sotheby’s securing the estate of the Argentine sugar heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, including a nine-figure Van Gogh flower painting and a Cézanne harlequin, with a US$450m guarantee ‘per her sources’; Maneker added that the deal was finalised earlier in the summer.
whispers.who: Katya Kazakina (Artnet News), as relayed by Marion Maneker in Puck’s Wall Power
whispers.detail: Part of Maneker’s piece on ‘property gathering’: Christie’s Americas chairman Marc Porter said August is his busiest month; Mari-Claudia Jimenez, former Sotheby’s president now at Withers, said early consignors get the marketing and late ones may get better guarantees. The Artnet report itself was not opened.
whispers.outcome: Confirmed in substance on 30 September 2026, when Sotheby’s announced the 12-painting collection at ‘in the region of $450m’ and Helena Newman confirmed a house guarantee of undisclosed size (The Art Newspaper).

whispers.t: Puck (9 Aug 2026) relayed Katya Kazakina’s Artnet report that three senior figures left White Cube’s New York operation in summer 2026: Jessie Washburne-Harris, hired as global director less than a year earlier, Courtney Willis Blair (to ‘return to academia’) and Sukanya Rajaratnam (to focus on ‘independent ventures’); White Cube took over the former Almine Rech space across the street for its 30-plus New York staff.
whispers.who: Katya Kazakina (Artnet News), as relayed by Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power)
whispers.detail: Maneker’s understanding was that the moves happened earlier in the summer. No statement from White Cube or Jay Jopling appears; no artists are named as leaving. White Cube’s UK accounts (year to 31 Mar 2025) showed turnover up from £10.6m to £15.3m (The Art Newspaper, 9 Mar 2026).

whispers.t: Heritage Auctions sold US$1.4bn in the first half of 2026 against just under US$1bn for all of 2025, Puck reported on 9 August 2026; The Art Newspaper (10 Jul 2026) put the half at a record US$1.4bn, up about 47% from US$962m.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck; Anna Brady, The Art Newspaper
whispers.detail: Maneker also noted Sotheby’s sale of a US$50m dinosaur skeleton and CEO Charles Stewart’s pitch of ‘SpaceX to T. rex’, and that almost US$2.6bn of art priced over US$5m sold in the past season.

whispers.t: Phillips announced on 22 July 2025 a new buyer’s premium from autumn 2025 of 29% to US$1m, 22% to US$6m and 15% above, and a ‘priority bidding’ discount (25%/20%/14%) for buyers who commit to at least the low estimate 48 hours before a live sale, Puck reported the same day, comparing Christie’s 26/21/15 and Sotheby’s 27/22/15.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), citing Phillips’s release quoting CEO Martin Wilson
whispers.detail: Sotheby’s had tried a fee reset a year earlier and reverted within a year. Phillips committed to priority bidding only through the autumn 2025 sales at the time.
whispers.outcome: Still in use in 2026: Phillips told The Art Newspaper (10 Jul 2026) that pre-sale priority bids were up 300% year on year and sales were often 40–50% sold before the auction started.

whispers.t: Puck (22 Jul 2025) reported that adviser Barbara Guggenheim had sued her former partner Abigail Asher about a year earlier and that, per Artnet (Katya Kazakina), Guggenheim alleges Asher misappropriated US$20.5m in commissions, fees and payments; Asher filed a counterclaim alleging Guggenheim misused company funds, and Guggenheim’s lawyer William Charron ‘flatly denied’ Asher’s claims.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck, citing Artnet News
whispers.detail: Both sides’ claims are allegations in civil filings, partly sealed; no judgment is reported in the pages opened. Maneker’s view is that it is a business dispute with little wider significance. Personal details printed by Puck are omitted here.
whispers.outcome: No outcome reported in the sources opened as of 12 November 2026.

whispers.t: Puck’s Inner Circle letter on the first half of 2026 (undated on the page; summer 2026) gave ARTDAI figures of US$4.409bn of art sold at Christie’s, Phillips and Sotheby’s, up 87% year on year, with nearly US$2.6bn (59%) in 156 lots above US$5m (up 208%), while the US$1m–5m band softened to US$841m; Maneker wrote that the market ‘may be just a few halves away from a full recovery’ but with ‘no guarantee’.
whispers.detail: Average lot price US$395,000 against peaks of US$473,000 (2018) and US$449,000 (2022); the 2H24 trough was US$2.3bn. Maneker’s theory: estimate levels drive the cycle, and ‘if consignors resist raising expectations, the market will have more room to run’. Apollo (1 Sep 2026) quotes Maneker’s US$4.4bn/+87% figure. The letter also noted Jessica Morgan’s appointment as Tate director, succeeding Maria Balshaw. Date approximate.
whispers.outcome: Open.

whispers.t: Gagosian planned ‘This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte’ at Grosvenor Hill, London, for the Frieze week, around Magritte’s La Lampe philosophique (1936) with museum and private loans and unannounced contemporary works, Puck reported in summer 2026; The Art Newspaper (31 Jul 2026) also listed the September show.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck; The Art Newspaper
whispers.detail: Loans, not sales, as described. Date of the Puck letter approximate.

whispers.t: The Joe Lewis collection made £306m (just over US$406m) at Sotheby’s London in June 2026, Puck reported: Modigliani’s seated nude nearly US$65m, Klimt’s Gertrud Loew nearly US$49m (Lewis paid US$39m 11 years earlier), Lucian Freud’s Sue Tilley US$39m and a Magritte gouache, La Belle promenade (1965), £16m (US$21.6m), a record for a work on paper; Asian buyers took more than £120m, over a third of the value.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), late June 2026
whispers.detail: Sotheby’s London week £420m (US$556m), including £97m from the various-owner evening sale, where Monet’s Nymphéas made nearly US$55m. Nahmad and Acquavella bid aggressively on the Magritte and bought Picasso and Degas works. ‘Astute auction watchers’ linked a front-row bidder to Patti Wong’s advisory; no buyer is named. Estimates were set low. Sotheby’s itself put the Lewis sale at US$406.2m (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026); ArtTactic counted US$390m (The Art Newspaper, 10 Jul 2026). Date of the letter approximate (late June 2026).

whispers.t: Christie’s London sold the Zabludowicz contemporary collection for £15.4m (US$20.4m) in June 2026, with Cecily Brown’s The Haunter (2010) at US$3.7m ‘apparently bought by a third-party guarantor’, Puck reported; Phillips London made £12m (US$15.8m), led by Hockney’s The Only One With Waves (1991) at US$3.2m.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), late June 2026
whispers.detail: Christie’s Postwar to Present sale £10.2m. Jadé Fadojutimi £425,000. Richard Prince cowboy US$2.1m (vs about US$1.75m in 2014); Nara’s Your Dog just over US$1m (vs US$566,000 in 2012). Date approximate.

whispers.t: Puck reported in late June 2026 that Sotheby’s New York would sell an anonymous private collection of more than 900 works, from antiquities to modern, on 17–22 October 2026, with three focused sales expected to make US$60m or more.
whispers.detail: The collector is not named by Puck. The result was not found in the pages opened.
whispers.outcome: Open; result not found in the sources opened.

whispers.t: Puck (14 Aug 2026) noted that Josh Baer had called Maneker about Dutch court cases favouring galleries that receive compensation when artists leave them.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck, relaying Josh Baer
whispers.detail: No case names or dates are given in the letter; carried as printed.

whispers.t: ArtTactic put Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips at a combined US$6.8bn for the first half of 2026 (including fees, excluding cars), up 70% and the best first half since 2022: Christie’s US$3.4bn (+71%), Sotheby’s US$2.8bn (+71%), Phillips US$505.4m (+59%); London rose 131% to US$1.42bn and Hong Kong almost 30% to US$764m, The Art Newspaper reported on 10 July 2026.
whispers.who: Anna Brady, The Art Newspaper, citing ArtTactic; Anders Petterson quoted
whispers.detail: Sell-through 91%; 131 white-glove sales; a record 33,474 online lots; memorabilia up 308% to US$96.1m. Petterson: the recovery is ‘proving to be far broader than the headline-grabbing results at the very top end’ and the top sales ‘flipped what looked like to be a terrible year into a positive one’. ArtTactic’s totals differ from the houses’ own (Sotheby’s US$3.4bn auctions, Christie’s US$3.5bn per Artlyst) because of scope.

whispers.t: ArtTactic’s September 2026 Contemporary Art Market Confidence Report put its indicator at 56 (from 43 in March), auction confidence at 78 and primary-market confidence at 51, with 60% of respondents expecting flat sales over the next six months; Anders Petterson said confidence ‘seems to be grounded in a real recovery in sales, rather than just a belief’ but that the recovery is ‘still concentrated in the above $1m segment’, Tim Schneider wrote in The Art Newspaper on 3 November 2026.
whispers.who: Tim Schneider, The Art Newspaper, citing ArtTactic; Anders Petterson and Adam Green quoted
whispers.detail: Only the third positive reading in more than four years (75 in Feb 2022 fell to 42 by July; 54 in Jan 2025 fell to 30 within six months). Adviser Adam Green sees ‘a noticeable shift’ of clients to auction houses and private resellers and believes the recovery is ‘broadening to some degree’, with its reach clear by year-end. Events watched ‘this month’: the New York marquee auctions, the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi and Art Collaboration Kyoto.
whispers.outcome: Open; the November 2026 New York sales will test it.

whispers.t: Phillips reported first-half 2026 sales of US$507m, up 60%, with watches (US$235m, from US$115m) outselling modern and contemporary art (US$224m, from US$149m); CEO Martin Wilson attributed the growth to ‘very conscious strategic choices’, The Art Newspaper reported on 10 July 2026.
whispers.who: Anna Brady, The Art Newspaper; Martin Wilson (Phillips) quoted
whispers.detail: Top lot Warhol’s Sixteen Jackies (1964) at US$16.2m in New York in May; an F.P. Journe Résonance at US$13.9m. The John L. Loeb Danish collection made US$18m over five sales. Phillips Assets Ltd’s UK filings show group losses narrowing from £45m (2023) to £8.7m (2024). The piece does not discuss the owners, Mercury Group, or any sale of the house.

whispers.t: Stephen Friedman Gallery entered liquidation on 2 February 2026 and its London and New York galleries closed, The Art Newspaper reported on 9 March 2026; the paper later reported (15 Oct 2026) that the gallery owed creditors £7.8m, including more than £800,000 to artists, and had represented 39 artists and estates.
whispers.who: Anna Brady and Anny Shaw; Phin Jennings, The Art Newspaper
whispers.detail: The 2023 accounts showed a £1.7m loss and about £11.4m owed to creditors due within a year; Alison Mosheim of the Pentland Group held 25–50% of the company. Friedman had announced in November 2025 that it would close its Tribeca gallery as a ‘strategic evolution’. The 11 Aug 2026 report gives £8m of debt outstanding.
whispers.outcome: Artists re-placed by October 2026: Denzil Forrester to Thaddaeus Ropac (show June 2027), Clare Woods to Victoria Miro (solo show February 2027), Holly Hendry to Josh Lilley, Sarah Ball to Pilar Corrias (since September 2026); Caroline Walker stays with Grimm and Ingleby (The Art Newspaper, 15 Oct 2026).

whispers.t: At Frieze London in October 2026, former Stephen Friedman artists sold out on the opening day: Denzil Forrester’s paintings went for £175,000 each within the first hour at Thaddaeus Ropac, and Clare Woods sold out at Victoria Miro (as she had at the Armory Show in September), The Art Newspaper reported on 15 October 2026.
whispers.detail: Ropac: Forrester’s paintings are ‘among the most enthralling and distinctive of his generation’. Victoria Miro’s Glenn Scott Wright: ‘It felt like a natural progression.’ Forrester: Friedman ‘did a lot of good for me, but I’m in the right place now’. Andreas Eriksson and Claire Barclay appeared to have no UK representation.

whispers.t: Apollo (1 Sep 2026) quoted Pace CEO Marc Glimcher: ‘The current gallery model isn’t only broken, it’s unfixable’, and ‘every gallery is currently making temporary fixes… to prop up a system that no longer works’; Pace was seeking to move from its 800 sq m Hanover Square gallery to a ‘less corporate’ part of London, and its eight-floor New York building carries a rumoured rent of US$9m a year.
whispers.detail: Marc Spiegler, in the New York Times in summer 2026: ‘Until, suddenly, it didn’t work. For anybody’; he urged galleries to ‘stop taking on more artists, stop doing more fairs and stop chasing the chimera of globalisation’. Jerry Saltz: ‘Pace feels as though it is built around a fantasy of endless growth.’ Apollo also lists Tiwani Contemporary, Project Native Informant and TJ Boulting among London closures, and at least 85 gallery openings in major cities in 2025 (Arts Economics).

whispers.t: Sid Motion Gallery in South Bermondsey, founded in 2016, will close in autumn 2026 after its 85th exhibition, Sid Motion telling The Art Newspaper on 11 August 2026: ‘We are stopping while we are ahead… the gallery is not in the financial position to fully honour the extraordinary potential of each of my artists.’
whispers.detail: Final show That Which Appears, 18 September–31 October 2026, travelling to Sheffield’s Millennium Gallery in April 2028. No new galleries for the artists are named.

whispers.t: UK filings reported by The Art Newspaper (9 Mar 2026): Bonhams’ Vantage Bidco posted a 2024 operating loss of £163m including £153.3m of impairments and owed £207.3m to Pemberton, which took ownership in October 2025 by a debt-for-equity swap; Phillips Assets Ltd’s auction sales fell about 20% to £381.8m with its parent Mercury Group committing a year of funding; Sotheby’s UK auction sales fell from £771.1m to £471.7m; Christie’s International PLC made an £86m profit.
whispers.who: Anna Brady and Anny Shaw, The Art Newspaper, from Companies House
whispers.detail: Phillips pays £3.7m a year in rent to a company owned by its beneficial owners and said the UK filings ‘do not capture the full breadth of our global performance’. Sotheby’s Holdings’ equity rose US$874.1m to US$1.8bn after the ADQ investment; a spokeswoman cited global sales of US$7.1bn, up 18% on 2024, and reduced debt (the page gives the year as 2026, presumably 2025). Christie’s art-financing debt was US$277m of a US$300m facility. Bonhams said the business ‘is in a strong position’. Thaddaeus Ropac Ltd turnover fell 27% to £36.4m; Hauser & Wirth’s UK pre-tax profit fell almost 90%; David Zwirner’s UK after-tax profit fell to £41,180; Pace’s 2024 accounts were unfiled.

whispers.t: MyArtBroker’s Sheena Carrington made five predictions for 2026: a major house would open a headline sale with a dedicated blue-chip print selection; a complete print set or unseen proof would reset a top price; a charity-led sale would produce a defining result; a major house would add a live pricing signal to its digital platform; and Banksy would stage a major exhibition.
whispers.who: Sheena Carrington, MyArtBroker (page last updated 29 Jun 2026; written ‘as 2026 begins’)
whispers.detail: She counts her 2025 prediction of a dedicated single-artist print sale as fulfilled by Sotheby’s September 2025 Lichtenstein prints sale. No price figures are given. Date approximate.
whispers.outcome: Open; not checked against events in the pages opened.
src: MyArtBroker, Five key art market predictions in 2026

whispers.t: On The Baer Faxt podcast recorded at Art Basel on 17 June 2026, Art Basel CEO Noah Horowitz discussed the ‘Basel Exclusive’ initiative, which withholds marquee works from preview PDFs to re-energise opening day, and ‘the return of high-value consignments to the fair floor’.
whispers.who: The Baer Faxt (Josh Baer), episode page, 25 Jun 2026
whispers.detail: The episode page gives topics only, no quotes or sales figures.
src: The Baer Faxt podcast page (25 Jun 2026)

whispers.t: Puck’s Wall Power of 7 July 2026 carried a teaser that Sotheby’s Blaquier-Arrieta sale in November ‘is expected to clear nearly half a billion dollars’, that London’s June week reached US$438m and that Hong Kong day sales nearly doubled.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), teaser text
whispers.detail: The underlying Puck article is paywalled; the teaser is carried as printed. The same letter reported 56 de Kooning works sold at auction in 2026 for more than US$77m, the most since 2022, and that Massimiliano Gioni would succeed Lisa Phillips as director of the New Museum; a paywalled teaser said the Independent 20th Century fair was moving to the Breuer building.
whispers.outcome: Confirmed in substance on 30 September 2026: Sotheby’s put the collection at ‘in the region of $450m’ with a house guarantee (The Art Newspaper).

whispers.t: Puck (6 Mar 2026) relayed Katya Kazakina’s Artnet report that 35–40 works from S.I. Newhouse’s collection, with a combined estimate of US$450m, were headed to Christie’s; Christie’s had not confirmed.
whispers.who: Katya Kazakina (Artnet News), as relayed by Marion Maneker, Puck
whispers.detail: Carried as an unconfirmed report at the time. The Artnet piece itself was not opened.
whispers.outcome: Came true in substance: The Art Newspaper (11 May 2026) previewed 16 Newhouse lots at up to US$450m, and the sale made US$630.8m on 18 May 2026 (HENI, 20 May 2026).

whispers.t: Puck (6 Mar 2026) reported Sotheby’s announcement of the Robert Mnuchin collection (24 works, US$130m estimate, Rothko’s Brown and Blacks in Reds at US$70m); Maneker wrote that he understood Sotheby’s secured it without competition and admitted he had wrongly predicted a few weeks earlier that there would be no sale.
whispers.detail: Viewing 11–15 March 2026; the dedicated evening sale was on 14 May 2026.
whispers.outcome: The Mnuchin evening sale made US$166.3m for 11 guaranteed lots, the Rothko US$85.7m (Apollo, 24 May 2026).

whispers.t: London’s March 2026 week made £197m (US$264m) at Christie’s, up 52% on the year, £154m (US$207m) at Sotheby’s and £13m at Phillips, Puck reported on 6 March 2026; Henry Moore’s King and Queen (1952–53) made £26.35m (US$35.3m) against a £10m estimate at Christie’s and Francis Bacon’s Selfie (1972), from the Joe Lewis collection, £16m against £8m at Sotheby’s.
whispers.detail: Dorothea Tanning’s Children’s Games (1942) nearly £4.7m against £1m; Leon Kossoff’s Children’s Swimming Pool (1969, Lewis collection) £5.2m against £600,000; Hockney iPad drawings £4.5m. ArtTactic later put London’s first half up 131% (The Art Newspaper, 10 Jul 2026).

whispers.t: Puck’s Inner Circle ranking of the first half of 2026 (ARTDAI data) put Picasso first at about US$350m (608 lots), Rothko second at about US$253m (nine paintings, all sold), then Twombly (US$205m), Pollock (US$200m) and Warhol (US$166m); the top 150 artists accounted for US$4.3bn of US$4.4bn, and Klimt had led the second half of 2025 at about US$394m, mostly from the three Lauder Klimts.
whispers.detail: Maneker: ‘the market has not reverted to its usual concentration on the big names of the past’; on South Asian modern art (M.F. Husain 87 sales, about US$28m; a Raja Ravi Varma pair over US$21m) he wrote ‘I expect those numbers to continue, and probably rise’. Female artists’ share of the top 150 rose from 10% to 12%. Date approximate (the page shows no date; content is summer 2026).
whispers.outcome: Open.

whispers.t: Puck (31 Jul 2026) reported that Marc Spiegler, former Art Basel director, argued in a June 2026 New York Times op-ed for ‘legally enforceable resale agreements’ to ‘block flipping’; Maneker countered that resale restrictions must be ‘reasonable’ under Wildenstein v. Wallis and that smaller dealers rarely litigate them.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), citing the New York Times
whispers.detail: Same letter: Heritage’s 2025 sell-through was ‘almost 98 percent’ (about 417,000 of 426,000 lots) per CEO Steve Ivy, against about 90–91% at the three fine-art houses in the first half of 2026; and the ADAA’s new fair runs 13–16 November 2026 at the Park Avenue Armory with 63 of its 200 members.

whispers.t: Puck’s 21 July 2026 letter carried teasers that Giovanna Bertazzoni, Christie’s head of Impressionist and Modern art, is retiring; that ‘Sotheby’s holds most high-value historical works, while Christie’s leans into Rashid Johnson, KAWS, Richard Prince and Yoshitomo Nara’; and that unnamed competitors call the parent of car auctioneer Broad Arrow a ‘Death Star’.
whispers.who: Marion Maneker, Puck (Wall Power), teaser text
whispers.detail: Teasers only; the articles are paywalled. Maneker also wrote that the gallery system ‘still has a tough time ahead’ and quoted an unnamed adviser that in slow periods ‘it always seems as if the very idea of collecting art is coming to an end’.

whispers.t: Frieze Abu Dhabi, which has taken over Abu Dhabi Art, holds its first edition on 19–22 November 2026 at Manarat Al Saadiyat with 84 galleries (The Art Newspaper, 27 Aug 2026; The National counted 89 on 10 Nov 2026), including Gagosian, Pace, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and Victoria Miro, against 142 at Abu Dhabi Art’s last edition.
whispers.who: Melissa Gronlund, The Art Newspaper; William Mullally, The National
whispers.detail: Frieze is part of Mari, Ari Emanuel’s company, in which Abu Dhabi’s IMI Media took a stake in October 2025; the Department of Culture and Tourism remains a financial partner, terms undisclosed. There had been concern the fair might be postponed because of the Iran conflict; Iranian drone attacks on the UAE had largely stopped by August. Frieze CEO Simon Fox: ‘I would love in all of the cities where we are for Frieze to be a year-round brand’; a permanent Abu Dhabi space ‘might well be something that we should think about… over time’. The National also reports Christie’s inaugural Abu Dhabi fine-art auction at US$8.94m and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opening on 11 December 2026.
whispers.outcome: Opens 19 November 2026.

whispers.t: Sotheby’s Luxembourg parent reported a 2024 pre-tax loss of US$248m, more than double 2023’s US$106m, with commission revenue down 18% to US$813m and long-term net debt cut from US$3.55bn to US$2.76bn; ADQ had invested US$909m for a 24% stake in Sotheby’s Holdings UK as part of a US$1bn capital injection agreed in August 2024, the FT reported (via The Irish Times, 11 Sep 2025).
whispers.who: Financial Times, syndicated by The Irish Times
whispers.detail: Severance US$29.2m; headcount 2,218. Patrick Drahi’s BidFair contributed US$85m to the 2024 raise. Sotheby’s declined to comment. For context, Sotheby’s later cited US$7.1bn of 2025 sales, up 18% (The Art Newspaper, 9 Mar 2026), a US$900m securitisation in January 2026 and an US$825m bond in April 2026 (Artlyst, 16 Jul 2026).

whispers.t: HENI’s 2025 review (1 Jan 2026) put the big three’s fine-art sales at US$6.5bn, up 13% but a third below the decade average (Christie’s US$3.17bn, Phillips US$358m), and recorded Sotheby’s US$1.2bn November 2025 week led by the Lauder Klimt Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer at US$236.4m, Kahlo’s El sueño (La cama) at US$54.66m and Cattelan’s gold toilet America, consigned by Steve Cohen, at US$12.1m; Christie’s Weis collection made US$218m.
whispers.detail: The Klimt became the most expensive modern painting at auction and the Kahlo the most expensive work by a woman artist. HENI graded 2025 C−, up from D in 2023 and 2024, and noted Phillips would have to operate without former chairwoman Cheyenne Westphal’s ‘rainmaking’. ‘The market still has ground to make up but is moving in the right direction.’
whispers.outcome: The first half of 2026 then rose 70% at the three houses (ArtTactic via The Art Newspaper, 10 Jul 2026).

whispers.t: Artnet’s Wet Paint (4 Mar 2026, guest writer Sammy Loren) relayed ‘a new round of whispers’ about New York galleries’ Los Angeles outposts: one unnamed ‘powerhouse’ transplant ‘may be considering a downsizing’, another ‘is said to be attempting to sublease its L.A. location’ and a third ‘may be nearing a closure’.
whispers.who: Artnet News, Wet Paint (as mirrored by USA Art News, 5 Mar 2026)
whispers.detail: No gallery is named. The column noted Tanya Bonakdar, Harper’s and Sean Kelly had already left Los Angeles, and that East Coast snow disrupted LA art week. The Artnet page itself could not be opened; the mirror is the source read.
whispers.outcome: Open; no named closure traced to these whispers in the pages opened.
src: USA Art News mirror of Artnet’s Wet Paint (5 Mar 2026)

whispers.t: Asked about the May 2026 sales, adviser Ed Dolman (former Phillips executive chairman) called it a market that has ‘corrected, stabilized, and moved on’; Meredith Darrow said the Pollock not soaring higher suggested a more measured collector class; Hugo Nathan pointed to the Marian Goodman Richter Abstraktes Bild (1995) making US$8.7m against US$3m–5m (Artnet, as mirrored by USA Art News, 27 May 2026).
whispers.who: Artnet News (mirrored by USA Art News); Ed Dolman, Meredith Darrow, Hugo Nathan, Andrea Hazen
whispers.detail: Hazen cited Sotheby’s Charles Stewart on millennial and Gen Z interest at the 2026 Art Business Conference; Christie’s reported more than 20,000 preview visitors. The Artnet page itself could not be opened.
src: USA Art News mirror of Artnet (27 May 2026)

whispers.t: Templon closed its 6,500 sq ft Chelsea gallery, opened in 2022, after the landlord sought a large increase on its US$55,000 monthly rent; Mathieu Templon said ‘It was way too, too much’ and is looking at Tribeca or the Upper East Side (ARTnews Morning Links, as mirrored by USA Art News, 9 Jun 2026).
whispers.who: ARTnews Morning Links (mirrored by USA Art News)
whispers.detail: The same round-up noted that Stephen Friedman and Timothy Taylor had closed their New York outposts. A related link dated 7 November (year not shown) says The Hole faces eviction from its Bowery space over unpaid rent; unverified here.
src: USA Art News mirror of ARTnews Morning Links (9 Jun 2026)

whispers.t: The Art Newspaper reported on 6 April 2026 that The Hole had permanently closed its West Hollywood space (final show down September 2025), owed more than US$120,000 in rent and tax arrears on its Tribeca space and more than US$60,000 on the Bowery, and had cut its fairs from 12 in 2023 to one in 2026; founder Kathy Grayson said ‘I’m recalibrating things here to focus on New York’.
whispers.detail: Of five artists interviewed, three remained unpaid. The piece also lists Blum’s closure (summer 2025), Tanya Bonakdar’s and Sean Kelly’s Los Angeles closures (2025), Stephen Friedman’s administration (February 2026) and Timothy Taylor’s New York closure.

whispers.t: Klimt’s Portrait of Fräulein Lieser (1917), hammered at €30m at Im Kinsky in Vienna in April 2024 to Patti Wong & Associates for an anonymous Hong Kong buyer in a sale that later fell through, stays off the market: Patricia Leahy, a granddaughter of Hans Lieser, sued Im Kinsky and the holder Eva Ropper in the New York Supreme Court in April 2026 claiming to be a rightful heir, and Louis Rönsberg, lawyer for the other claimants, says that while the case is pending ‘a sale is impossible’, The Art Newspaper reported on 20 October 2026.
whispers.detail: As of mid-October 2026 Ropper had not been served; her lawyer Robert Bachner said the suit lacked justification and that ‘the plaintiff’s primary objective was to achieve the greatest possible publicity with minimal effort’. Leahy’s lawyer did not respond. Under the 2024 settlement claimants were to receive 60% of proceeds and Ropper 40%; the consignor and original claimants had agreed to try again at a major international house. Ropper has commissioned a fuller provenance report. These are the parties’ positions as the paper states them; no judgment is reported.
whispers.outcome: Open; no sale possible while the New York case is pending, per the claimants’ lawyer.

whispers.t: Kenny Schachter wrote (Artnet News, reposted on his site 21 Oct 2025) that Kerry James Marshall’s Past Times (1997), bought by Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs for US$21m and sold ‘at the onset of his, uh, legal situation’, had been sold, as Mark Godfrey confirmed to him; a ‘prominent birdie’ told him the buyer was ‘Larry G’ after a US$29m offer was declined, and that the work ‘went to Gagosian for $30 million, or just above’. Larry Gagosian did not respond to his request for comment.
whispers.who: Kenny Schachter, Artnet News column (as reposted on kennyschachter.art)
whispers.detail: Schachter labels the buyer identification as hearsay (‘the birdie whispered’) and says the work did not go to Ken Griffin; a Jeff Bezos suggestion is his own speculation. The same column: Inigo Philbrick is developing a mushroom-coffee product (Nimrod Kamer, quoted); Simon Lee’s London space was shut by HMRC and he entered receivership (per a 2024 Art Newspaper link); Schachter calls rumours of a retreat by an unnamed bicoastal gallery ‘persistent, spiteful rumors’ and false; and he predicted Art Basel Paris would ‘best’ Frieze.
whispers.outcome: The buyer has not been confirmed in the pages opened.

whispers.t: The estate of Robert Therrien (1947–2019) left Gagosian for David Zwirner after almost 30 years and 11 Gagosian shows, following the Broad’s 120-work survey in Los Angeles; Zwirner called himself a ‘superfan’ (ARTnews, as mirrored by USA Art News, 24 May 2026).
whispers.detail: The mirror also recalls Carol Bove’s 2023 move from Zwirner to Gagosian and Jeff Koons’s return to Gagosian in 2025 after four years at Pace. The ARTnews page itself was not opened.
src: USA Art News mirror of ARTnews (24 May 2026)

whispers.t: Citi Wealth’s ‘State of the Art Market 2026: Don’t Call It A Comeback’ (Betsy Bickar) said that ‘as of early 2026, confidence has returned to the art market, but not uniformly’, with optimism at the high and accessible ends and the middle ‘selective and cautious’; the November 2025 New York sales made US$2.2bn, up 77% on the year but 30% below the 2022 peak, WealthBriefing reported on 7 May 2026.
whispers.who: Betsy Bickar, Citi Wealth, as reported by Tom Burroughes, WealthBriefing
whispers.detail: Bickar: ‘Rather than broad upward momentum, the market is characterised by buyer discernment.’ Gallery closures of 2025 (Blum, Venus Over Manhattan) ‘continued into this year’. She said the inaugural Art Basel Qatar ‘has elevated the Middle East’s standing’, held before the US and Israeli clashes with Iran. The Citi report itself was not opened.
whispers.outcome: Partly borne out: the May 2026 sales set records at the top (Pollock US$181.2m) while the US$1m–5m band softened (Puck, summer 2026) and galleries kept closing (The Art Newspaper, 17 Sep 2026).

forecasters.outlet: Arts Economics; The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report
forecasters.beat: annual global sales estimate and dealer/auction sentiment surveys

record.said: 2025 was ‘a shift in direction… to modest growth’; 43% of dealers expected 2026 sales to improve, 19% a decline
‘sustained growth will depend on bringing exceptional works to market’

forecasters.outlet: Puck (Wall Power); formerly Art Market Monitor
forecasters.beat: auction data, house strategy, the top 50/150 artists

record.said: the first half of 2026 ‘marked the takeoff phase of a new auction cycle’
‘I would resist naming this as a broader based bull run, at least not yet’; a ‘really bifurcated market’

forecasters.outlet: collector, quoted in The Art Newspaper

record.said: ‘more dramatic rightsizing will be necessary, particularly to compete with more efficient auction houses’

forecasters.outlet: The Art Newspaper; The Gray Market; No Reserve from The Baer Faxt

record.said: mega-dealers’ real-estate retreat is ‘a wake-up call but not a sector-wide death knell’; galleries ‘will need more extreme resizing’
the decline ‘has leveled off’; ‘when we do source great material, the buyers are there’
discretionary sellers who came to market in 2026 would keep doing so; ‘nobody has a crystal ball’; no forecast beyond three to four months

forecasters.beat: letter grades for each marquee week; guarantees, bidders per lot

record.said: ‘even a modest rebound would lift the HENI Auction Index this November’
‘2026 will not be a spectacular recovery year’; the top segment above US$10m ‘remains vulnerable’; ‘a quiet correction, not a revolution’

forecasters.outlet: Sotheby’s (executive vice-president, global fine art and major collections)

record.said: ‘What was needed was material worthy of it, and lately that material has been surfacing’

forecasters.outlet: The Baer Faxt; No Reserve; The Baer Faxt podcast
forecasters.beat: who bid, who bought, who is consigning

record.said: reported that Iwan Wirth bid to about US$150m on Pollock’s Number 7A (as quoted by Apollo)

src: No Reserve from The Baer Faxt, issue 48 (11 Aug 2026)

playbooks.n: Consigning a work to a major auction house (Sotheby’s, Christie’s): from estimate to settlement
playbooks.for: seller, collector’s adviser, executor, dealer

steps.n: Request the estimate
steps.do: Submit photographs and details through the house’s online estimate portal; a specialist reviews them and returns a low-to-high estimate based on comparable sales, demand and the object’s qualities (Sotheby’s describes the online estimate as complimentary). Sotheby’s cites, for 2025, an average of 4.5 bidders per lot sold and lots selling on average at 139% of the low estimate.
steps.who: the specialist department
steps.doc: photographs, dimensions, medium, provenance, exhibition and literature history, any condition issues
src: Sotheby’s, ‘How to Sell with Sotheby’s: A Step-by-Step Guide’ (17 July 2026)

steps.n: Sign the consignment agreement and agree the reserve
steps.do: The consignment agreement sets the terms of sale; the reserve is a confidential minimum agreed with the specialist, always at or below the low estimate; if bidding does not reach it the lot is unsold and remains the seller’s. Sotheby’s states no standard seller’s commission: the terms, including any commission, are set in the agreement case by case, and the specialist explains the net proceeds before the seller commits. The buyer’s premium is paid by the buyer. (The property receipt, the insurance or loss-and-damage fee, catalogue and marketing charges, the withdrawal and unsold fees and the guarantee terms are not published on the pages opened; they are set in the agreement — vf U for their levels.)
steps.who: the house (consignment agreement)
steps.doc: the consignment agreement, the schedule of property, the reserve letter
steps.fee: seller’s commission and expenses as negotiated (no published rate, Sotheby’s 2026)
src: Sotheby’s, ‘How to Sell with Sotheby’s: A Step-by-Step Guide’ (17 July 2026)

steps.n: Pass the house’s AML and agent checks
steps.do: Christie’s runs a global anti-money-laundering programme with customer, transaction and artwork due diligence, monitoring and record-keeping; it applies strict cash limits and refuses third-party payments. Where an agent introduces the consignment, Christie’s may pay an introduction commission; the agent must disclose any economic interest to the person who appointed them, and the seller should ask. Expect to provide identity and beneficial-ownership documents before the agreement is countersigned (the exact list is not published on the page opened — vf U).
steps.who: the house’s compliance department
steps.doc: passport or ID, proof of address, company documents and beneficial-owner identification for a corporate seller, proof of title (invoice, inheritance papers)
src: Christie’s, Selling guide, ‘Important information’ (terms dated 1 April 2019; AML and agents sections)

steps.n: Loss and damage while in the house’s custody
steps.do: Under Christie’s terms (1 April 2019) its liability covers lots lost or damaged while under an agreement, excluding moths and pests, natural wear, inherent defects, atmospheric change, war, terrorism and environmental causes; for partial damage it pays reasonable repair costs plus the resulting loss in value. The seller must notify Christie’s immediately of any reportable event and in writing within 30 days. Christie’s gives 45 days’ notice before amending the terms. If Christie’s pays out for a lost lot and later recovers it, it takes title once the seller repays the compensation.
steps.who: the house
steps.time: written notice within 30 days of a loss
steps.fee: the loss-and-damage charge is set in the agreement (level not published — vf U)
steps.doc: condition report at delivery, photographs, the property receipt
src: Christie’s, Selling guide, ‘Important information’ (terms dated 1 April 2019)

steps.n: Cataloguing, marketing and the sale
steps.do: The house catalogues, photographs, researches and markets the object ahead of the sale; some objects are cleaned, reframed or tidied before sale. The buyer pays the buyer’s premium on the hammer price: at Sotheby’s, since 13 February 2026, 28% up to and including US$2m (£1.5m in London), 22% from US$2m to US$8m (£1.5m–£6m), 15% above; at Christie’s, since September 2025, 27% up to US$1.5m (£1m), 22% to US$8m (£6m), 15% above.
steps.who: the house
steps.time: a sale calendar slot is usually months away (not stated by the house)
steps.fee: none to the seller beyond the agreed expenses
steps.doc: the catalogue entry proof, the condition report for buyers
src: Sotheby’s, ‘How to Sell with Sotheby’s: A Step-by-Step Guide’ (17 July 2026)
The Art Newspaper, ‘Sotheby’s adjusts buyer’s premiums…’ (17 February 2026)

steps.n: Settlement
steps.do: The seller is paid once the buyer has settled, typically about a month after the auction (Sotheby’s). An unsold lot stays the seller’s and is returned or re-offered on new terms.
steps.who: the house’s client accounts
steps.time: about one month after the sale, subject to the buyer’s payment
steps.fee: the agreed commission and expenses deducted from the hammer price
steps.doc: the settlement statement
src: Sotheby’s, ‘How to Sell with Sotheby’s: A Step-by-Step Guide’ (17 July 2026)

pitfalls: The seller is paid only when the buyer pays; a defaulting buyer delays or voids the settlement.
The reserve is at or below the low estimate; an estimate pushed up to flatter the consignor lowers the chance of a sale.
Loss or damage must be reported to Christie’s in writing within 30 days; later claims fall outside its terms.
An introducing agent may be paid by the house as well as by the seller; ask for the disclosure.
The levels of the loss-and-damage fee, catalogue costs, withdrawal and unsold fees are not published; they are in the consignment agreement and are negotiable.
playbooks.cost: Seller’s commission and expenses as negotiated (the houses publish no standard rate in 2026); the buyer’s side adds 27–28% on the first tier (Christie’s Sept 2025, Sotheby’s Feb 2026)
playbooks.time: estimate to sale: a season (months); settlement about one month after the sale
src: Sotheby’s, ‘How to Sell with Sotheby’s’ (17 July 2026)

playbooks.n: Buying at a major auction house as a foreign buyer: registration, the deposit, the premium, payment and collection
playbooks.for: collector, adviser bidding as agent, corporate buyer, family office

steps.n: Register at least 24 hours before a live sale
steps.do: Christie’s recommends registering at least 24 hours before the start of any live auction (online sales can be joined during the sale); bring a photo ID and a proof of address to collect a paddle in person; ‘for some auctions, you may also be asked for a financial reference and/or a deposit as a condition of allowing you to bid’ (no trigger value published on the page). For a company, expect the certificate of incorporation, the beneficial-ownership evidence and the signatory’s authority; for an agent, the principal’s identity and written authority (company and agent lists are from the houses’ conditions of sale, not the page opened — vf U). Bidding methods: in the room with a paddle, telephone (leave an emergency absentee bid too), absentee (priority over an equal bid in the room or on the phones), Christie’s LIVE online; increments of up to 10% at the auctioneer’s discretion.
steps.who: the house’s Client Services / Bids department
steps.fee: none for registration; deposit where required
steps.doc: passport or ID, proof of address, company documents, authority letter for an agent, bank reference for high-value sales

steps.n: Budget the buyer’s premium
steps.do: Sotheby’s since 13 February 2026: 28% of the hammer up to and including US$2m (£1.5m in London), 22% from US$2m to US$8m (£1.5m–£6m), 15% above. Christie’s since September 2025: 27% up to US$1.5m (£1m), 22% to US$8m (£6m), 15% above. Phillips (September 2025) charges a significantly lower premium to a bidder whose binding written bid at or above the low estimate placed 48 hours before the sale wins. VAT or sales tax applies on the premium (and on the hammer where the lot is imported under temporary admission or sold under the standard scheme).
steps.who: the house
steps.doc: the sale’s conditions of sale and the lot symbols (import VAT, artist’s resale right)
src: The Art Newspaper, ‘Sotheby’s adjusts buyer’s premiums…’ (17 February 2026)

steps.n: Pay the invoice
steps.do: The house issues the invoice in the sale currency to the registered bidder only; Christie’s applies strict cash limits and refuses third-party payments under its AML programme. The payment deadline and late-payment interest are in the conditions of sale (seven calendar days at Christie’s from memory — vf U; the PDF conditions returned a bot-check page in this session). Pay by wire from an account in the buyer’s own name.
steps.who: the house’s client accounts / post-sale services
steps.doc: the invoice, proof of the payer’s identity matching the registration
src: Christie’s, Selling guide, ‘Important information’ (AML programme: cash limits, no third-party payments)

steps.n: Collect, store and export
steps.do: Sotheby’s releases property only once payment has been received and cleared (Paris: ‘must be paid for immediately after the sale’) and asks for collection or delivery within 30 calendar days of the sale date in New York, London, Paris, Hong Kong, Cologne and Geneva (60 days for Sotheby’s Preferred members); later collection carries a late-collection fee, and London lots uncollected after 90 calendar days move to Greenford Park storage (London wine: £2 per case per week after 30 days; Paris wine: €10 per lot per month). For export, the house’s shipping desk or the buyer’s shipper handles the export licence (UK: Arts Council; France: certificat; Italy: attestato) and the CITES permit for lots with endangered material; VAT on the hammer paid under temporary admission may be refunded on proof of export within the time limit (U).
steps.who: the house’s post-sale services; the shipper; the licensing authority
steps.time: collect within 30 calendar days (Sotheby’s); licence times per the export playbooks (5–28 business days in the UK)
steps.fee: late-collection and storage fees after 30 days (Sotheby’s); shipping and licence costs
steps.doc: the paid invoice, the export licence, the CITES permit, the shipper’s instructions
src: Sotheby’s, ‘Guide for Buyers: Collection, Shipment, Export, Storage’
Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters (2021)

pitfalls: A deposit or bank reference may be required for high-value sales; registering on the day fails.
Third-party payments are refused; the paying account must be the registered bidder’s.
VAT on the premium is generally not refunded on export (Barnebys, 2025).
The premium tiers moved at both houses within the last 14 months; quote from the sale’s own conditions.
playbooks.cost: Hammer plus 27–28% on the first tier (2025–26), plus VAT or sales tax on the premium, plus shipping, licence and storage
playbooks.time: registration 24 hours before; payment within the conditions-of-sale period; export licence days to weeks
links: The Art Newspaper on the 2026 premium changes

playbooks.n: Exporting a work from the UK: the OGEL, the individual licence, the Waverley stop
playbooks.for: dealer, auction house shipping desk, collector’s agent, registrar

steps.n: Check whether the object needs an individual licence
steps.do: Rule of thumb from the Arts Council’s Guidance for Exporters (Issue 2, 2021): any object less than 50 years old at export is outside the control (Table 1). For older objects compare the value with the Open General Export Licence limits (Table 2): £65,000 for any article over 50 years not in another category; £180,000 for an oil or tempera painting over 50 years (except portraits of British historical personages); £35,000 for firearms over 100 years and other arms or armour over 50 years; £12,000 for textiles; £10,000 for photographs and for portraits of British historical personages; £0 (always licensable) for archaeological material from UK soil or waters, manuscripts and documents, archives and hand-produced architectural, scientific or engineering drawings. Below the limit: export under the OGEL, no application, quote the OGEL title in the export documents. At or above it: apply for an individual licence.
steps.who: Export Licensing Unit, Arts Council England (acting for the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport)
steps.doc: a valuation on the exporter’s own assessment, the date of making, the invoice if sold
src: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters, Issue 2 (2021), Tables 1–2, paras 3–8

steps.n: Apply for the individual licence on ELU Form C
steps.do: Download ELU Form C from the Arts Council site. Apply as soon as the export is known, naming the consignee and address. Attach full provenance and ownership history, high-resolution digital photographs (clocks: a photograph of the works; vehicles: logbook, engine and chassis numbers; archives: a list or calendar). If the object was imported within the last 50 years attach evidence of legal arrival (shipping documents or the C88). For an object that was in another EU member state on or after 1 January 1993 attach evidence of lawful, definitive export from that state (para 13). Send to the Export Licensing Unit, The Arts Council, 21 Bloomsbury Street, London WC1B 3HF, or elu@artscouncil.org.uk.
steps.who: Export Licensing Unit, Arts Council England; the Expert Adviser at the relevant national museum
steps.time: Expert Adviser asked to respond within 15 business days; normally 28 business days in all if no objection; normally 5 business days if there is no referral (the object arrived in the UK within the last 50 years and the arrival is evidenced)
steps.doc: ELU Form C, photographs, provenance file, shipping or C88 evidence of arrival, EU export evidence where relevant
src: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters, Issue 2 (2021), paras 9–13 and Appendix A

steps.n: If the Expert Adviser objects: the Reviewing Committee and the Waverley criteria
steps.do: The case goes to the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (eight permanent members plus three independent assessors), normally heard within two to three months. The object is a national treasure if it meets any one of the three Waverley criteria: closely connected with our history and national life; of outstanding aesthetic importance; of outstanding significance for the study of some particular branch of art, learning or history. The Committee then recommends a deferral of the licence: a first period, normally two to four months, for a serious expression of interest to buy at the fair market price; a second, usually up to six months, for the sale to complete. If no serious expression of interest arrives in the first period the licence is normally granted at its end.
steps.who: Reviewing Committee (RCEWA); the Secretary of State decides
steps.time: 2–3 months to the hearing; then deferral of 2–4 months, extendable by up to 6 months
steps.doc: the exporter’s written case, the valuation evidence (the fair market price is the matching price)
src: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters, Issue 2 (2021), paras 38–42 and 77

steps.n: Temporary export (loan, fair, restoration)
steps.do: Use the same form; a temporary application is not scrutinised for national importance, the Expert Adviser comments on fitness to travel and the assurances of return. A temporary licence normally runs for up to three years with one extension of up to three years, applied for before the return date. For a national treasure the maximum is three years, normally for display in a public institution, with no extension, and the object must then stay in the UK for three years before a new application. The OGEL itself covers certain temporary exports of under six months (some musical instruments and motor vehicles, Appendix B).
steps.who: Export Licensing Unit, Arts Council England
steps.time: as for an individual licence; licence valid up to 3 years
steps.doc: loan agreement or fair contract, return undertaking, condition report
src: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters, Issue 2 (2021), paras 25–30 and Appendix B

pitfalls: Failure to return a temporarily exported object is an offence under section 5(b) of the Export of Objects of Cultural Interest (Control) Order 2003.
An object that came from an EU member state on or after 1 January 1993 needs evidence of lawful export from that state before the UK licence is granted; without it the application stalls.
The OGEL value limits above are those printed in the 2021 guidance (Issue 2); check the current OGEL text before relying on them, as the limits are revised from time to time.
A deferral under the Waverley procedure can hold a sold work in the UK for close to a year; auction and private-sale contracts should make the sale conditional on the licence.
playbooks.cost: No licence fee is mentioned in the Arts Council guidance (2021); the cost is the shipper’s or agent’s handling and the photographs and research for the file. (vf U for the absence of any fee today.)
playbooks.time: 5 business days (evidenced recent import) to 28 business days (no objection); 2–3 months plus 2–10 months of deferral if the object is referred to the Reviewing Committee
links: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters (Issue 2, 2021)
src: Arts Council England, Guidance for Exporters, Issue 2 (2021)

playbooks.n: Exporting a work from France: the certificat d’exportation, the EU licence, the temporary authorisation, the 6.5% export tax
playbooks.for: dealer, auction house, collector’s agent, shipper (commissionnaire en douane)

steps.n: Check the category thresholds
steps.do: A certificate is needed when the good exceeds the age and value thresholds of its category: paintings over 50 years and €150,000 or more; sculptures over 50 years and €50,000; watercolours, gouaches and pastels over 50 years and €30,000; engravings and prints over 50 years and €15,000; archaeological objects over 100 years at any value (the service-public guide, last updated 27 September 2016, lists these; drawings, photographs, furniture, books and archives have their own thresholds in the annex to the Code du patrimoine, not shown on the page opened — vf U for those). Below the thresholds the work leaves France without a certificate.
steps.who: the owner or the shipper (self-assessment)
steps.doc: invoice or valuation, date of execution
src: service-public.fr guide F1277 (mirror), ‘Exportation d’un bien culturel’ (updated 27 September 2016)

steps.n: Apply for the certificat d’exportation (Cerfa n°02 0075)
steps.do: File online through the ministry’s procedures portal or by post with the competent service (Service des Musées de France for paintings and objets d’art; Service interministériel des Archives de France; Service du livre et de la lecture; Service du patrimoine), contact exportation-biensculturels@culture.gouv.fr. The certificate allows a permanent exit or any number of temporary exits without limit of duration. Silence of the administration for 4 months counts as grant. The certificate is permanent except for goods under 100 years old, which must be renewed after 20 years; it stays with the object and passes to the buyer.
steps.who: Ministère de la Culture (Direction générale des patrimoines et de l’architecture)
steps.time: up to 4 months; silence after 4 months = granted
steps.doc: Cerfa 02 0075, photographs, description, provenance, proof of ownership

steps.n: If refused: the 30-month window
steps.do: A refusal makes the work a trésor national, which may leave France only temporarily with a compulsory return. The State then has 30 months to make an offer to buy at the international market price; if it does not, a new application is normally needed and the certificate is granted, and the work is no longer a trésor national.
steps.who: Ministère de la Culture; the Commission consultative des trésors nationaux
steps.doc: the refusal decision, an independent valuation for the price negotiation

steps.n: Export outside the EU: add the EU licence (Cerfa n°11033*03)
steps.do: For a destination outside the Union apply for the licence d’exportation under the EU regime (Cerfa n°11033*03, temporary or permanent), issued by the ministry; the certificate alone does not clear the EU border. Silence after 2 months counts as grant; the licence is usable once within one year.
steps.who: Ministère de la Culture
steps.time: 2 months (silence = granted); valid one year, single use
steps.doc: Cerfa 11033*03, the certificat d’exportation, the invoice

steps.n: Temporary exit (restoration, expertise, exhibition, sale abroad)
steps.do: For a bien culturel without certificate: the autorisation de sortie temporaire, Cerfa n°02 0083, valid for a period proportionate to the purpose; silence after 2 months = granted. For a trésor national the AST is exceptional (restoration, expertise, cultural event, exhibition, deposit in a public collection) with a stated return date, extendable on the prorogation sheet Cerfa n°02 0076 no later than 15 days before expiry. A feuille d’itinérance accompanies temporary exits.
steps.who: Ministère de la Culture
steps.doc: Cerfa 02 0083 (or 02 0076 for a prorogation), the loan or restoration contract, the return guarantee

steps.n: Pay the taxe forfaitaire on a definitive export outside the EU
steps.do: A definitive export outside the EU of art, collectibles or antiques worth €5,000 or more by a French tax resident attracts the flat tax of 6% of the price or customs value plus CRDS of 0.5% (non-residents are exempt from the CRDS), payable within a month on form n°2091-SD; exemptions include sales to public museums or libraries, temporary exports and export by the artist of their own work.
steps.who: Direction générale des Finances publiques (customs on export)
steps.fee: 6% + 0.5% CRDS of the value (figures per the 2016-updated guide — vf S)
steps.doc: form 2091-SD, the invoice or valuation

pitfalls: Illegal export of a trésor national or other cultural good: up to 2 years’ imprisonment and a fine up to €450,000 (guide F1277).
The certificate for a work under 100 years old lapses after 20 years; check the date on an old certificate before shipping.
The EU licence is single-use and lapses after one year; a sale that falls through wastes it.

The service-public guide was last updated in 2016; the thresholds printed there were revised in January 2021 (the ministry links a PDF not opened here) — confirm with the ministry before relying on a threshold.
playbooks.cost: No administrative fee for the certificate, the AST or the EU licence; the 6.5% flat export tax applies on definitive non-EU exports from €5,000 unless exempt (figures from the 2016 guide, vf S)
playbooks.time: up to 4 months for the certificate (silence = grant), 2 months for the EU licence or an AST; 30 months more if refused
links: Ministère de la Culture, procédures d’exportation (forms and contacts)

playbooks.n: Exporting a work from Italy: the autocertificazione, the attestato di libera circolazione on the SUE portal, the 2025–26 reforms
playbooks.for: dealer, auction house, collector’s agent, spedizioniere

steps.n: Place the work by age and author
steps.do: Work by a living artist or made less than 50 years ago: free export after an autocertificazione filed with the competent Ufficio Esportazione through the SUE portal (Sportello Unico per l’Esportazione). Work made more than 50 but less than 70 years ago: autocertificazione too, but the office may ask for further documents and check the cultural interest and the declared value. Work more than 70 years old by an author no longer living: definitive export needs the attestato di libera circolazione (and, for a non-EU destination, the licenza di esportazione). A notified (vincolato) work cannot be exported definitively; only a temporary exit can be authorised.
steps.who: Ufficio Esportazione of the Soprintendenza, via the SUE portal
steps.doc: autocertificazione form, photographs, the artist’s dates, proof of value
src: We Wealth, Negri Clementi, Ligasacchi and Tommasi, ‘La circolazione delle opere d’arte è (più) libera oggi?’ (18 March 2026)

steps.n: Check the value threshold: €50,000 since Law no. 40/2026
steps.do: The DGABAP circular of 24 April 2026 records that Law no. 40/2026 raised the threshold of relevance (soglia di rilevanza) from €13,500 to €50,000, excluding library material. Works over 70 years old by dead authors below the threshold go through the declaratory route; above it, the attestato procedure with the office’s discretionary assessment of cultural interest.
steps.who: Ufficio Esportazione
steps.doc: proof of value (invoice, auction estimate, insurance valuation)
src: Ministero della Cultura, DGABAP Servizio IV, circolare 24 aprile 2026 on Constitutional Court judgment no. 51/2026

steps.n: Apply for the attestato di libera circolazione on SUE
steps.do: Lodge the application with the Ufficio Esportazione through the SUE portal with photographs, description, provenance and value; the office examines the work (physical presentation) and either issues the attestato, valid five years, or refuses and starts the procedure to declare the work of particular cultural interest. For a non-EU destination the licenza di esportazione under the EU regime is issued with it. The administration’s power to annul an authorising act on its own initiative was cut from twelve to six months by Law no. 182 of 2 December 2025 (Legge Semplificazioni, in force 18 December 2025).
steps.who: Ufficio Esportazione (Soprintendenza); Ministero della Cultura
steps.time: the statutory decision period is not on the pages opened (40 days from memory — vf U); the attestato is valid 5 years
steps.fee: none stated on the pages opened (stamp duty and office fees from memory — vf U)
steps.doc: the SUE application, two photographs, the work’s file, the sale documents

steps.n: Works brought into Italy: ask for the certificazione di ingresso (CAI/CAS)
steps.do: On entry, ask the Ufficio Esportazione for the certificazione di ingresso (certificato di avvenuta importazione / spedizione): Law no. 40/2026 removed any limit of value, age or author status, and Constitutional Court judgment no. 51/2026 declared art. 72(1) of the Codice unconstitutional in so far as it denied the certification to the goods of art. 65(4)(a) and (b). The certification works as a temporary shield tied to re-export: the work leaves again ‘a scarico’, with an identity check only, without a discretionary assessment of cultural interest. The certification can be extended on request.
steps.who: Ufficio Esportazione
steps.time: offices instructed to receive and process CAI/CAS requests without limits of value, age or author (circular of 24 April 2026, immediate effect)
steps.doc: the import documents, photographs, the foreign export licence or invoice
src: Ministero della Cultura, DGABAP circolare 24 aprile 2026

steps.n: Compulsory purchase (acquisto coattivo): where it can still bite
steps.do: The Court held the questions on the acquisto coattivo (arts 70, 68 and 65(3)(a)) unfounded: subordinating the purchase power to a value threshold is not unreasonable. The circular instructs offices that the power is exercisable only in the cases provided by primary law and not in declaratory or simplified procedures; arts 6(4) and 7(5) of DM 246/2018 are disapplied where incompatible. Problems in SUE handling are to be reported to the Direzione Generale.
steps.who: Ministero della Cultura
steps.doc: n/a
src: Ministero della Cultura, DGABAP circolare 24 aprile 2026

pitfalls: A refusal of the attestato starts the notification (vincolo) procedure; the work may become unexportable.
The six-month self-annulment window (Law 182/2025) still allows the office to revoke an attestato after issue; do not ship on the day of issue if the file is thin.
The €50,000 threshold is new (Law 40/2026); forms and portal screens may still show €13,500 — the circular asks offices to apply the new rule uniformly and report SUE problems.
The attestato lapses after five years.
playbooks.cost: No fee is stated on the official page opened; stamp duty and shipper’s handling apply (vf U)
playbooks.time: autocertificazione at filing; attestato: the office’s statutory period plus physical presentation (period not confirmed here); five-year validity
links: DGABAP circular of 24 April 2026 on judgment 51/2026
src: Ministero della Cultura, DGABAP circolare 24 aprile 2026

playbooks.n: Moving a work in or out of Switzerland under the Cultural Property Transfer Act: the detailed customs declaration (revised 1 January 2026), the registers, the bilateral agreements
playbooks.for: shipper, dealer, auction house, collector, free-port tenant

steps.n: Declare cultural property ‘as such and in detail’ at customs
steps.do: Under the CPTA (KGTG) cultural property must be declared as such and in detail. The revised Cultural Property Transfer Ordinance (CPTO, SR 444.11; revision AS 2025 634, in force 1 January 2026) requires the typology of the cultural property, information as accurate as possible on the place of manufacture (for archaeological finds, the place of discovery), and now also the dating and the dimensions. Cultural property is an object in a category of Article 1 of the 1970 UNESCO Convention that is significant for archaeology, prehistory, literature, art or science (CPTA art. 2(1)). Travellers importing or exporting cultural property declare it electronically at a customs office competent for merchandise.
steps.who: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (FOCBS/BAZG); the Federal Office of Culture’s Specialised Body for the International Transfer of Cultural Property (kgt@bak.admin.ch)
steps.fee: none for the declaration; import VAT on release (8.1% standard rate from memory — vf U)
steps.doc: description with typology, place of manufacture or discovery, dating, dimensions; invoice; photographs
src: Federal Office of Culture, ‘Import, transit and export of cultural property’ (CPTO revision in force 1 January 2026)
FOCBS, ‘Transfer of cultural property: legal requirements’

steps.n: Imports from a bilateral-agreement state need the origin state’s export permit
steps.do: Switzerland has bilateral agreements on archaeological cultural property; as of January 2015 with Egypt, China, Greece, Italy, Colombia and Cyprus (further agreements since are not on the page — vf U). For imports from these states an official export permit of the country of origin must be presented to Swiss customs. The import of stolen and pillaged cultural property is prohibited; archaeological items may be subject to export bans or authorisation requirements in many states.
steps.who: FOCBS at the border
steps.doc: the origin state’s export permit
src: FOCBS, ‘Transfer of cultural property: legal requirements’

steps.n: Storage in a customs warehouse or free port counts as an import
steps.do: Storing cultural property in a customs warehouse ‘is considered an import in the terms of the CPTA’ and requires a written declaration to the customs authorities (art. 19 KGTG, art. 26 CPTO). The EU’s Regulation (EU) 2019/880 applies to the onward introduction of cultural property from Switzerland into the EU.
steps.who: FOCBS; the free-port operator
steps.doc: the written CPTA declaration with the inventory entry
src: Federal Office of Culture, ‘Import, transit and export of cultural property’

steps.n: Exporting an object listed in the Federal Register or a cantonal register
steps.do: Objects in the Federal Register of cultural property owned by the Confederation, and objects in cantonal registers where the canton so provides, may be exported only with a permit from the Federal Office of Culture (temporary export for exhibitions, research or restoration). Objects not listed leave without a Swiss export permit; only the customs declaration applies. (vf U: the permit rule is carried from the CPTA text from memory; the BAK page on the registers was not opened.)
steps.who: Federal Office of Culture (federal register); the cantons
steps.doc: the register entry, the loan agreement
src: Federal Office of Culture, ‘Import, transit and export of cultural property’

pitfalls: Since 1 January 2026 the customs declaration must carry the dating and dimensions as well as typology and place of manufacture; a shipper’s generic ‘painting’ line is non-compliant.
Putting a work into a Swiss free port is an import under the CPTA and needs the written declaration; the free port is not outside the Act.
Archaeological objects from a bilateral-agreement state are refused entry without the origin state’s export permit.
Art-trade due-diligence duties under CPTA art. 16 (identity of the seller, written declaration of entitlement, 30-year records) are from memory and not confirmed on the pages opened (vf U).
playbooks.cost: No fee for the declaration; import VAT on release into Switzerland (rate not confirmed here)
playbooks.time: at the border; register-object permits take longer (not confirmed)
links: Federal Office of Culture, import, transit and export of cultural property

playbooks.n: Exporting a work from India: the ASI non-antiquity certificate and the Navratna permit
playbooks.for: dealer, auction house, collector, shipper, licensed antiques dealer

steps.n: Check the object against the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972
steps.do: An antiquity includes coins, sculptures, paintings and works of art or craftsmanship at least 100 years old (manuscripts 75 years — from memory, vf U); export of antiquities is reserved to the central government. Works of nine ‘Navratna’ artists declared art treasures by notifications of 1976 and 1979 (Rabindranath Tagore, Amrita Sher-Gil, Jamini Roy, Nandalal Bose, Raja Ravi Varma, Gaganendranath Tagore, Abanindranath Tagore, Sailoz Mookherjea and Nicholas Roerich) need a specific permit from the Director General of the ASI to leave India. The Act regulates, and does not prohibit, dealing in antiquities and art treasures; the Rules of 1973 set the procedure.
steps.who: Archaeological Survey of India
steps.doc: the object’s date and authorship
src: Chambers Global Practice Guide, Art and Cultural Property Law 2026, India chapter (Khaitan & Co)

steps.n: Apply for the certificate of non-antiquity
steps.do: File the ‘Application form for the issue of certificate of non-antiquity for the export of art objects, arms’ in duplicate for each category of object with the Superintending Archaeologist of the ASI circle (Chennai Circle: Fort St George, Chennai 600009; other circles have their own committees), giving the applicant, handling agent, owner and consignee details, the dealer licence number if licensed, the port of embarkation (air, sea or post office), each object’s name, material, size in cm and number, 8 × 6 inch photographs, whether the object is registered under the Act, any previous committee review, and a consolidated statement of size, material, sale price and source. The Experts’ Advisory Committee on the Export of Non-antiquities examines the objects and issues the certificate, valid 180 days from issue.
steps.who: Superintending Archaeologist, ASI circle; the Experts’ Advisory Committee
steps.time: committee sittings; the form states no processing time; certificate valid 180 days
steps.doc: the form in duplicate, photographs 8 × 6 inch, invoice, dealer licence
src: ASI Chennai Circle, application form for the certificate of non-antiquity

steps.n: Present the certificate to customs
steps.do: Customs releases the export against the non-antiquity certificate (and the DG ASI permit for a Navratna work). (vf U: customs practice from memory.)
steps.who: Indian Customs
steps.doc: the certificate, invoice, shipping bill

pitfalls: The certificate lapses 180 days after issue; a delayed shipment needs a new application.
Works by the nine Navratna artists cannot be exported on a non-antiquity certificate alone; the DG ASI permit is required and in practice rarely granted (practice from memory — vf U).
Each category of object needs its own application in duplicate.
playbooks.cost: No fee stated on the ASI form; the agent’s handling
playbooks.time: the next committee sitting; validity 180 days
links: ASI Chennai Circle, non-antiquity certificate application form
src: Chambers, Art and Cultural Property Law 2026, India

playbooks.n: Exporting a work from China: the fine-art export approval and the cultural-relics verification
playbooks.for: dealer, auction house, artist’s studio, shipper

steps.n: Separate fine art from cultural relics
steps.do: Fine art (paintings, sculpture, photographs and limited-edition reproductions signed by the artist; not mass-produced handicrafts and not cultural relics) is governed by the Provisions on the Management of the Import and Export of Fine Art (effective 1 August 2009). Cultural relics fall under the Law on the Protection of Cultural Relics (1982, amended 2013): their export is prohibited unless authorised with State Council approval and must undergo examination and verification by the authorities designated under the State Council. (The 1949/1911 cut-offs and the appraisal stations’ seals are from memory — vf U; the note opened does not give them.)
steps.who: Ministry of Culture and Tourism (fine art); National Cultural Heritage Administration and the provincial appraisal offices (relics)
steps.doc: the work’s date, the artist, photographs
src: Eiger Law, Tian Xu and Belinda Zhou, ‘Conditions and requirements for the export of art from China’ (March 2014)

steps.n: Fine art: obtain the provincial approval
steps.do: Apply to the culture bureau of the province where the export port is located (Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin and Chongqing apply to the municipal bureau); a response is due within 15 days of application. The bureau checks the 11 prohibited-content categories of the 2009 Provisions (including content that ‘deliberately tampers with history or severely distorts history’).
steps.who: the provincial or municipal culture bureau
steps.doc: application with images and description of each work, the exporter’s business licence

steps.n: Clear customs
steps.do: Customs releases the shipment against the approval; for relics the verification seal is required (U). Note the 2009 US–China Memorandum of Understanding restricting US imports of Chinese archaeological material through the Tang dynasty (to 907 AD), renewed since (renewals from memory — vf U).
steps.who: General Administration of Customs of China
steps.doc: the approval, invoice, export declaration

pitfalls: The only note opened dates from 2014; the Cultural Relics Protection Law was further amended in 2024 (from memory — vf U); confirm the current text before advising.
Content review can stop a contemporary work with political or historical subject matter.
Relics mis-declared as fine art are seized.
playbooks.cost: No fee stated; agent’s handling
playbooks.time: 15 days for the fine-art approval (2014 note); relics verification longer (unconfirmed)

playbooks.n: Exporting a cultural valuable from Russia: the Ministry of Culture permit, the expert conclusion, the EAEU frame
playbooks.for: collector, dealer, museum registrar, shipper

steps.n: Know the frame
steps.do: Export and import of cultural valuables to and from non-EAEU states is regulated by Federal Law 4804-1 of 1993 as amended by Federal Laws 435-FZ and 430-FZ (2017); movement between EAEU member states follows EAEU law (the EEC Board Decision No. 30 of 21 April 2015, section 2.20 of the unified list, from memory — vf U). The Ministry of Culture’s summary: individuals need a Ministry permit to export cultural valuables for personal use; a new category of ‘особо значимые’ (especially significant) valuables is banned from permanent export; lists of documents and grounds for refusal are fixed; an attestation of experts and a register of experts are introduced; expertise of imported items is optional at the applicant’s request; temporarily exported items from state or municipal museums and archives must be insured; a new state duty applies to passports for musical instruments.
steps.who: Министерство культуры Российской Федерации (Ministry of Culture); attested experts
steps.fee: state duty under a ‘new procedure and amount’ (figures not on the page — vf U)
steps.doc: the expert conclusion, photographs, proof of ownership, the application
src: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation, information on the import and export of cultural valuables (ConsultantPlus copy)

steps.n: Obtain the expert conclusion and the permit
steps.do: An attested expert examines the object and issues the заключение (conclusion) on whether it is a cultural valuable and whether it may leave; the Ministry (or its territorial body) issues the permit (разрешение) for permanent or temporary export; customs releases against it. Age thresholds and the duty rate are not confirmed on the page opened (vf U).
steps.who: Ministry of Culture; Federal Customs Service
steps.doc: expert conclusion, permit, customs declaration
src: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation (ConsultantPlus copy)

pitfalls: Sanctions and counter-sanctions since 2022 affect payments, insurance and carriers for any movement to or from Russia (not covered by the page opened — vf U).
An ‘especially significant’ valuable cannot leave permanently at all.
The thresholds, duty rates and processing times could not be confirmed in this session; treat this playbook as a frame only.
playbooks.cost: state duty on the permit (amount not confirmed)
playbooks.time: not confirmed
src: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation (ConsultantPlus copy)

playbooks.n: Importing a cultural good into the EU: the ICG licence or importer statement (since 28 June 2025)
playbooks.for: importer of record, customs broker, dealer, auction house, collector’s shipper

steps.n: Classify the object under the Annex of Regulation (EU) 2019/880
steps.do: Three parts. Part A: cultural goods illicitly removed from the country where they were created or discovered may not be introduced at all. Part B (import licence): archaeological objects and parts of monuments that have been dismembered, over 250 years old, whatever the value. Part C (importer statement): the less-at-risk categories (rare collections and specimens, property of historical interest, antiquities, ethnological objects and the other listed categories) over 200 years old and with a customs value above €18,000. Below those ages and values no ICG document is needed; the ordinary customs declaration stands.
steps.who: the importer (self-classification); the member state’s competent cultural authority checks
steps.doc: description, photographs, date and country of creation or discovery, the customs value
src: European Commission, Access2Markets, ‘EU introduces new import controls of cultural goods’ (2025)

steps.n: Part B: apply for the import licence in the ICG system before import
steps.do: The licence must be obtained before the goods are released. Apply electronically in the ICG system (the centralised Import of Cultural Goods system hosted by the Commission and connected to the EU Single Window Environment for Customs, EU CSW-CERTEX; reached through the TRACES login), mandatory since 28 June 2025 for licence applications, importer statements and the exchange of information between national authorities. One licence per object. Attach a detailed description, photographs, the export documents and a legal-export declaration, with evidence that the object was lawfully exported from its country of origin or that no export law existed when it left (Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/1079 sets the substitute evidence). A licence issued by one member state is valid throughout the EU; it is not proof of legal provenance or ownership.
steps.who: the competent authority of the member state of import (for Germany: Kunstverwaltung des Bundes)
steps.time: up to 90 calendar days after receipt of the complete application; the authority may ask for more documents within 21 days of receipt; apply well before the planned import
steps.fee: none stated by the Commission or the German authority
steps.doc: export licence of the source country or the 2021/1079 substitute evidence, photographs, provenance
src: European Commission, Access2Markets, ‘EU introduces new import controls of cultural goods’ (2025)

steps.n: Part C: lodge the importer statement in the ICG system before import
steps.do: A self-certification: the importer declares that the goods were lawfully exported from the country of creation or discovery and attaches a standardised description. Lodge it in the ICG system; the customs declaration then references it.
steps.who: the importer, in the ICG system; customs checks the reference
steps.doc: the standardised description, photographs, the evidence of lawful export kept on file
src: European Commission, Access2Markets, ‘EU introduces new import controls of cultural goods’ (2025)

steps.n: Check the exemptions: fairs, returned goods, research
steps.do: Art fairs: goods can be brought in temporarily for exhibition under the importer-statement procedure; a licence is needed only if they stay in the EU, for example because they are sold; goods re-exported after the fair are exempt. Returned goods that left the EU only temporarily (a viewing in Switzerland, say) are exempt. Public institutions with the ‘exemption beneficiary’ role may import for education, science or research without licence or statement, filing only a general description in the ICG system, and only under temporary admission. Temporary admission otherwise counts as an ‘import’ under the Regulation.
steps.who: customs; the competent authority for the exemption-beneficiary role
steps.doc: the fair contract or loan agreement; the earlier export declaration for returned goods

pitfalls: The duty falls on the importer of record, usually the shipper or broker; a consignor who cannot document the lawful export from the source country cannot import a Part B object at all.

The ‘country of creation or discovery’ test, not the country of last ownership, governs the evidence: an antiquity bought legally in London still needs its source-country evidence or the 2021/1079 substitute.
Temporary admission for a fair or an auction view is an import under the Regulation; plan the ICG filing before the truck leaves.
