playbooks.cost: No ICG fee is stated by the Commission; the cost is the broker’s filing and the provenance research.
playbooks.time: Importer statement: at filing. Import licence: up to 90 calendar days after a complete application (Kunstverwaltung des Bundes).
links: European Commission, Access2Markets news page on the new import controls
Kunstverwaltung des Bundes, import licences (ICG via TRACES)
src: European Commission, Access2Markets, ‘EU introduces new import controls of cultural goods’ (2025)

playbooks.n: Importing a work into the UK: the 5% effective import VAT, the CDS entry, the dealer’s margin-scheme option
playbooks.for: importer of record, customs agent, dealer, auction house, collector’s shipper

steps.n: Declare the import on CDS through a customs agent at the reduced VAT valuation
steps.do: For works of art, antiques and collectors’ items the value for VAT purposes only is 25% of the customs value; VAT is then charged as normal at the standard rate. HMRC’s own example: customs value £10,000 → value for VAT £2,500 → VAT at 20% £500, i.e. 5% of the customs value. The agent enters the reduced valuation on the Customs Declaration Service entry. The import must be into Great Britain from outside the UK, or into Northern Ireland from outside the EU and the UK.
steps.who: HMRC, via the customs agent lodging the CDS declaration
steps.fee: VAT at 20% on 25% of the customs value (= 5% effective), HMRC guidance updated 2 November 2026; the agent’s entry fee is commercial
steps.doc: the commercial invoice or valuation, the shipper’s airway bill or CMR, the description establishing the goods as works of art, antiques or collectors’ items
src: HMRC, ‘Import works of art, antiques and collectors’ items using the VAT margin or global accounting scheme’ (updated 2 November 2026)

steps.n: Dealer: opt to sell the imported goods under the margin scheme
steps.do: Tell HMRC in writing before starting, stating the start date; use the option for at least two years and for all such imported goods, not a selection; tell HMRC in writing on stopping. Input tax on the goods cannot be recovered until the VAT period in which the sale or export is accounted for; goods may be sold outside the scheme (for example when exported). All margin-scheme purchases and sales go on the VAT return.
steps.who: HMRC
steps.time: written notice before the first use; minimum two years in the scheme
steps.doc: the written notice to HMRC, the stock book, the import entries
src: HMRC, ‘Import works of art, antiques and collectors’ items using the VAT margin or global accounting scheme’ (updated 2 November 2026)

steps.n: Temporary Admission for an auction view or a fair
steps.do: Goods entered under Temporary Admission are released to free circulation only on sale; VAT is accounted for at release, with the reduced valuation applied. The customs agent lodges the TA entry and the later release.
steps.who: HMRC, via the customs agent
steps.fee: VAT at release on the reduced valuation; agent fees commercial
steps.doc: the TA authorisation, the sale invoice at release
src: HMRC, ‘Import works of art, antiques and collectors’ items using the VAT margin or global accounting scheme’ (updated 2 November 2026)

pitfalls: The reduced valuation applies only to goods that meet the legal definitions of works of art, antiques (over 100 years) and collectors’ items; a design object or a frame declared under the wrong heading pays full VAT (the definitions sit on HMRC’s separate valuation page, not opened here).
A dealer who opts in is bound for two years and for all such goods.
HMRC says the margin-calculation section of its guidance is ‘currently under review’ (November 2026); check it before filing a return.
playbooks.cost: 5% of the customs value in VAT; customs duty on original works of art is nil under Chapter 97 (vf U: not on the page opened); agent’s entry fee commercial
playbooks.time: at entry; a release from Temporary Admission on sale
src: HMRC, ‘Import works of art, antiques and collectors’ items using the VAT margin or global accounting scheme’ (updated 2 November 2026)

playbooks.n: Importing a work into the United States: the CBP entry, Chapter 97, the 2026 tariff position, the Fish and Wildlife declaration
playbooks.for: importer of record, customs broker, auction house, dealer, collector’s shipper

steps.n: Enter the work through a licensed customs broker under HTS Chapter 97
steps.do: The broker files the CBP entry (ACE) classifying the work under heading 9701 (paintings, drawings, pastels executed by hand), 9702 (original prints), 9703 (original sculpture) or 9706 (antiques over 100 years). The general duty rate for these headings is free (vf U: from memory, the HTS page was not opened in this session). Attach the commercial invoice, the artist’s name and date, and the country of origin.
steps.who: US Customs and Border Protection
steps.fee: no duty on Chapter 97 originals (vf U); merchandise processing fee and broker’s fee commercial
steps.doc: commercial invoice, airway bill, packing list, provenance letter, power of attorney for the broker
src: The Art Newspaper, ‘New Trump tariffs largely exempt art, antiques’ (28 July 2026)

steps.n: Apply the 2026 tariff position
steps.do: The IEEPA tariffs were held unlawful by the Supreme Court in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (20 February 2026, 6–3) and terminated by proclamation; CBP stopped collecting them for entries after 12:00 a.m. ET on 24 February 2026. A Section 122 tariff of 10% on all countries ran from 12:01 a.m. on 24 February 2026 for 150 days, to 24 July 2026, with ‘informational materials, such as publications, films, and artworks’ among the exemptions. On 28 July 2026 The Art Newspaper reported new Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on imports from around 80 countries, with works of art, antiques and collectors’ items ‘largely declared exempt’ in a USTR fact sheet of 23 July 2026; separately, 50% tariffs on Canadian imports announced on 20 July 2026 do apply to art, antiques, antiquities, stamps, coins and most collectibles. Check the current HTS Chapter 99 notes with the broker on the day of entry.
steps.who: USTR; CBP
steps.fee: nil on exempt art; 50% on Canadian-origin art (as reported 28 July 2026)
steps.doc: country-of-origin evidence for the work
src: Covington & Burling, ‘IEEPA tariffs terminated; replacement Section 122 tariffs take effect’ (27 February 2026)

steps.n: Claim back IEEPA duties paid on art in 2025–26
steps.do: The Court declared the IEEPA tariffs invalid ab initio but did not address remedies; Covington advises importers to track liquidation dates, post-summary-correction deadlines and protest deadlines, and reports that CBP may require a court order before refunding. File protests on liquidated entries and consider suit.
steps.who: CBP; the US courts
steps.time: protest deadlines run from liquidation (180 days under the statute — vf U)
steps.doc: entry summaries (CBP Form 7501), proof of duty paid

steps.n: Wildlife materials (ivory, tortoiseshell, coral, feathers): file FWS Form 3-177
steps.do: File the Declaration for Importation or Exportation of Fish or Wildlife (USFWS Form 3-177, Rev. 12/2017, continuation sheet 3-177a) with the wildlife inspection office, CBP office or regional law-enforcement office at a designated port, preferably through eDecs (edecs.fws.gov); paper filers submit the original plus up to two copies. Enter the foreign CITES permit number (box 17a) and the US CITES permit number (17b), the purpose code (P personal, T commercial) and attach a copy of a Designated Port Exception Permit where applicable. Failure to file when required is a violation of the Endangered Species Act (50 CFR Part 14).
steps.who: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Office of Law Enforcement
steps.fee: the inspection and licence fees are not on the form page opened (vf U)
steps.doc: Form 3-177, the CITES export permit of the origin country, the invoice, the antique-exemption evidence for ESA antiques
src: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Form 3-177 and 3-177a with instructions (updated 2022)

pitfalls: A frame, a design object or a work of applied art falls outside Chapter 97 and may carry duty and the current ad valorem tariffs.
Canadian-origin art is reported to carry a 50% tariff since July 2026 (The Art Newspaper); verify the HTS Chapter 99 note before shipping from Canada.
Shipments with ivory, tortoiseshell or rosewood without a CITES permit and a 3-177 are seized at the port.
The tariff position has changed three times since February 2026; a quote given to a client a month ago may be wrong.
playbooks.cost: Duty nil on original works (U); broker’s entry fee commercial; Fish and Wildlife fees where applicable
playbooks.time: same day to a few days at the port; wildlife inspections add days
src: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Form 3-177

playbooks.n: Importing a work into Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, Korea or China: the tax at the border
playbooks.for: importer, customs broker, auction house, dealer

steps.n: Hong Kong: no import duty
steps.do: Hong Kong is a free port and generally imposes no import duty on art; there is no VAT. The import is declared to Hong Kong Customs through the shipper (the import declaration within 14 days of import is from memory — vf U).
steps.who: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department
steps.doc: invoice, airway bill
src: Barnebys Magazine, ‘What art buyers need to know about VAT in 2025’ (25 July 2025)

steps.n: Singapore: 9% GST
steps.do: GST at 9% is charged on import on the CIF value; no customs duty on art. Works entering a licensed warehouse or the Le Freeport facility are GST-suspended until release (suspension detail from memory — vf U).
steps.who: Singapore Customs (GST collected on behalf of IRAS)
steps.doc: invoice, permit via TradeNet lodged by the forwarder

steps.n: Japan: 10% consumption tax
steps.do: Consumption tax of 10% on import; original works of art are duty-free under Chapter 97 (duty-free status from memory — vf U).
steps.who: Japan Customs
steps.doc: invoice, import declaration by the broker

steps.n: South Korea: 10% VAT
steps.do: VAT at 10% on import; works by living artists and certain original art are exempt under the VAT Act (exemption from memory — vf U); no customs duty on Chapter 97 originals (U).
steps.who: Korea Customs Service
steps.doc: invoice, import declaration

steps.n: China: 13% VAT plus duty
steps.do: Import VAT at the general rate of 13%; a customs duty applies on top (the current MFN rate for 9701 is not on the page opened — vf U); works by living artists imported for sale need the Ministry of Culture import approval for fine art (Provisions of 2009, effective 1 August 2009), with the provincial bureau responding within 15 days (Eiger Law note, 2014). Bonded zones (Shanghai West Bund, Beijing) defer the tax until sale (from memory — vf U).
steps.who: General Administration of Customs of China; the provincial culture bureau for the import approval
steps.time: 15 days for the fine-art import/export approval (2014 note)
steps.fee: 13% VAT plus duty (Barnebys, July 2025; duty rate unconfirmed)
steps.doc: invoice, the import approval, photographs and content description for the approval
src: Eiger Law, ‘Conditions and requirements for the export of art from China’ (March 2014)

steps.n: The Gulf and India
steps.do: UAE: 5% VAT and 5% customs duty on import, with the Dubai free zones deferring both (from memory — vf U; not covered by the pages opened). India: basic customs duty plus IGST on works of art (rates not confirmed — vf U).
steps.who: UAE Federal Tax Authority and Customs; Indian Customs
steps.doc: invoice, import declaration
src: Barnebys Magazine, 25 July 2025 (does not cover the UAE or India)

pitfalls: The rates above are a trade-press table (July 2025); each is to be confirmed with the national customs tariff before quoting a landed cost.
China’s fine-art import approval is a content review (11 prohibited categories under the 2009 Provisions); a work with sensitive subject matter can be refused.
Singapore and Hong Kong freeport or bonded storage defers tax only while the work stays in the facility; a sale to a local buyer triggers it.
playbooks.cost: Hong Kong nil; Singapore 9% GST; Japan 10%; Korea 10%; China 13% VAT plus duty (Barnebys, July 2025; vf S)
playbooks.time: at entry; China’s approval 15 days
src: Barnebys Magazine, ‘What art buyers need to know about VAT in 2025’ (25 July 2025)

playbooks.n: Importing a work into the EU: the reduced import VAT by member state after the 2025 reform
playbooks.for: importer, customs broker, dealer, auction house, collector

steps.n: Pick the member state of import by its reduced rate
steps.do: Import VAT on works of art, antiques and collectors’ items (Barnebys, July 2025): France 5.5%; Germany 7% (reinstated, no effective date given on the page); Italy 5% from 1 July 2025 (down from 22%, applying to import VAT too, reported as pending parliamentary ratification); the Netherlands 9%; Belgium 6%; Austria 13%; Sweden 12% on sale and import; Denmark 25% standard with a 5% ‘artist VAT’ on first sales by the artist or heirs above DKK 300,000 a year. Customs duty on original works under Chapter 97 is nil (from memory — vf U).
steps.who: the member state’s customs on the import declaration
steps.fee: the reduced rate on the customs value
steps.doc: invoice, the description establishing the work as an original under the VAT directive’s annex
src: Barnebys Magazine, ‘What art buyers need to know about VAT in 2025’ (25 July 2025)

steps.n: Mind the margin-scheme change of 1 January 2025
steps.do: Since 1 January 2025, under Directive (EU) 2022/542, VAT is charged on the full hammer price where the seller acquired the work at a reduced VAT rate, instead of on the margin; VAT on the buyer’s premium is generally not refundable on export. A dealer who imports at the reduced rate cannot then resell under the margin scheme.
steps.who: the member state’s tax authority
steps.fee: VAT on the full price on resale
steps.doc: the import VAT receipt kept with the stock record

steps.n: File the ICG document where the object is old enough
steps.do: For objects over 200 years and €18,000 (importer statement) or archaeological objects over 250 years (licence) the ICG filing precedes the customs declaration — see the ‘import-eu-icg’ playbook.
steps.who: the competent cultural authority; customs
steps.doc: the ICG reference

pitfalls: Italy’s 5% rate was reported as pending ratification in July 2025; confirm its status before relying on it.
Importing at a reduced rate and reselling under the margin scheme is no longer possible since 1 January 2025.
VAT paid on the buyer’s premium is generally not recoverable on export.
playbooks.cost: 5%–13% of the customs value depending on the member state (Barnebys, July 2025)
playbooks.time: at entry

playbooks.n: Moving a work into a Swiss free port (Geneva, Zurich): the inventory with the owner’s name, the six-month limit for export goods
playbooks.for: collector, dealer, shipper, freeport operator’s client

steps.n: Understand the 2016 rule
steps.do: Since the amendment of the Swiss Customs Act in force on 1 January 2016, managers of bonded warehouses and free ports must register the goods and their owners in an inventory record, and goods intended for export may be stored for up to six months, extendable by the Federal Customs Administration on proper grounds. (Artnet reported the change; the operators’ own onboarding pages were not opened — the identity, insurance, condition-report and storage-contract steps below are carried from trade practice and flagged U.)
steps.who: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security (formerly Federal Customs Administration); the free-port operator
steps.doc: proof of ownership and identity of the owner for the inventory

steps.n: Onboard with the operator
steps.do: The tenant signs a storage contract with the operator or with a tenant logistics company (the Geneva free port leases space; the art-handling firms within it hold the goods); provides identity and beneficial-ownership documents for the inventory; lodges an inventory declaration with the customs value and description; and delivers a condition report and an insurance certificate naming the location. (vf U: operator pages not opened.)
steps.who: the free-port operator / the logistics tenant; customs for the inventory
steps.fee: storage rent and handling as quoted (U)
steps.doc: ID, company documents, invoice or valuation, condition report, insurance certificate

steps.n: Keep the customs status straight
steps.do: Goods in the free port remain outside Swiss VAT and duty until released; goods declared as intended for export must leave within six months unless customs extends the period. Release into Switzerland triggers import VAT (8.1% standard rate since 1 January 2024 — vf U, not on a page opened).
steps.who: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security
steps.doc: the inventory entry, the export declaration on exit

steps.n: File the CPTA written declaration on entry to the warehouse
steps.do: The Federal Office of Culture states that storing cultural property in a customs warehouse ‘is considered an import in the terms of the CPTA’ and requires a written declaration to the customs authorities (art. 19 KGTG, art. 26 CPTO). Since 1 January 2026 the revised ordinance (AS 2025 634) requires the declaration to give the typology, the place of manufacture or discovery, the dating and the dimensions of the object.
steps.who: Federal Office for Customs and Border Security; Federal Office of Culture (Specialised Body)
steps.doc: the CPTA declaration with typology, origin, dating and dimensions
src: Federal Office of Culture, ‘Import, transit and export of cultural property’ (2026)

pitfalls: The inventory names the owner; an undisclosed principal behind a logistics company is not an option since 2016.
Export goods left beyond six months without an extension lose their status and face customs action.
Insurance for free-port storage is a separate location on the policy schedule; an unlisted location is uninsured.
playbooks.cost: Rent and handling as quoted by the operator (not opened); no customs fee at entry
playbooks.time: days to onboard; six-month limit for export goods
links: Artnet News on the 2016 Swiss free-port rules

playbooks.n: Choosing a free port outside Switzerland: Delaware (and its foreign-trade zone), Luxembourg, Singapore, UK bonded warehouses
playbooks.for: collector, dealer, shipper, adviser

steps.n: Delaware Freeport and its foreign-trade zone
steps.do: Run by Fritz Dietl; shipments can be held duty-free in the adjoining FTZ before customs clearance, which matters while US tariffs apply to design, furniture and some antiques (an extra 10%), to items with steel or aluminium (10% or 25%) and to Chinese antiques (7.5%) and furniture (25%) as reported in June 2025. A free port must sit in a state without sales or use tax (Oregon, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, Alaska) to avoid triggering use tax on delivery. Onboarding (identity, inventory, insurance certificate, condition report, storage contract) follows the operator’s own terms, not opened here (vf U).
steps.who: Delaware Freeport (operator); US Customs and Border Protection for the FTZ admission
steps.fee: rates not published on the page opened
steps.doc: ID and company documents, invoice, insurance certificate, condition report
src: The Art Newspaper, Anna Brady, ‘Anxious collectors are increasingly turning to freeport havens, experts say’ (19 June 2025)

steps.n: Luxembourg, Singapore and UK bonded warehouses
steps.do: Named by Convelio’s Edouard Gouin as the non-EU options (Luxembourg’s facility is inside the EU customs territory but operates as a free zone — from memory, vf U) alongside UK bonded warehouses; duties and VAT are deferred while the work stays in the zone. Gouin expects non-EU free ports to face ‘increased regulatory scrutiny’, and Katalin Andreides cites growing disclosure requirements about who owns what. Since 28 June 2025 Regulation (EU) 2019/880 requires proof of lawful export from the country of origin for cultural goods entering the EU, which pushes some sellers to ‘friendlier jurisdictions’.
steps.who: the operators (Le Freeport Luxembourg; Le Freeport Singapore — names from memory, vf U); the national customs for the free-zone status
steps.fee: not published on the page opened
steps.doc: as above; for the EU, the ICG evidence on later release

steps.n: Geneva
steps.do: Natural Le Coultre manages a large part of the Geneva Freeport; its director reports a significant increase in clients over the past three years (June 2025), with collectors moving art there since the war in Ukraine began; Zurich, Basel and Chiasso are the other Swiss locations. See the Swiss free-port playbook for the 2016 inventory rule and the 2026 CPTA declaration.
steps.who: Ports Francs et Entrepôts de Genève; the tenant logistics firms
steps.doc: see freeport-switzerland

pitfalls: A US free port in a sales-tax state triggers use tax on delivery; the five no-tax states are the only safe locations (The Art Newspaper, 2025).
One client’s design furniture cost US$200,000 in import duties when cleared (Dietl, 2025); the free port defers, it does not cancel.
The EU import regulation makes later release into the EU harder for goods without source-country export evidence.
playbooks.cost: Operators’ rates not published on the page opened
playbooks.time: n/a
links: The Art Newspaper on free ports (June 2025)

playbooks.n: Borrowing against a work from Sotheby’s Financial Services: equity loan, consignor advance, acquisition finance
playbooks.for: collector, family office, dealer, estate

steps.n: Choose the product
steps.do: Sotheby’s Financial Services offers three products: the Equity Loan (a 12- to 36-month loan unlocking part of the equity in a collection while the client continues to own it), the Consignor Advance (an advance against property consigned for sale) and Acquisition Financing. Loans run from US$1 million up to US$250 million across 70+ collateral categories (fine art, automobiles, whisky, wine, jewellery).
steps.who: Sotheby’s Financial Services (in California: Sotheby’s Financial Services California, Inc., licensed California Finance Lender 6030237)
steps.fee: rates, terms and programmes ‘subject to change without notice’; no rate published
steps.doc: a list of the collateral with provenance and prior valuations

steps.n: Valuation and diligence
steps.do: Sotheby’s specialists value the collateral; a diligence and compliance review is conducted (identity, source of funds, title). The page says no personal financial disclosure or covenants are required. Loan-to-value is not published: the illustrative case study shows a US$25m loan against a US$50m work (the page presents it as an example, not a policy).
steps.who: Sotheby’s specialist departments and compliance
steps.doc: invoices and provenance, condition reports, insurance schedule, ID and beneficial-ownership documents

steps.n: Possession and perfection of the security
steps.do: The client may keep the collection on display with ‘an option for in-residence collateral in certain locations’; otherwise the collateral is held in Sotheby’s custody. The lender perfects its interest by filing (in the US, a UCC-1 financing statement against the borrower — vf U, not on the page opened). Loans ‘may not be available in all locations’.
steps.who: Sotheby’s Financial Services; the state filing office for the UCC-1
steps.doc: the loan agreement, the security agreement, the insurance endorsement naming the lender as loss payee

steps.n: Closing
steps.do: Sotheby’s aims to close loans within six weeks of the initial consultation, depending on the collateral, its location and other factors; tenor between 12 and 36 months.
steps.who: Sotheby’s Financial Services
steps.time: about six weeks to close; 12–36-month tenor
steps.fee: origination and interest as agreed (not published)
steps.doc: executed loan documents

pitfalls: In-residence collateral is offered only in certain locations; elsewhere the works move to the lender’s storage.
The loan-to-value, rate and fees are not published; the example of 50% (US$25m on US$50m) is illustrative.
A consignor advance ties the works to a Sotheby’s sale; withdrawing them triggers the repayment and the sale’s withdrawal terms.
playbooks.cost: Interest and fees as agreed; no public rate (Sotheby’s 2026). Trade-press ranges for art-secured lending are not cited here because no such page was opened in this session.
playbooks.time: about six weeks from consultation to closing; tenor 12–36 months

playbooks.n: Borrowing against a work from the banks and specialist lenders: what the market charges
playbooks.for: collector, family office, dealer, adviser

steps.n: Expect about 50% loan-to-value
steps.do: The Art Newspaper (8 March 2023) reports that all the firms lend around 50% of the appraised value, some with in-house appraisers and some external. Sotheby’s Financial Services offered buyers an immediate loan of 50% of the hammer price on purchases over US$2m at its auctions, ‘from application to funding in 30 days’ (2023; its 2026 page says six weeks to close). Athena Art Finance (owned by Yieldstreet) had funded over US$500m. Bank of America’s art credit business grows about 10% a year (Deborah Larrison). The Fine Art Group (Freya Stewart) lends where banks have less appetite. Minimums at the main lenders are typically US$1m–US$2m.
steps.who: Sotheby’s Financial Services; Athena Art Finance; Bank of America; The Fine Art Group; (Christie’s, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, Citi and Gurr Johns were not covered by the page opened — vf U)
steps.time: 30 days to six weeks to fund
steps.fee: rates not published; ‘much lower’ than pawn-style lenders
steps.doc: appraisal, provenance and title documents, insurance schedule
src: The Art Newspaper, Georgina Adam, ‘The rise of art-backed loans is spectacular—here’s how they work’ (8 March 2023)

steps.n: Pawn-style lending for small sums
steps.do: Borro offers short-term non-recourse loans on one or more works and other assets from about US$10,000: ‘the larger the loan the lower the rate. On average, you are looking at 3% to 4% per month.’
steps.who: Borro
steps.doc: the work itself (possession taken), ID

steps.n: Perfect the lien
steps.do: US lending dominates because the Uniform Commercial Code records liens: the lender files a UCC-1 financing statement against the borrower in the state of the borrower’s location, which lets the borrower keep possession (the mechanics are from memory — vf U; the article cites the UCC as the reason the US market is larger). The sector was worth US$24bn–US$28.2bn in 2021.
steps.who: the lender; the Secretary of State filing office
steps.doc: security agreement, UCC-1, insurance endorsement

pitfalls: Non-recourse is the exception; most loans are full recourse to the borrower.
A lender’s in-house appraisal is at the lender’s number; an independent appraisal strengthens the LTV negotiation.
Outside the US the lender usually takes possession because there is no UCC-style register.
playbooks.cost: About 50% LTV; rates unpublished at the main lenders; 3–4% a month at pawn-style lenders (2023)
playbooks.time: 30 days to six weeks
links: The Art Newspaper on art-backed loans (2023)

playbooks.n: Donating a work to a US museum: the qualified appraisal, Form 8283, the Art Advisory Panel, the Statement of Value
playbooks.for: donor, donor’s tax adviser, appraiser, museum registrar

steps.n: Obtain a qualified appraisal and complete Form 8283 Section B
steps.do: For an income-tax charitable contribution of art the appraisal must be a qualified appraisal by a qualified appraiser, and the appraisal summary (Section B of Form 8283) must be completed and signed by the appraiser and the donee. (The related-use rule, the 30% of AGI ceiling for appreciated property given to public charities and the fractional-gift rules are carried from memory — vf U; the IRS page opened covers the valuation machinery.)
steps.who: the donor; the qualified appraiser; the donee museum signs Form 8283
steps.time: appraisal dated no earlier than 60 days before the gift and before the return’s due date (vf U)
steps.doc: Form 8283 Section B, the qualified appraisal, photographs, the deed of gift and the museum’s acceptance
src: IRS Internal Revenue Manual, Art Appraisal Services (effective 14 May 2025; page reviewed 30 April 2026)

steps.n: Know the US$50,000 trigger
steps.do: For a single work of art with a claimed value of US$50,000 or more, IRS examiners must refer the valuation to Art Appraisal Services; Appeals refers any case with a single artwork valued over US$50,000. Items under US$50,000 get telephone assistance through the Specialist Referral System. The Commissioner’s Art Advisory Panel (nationally prominent museum directors, curators and dealers, serving without pay) meets twice a year for paintings and sculpture (spring and fall; referrals by 15 January and 15 June) and ad hoc for decorative arts; it gives oral recommendations and AAS makes the final value determination.
steps.who: IRS Art Appraisal Services; the Commissioner’s Art Advisory Panel
steps.time: the appraiser’s initial case analysis within 30 calendar days of receipt; referrals assigned within five business days
steps.doc: the return, Form 8283, the appraisal, photographs
src: IRS Internal Revenue Manual, Art Appraisal Services (effective 14 May 2025; page reviewed 30 April 2026)

steps.n: Optional: ask for a Statement of Value before filing (Rev. Proc. 96-15)
steps.do: For an item appraised at US$50,000 or more the donor may request an advance IRS review. Pay the user fee on Pay.gov (the amount is updated biannually; the US$7,500 for up to three items / US$400 per further item from memory — vf U), mail the written request to AAS in Washington DC with the qualified appraisal, the completed Form 8283 Section B, a professional-quality photograph (8 × 10 inch colour preferred) or a high-resolution digital image, and the Area Office with jurisdiction. Requests received 16 January–15 July are to be issued by 31 December; those received 16 July–15 January by 30 June. Missing information must be supplied within 30 calendar days of notice; the request can be withdrawn before issue; if the IRS declines to issue, the fee is refunded.
steps.who: IRS Art Appraisal Services, Washington DC
steps.time: up to about 11 months (issue by 31 December or 30 June)
steps.fee: user fee via Pay.gov (amount updated biannually)
steps.doc: written request, appraisal, Form 8283 Section B, photograph, proof of payment
src: IRS Internal Revenue Manual, Art Appraisal Services (effective 14 May 2025; page reviewed 30 April 2026)

pitfalls: A single work claimed at US$50,000 or more is always referred to Art Appraisal Services; a weak appraisal is challenged there.
The Panel issues no written report; the taxpayer sees only AAS’s determination.
A Statement of Value binds the IRS but takes up to a year; plan the gift and the filing calendar together.
The related-use rule (the museum must use the work in its exempt purpose) and the AGI ceilings are not covered by the page opened; confirm them with counsel.
playbooks.cost: The appraisal fee; the Statement of Value user fee (updated biannually); counsel
playbooks.time: the gift can close in weeks; the Statement of Value up to 11 months; the Panel sits spring and fall
links: IRS Internal Revenue Manual, Art Appraisal Services
src: IRS Internal Revenue Manual, Art Appraisal Services (effective 14 May 2025)

playbooks.n: Giving a work to the nation in the UK: the Cultural Gifts Scheme (and Acceptance in Lieu)
playbooks.for: donor, donor’s tax adviser, museum director, executor (AIL)

steps.n: Check eligibility and the tax reduction
steps.do: Individuals in a private capacity with a UK income-tax or capital-gains-tax liability, and companies with a corporation-tax liability, may offer a pre-eminent object; trusts, trustees and personal representatives may not. The reduction is 30% of the agreed value for income tax and CGT (spreadable over up to five tax years from the year of registration) and 20% for corporation tax (not spreadable). The CGS and Acceptance in Lieu share a £40 million annual limit. Hybrid offers are not allowed under CGS.
steps.who: Arts Council England (administers); the Acceptance in Lieu Panel advises; the Minister decides
steps.doc: a tax computation of the liability to be offset
src: DCMS, Cultural Gifts Scheme: scheme and guidance (6 December 2011; published 27 January 2015)

steps.n: Apply in writing to Arts Council England
steps.do: Send full object details and provenance, a valuation with supporting evidence, evidence of title, at least three colour photographs and a high-resolution jpeg, a current condition report, a statement of why the object is pre-eminent (national, scientific, historic or artistic interest, alone or as a collection, or association with a significant building), contact and inspection details, an Interim Tax Schedule, any preferred eligible institution and a signed declaration. Applications are taken first come, first served against the annual limit.
steps.who: Arts Council England, Acceptance in Lieu Panel
steps.time: registration normally within 30 days of a complete application
steps.doc: the application pack listed

steps.n: Valuation and acceptance
steps.do: The value is the fair market value fixed at the registration date, excluding costs of disposal, professional fees and tax; the Panel may seek its own advice and negotiate. The donor has 30 days to accept the letter of acceptance. Negotiations should conclude within two years of registration (the Panel reviews at that point) and the offer must be rejected after three years.
steps.who: Acceptance in Lieu Panel; the Minister
steps.time: up to two years; three-year hard stop
steps.doc: valuation evidence, the letter of acceptance

pitfalls: The £40m annual limit is shared with Acceptance in Lieu and is first come, first served; late-year offers can be deferred to the next year.
Trusts and personal representatives cannot use CGS; an estate uses Acceptance in Lieu instead (the AIL ‘douceur’ of 25% of the tax forgone is from memory — vf U, not in the document opened).
The guidance opened dates from 2011/2015; a 2024 consultation on reforming the scheme exists (gov.uk) but was not opened — check for changes before advising.
playbooks.cost: No fee; the donor bears the valuation and legal costs
playbooks.time: registration within 30 days; acceptance usually within months, up to two years

playbooks.n: Paying French inheritance, gift or wealth tax with a work of art: the dation en paiement
playbooks.for: heir, donee, IFI taxpayer, notaire, tax counsel, museum curator

steps.n: Check the tax and the object qualify
steps.do: Only droits de mutation à titre gratuit (succession, donation), the droit de partage and the impôt sur la fortune immobilière may be paid by dation (CGI art. 1716 bis), for taxes already due of at least €10,000 per tax. Eligible objects: œuvres d’art, livres, objets de collection or documents ‘de haute valeur artistique ou historique’ (also certain coastal or forest land). The offeror must be the full, direct owner at the offer date; goods held less than five years are inadmissible unless acquired by gift or inheritance; goods refused twice cannot be re-offered; the offer must be pure and simple (no soulte, no reserved enjoyment).
steps.who: the service des impôts that registers the act or receives the IFI return; the Bureau des agréments et rescrits (DGFiP) instructs
steps.doc: proof of ownership and of the acquisition date
src: BOFIP, BOI-SJ-AGR-50-20 (6 November 2018), dation en paiement

steps.n: File the offre de dation with the return
steps.do: Lodge the offer with the service des impôts that registers the act or declaration (or receives the IFI return), within the same deadline as that filing, in four copies with two photographs of each object and the documents proving acquisition; the DGFiP comptable issues a receipt. The DRFiP/DDFiP checks the file and the taxpayer’s compliance and forwards it to the Bureau des agréments et rescrits. The offer cannot be withdrawn within six months of filing (extendable by three months by reasoned decision).
steps.who: DGFiP
steps.time: with the tax return; six-month lock-in
steps.doc: the offer in four copies, two photographs per object, acquisition documents, the tax return

steps.n: The commission and the agrément
steps.do: The interministerial commission (a representative of the Prime Minister in the chair, two of the budget minister, two of the culture minister; arrêté of 6 April 1982) gives a consultative opinion on artistic or historic interest and on value (CGI ann. II art. 310 G); it may retain only some goods or propose substitutes or additions. The budget minister decides the agrément and sets the valeur libératoire, the maximum tax the goods can discharge. If the State retains a value different from the offer the taxpayer has 30 days from the registered letter to accept or withdraw; silence is withdrawal and the tax falls due. A value above the tax gives no soulte; below it, the taxpayer pays the difference. For objets d’art, no decision within two years of the receipt means refusal.
steps.who: Commission interministérielle d’agrément; the budget minister
steps.time: up to two years (deemed refusal after two years for objets d’art); 30 days to accept the value
steps.doc: the agrément decision, the written acceptance

steps.n: Interest and payment
steps.do: No interest or penalties run while the offer is pending; the tax becomes payable within 30 days of the end of the acceptance period, of a refusal, or of the two-year period. A taxpayer who renounces after the 30 days owes interest from the first day of the following month (CGI art. 1727); a withdrawal after the six-month lock-in but before notification of the agrément also carries interest.
steps.who: DGFiP
steps.doc: the payment or the delivery of the works

pitfalls: A work bought less than five years before the offer is inadmissible unless inherited or received as a gift.
The State can accept at a lower value; the heir then pays the balance in cash, so budget for the gap.
The offer is locked for six months; selling the work at auction meanwhile is not an option.
Silence after the value notice is a withdrawal, with the tax due within 30 days.
playbooks.cost: No fee; the work discharges tax at the valeur libératoire; interest only on late renunciation
playbooks.time: months to two years; deemed refusal at two years for objets d’art

playbooks.n: Shipping a work abroad temporarily on an ATA carnet (fair, exhibition, viewing) from the UK
playbooks.for: gallery, art fair exhibitor, shipper, registrar

steps.n: Decide whether the carnet fits
steps.do: An ATA carnet is a temporary-admission document, ‘a passport for goods’, for commercial samples, professional equipment and trade-fair and exhibition goods, including ‘works of art to be exhibited at galleries and museums’. It is accepted in over 100 destinations (the EU, Switzerland, the USA, Canada, China, Japan, Australia among them; Taiwan needs a separate CPD carnet). Paintings are described by type, title, artist and year. Controlled art and antiques still need the Arts Council export licence (FAQ 19).
steps.who: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry (issuing body)
steps.doc: the general list of goods with values, the Arts Council licence where the object is licensable
src: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry, ATA Carnet FAQs (2026)

steps.n: Apply and pay
steps.do: Apply online to the Chamber; standard applications are reviewed within 24 hours, express within 2 hours; carnets are released only after payment. Issuing fee: £215 + VAT (member), £355 + VAT (non-member); express service £215 + VAT on top. Security: the Carnet Security Scheme (a non-refundable one-off premium for 2, 6 or 12 months, priced on the countries visited, the duration and the goods), or a refundable banker’s draft or cash deposit, or a bank guarantee from a listed bank.
steps.who: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry
steps.time: 24 hours standard, 2 hours express, plus postage or collection
steps.fee: £215 + VAT (member) / £355 + VAT (non-member); express +£215 + VAT; security premium or deposit on top (LCCI, 2026)
steps.doc: the general list, the company details, the security arrangement
src: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry, ATA Carnet FAQs (2026)

steps.n: Travel and discharge
steps.do: The carnet is valid 12 months from issue but usable only for the period the security covers (2, 6 or 12 months). Have customs stamp the exportation and importation vouchers on each leg; re-export within the permitted time and return the carnet to the Chamber for discharge. Lost or stolen goods attract customs charges in most cases; goods not re-exported attract the destination’s duties and taxes and ‘large fines can be imposed over their value’.
steps.who: customs at each border; the Chamber at discharge
steps.fee: duties and taxes if not re-exported
steps.doc: the stamped carnet
src: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry, ATA Carnet FAQs (2026)

pitfalls: A sale at the fair breaks the carnet: the work must then be entered definitively in the destination and the carnet voucher adjusted; plan the alternative (temporary admission under local rules) with the shipper.
EU trips often need extra transit stamps; a missing stamp leaves the carnet undischarged and the security at risk.
The carnet does not replace the Arts Council licence for a licensable object.
playbooks.cost: £215–£355 + VAT issuing fee plus the security premium or deposit (LCCI, 2026)
playbooks.time: 24 hours (standard) or 2 hours (express) to issue; valid 12 months
src: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry, ATA Carnet FAQs (2026)

playbooks.n: Shipping a work with endangered-species material from the UK: the CITES permit and the Ivory Act certificate
playbooks.for: shipper, dealer, auction house, collector

steps.n: Apply for the CITES export or re-export permit
steps.do: Apply through the online ‘apply for a CITES permit’ service run by the Animal and Plant Health Agency, which has replaced the paper CITES forms; questions, replacement and retrospective permits go to wildlife.licensing@apha.gov.uk. APHA aims to process an application within 30 days. A travelling-exhibition certificate (for a specimen you do not own, with the owner’s written authorisation) is valid 3 years; a musical-instrument certificate carries no fee. The fee table is on a separate ‘CITES application fees’ page not opened here (vf U for amounts).
steps.who: Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), on behalf of Defra
steps.time: APHA aims for 30 days (page updated 23 June 2026)
steps.fee: see APHA fee page (not opened — vf U)
steps.doc: photographs, description with species, proof of age for pre-Convention/antique specimens, the importer’s details and the destination’s import permit where required
src: gov.uk, ‘Endangered species: application for import and export permit’ (updated 23 June 2026)

steps.n: Ivory: get the Ivory Act 2018 certificate or registration before dealing
steps.do: Dealing in ivory is banned unless an exemption applies. For a pre-1918 item of outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historical value (an exemption ‘designed to be narrow’) apply through the ivory service: application fee £250, non-refundable; APHA refers the application to an expert at one of the 12 prescribed institutions (the V&A and the Ashmolean among them; National Museums NI, National Museums Liverpool and the National Museum of Wales added 15 May 2025); the expert may inspect; assessments take approximately 3 months. Since 28 January 2025 the guidance covers ivory of elephant, hippopotamus, killer whale, narwhal and sperm whale. A £20 fee applies to notify APHA of the sale or hire of an item already certified to someone else; updating the owner’s details is free. The standard registrations (de minimis, pre-1975 musical instruments, portrait miniatures, museum sales) are on the separate dealing-in-ivory guidance (not opened — vf U).
steps.who: APHA for the Secretary of State; the prescribed institution’s expert
steps.fee: £250 application (non-refundable); £20 sale notification of a certified item
steps.doc: photographs, provenance and dating evidence, the expert’s assessment
src: gov.uk, ‘Ivory: apply for an exemption certificate to deal in pre-1918 outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historical value items’ (updated 15 May 2025)

steps.n: Pair the UK permit with the destination’s rules
steps.do: For the United States file FWS Form 3-177 at a designated port with the CITES permit numbers (see the US import playbook); for the EU the import permit of the member state is needed for Annex A specimens (from memory — vf U).
steps.who: the destination’s CITES management authority
steps.doc: the UK export permit, the destination import permit
src: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Form 3-177

pitfalls: An ivory item without a certificate or registration cannot be sold in the UK at all, whatever its age; the certificate takes about three months.
The APHA 30-day target runs from a complete application; missing species identification restarts it.
Tortoiseshell, rosewood (Dalbergia) and coral inlays in furniture and frames are CITES-listed; the shipper’s packing list must name them.
playbooks.cost: £250 for an Ivory Act certificate; CITES permit fees per the APHA table (not opened)
playbooks.time: 30 days (CITES target); about 3 months (ivory certificate)

playbooks.n: Shipping a work internationally: the shipper, the crate, the courier, the lead times and what it costs
playbooks.for: collector, gallery, auction house post-sale desk, registrar

steps.n: Book a fine-art shipper early
steps.do: Before the pandemic a work typically arrived within about 72 hours of dispatch; by mid-2021 the first available collection and crate-fabrication slot at one shipper was six weeks out, with a waitlist (Artnet, July 2021). Shippers quoted: Crozier, Fortress, ARTA, Masterpiece. Instruct the shipper with the dimensions, medium, value and the licences in hand (export licence, CITES, ATA carnet where temporary).
steps.who: the fine-art shipper (Crozier, Momart, Gander & White, Convelio, Hasenkamp, Dietl and others — only the first is on the page opened)
steps.time: 72 hours door to door in normal conditions; weeks in a capacity squeeze
steps.doc: the work’s data, the licences, the insurance instruction
src: Artnet News, Eileen Kinsella, ‘Art shipping in the age of Covid…’ (19 July 2021)

steps.n: Expect the cost to move with freight rates
steps.do: In 2021 air-freight rates were about four times pre-pandemic levels and sea freight about double (Crozier); one transatlantic quote came in 50% above the gallery’s estimate; for a small painting the shipping cost reached 10% of the sale price. No current London–New York crate-and-air price was found on a page opened in this session (vf U); obtain two quotes.
steps.who: the shipper
steps.doc: two quotes

steps.n: Packing, climate and the condition report
steps.do: Museum-standard packing: a sealed, climate-buffered crate (plywood with foam cavity packing or a travel frame), climate-controlled air-ride truck to and from the airport, a courier for high values, condition reports at packing and unpacking signed by both sides, nail-to-nail transit insurance under the collector’s policy or the shipper’s (standards from trade practice — vf U; not on a page opened).
steps.who: the shipper; the registrar or courier
steps.doc: the condition report, the packing list, the insurance certificate

steps.n: Customs and licences
steps.do: The shipper’s customs broker lodges the export declaration against the licences and the import entry at destination (see the export and import playbooks); temporary movements use the ATA carnet or temporary admission; endangered materials need the CITES permit on both sides. Italy’s export office opening only two days a week was cited as a delay factor in 2021.
steps.who: the customs broker
steps.time: licence times per the export playbooks
steps.doc: licences, invoice, packing list
src: London Chamber of Commerce and Industry, ATA Carnet FAQs

pitfalls: Shipping cost can reach 10% of the price on a small work; quote before bidding.
A crate slot can be weeks away in a busy season; book at purchase.
Brexit customs and short export-office hours add days on the Continent.
playbooks.cost: Not confirmed for 2026; 2021 air rates were four times pre-pandemic (Artnet)
playbooks.time: 72 hours door to door in normal conditions; add licence time

playbooks.n: Insuring a private collection: the fine-art policy, the schedule, the valuation cycle, the premium, the loss
playbooks.for: collector, family office, adviser, broker

steps.n: Choose the policy form
steps.do: A standalone fine-art policy (typically all-risk) rather than a homeowners rider (standard homeowners sub-limits for art and collectibles are roughly US$1,000–US$5,000). Scheduled cover gives each work an agreed value; blanket cover sets one limit for the collection with no per-item cap; a hybrid schedules the top pieces. Agreed value pays the fixed sum on a covered total loss without depreciation; market value is established after the loss. Chubb: 100% of the agreed value as cash on a covered total loss; worldwide cover including gallery and storage; newly acquired works covered automatically for 90 days up to 25% of the itemised amount; market appreciation paid up to 150% of the itemised amount; most fine-art losses with no deductible.
steps.who: the carrier (Chubb, AXA XL, AIG Private Client, Hiscox, Huntington T. Block are named) through a broker
steps.doc: the inventory with images, invoices, provenance and condition reports
src: Masterworks Research, ‘How to insure fine art’ (2 July 2026)

steps.n: Set the valuation cycle
steps.do: Chubb requires a formal appraisal only for items valued at US$500,000 or more; below that a detailed description and estimated value suffice. Insurers generally recommend refreshing valuations every three to five years, closer to every two years for fast-moving contemporary art.
steps.who: the appraiser; the carrier
steps.doc: the appraisal, the updated schedule

steps.n: Budget the premium
steps.do: Premiums commonly run about 0.1% to 2% of insured value a year (Masterworks, July 2026): roughly US$100–US$2,000 on a US$100,000 work and US$1,000–US$20,000 on a US$1m work; a well-documented, well-secured collection in a low-risk home can price below 0.5%. Rating factors: location (flood, wildfire, crime), alarms, fire suppression and climate control, how often the works travel or are lent, fragile media.
steps.who: the carrier
steps.doc: security and environmental details of the residence and storage
src: Masterworks Research, ‘How to insure fine art’ (2 July 2026)

steps.n: The loss
steps.do: Notify the carrier at once; an agreed-value policy pays the scheduled sum on a covered total loss; provenance and documentation (photographs, receipts, condition reports) speed the claim by establishing what the work is and that you own it. Partial losses are settled on repair cost plus loss in value under the policy wording (vf U: not on the pages opened). Chubb’s loss-control specialists review loan and consignment agreements and advise before renovations.
steps.who: the carrier’s claims and loss-control teams
steps.doc: the schedule, images, the conservator’s report

pitfalls: A homeowners policy caps art at a few thousand dollars; a single work above that needs a schedule or a standalone policy.
A stale valuation under-insures; the 150% appreciation clause is a cushion, not a substitute.
Frequent loans and shipping raise the rate; declare them.
Storage and free-port locations must be named on the policy.
playbooks.cost: 0.1%–2% of insured value a year (trade estimate, July 2026); appraisals from US$500,000 at Chubb
playbooks.time: days to bind; revalue every 3–5 years
links: Masterworks, how to insure fine art (2026)

playbooks.n: Lending a work to a UK exhibition under the Government Indemnity Scheme
playbooks.for: lender (private or institutional), borrowing museum’s registrar, insurer

steps.n: Check the loan qualifies
steps.do: The scheme indemnifies objects on loan to UK museums, galleries, libraries, the National Trust and similar bodies for temporary exhibitions, long-term loans, or study and research to be published; lenders may be private individuals or public collections in the UK or abroad (loans from UK national institutions directly funded by government are excluded). The criterion is public benefit, because ‘the underwritten risk is carried by the UK public purse’. Cover is nail to nail. Minimum object value £1,001 (England, Northern Ireland, Wales), £301 (Scotland); Wales sets a £10m guideline ceiling per object for long-term loans. Legal basis: National Heritage Act 1980.
steps.who: Arts Council England (non-national borrowers in England); DCMS for nationals; the devolved bodies in Scotland and Wales
steps.doc: the loan request with the object’s open-market value at the time of loan
src: Arts Council England, ‘Government Indemnity Scheme’ (consolidated guidance published January 2024)

steps.n: The borrower applies
steps.do: Non-national borrowers apply to the Arts Council at least three months before the indemnity starts; nationals at least five working days before. The application needs a security risk assessment of transport, venue and exhibition areas, environmental approval of the exhibition or research space (non-nationals supply environmental data including charts for week 1 of the exhibition and data-logger readings at 30-minute intervals), the object value as a fair estimate of open-market value, compliance with the government conditions (section 2 of the Guidelines, clause 2 of the standard undertaking, Annexes D, E and F) and a signed Irrevocable Undertaking (Annex B for nationals and other non-nationals; Annex B2 annually for Designated collections). The 16°C temperature minimum has been temporarily suspended and ‘split courier’ arrangements are accepted permanently (both since 20 October 2023).
steps.who: the borrowing institution to Arts Council England
steps.time: at least 3 months before (non-nationals); 5 working days (nationals)
steps.doc: facility report-type security and environmental data, the valuation, the undertaking, the lender’s loan agreement

steps.n: Understand the borrower’s minimum liability (the excess)
steps.do: England and Northern Ireland: £25,000 per financial year for nationals and for non-nationals with Designated collections that opt in; other non-nationals £300 per application plus 1% of the value of objects over £4,000. Wales: £15,000 per year for nationals; non-nationals £300 + 1% over £4,000. Scotland: £5,000 for nationals; non-nationals £300 + 1% over £4,000. The lender bears nothing; the borrower carries the excess, usually through its own insurance.
steps.who: the borrowing institution
steps.fee: the excess as above (Arts Council England)
steps.doc: the borrower’s insurance for the excess

pitfalls: Three months’ lead time for non-national borrowers; a late application leaves the loan on commercial insurance.
Environmental conditions must be evidenced with logger data; a venue without loggers cannot be approved.
The value declared must be a fair estimate of open-market value; an inflated value is challenged and a low one under-indemnifies.
playbooks.cost: No premium; the borrower pays the excess (£300 + 1% over £4,000 per application for most non-nationals) and its own security and environmental compliance
playbooks.time: apply 3 months ahead (non-national) or 5 working days (national)
links: Arts Council England, Government Indemnity Scheme
src: Arts Council England, ‘Government Indemnity Scheme’ (guidance January 2024)

playbooks.n: Lending to a US exhibition under the Arts and Artifacts Indemnity Program (international indemnity, FY27)
playbooks.for: lender, US borrowing museum, registrar, insurer

steps.n: Check the borrower and the exhibition qualify
steps.do: The Federal Council on the Arts and the Humanities (FCAH) makes indemnity agreements under the Arts and Artifacts Indemnity Act (P.L. 94-158, 20 USC 971 et seq.), administered by the National Endowment for the Arts. Applicants are US non-profit, tax-exempt organisations and governmental units that have organised at least one exhibition with borrowed objects; participating venues must have organised or hosted one. The exhibition must be certified as in the national interest. Limits: US$1.8 billion per exhibition; US$150 million per conveyance; objects valued above US$100 million are generally covered to US$100 million; generally five venues or fewer and two years or less. Apply no more than one year and three months before the indemnity period starts.
steps.who: FCAH; NEA Indemnity staff
steps.doc: the exhibition plan and venue list
src: NEA, FY27 International Indemnity Application Instructions

steps.n: Meet the deadlines
steps.do: Two rounds a year. September round: Part 1 (SF-424 on Grants.gov) due 14 September 2026, Part 2 (NEA Applicant Portal) due 18 September 2026, both 11:59 pm ET. March round: Part 1 due 8 March 2027, Part 2 due 12 March 2027.
steps.who: NEA
steps.time: Part 1 and Part 2 within the same week; two rounds a year
steps.doc: SF-424 with AOR certifications
src: NEA, FY27 International Indemnity Application Instructions

steps.n: Assemble Part 2
steps.do: Item 1 the indemnity narrative (packing, shipping, environmental, security, condition reporting); Item 2 the object list in Excel with description, lender, lender value in US dollars, source of value and a third-party opinion of value; Item 3 floor plans with guard placement; Item 4 facility reports dated within six months; Item 5 images of each object; Item 6 images of the top ten highlights. Dated loan agreements with US-dollar valuations and the lender’s agreement to federal indemnity must be in hand before the first condition report. Security: 24/7 human presence in buildings holding indemnified objects, electronic surveillance, fire protection, seismic measures. Environment: temperature, relative humidity and light for each venue and store, light generally not above 25 fc for paintings and 5 fc for works on paper. Conservation: a qualified professional confirms the objects can withstand packing, shipping and installation; condition reports at the lender, each venue and on return.
steps.who: the borrowing museum’s registrar; the lender signs the loan agreement
steps.time: facility reports within six months of application
steps.doc: loan agreement, facility report, object list with values and third-party opinion, condition reports, floor plans
src: NEA, FY27 International Indemnity Application Instructions

steps.n: Carry the deductible and insure above the limit
steps.do: The indemnitee pays a deductible per exhibition: US$15,000 up to US$2m indemnified value; US$25,000 from US$2m to under US$10m; US$50,000 from US$10m to under US$125m; US$100,000 to under US$200m; US$200,000 to under US$300m; US$300,000 to under US$400m; US$400,000 to under US$500m; US$500,000 at US$500m or more. Losses above the indemnified amount must be insured by the indemnitee or another party. The Certificate of Indemnity’s object list and US-dollar values are the basis of any certified claim; losses are reported to NEA Indemnity staff immediately.
steps.who: the indemnitee; FCAH on claims
steps.doc: the Certificate of Indemnity, the insurance for the excess layer
src: NEA, FY27 International Indemnity Application Instructions

pitfalls: Unauthorised changes to the shipping, venue or security plan void the FCAH’s responsibility for the resulting loss.
Facility reports older than six months are rejected.
An object worth over US$100m is covered only to US$100m; the lender needs commercial insurance for the top layer.
Immunity from judicial seizure (22 USC 2459) is a separate State Department application, not covered by the instructions opened (vf U).
playbooks.cost: No fee; the deductible (US$15,000–US$500,000 per exhibition) and the excess-layer insurance
playbooks.time: apply up to 15 months ahead at one of two annual deadlines
src: NEA, FY27 International Indemnity Application Instructions

playbooks.n: Lending to an exhibition with immunity from seizure: the UK approved-museum regime and the US Federal Register notice
playbooks.for: foreign lender, borrowing museum, registrar, counsel

steps.n: UK: lend only to an approved museum and have the object published
steps.do: The Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 gives immunity from seizure to an object loaned from overseas for a temporary public exhibition at an approved museum or gallery, provided it is usually kept outside the UK, is not owned by a UK resident, is imported without contravening any law, and the museum publishes the information about it that the regulations require. Approval is by the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport (Welsh and Scottish Ministers, and the Northern Ireland department, in the devolved nations) on the institution’s procedures for establishing provenance and ownership and its compliance with the published guidance. Forty-one institutions are listed on the Arts Council page, among them the British Museum, the National Gallery, Tate, the V&A, the Royal Academy, the Ashmolean, the Fitzwilliam, National Galleries Scotland, National Museums Liverpool, the Courtauld and the Wallace Collection. (The publication lead time and the 12-month limit are in the 2008 Regulations, not on the page opened — vf U.)
steps.who: DCMS (approval); the approved museum (publication); Arts Council England (information)
steps.time: publication before the object arrives (period not confirmed here)
steps.doc: the loan agreement, the provenance file, the published object entry

steps.n: US: the 22 U.S.C. § 2459 determination and Federal Register notice
steps.do: Before importation the President or his designee must determine that the object ‘is of cultural significance’ and that its temporary exhibition or display (since the 2021 amendment, Pub. L. 116-283, also storage, conservation and scientific research) by a qualifying institution is in the national interest, and publish ‘a notice to that effect’ in the Federal Register. Then no court ‘may issue or enforce any judicial process, or enter any judgment, decree, or order’ depriving the institution or a carrier of custody or control. The United States attorney may intervene; actions to enforce the loan agreement or carrier contracts remain possible; a transfer from a foreign mission in the US to a US institution counts as importation. Executive Order 12047 assigned the function to the USIA Director in consultation with the Secretary of State; the USIA’s functions passed to the Department of State (the page notes the transfer under 22 U.S.C. §§ 6531–6551 without naming the current designee). The 2016 Nazi-era exception (Foreign Cultural Exchange Jurisdictional Immunity Clarification Act) is not reproduced on the page opened (vf U).
steps.who: US Department of State, Office of the Legal Adviser (designee — vf U); the borrowing institution applies
steps.time: apply well before import so the notice is published first (the Department’s lead-time guidance was not opened — vf U)
steps.doc: the application with the object list, provenance and the loan agreement

pitfalls: UK immunity is lost if the museum fails to publish the required information before the object arrives.
The US notice must be published before importation; an object that lands first is unprotected.
Neither regime cures a title defect; both presuppose the museum’s provenance diligence.
playbooks.cost: No fee; counsel and provenance research
playbooks.time: weeks before shipment (both regimes require publication before arrival)
links: Arts Council England, immunity from seizure

playbooks.n: Checking title before a purchase or consignment: the Art Loss Register search
playbooks.for: buyer, dealer, auction house cataloguer, lender, insurer

steps.n: Order the search
steps.do: Submit the object with the minimum current-ownership information (for antiquities, tribal and Asian art the ALR requires provenance prior to 2000). Single search £85 / €100 / US$110 plus VAT where applicable; subscriptions valid one year: up to 10 searches £700 / €800 / US$850, up to 25 searches £1,500 / €1,750 / US$2,000; urgent search £300 / €350 / US$400, or £215 / €250 / US$290 to upgrade a standard search. Auction houses pay per lot: UK £3.66, US US$4.95, DACH €5.60, rest of Europe €5.10 (ex VAT), minimum annual fee £800 / €900 / US$1,000; specialist items (antiquities, coins, books, musical instruments) cost more.
steps.who: The Art Loss Register (London)
steps.time: urgent search answered within one working day if all information is supplied and no detailed provenance research is needed; standard searches have no stated turnaround; items without provenance take longer
steps.doc: images, description, dimensions, the current-ownership information, provenance for antiquities

steps.n: Read the certificate for what it is
steps.do: The ALR certificate records that the item was not found in the database of over 700,000 items at the date of search; the ALR says ‘no database of stolen art, antiques and collectables can be complete’ and that a certificate is an important defence and demonstration of due diligence in good faith, not a guarantee. A certificate may be refused, most commonly when requested provenance information or documentation is not supplied.
steps.who: The Art Loss Register
steps.doc: the certificate filed with the invoice

steps.n: Registering a loss and recovery terms
steps.do: A theft is registered for an administrative fee of £15 / €17.50 / US$20 (plus VAT where applicable); if the item is located a Location Fee of 5% of the ultimate net benefit is due; if the registrant appoints the ALR to recover the object the fee is 20% of the ultimate net benefit and no Location Fee is payable.
steps.who: The Art Loss Register
steps.fee: £15 registration; 5% location fee or 20% recovery fee of the net benefit
steps.doc: police report, images, proof of ownership

pitfalls: A clean certificate does not clear a Nazi-era or an export-law problem; pair it with a Lost Art search and the provenance file.
The certificate is refused if provenance is withheld; a seller who will not give provenance is the red flag.
Title insurance (ARIS and others) is the product that transfers the residual risk; it is not covered by the page opened (vf U).
playbooks.cost: £85–£300 per item depending on urgency; per-lot rates for auction houses (ALR, 2026)
playbooks.time: one working day (urgent); longer for a standard search or thin provenance
links: The Art Loss Register FAQs and tariff

playbooks.n: Restitution and Nazi-era provenance: the research standard, the Lost Art database, the German arbitration court, the 2024 Best Practices
playbooks.for: museum, dealer, auction house, collector, claimant’s counsel, provenance researcher

steps.n: Apply the research standard to any object that existed before 8 May 1945
steps.do: The German Guidelines (new edition 2025, implementing the Common Statement of 9 December 1999 and the Washington Principles) set the scope: items of unknown, incomplete or uncertain provenance that existed before 8 May 1945 and changed hands between 1933 and 1945, reviewed for the whole period from 30 January 1933 to the present. Four questions: where the item changed hands, how it entered the collection, who sold or confiscated it, and how the property changed hands. ‘A passive approach – taking action only in response to information that may come to light – is insufficient.’ A gap for 1933–45 does not of itself mean looting, but a reasonable suspicion obliges a decision on the object. Databases named: Lost Art and Proveana.
steps.who: the holder (museum, dealer, collector); the German Lost Art Foundation (DZK)
steps.fee: Lost Art and Proveana searches are free (vf U: fee not stated on the page)
steps.doc: the provenance file: invoices, labels, exhibition and literature history, dealer stock books
src: BKM, Guidelines for implementing the Common Statement of 1999 on the tracing and return of Nazi-confiscated art (new edition 2025, published May 2026)

steps.n: Report findings to Lost Art
steps.do: Report to the German Lost Art Foundation for entry in the Lost Art database (www.lostart.de), even when provenance is not fully proven but loss cannot be ruled out; reports of research that found no looted items are also accepted; restitutions and agreed solutions go through the Foundation’s online restitution form.
steps.who: Deutsches Zentrum Kulturgutverluste (Magdeburg)
steps.doc: the research report, images, the object’s data

steps.n: Claims in Germany: the Court of Arbitration for Nazi-looted Cultural Property
steps.do: The Court of Arbitration replaces the Advisory Commission and was due to begin work on 1 December 2025; its Assessment Framework was adopted at the High-Level Cultural Policy Meeting on 26 March 2025. Victims of Nazi art theft and their legal successors can initiate arbitration unilaterally, without the institution’s express agreement, on the basis of standing offers; a direct procedure between the parties must be attempted first, with arbitration following if no agreement is reached within the time limit. ‘The costs of the Arbitration Panel are not charged to the parties’; each side bears its own counsel and travel. The primary just and fair solution is restitution; alternatives are restitution followed by repurchase or loan, sharing of sale proceeds, compensation with the object remaining, or retention with the provenance displayed.
steps.who: Schiedsgericht für NS-Raubgut (Court of Arbitration); the Länder and the federal government
steps.time: direct negotiation first (time limit not stated); arbitration from 1 December 2025
steps.fee: no panel costs charged to the parties
steps.doc: the claim, the proof of succession, the provenance evidence

steps.n: Internationally: the 2024 Best Practices
steps.do: The Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art (6 February 2024) are endorsed by 14 states (Austria, Canada, Croatia, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, Luxembourg, Moldova, the Netherlands, Romania, the United Kingdom, the United States). They cover what was looted, confiscated, sequestered and spoliated by the Nazis, the Fascists and their collaborators, including ‘forced sales and sales under duress, during the Holocaust era between 1933-45’; sales by persecuted persons ‘can be considered equivalent to an involuntary transfer of property based on the circumstances of the sale’; ‘the primary just and fair solution is restitution’; owners or heirs identified through research should be proactively sought; provenance research should be published on the internet; countries should create independent expert bodies and consider exceptions to barriers such as statutes of limitations and anti-deaccessioning rules.
steps.who: the endorsing governments; national claims commissions (UK Spoliation Advisory Panel, French CIVS, Dutch Restitutiecommissie, Austrian Beirat — names from memory, vf U)
steps.doc: the claim file
src: Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art (6 February 2024), copy on the Greek Foreign Ministry site
https://mfa.gr/archive/1/docs/2024/2024-02-06 Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.pdf

pitfalls: A 1933–45 gap in a German-, Austrian- or French-provenance work is the trigger; research before cataloguing, not after a claim.
In Germany a claimant can now force arbitration against a public institution; a museum’s standing offer binds it.
A sale by a persecuted person in 1933–45 is treated as involuntary under the 2024 Best Practices even with a receipt.
Statutes of limitation remain a defence in many courts; the Best Practices ask states to consider exceptions, they do not remove them.
playbooks.cost: Research time and counsel; the German arbitration panel charges no costs to the parties
playbooks.time: months to years for a claim; a database search is immediate
links: Lost Art database and the BKM Guidelines (English)
https://mfa.gr/archive/1/docs/2024/2024-02-06 Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.pdf
src: Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles (6 February 2024)
https://mfa.gr/archive/1/docs/2024/2024-02-06 Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art.pdf

playbooks.n: Opening a gallery or dealership in the UK: registering with HMRC as an art market participant
playbooks.for: gallery owner, dealer, auction house, art adviser acting as intermediary, free-port operator

steps.n: Decide whether you are an ‘art market participant’
steps.do: You must register if, by way of business, you trade in or act as an intermediary in the buying or selling of works of art where the value of a transaction, or a series of linked transactions, is €10,000 or more; or if you operate a free port storing works of art where the value stored for a person is €10,000 or more. ‘Work of art’ takes the VAT Act 1994 s.21 definition. Intermediaries must negotiate prices with another participant or act on a customer’s behalf; advisers, research and provenance providers, introducers and non-regulated service providers need not register, nor do artists selling only their own work.
steps.who: HMRC (supervisor under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017)
steps.doc: a note of the business model and the transaction values
src: HMRC, ‘Money laundering supervision for art market participants’ (updated 6 August 2024)

steps.n: Register online and pay the fees
steps.do: Apply through HMRC’s online money-laundering supervision service, listing every premises and the persons to be approved. Fees from 1 December 2025: application fee £300 (one-off, non-refundable; waived for businesses eligible for the small-business reduction); premises registration fee £400 per premises, payable annually; approval-process fee £40 per person tested for art market participants (the £500 fit-and-proper fee applies to money service businesses and trust or company service providers, not to the art trade). Businesses with turnover under £5,000 pay in full and receive a £500 refund on acceptance (then £200 a year), by e-mailing AMLS.Fees@hmrc.gov.uk with ‘Turnover Reduction’ in the subject; refunds within 30 days. Quote the 14-character payment reference (starting with X).
steps.who: HMRC, Economic Crime Supervision
steps.time: HMRC states no processing time on the pages opened; the annual declaration and fee fall due each registration period
steps.fee: £300 application + £400 per premises per year + £40 per approved person (HMRC, fees from 1 December 2025; page updated 10 November 2026)
steps.doc: company details, premises list, the responsible persons’ identities for approval, the nominated officer
src: HMRC, ‘Fees you’ll pay for money laundering supervision’ (updated 10 November 2026)
HMRC, ‘Money laundering supervision for art market participants’

steps.n: Put the compliance programme in place
steps.do: Follow HMRC’s art-market participant guidance on protecting against money laundering and terrorist financing and reporting suspicious activity: a written risk assessment, customer due diligence at the €10,000 threshold, a nominated officer, staff training and record-keeping (the content of these duties is in the separate HMRC guidance, not the page opened — vf S for the list). Each registration period HMRC sends a notice to update the registration and pay the annual fee on all premises; non-payment can lead HMRC to cancel the registration and remove the business from the register.
steps.who: HMRC
steps.doc: the risk assessment, CDD procedures, the nominated-officer appointment, training records
src: HMRC, ‘Money laundering supervision for art market participants’ (updated 6 August 2024)

pitfalls: A single linked series of sales to one client crossing €10,000 brings a small gallery into scope.
Trading while unregistered is an offence; the Art Newspaper reported the original registration deadline as 10 June 2021 (not opened here — vf U).
Each premises pays £400 a year; a pop-up or a second showroom is a premises.
The fee page changed on 1 December 2025 and again on 10 November 2026 (small-business section); check it at renewal.
playbooks.cost: £740 for a single-premises gallery with one approved person in year one (£300 + £400 + £40), then £400 a year per premises (HMRC, fees from 1 December 2025)
playbooks.time: online application; HMRC gives no stated turnaround on the pages opened
links: HMRC, money laundering supervision for art market participants
HMRC, fees for money laundering supervision
src: HMRC, ‘Money laundering supervision for art market participants’ (2024)
HMRC, ‘Fees you’ll pay for money laundering supervision’ (10 November 2026)

playbooks.n: Opening a gallery in the EU: the national AML regime today and the single rulebook (AMLR) from 10 July 2027
playbooks.for: gallery owner, dealer, auction house, free-port operator, compliance officer

steps.n: Register or notify under the current national regime
steps.do: Until 10 July 2027 each member state applies its transposition of the AML directives: art dealers and intermediaries at €10,000 and free ports storing art are obliged entities under the fifth directive as transposed (vf U: carried from memory; the page opened does not list works of art). In France the supervisor for the art trade is the DGCCRF with Tracfin receiving reports; in the Netherlands the Bureau Toezicht Wwft of the Belastingdienst (vf U: not opened in this session). Register or notify where the national law requires it before the first transaction above the threshold.
steps.who: the national AML supervisor for the art trade
steps.doc: company registration, beneficial-owner declaration (UBO register), the nominated compliance officer
src: Norton Rose Fulbright, ‘The new EU AML/CFT regime has arrived – are you ready?’ (2024)

steps.n: Prepare for the AMLR single rulebook (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624)
steps.do: The package published in the Official Journal on 19 June 2024 comprises the AMLA Regulation (EU) 2024/1620, the AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and Directive (EU) 2024/1640 (sixth directive). The AMLR applies from 10 July 2027 (10 July 2029 for the entities in Article 3(3)(n) and (o)). It harmonises customer due diligence across the EU; obliged entities must perform CDD on cash transactions above €3,000 (Article 19). New obliged entities include traders in high-value goods (jewellery, clocks and watches, luxury motor vehicles over €250,000, planes and boats over €7.5m), precious metals and stones, crypto-asset service providers, crowdfunding platforms, residence-permit operators and professional football clubs and agents.
steps.who: the national supervisor; AMLA (Frankfurt) coordinates and directly supervises selected financial institutions from 2028
steps.doc: updated risk assessment and CDD procedures aligned with the AMLR
src: Norton Rose Fulbright, ‘The new EU AML/CFT regime has arrived – are you ready?’ (2024)

steps.n: Apply the EU-wide cash limit
steps.do: Under Article 80 AMLR persons trading in goods or providing services may accept or make cash payments only up to €10,000, including linked operations, subject to exceptions; stricter national limits (France €1,000 for residents, Italy €5,000 — vf U) continue to apply and were notified to the Commission by 10 October 2024.
