steps.who: national authorities
steps.doc: cash-handling policy
src: Norton Rose Fulbright, ‘The new EU AML/CFT regime has arrived – are you ready?’ (2024)

pitfalls: The AMLR replaces national variation with one rulebook in July 2027; procedures written for one state’s transposition will need rewriting.
Cash above €10,000 is banned EU-wide from 2027; several states already ban far lower sums.
The free-port operator is an obliged entity for art stored above €10,000 per client under the current directive (vf U).
The page opened does not confirm the art-trade provisions of the AMLR text; confirm Article 3 of Regulation 2024/1624 on EUR-Lex before advising.
playbooks.cost: No EU fee; national registration fees vary; the compliance programme is the cost
playbooks.time: national registration before trading; AMLR from 10 July 2027
links: Norton Rose Fulbright on the EU AML package
src: Norton Rose Fulbright, ‘The new EU AML/CFT regime has arrived – are you ready?’ (2024)

playbooks.n: Opening a gallery in the United States: the state sales-tax registration and the resale certificate (New York)
playbooks.for: gallery owner, dealer, adviser selling as principal, art fair exhibitor

steps.n: Register as a sales-tax vendor and hold a Certificate of Authority
steps.do: A seller making taxable sales in New York must hold a valid Certificate of Authority from the Department of Taxation and Finance; most sellers must hold one before they may accept an exemption certificate from a buyer. (The registration route — online through Business Express or Form DTF-17 — and the advance period before opening are from memory and were not on the bulletin opened — vf U.) There is no federal sales tax; each state with a sales tax has its own registration, and the use tax follows the work to the buyer’s state.
steps.who: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance (and each other state’s revenue department where the gallery has nexus)
steps.time: before the first sale (period not confirmed)
steps.fee: none for the New York Certificate of Authority (from memory — vf U)
steps.doc: the registration application, the business’s EIN, the owners’ details
src: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, Tax Bulletin TB-ST-240, ‘Exemption certificates for sales tax’ (26 March 2010)

steps.n: Buy inventory tax-free on a resale certificate
steps.do: A gallery buying works for resale gives the seller Form ST-120 (Resale Certificate) instead of paying sales tax; the certificate must be given within 90 days of the sale. A work bought for the owner’s personal use cannot go on a resale certificate and attracts the tax. Sellers keep the exemption certificates for at least three years after the due date of the return covering the last sale in which they were used.
steps.who: the selling dealer or auction house accepts the certificate; the Department audits
steps.doc: Form ST-120, the Certificate of Authority number
src: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, Tax Bulletin TB-ST-240 (26 March 2010)

steps.n: Charge the tax by destination
steps.do: Sales tax is charged by the buyer’s shipping address at state rates of roughly 4% to over 10%, nil in some states (Barnebys, July 2025); a work shipped out of state by common carrier is not taxed in New York but the buyer owes use tax at home (the shipping rule is from memory — vf U). Keep the shipping documents as proof of delivery out of state.
steps.who: the gallery as collecting vendor; the buyer’s state for use tax
steps.doc: the invoice with the delivery address, the carrier’s proof of delivery
src: Barnebys Magazine, ‘What art buyers need to know about VAT in 2025’ (25 July 2025)

pitfalls: Taking a work ‘for resale’ and then hanging it at home is the classic audit finding; New York has prosecuted art sales-tax evasion (Artnet reported investigations, not opened here — vf U).
An exemption certificate accepted from a buyer without a Certificate of Authority is invalid; the gallery owes the tax.
Selling at a fair in another state creates nexus and a registration duty there.
playbooks.cost: No registration fee in New York (U); the compliance is the cost
playbooks.time: before opening; certificates within 90 days of each purchase
src: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, TB-ST-240 (2010)

unconfirmed: Christie’s current conditions of sale (bidder registration list for companies and agents, the deposit trigger for high-value lots, the payment deadline and late-payment interest): the christies.com.cn PDF returned a bot-check script and was not read; the help page gives only ‘photo ID and proof of address’, ‘register 24 hours before’ and ‘a financial reference and/or a deposit for some auctions’. Sotheby’s Conditions of Business for Buyers were not opened; its buyer guide gives only the 30-day collection rule.

Seller’s side at the major houses: the levels of the seller’s commission, the loss-and-damage (insurance) charge, catalogue and marketing costs, the withdrawal and unsold fees and guarantee terms are not published on the pages opened; Sotheby’s says they are set case by case in the consignment agreement.

France: the thresholds for drawings, photographs, furniture, books and archives, and the January 2021 revision of the thresholds, were not opened (the service-public mirror is dated 2016); the 6%+0.5% export tax figures are from that 2016 page.

Italy: the statutory decision period for the attestato di libera circolazione (40 days from memory), the fees (stamp duty) and the exact text of Law no. 40/2026 were not opened; the €50,000 threshold and the CAI/CAS change rest on the DGABAP circular of 24 April 2026, and the 50/70-year tiers on a March 2026 We Wealth article.
EU ICG: the 90-day decision period, the 21-day document request and the fair exemption come from the German authority’s page; the Regulation text itself was not opened.
UK export: the OGEL value limits are those of the Arts Council’s Issue 2 (2021) guidance, not re-verified for 2026; the absence of a licence fee likewise.
UK import: nil customs duty on Chapter 97 originals is from memory; HMRC’s page gives only the 25% VAT valuation (5% effective).

US import: the free general duty rate for headings 9701–9706 is from memory (the HTS was not opened); the tariff position is from Covington (27 February 2026) and The Art Newspaper (28 July 2026), not from the USTR fact sheet itself; the 180-day protest deadline is from memory.

Switzerland: the 8.1% import VAT, the Federal Register export-permit rule and the CPTA art. 16 due-diligence duties are from memory; the BAK page confirms only the 2026 declaration content and the warehouse-as-import rule; bilateral agreements beyond the 2015 list are not confirmed.

Asia and the Gulf: all rates (HK nil, SG 9%, JP 10%, KR 10%, CN 13%) are from a July 2025 trade-press table; China’s duty rate, the UAE 5%/5%, India’s duty and IGST, Korea’s living-artist exemption and Japan’s duty-free status are from memory.
China export: the only note opened dates from March 2014; the 1949/1911 cut-offs, the appraisal stations’ seals and the 2024 amendment of the Cultural Relics Protection Law are from memory.

Russia: the Ministry of Culture summary (ConsultantPlus) confirms the frame (Laws 435-FZ/430-FZ, the ‘especially significant’ ban, attested experts) but not thresholds, duty rates or times; the EEC Decision No. 30 of 2015 was not opened.
India: the Navratna list and the 100-year definition are from the Chambers 2026 India chapter; the 75-year manuscript rule, the committee’s timing and customs practice are from memory.

Free ports: no operator onboarding page (Geneva, Luxembourg, Singapore, Delaware) was opened; the identity, inventory, insurance and storage-contract steps are trade practice; the Swiss 2016 inventory rule rests on an Artnet report and the 2026 CPTA declaration on the BAK page.

Lending: LTV ‘around 50%’ and the lender names rest on a March 2023 Art Newspaper piece; Christie’s, JPMorgan, Deutsche, Citi and Gurr Johns terms were not found; the UCC-1 mechanics are from memory; no 2026 rate was found.

Donations: the US related-use rule, the 30% AGI ceiling, the 60-day appraisal window and the Statement of Value fee amounts are from memory (the IRS IRM page says fees are updated biannually); the UK AIL 25% douceur is from memory and the 2024 CGS reform consultation was not opened.
CITES UK: the APHA fee table was not opened; the Ivory Act standard exemptions (de minimis, pre-1975 instruments, portrait miniatures) are on a page not opened.
Shipping: no 2026 London–New York crate-and-air price was found on a page opened; the 2021 Artnet figures are the only sourced ones; packing standards are trade practice.
Insurance: the 0.1%–2% premium range is a July 2026 Masterworks estimate; partial-loss settlement wording and exclusions were not opened.
Immunity from seizure: the UK publication lead time and 12-month limit (2008 Regulations) and the US 2016 Nazi-era exception and current State Department designee are not on the pages opened.

Title insurance (ARIS and others), the AAM standard facility report, the Dutch Bureau Toezicht Wwft and French DGCCRF/Tracfin AML registrations, and the AMLR’s own Article 3 text on art dealers and free ports were not opened; the EU AMLR playbook rests on a Norton Rose Fulbright summary that does not mention works of art.

US sales tax: the New York registration route (Business Express / DTF-17), the 20-day advance rule, the no-fee Certificate of Authority and the common-carrier shipping rule are from memory; TB-ST-240 (2010) confirms only the resale-certificate rules.

cases.task: I want a Richter abstract in the US$2–4m band at the New York evening sales, delivered to Singapore, and I want to know what it really costs and how long it takes.
cases.sum: US$2–4m hammer; worked at US$3m hammer (the band is the persona’s; the premium tiers are Sotheby’s and Christie’s as published in 2026)
cases.reading: The Richter market in 2026 is a two-speed market. At Christie’s 21st Century evening sale in New York on 20 May 2026 the trophy Kerze (1982) hammered at US$30m (US$35m with fees) against a US$35–50m estimate, and the Marian Goodman Richters mostly hammered within or at the top of their estimates, with strong bidding reported from China and the Middle East; the adviser Lorinda Ash told The Art Newspaper that buyers ‘are just not spending money in the middle’ (The Art Newspaper, 21 May 2026). At Sotheby’s London Contemporary evening sale on 15 October 2026 Abstraktes Bild (1992) hammered at £5.4m (£6.7m with fees), slightly below its £6m low estimate but well above its £3.6m price at Christie’s London in 2011; the sale made £36.9m at hammer against a £39.5m low estimate, 82% sold by lot, and a 2021 Kusama hammered at £250,000, a quarter of its £1m low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026). The trade’s reading is caution: the dealer Thomas Stauffer told the paper that collectors ‘are not willing to take big risks’ and set their limits conservatively (same source). For the US$2–4m band this means a well-chosen 1980s–90s abstract bought on or under the low estimate is the realistic outcome; a Kusama in the same band is the weaker choice on the October 2026 evidence. The Singapore side of the market is active but smaller: Art SG 2026 (22–25 January 2026, Marina Bay Sands) drew over 43,000 visitors with 106 exhibitors from 30 countries, co-presented for the first time with S.E.A. Focus, UBS as lead partner (Art SG press release, January 2026; The Art Newspaper, 20 January 2026).
cases.money: Line by line at a US$3,000,000 hammer. (1) Buyer’s premium: Sotheby’s charges 28% of the hammer up to and including US$2m, 22% from US$2m to US$8m and 15% above US$8m, worldwide since 13 February 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026; Grossman LLP, 14 May 2026) — computed from those tiers the premium on US$3m is US$560,000 + US$220,000 = US$780,000, total US$3,780,000. Christie’s charges 27% up to US$1.5m, 22% from US$1.5m to US$8m and 15% above US$8m since September 2025 (same sources) — computed, US$405,000 + US$330,000 = US$735,000, total US$3,735,000. Phillips charges 29% up to US$2m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above, with a 1–4 point reduction for a binding written bid at or above the low estimate lodged 48 hours before the sale (Grossman LLP, 14 May 2026). Sotheby’s 1% ‘overhead premium’ was scrapped in February 2025 except for wine and spirits (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024). (2) New York sales tax: none is due if the house or its arranged carrier ships the work out of state, because New York sales tax is a destination tax fixed by the point of delivery (20 NYCRR 525.2(a)(3); NY Advisory Opinion TSB-A-16(17)S, 2 May 2016); if the collector’s own fine-art shipper collects in New York the sale is taxable at the New York City rate (Frankfurt Kurnit Klein & Selz on the NY Tax Bulletin, 16 October 2015). The New York City combined rate is 8.875% from memory (U) — on US$3.78m that would be about US$335,000, which is the cost of getting the shipping arrangement wrong. (3) Crate, air freight and transit insurance: an aggregator’s 2026 guide gives US$850 for a museum-standard crate on a Berlin–London example, transit insurance of 1–3% of declared value with cover written at 110% of value, and advises booking 4–8 weeks ahead; it gives no per-kilo New York–Singapore air rate (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026 — a freight marketplace’s blog, S). A house quote is the only firm number; budget on the order of 0.5–1% of value for crate, air freight and transit cover combined (U, from memory of trade practice). (4) Singapore import GST: 9% since 1 January 2024 (8% in 2023, 7% before), collected at importation on goods above the S$400 low-value threshold (IRAS, Taxbytes, 2024). On a US$3.78m invoice that is about US$340,000 at 9%, on whichever value Singapore Customs applies (the CIF basis is from memory, U). Singapore levies no customs duty on works of art (from memory, U). (5) The Le Freeport alternative: goods stored in an Approved Specialised Warehouse under IRAS’s Specialised Warehouse Scheme — ‘qualifying goods (e.g. works of art, antiques, precious metals and stones)’ — have storage, auction, broking and valuation services zero-rated when supplied to overseas persons, and the operators are Zero-GST or Licensed warehouse operators approved warehouse by warehouse (IRAS, SWS page); GST is suspended while the goods stay in the Zero-GST warehouse and falls due at 9% only if the work is released into Singapore (from memory of the Zero-GST Warehouse Scheme, U). (6) Storage at the freeport, a condition report on arrival, and all-risks cover in Singapore are quoted case by case (no published tariff opened).

road.n: Register to bid, lodge the paddle and the KYC documents, and settle the premium tier with the house
road.who: Sotheby’s or Christie’s New York, Contemporary department
road.doc: bidder registration, identification, source-of-funds where the house asks
road.time: before the sale; the house publishes its tiers

road.n: Instruct the house to arrange the shipment out of state itself, so the sale is delivered outside New York
road.who: the house’s shipping desk; the house’s carrier
road.doc: shipping instruction and invoice showing delivery to Singapore; the house’s record of the point of delivery

road.n: Pay the invoice: hammer plus premium, no New York sales tax when shipped out of state by the vendor or a common carrier
road.who: the house’s client accounts
road.doc: invoice; wire
road.time: the house’s payment terms (not opened; U)

road.n: Crate, insure and fly the work New York–Singapore
road.who: a fine-art shipper engaged by the house; the transit insurer
road.doc: packing list, airway bill, condition report, certificate of insurance at 110% of value
road.time: book 4–8 weeks ahead for a complex international route (FreightAmigo, 2026)
road.fee: crate from about US$850 in a European example; transit cover 1–3% of value (FreightAmigo, 2026, S)

road.n: Import into Singapore: either clear for home use and pay 9% GST, or deposit into a Zero-GST warehouse under the Specialised Warehouse Scheme with GST suspended
road.who: the shipper’s declaring agent; Singapore Customs; the warehouse operator
road.doc: import permit; GST payment or warehouse deposit
road.fee: 9% GST on import value (IRAS); storage per the operator’s tariff

walls.n: New York State and City sales tax on tangible personal property delivered in New York
walls.cite: NY Tax Law §1105; 20 NYCRR 525.2(a)(3); Advisory Opinion TSB-A-16(17)S
walls.authority: New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
walls.threshold: any sale delivered in New York; the point of delivery, not the passing of title, decides
walls.date: opinion of 2 May 2016; bulletin reported October 2015
walls.what_it_does: makes the sale taxable where the purchaser or the purchaser’s own private or contract carrier takes possession in New York, and non-taxable where the vendor or a common carrier delivers out of state
walls.case: the opinion found no New York tax where a Florida buyer’s carrier took possession in Germany, and said in a footnote that the result would differ had the carrier been a common carrier (TSB-A-16(17)S); the enforcement cases against collectors and a house are not on a page opened in this session (U)

walls.n: Singapore Goods and Services Tax on import
walls.cite: Goods and Services Tax Act 1993; rate 9% from 1 January 2024
walls.authority: Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore; Singapore Customs collects at the border
walls.threshold: all imported goods; low-value goods at or below S$400 are taxed at the point of sale instead
walls.what_it_does: charges 9% on the import value at the border unless the goods go into a Zero-GST or Licensed warehouse
walls.case: no enforcement case opened in this session (U)

walls.n: Specialised Warehouse Scheme (Approved Specialised Warehouses)
walls.cite: IRAS SWS; approvals granted warehouse by warehouse by the Comptroller of GST
walls.authority: Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore
walls.threshold: operators of Zero-GST or Licensed warehouses predominantly storing qualifying goods (works of art, antiques, precious metals and stones)
walls.date: approvals listed from 15 December 2011, 13 February 2012 and 1 March 2012; one operator shown as ‘Ceased – effective till 31 Dec 2025’
walls.what_it_does: zero-rates storage, auction, broking and valuation services on the stored goods when supplied to overseas persons, and leases of storage space to overseas persons
walls.case: none; the scheme is a relief, not an enforcement control

cases.people: The Contemporary specialists at Sotheby’s and Christie’s New York, who will also quote the shipment; the house’s shipping desk, which must be the party arranging the carrier for the sales-tax position; a fine-art shipper on the Singapore end for customs declaration and delivery (the Art SG exhibitor portal names Helutrans, Lotus and Eythos as its official shipping partners — page not opened, U); a GST declaring agent; a fine-art insurer for the Singapore all-risks policy; the operator of the Zero-GST warehouse if the work is to be held in suspension. Le Freeport Singapore, built in 2010 for S$100m, was sold in July 2022 to a company of the crypto entrepreneur Jihan Wu for a reported US$28.4m (USA Art News, 20 September 2022, relaying The Art Newspaper); its current operating status is not confirmed on a page opened in this session (U).
cases.calendar: The New York November evening sales fall in the week of 16 November 2026 if the houses keep last year’s pattern (Christie’s 20th Century sale was 17 November 2025 — headline seen, article not opened, U); Sotheby’s London Contemporary evening sale was 15 October 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026); Christie’s 21st Century evening sale New York was 20 May 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 21 May 2026). Art SG 2026 ran 22–25 January 2026 and the 2027 edition is announced for January within Singapore Art Week (Art SG press release, January 2026; dates not given). Book the shipper 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, 2026). Singapore’s GST year is the calendar year; the rate has been 9% since 1 January 2024 (IRAS).
cases.whispers: The Art Newspaper (21 May 2026) reported Christie’s Richter trophy Kerze selling below estimate at US$35m with fees while the Goodman Richters drew bidding from China and the Middle East, and quoted an adviser that buyers ‘are just not spending money in the middle’. The Art Newspaper (16 October 2026) reported Sotheby’s London Contemporary sale at £45.9m with fees, below last October’s £47.6m, with a Richter at £6.7m and a Kusama at a quarter of its low estimate, and called the unsold Yiadom-Boakye and Fadojutimi lots ‘concerning’ for the ultra-contemporary segment. The Art Newspaper (17 February 2026) reported Sotheby’s raising its lower-tier premium to 28% and lifting the tier ceiling to US$2m from 13 February 2026. The Art Newspaper (20 January 2026) reported Art SG 2026 with 106 exhibitors from 30 countries and noted gallery closures in the region over the previous year.
risks: Paying New York sales tax by mistake: if the collector’s own shipper collects the work in New York the sale is taxable, whereas vendor-arranged or common-carrier delivery out of state is not (FKKS, 2015; TSB-A-16(17)S) — at a New York City rate of 8.875% (from memory, U) that is about US$335,000 on a US$3.78m invoice.

Buying ‘in the middle’ of a two-speed Richter market: Kerze hammered US$5m below its low estimate and the London Abstraktes Bild hammered £600,000 below its low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 21 May and 16 October 2026) — bid at or below the low estimate and expect to.
A Kusama alternative carries more downside on current evidence: the 2021 Infinity-net type work in London hammered at a quarter of its £1m low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026).

GST at 9% on the full import value is the largest cost after the premium (IRAS, 2024); the Zero-GST warehouse route only defers it, and one Approved Specialised Warehouse operator is listed as ceased at 31 December 2025 (IRAS SWS page).
Shipping lead time: 4–8 weeks to book a complex international route (FreightAmigo, 2026, S); the house charges storage after its free period (terms not opened, U).
cases.value_left: The houses publish the buyer’s premium but not the landed cost: no house page opened in this session gives a New York–Singapore shipping tariff, the Singapore GST line, or the Zero-GST warehouse alternative, and the seller-side terms are ‘bespoke’ (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024). The sales-tax position turns on who arranges the carrier, which the house’s invoice desk will do right only if asked (FKKS, 2015). Shipping cost benchmarks come from freight aggregators, not the trade (FreightAmigo, 2026). The Singapore art-market statistics the brief asks for (2024–26 totals, National Gallery Singapore attendance) are not on any page opened; Art SG reports attendance, not sales (Art SG press release, January 2026). A terminal that shows the premium tier, the no-tax shipping condition, the 9% GST line and the warehouse option on one page, before the bid, is what the persona cannot get from the houses today.
next: Pick the house by premium: at a US$3m hammer Christie’s premium is US$735,000 and Sotheby’s is US$780,000 on the 2026 tiers (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026; Grossman LLP, 14 May 2026).
Set a limit at or below the low estimate for a 1980s–90s Richter abstract; the May and October 2026 comparables both hammered under their low estimates (The Art Newspaper).
Instruct the house in writing, before invoicing, to arrange shipment to Singapore itself so no New York sales tax is due (TSB-A-16(17)S; FKKS, 2015).

Decide before the work leaves New York whether it clears into Singapore at 9% GST (IRAS) or is deposited in a Zero-GST warehouse under the Specialised Warehouse Scheme (IRAS SWS); confirm which operators are still approved after 31 December 2025.
Book the fine-art shipper and transit cover at 110% of value 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, 2026) and get the house’s crate and freight quote in writing.

cases.task: I want to consign a Zao Wou-Ki or a Richter from Singapore to the Hong Kong autumn evening sale and know what the house keeps, what the shipping costs and when the paperwork has to be in.
cases.sum: HK$30–45m (US$4–6m) band, after the two Zao Wou-Ki results at Sotheby’s Hong Kong on 29 March 2026
cases.reading: Hong Kong’s evening sales recovered in spring 2026. Sotheby’s Modern & Contemporary Evening Auction on 29 March 2026 made HK$548,421,200 (US$70,310,410), up more than 50% on March 2025, with 100% of 54 lots sold and nearly half above their high estimates; Zao Wou-Ki’s Nuage (1956) made HK$40,550,000 (US$5,176,613) and Terre rouge – 16.01.2005 made HK$32,010,000 (US$4,086,397) after 16 bids, while Joan Mitchell’s La Grande Vallée VII (1983) at HK$137,350,000 (US$17,608,974) was the top lot sold in Asia that season and a newly discovered Sanyu made HK$47,260,000 (Sotheby’s, March 2026). The autumn 2026 season has just closed: a South China Morning Post headline seen on 13 November 2026 reports the Hong Kong autumn 2026 art auctions topping HK$2bn with a cool reception for Kusama works, but the page refused to load and its figures are not carried here (U). A year earlier The Art Newspaper’s headline of 5 October 2025 recorded Christie’s Hong Kong autumn sale down 46% on the prior year while setting Picasso’s record in Asia (headline only, not opened, U). For a Zao Wou-Ki of the 1950s–60s the March 2026 evidence supports a HK$30–45m estimate and a Hong Kong sale rather than New York or London, where the March 2026 bidding was deepest for this material (Sotheby’s, March 2026).
cases.money: Line by line. (1) Seller’s commission: Sotheby’s returned sellers to ‘bespoke terms’ from 17 February 2025, ending the flat 10% for works estimated up to US$5m capped at US$50,000 that it had published in 2024; its 2% success fee on hammer above the high estimate remains (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024). Christie’s does not publish a seller’s rate (not opened; U). In practice a lot in this band is negotiated to a low or zero seller’s commission with the house earning the buyer’s premium (from memory of trade practice, U). (2) The buyer’s premium the house earns on the lot is not the seller’s cost, but it sets the buyer’s all-in price: Sotheby’s charges 28% up to the first tier, 22% to the second and 15% above, worldwide since 13 February 2026, with the tier breaks at US$2m and US$8m in New York and £1.5m and £6m in London (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026); the Hong Kong dollar breaks are not on a page opened (U). (3) Shipping Singapore–Hong Kong: a crate, air freight and transit cover at 110% of value quoted by a fine-art shipper; an aggregator’s guide gives transit insurance at 1–3% of declared value and advises booking 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S). The house usually quotes shipping to the saleroom and may absorb it for a lot of this size (U). (4) Singapore GST on the way out: a work sitting in a Zero-GST warehouse under the Specialised Warehouse Scheme can be exported with its auction and broking services zero-rated where supplied to an overseas person (IRAS, SWS page); a work already cleared into Singapore at 9% GST (IRAS, 2024) recovers nothing on export for a private seller (from memory, U). (5) Hong Kong: no VAT or GST and no import duty on works of art (from memory, U — no Hong Kong government page opened in this session). (6) Insurance while at the house: the house’s own cover under its consignment terms, charged at a published percentage of the hammer or the mid-estimate (terms not opened, U). (7) Tax on the gain: Singapore has no capital gains tax for a private collector (from memory, U); Hong Kong taxes no gain for a non-trading seller (from memory, U). (8) Catalogue, photography and marketing charges: per the consignment agreement (U).

The Singapore seller gets no published guidance on what the Zero-GST warehouse route does on export, and no Hong Kong government page on the no-tax position was opened in this session. The persona cannot today compare the houses’ net-to-seller proposals on one screen with the March 2026 comparables beside them; the terminal can.

cases.task: I am bidding on a £1–2m painting in London in the February sales and want it on my wall in Dubai, or in a free zone, without a surprise from the export licence or the UAE tax.
cases.category: Modern and contemporary (a painting over 50 years old, so the licence rule bites)
cases.sum: £1–2m hammer; worked at £1.5m
cases.reading: London’s contemporary market is cautious. Sotheby’s Contemporary evening sale on 15 October 2026 made £36.9m at hammer against a £39.5m low estimate and £45.9m with fees, with 82% sold and six of 34 lots unsold; a de Kooning set a European record at £9.8m but opened below its low estimate, and a Richter made £6.7m with fees (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026). The house reported London’s 2026 year-to-date sales at US$1bn, with modern and contemporary at its highest year-to-date total since 2015 (same source). The Gulf is the growth story the houses are courting: Sotheby’s inaugural Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week, 2–5 December 2025 at the St Regis Saadiyat Island, made US$133.4m across a five-part live auction of handbags, jewels, watches, cars and property — no art was offered; Banksy’s Girl Without Balloon and the Guennol Lioness were shown in an exhibition only — with buyers from 35 countries, about a quarter from the UAE (The Art Newspaper, 10 December 2025). Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism followed in February 2026 with a full waiver of the 5% customs duty on eligible works valued from AED 10m (US$2.72m) that stay in the emirate for at least three years, with due diligence, documented provenance and a review by a committee of experts (WealthBriefing, 19 February 2026). For a £1.5m painting that waiver is out of reach, so the UAE lines are 5% duty and 5% VAT unless the work enters a designated zone.
cases.money: Line by line at a £1,500,000 hammer. (1) Buyer’s premium: Sotheby’s charges 28% up to and including £1.5m, 22% from £1.5m to £6m and 15% above £6m since 13 February 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026) — computed, £420,000, total £1,920,000. Christie’s charges 27% up to £1m, 22% from £1m to £6m and 15% above since September 2025 (same source) — computed, £270,000 + £110,000 = £380,000, total £1,880,000. (2) UK VAT on the premium: charged at 20% on the buyer’s premium for a UK delivery and refundable or not charged when the house exports the lot (from memory, U; no HMRC page opened). (3) Export licence: an individual licence is required for cultural goods at or above the age and value thresholds, whether the export is permanent or temporary (Arts Council England, export licensing page, last updated 25 January 2023); the Open General Export Licence value limits are £180,000 for oil or tempera paintings over 50 years old, £65,000 for general articles over 50 years old, £10,000 for photographs over 50 years old, £12,000 for textiles, £10,000 for portraits of British historical personages, and £0 for manuscripts, archives and UK archaeology, all on the customs declared value (Arts Council England, UK OGEL value limits); a painting under 50 years old needs no licence. There is no licence fee (from memory, U); the Arts Council’s stated processing time is not on the page opened (U). (4) Shipping London–Dubai: crate, air freight and transit cover quoted by a fine-art shipper; an aggregator’s guide gives transit cover at 1–3% of declared value and advises booking 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S). (5) UAE import: customs duty at the standard 5% and import VAT at 5% (WealthBriefing, 19 February 2026, citing M/HQ) — computed on a £1.92m invoice that is roughly £96,000 each, before the shipper’s brokerage. (6) Designated zone: goods brought into a designated zone from outside the UAE are treated as outside the UAE, so no VAT is charged; moving them into the mainland is an import on which import VAT is payable by the importer; goods consumed in the zone are taxed under normal rules, and resale is not consumption (FTA, Designated Zones VAT Guide VATGDZ1, July 2018). A freeport facility at Dubai South offers storage in a designated zone and an airfield zone the trade press describes as outside any customs authority (WealthBriefing, 19 February 2026, S). (7) Storage, condition report and all-risks cover in Dubai: quoted case by case.

WealthBriefing (19 February 2026) reported Abu Dhabi’s duty waiver for works from AED 10m kept three years, aimed at family offices and ultra-high-net-worth collectors. Paying UAE VAT twice: consumption inside a designated zone is treated as an import (FTA guide, 2018); hanging the work at home from the zone is the taxable event.
The Abu Dhabi waiver starts at AED 10m and demands three years in the emirate (WealthBriefing, 2026); it does not help a £1.5m purchase.
Buying into a soft London market: six of 34 lots unsold on 15 October 2026 (The Art Newspaper) — bid at the low estimate.
Shipping lead time of 4–8 weeks (FreightAmigo, 2026, S) on top of the licence.
cases.value_left: Neither house page opened shows the export-licence test against the lot’s age and declared value, the UK VAT position on export, or the UAE duty and VAT lines; the Arts Council publishes the value limits but not its processing time on the page opened. The designated-zone rule is in an FTA guide of 2018 that no house relays. Abu Dhabi’s waiver is published through the trade press, not on a page a collector can test a work against. A terminal that runs the £180,000/50-year test, the 5%+5% mainland line and the zone alternative on one screen is what the persona cannot get from the houses today.

cases.where: Mumbai, buying in New York or London
cases.task: I want a Husain, a Gaitonde or a Souza at the New York or London South Asian sale and I want it home in Mumbai — what does India charge at the border, and which works can never leave again?
cases.artist: M. F. Husain (also V. S. Gaitonde, F. N. Souza)
cases.sum: US$1–3m hammer; worked at US$2m hammer at Christie’s New York
cases.reading: The Indian modern market set two records in thirteen months. At Christie’s New York on 19 March 2025 M. F. Husain’s thirteen-panel Untitled (Gram Yatra) of 1954, consigned by Oslo University Hospital, made US$13.7m with fees against a US$3.5m high estimate, bought by an unnamed institution on the phone after five bidders competed; the sale totalled US$24.8m against an US$11.7m high estimate, the previous Husain record was Untitled (Reincarnation) at US$3.2m in September 2024, and the previous record for modern Indian art was Amrita Sher-Gil’s The Storyteller (1937) at Saffronart in Mumbai in 2023 (The Art Newspaper, 19 March 2025). Then in early April 2026 Saffronart sold Raja Ravi Varma’s Yashoda and Krishna (1890s) in Delhi for about €15.3m (US$17.9m) against an estimate of about €11m, the most expensive Indian work ever sold at auction, to a buyer the press named as the industrialist Cyrus S. Poonawalla; Varma’s works are classed by the Indian government as non-exportable national treasures (Euronews, 8 April 2026). The trade press has also noted a Souza record at Sotheby’s London (The Art Newspaper teaser, 6 October 2025, figure not opened, U) and the Gaitonde record of £3.4m in 2020 (The Art Newspaper headline, September 2020, not opened, U). Indian gallerists called the market a ‘crazy boom’ after the Husain (press headlines, March 2025, not opened, U). For a US$2m Husain the lesson of both records is that the deep bidding is Indian and institutional, and that the top works now sell in India as readily as abroad.
cases.money: Line by line at a US$2,000,000 hammer at Christie’s New York. (1) Buyer’s premium: Christie’s charges 27% up to US$1.5m, 22% from US$1.5m to US$8m and 15% above since September 2025 (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026) — computed, US$405,000 + US$110,000 = US$515,000, total US$2,515,000; at Sotheby’s (28% to US$2m) the premium would be US$560,000 (same source). (2) New York sales tax: none when the house ships the work out of state (NY Advisory Opinion TSB-A-16(17)S, 2016; FKKS on the NY Tax Bulletin, 2015). (3) Shipping New York–Mumbai: crate, air freight, transit cover at 1–3% of value, booked 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S). (4) Indian customs duty on paintings (HS 9701): basic customs duty 10%, social welfare surcharge 10% of the duty (so one further point), and IGST 12% on top, per a tariff reference whose latest entry is dated 2 February 2018 (Eximguru, S — possibly out of date). Computed on a US$2.515m invoice that is about US$251,500 duty, US$25,150 surcharge and 12% IGST on the duty-inclusive value, roughly US$335,000 — some US$610,000 at the border. A 2026 headline reports a CBIC notification exempting basic customs duty on works of art and antiques, apparently for public exhibitions (Taxscan and others, headlines seen, pages not opened, U); if it applies to a private import the duty line falls away and the terminal should re-run it. (5) GST on the domestic resale later: 12% on paintings (from memory, U). (6) Registration: a work over 100 years old is an antiquity under the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 and cannot be exported again except through the central government; works by artists declared ‘art treasures’ (Varma, Sher-Gil, Tagore and others, by notification) are non-exportable (Euronews, 8 April 2026 for Varma; the Act and the notification from memory, U). A 1950s Husain is neither, and can be exported again (U). (7) Insurance and storage in Mumbai: quoted case by case.

cases.task: I want a 1950s–60s Zao Wou-Ki at the Hong Kong evening sale, and I need to decide whether it stays in Hong Kong, goes into the Shanghai free-trade-zone bonded warehouse, or clears into the mainland with the duty and VAT paid.
cases.sum: HK$30–45m (US$4–6m) hammer band; worked at HK$35m
cases.reading: The Zao Wou-Ki market is the deepest part of the Hong Kong evening sales. At Sotheby’s Hong Kong Modern & Contemporary Evening Auction on 29 March 2026 Nuage (1956) made HK$40,550,000 (US$5,176,613) and Terre rouge – 16.01.2005 made HK$32,010,000 (US$4,086,397) after 16 bids, in a white-glove sale of 54 lots totalling HK$548,421,200 (US$70,310,410), up more than 50% on March 2025, with nearly half the lots above their high estimates; the same sale set the season’s top price in Asia with a Joan Mitchell at HK$137,350,000 sold to an online bidder and made HK$47,260,000 for a newly discovered Sanyu (Sotheby’s, March 2026). The autumn 2026 season has just closed with the Hong Kong art auctions reported above HK$2bn in a South China Morning Post headline seen on 13 November 2026 (page not opened, U). On the mainland side, Shanghai’s free-trade-zone bonded art warehouse has had a policy footing since 12 October 2020, when the Ministry of Finance, the General Administration of Customs and the State Taxation Administration jointly issued preferential customs duty, VAT and consumption-tax treatment for exhibited cultural relics, and since the 10 November 2020 pact between the State Administration of Cultural Heritage and the Shanghai municipality that removed the six-month legal window for imported artworks and antiques at the bonded warehouse and let foreign auction companies sell pre-1949 works by foreign artists who died after 1949 (China Daily / China Services Info, 15 December 2020). For a US$4–6m Zao Wou-Ki the economics turn on one line: the mainland’s import VAT and duty, which no page opened in this session states in current figures.
cases.money: Line by line at a HK$35,000,000 hammer. (1) Buyer’s premium: Sotheby’s charges 28%, 22% and 15% in three tiers worldwide since 13 February 2026 and Christie’s 27%, 22% and 15% since September 2025 (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026); the Hong Kong dollar tier breaks are not on a page opened (U), so the premium on HK$35m is in the order of HK$8–9m (computed on the US$ breaks at a rough HK$7.8 rate; U). (2) Hong Kong: no VAT, GST or import duty on art (from memory, U). (3) Shipping Hong Kong–Shanghai: crate, freight and transit cover quoted by a fine-art shipper; book 4–8 weeks ahead and insure at 1–3% of value (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S). (4) Mainland import, if the work clears for home use: import duty on paintings at a low provisional rate and import VAT at 13% (both from memory, U — the law-firm guide that would have confirmed them refused to load); on a HK$44m duty-paid invoice the VAT alone is in the order of HK$5.7m (computed, U). (5) The Shanghai FTZ bonded warehouse: duty and VAT suspended while the work is in bond and for bonded exhibition, under the 2020 policy (China Daily / China Services Info, 2020); storage and handling per the operator’s tariff (not opened, U). (6) Cultural-relics clearance: the import of a 1950s Zao Wou-Ki is not a relic import, but any onward export from the mainland of works by deceased artists goes through the cultural-relics export review (from memory, U). (7) Insurance and storage in Hong Kong if the work stays there: quoted case by case; the houses and the fine-art warehouses in Hong Kong offer it (U).

cases.task: I want my first Enwonwu or El Anatsui at Bonhams in London and I want to know the all-in price, how to get it to Lagos safely, and whether the London scene is the right place to buy it at all.
cases.artist: Ben Enwonwu (also El Anatsui, Amoako Boafo)
cases.sum: £60,000–200,000 hammer; worked at £150,000 (the low estimate of Enwonwu’s Negritude at Bonhams, 8 October 2025)
cases.reading: Bonhams London is the specialist room for this material. Its Modern & Contemporary African Art sale of 8 October 2025, on view at New Bond Street and timed with the Tate Modern exhibition of Nigerian modernism that opened the same day, offered Ben Enwonwu’s Negritude at £150,000–200,000, Clara Etso Ugbodaga-Ngu’s The labourer’s song at £100,000–150,000, Uzo Egonu’s Coffee House at Bad Orb at £25,000–35,000, El Anatsui’s Change goes on at £70,000–100,000, a Kentridge at £150,000–200,000, Papa Ibra Tall at £60,000–90,000, Gerard Sekoto at £60,000–90,000 and Pascale Marthine Tayou at £25,000–35,000; the head of department Helene Love-Allotey called it ‘a rare opportunity to engage with the foundational voices of Nigerian modernism’ (Bonhams press release, pre-sale, 2025). The results of that sale and of the March 2026 sale were not opened in this session; HENI’s headlines put the March 2026 London sale at US$2.35m, the March 2025 sale at US$2m led by Sekoto and the 2024 sale at US$1.65m led by Enwonwu (headlines only, not opened, U), and a trade headline reports an Irma Stern record in the autumn 2026 African sales (not opened, U). The segment is small — a whole sale at US$2m — and thin at the top: a single Enwonwu lot at estimate is a tenth of the sale. The wider contemporary market is cautious: Sotheby’s London Contemporary evening sale on 15 October 2026 left six of 34 lots unsold, and the paper called the unsold young-artist lots ‘concerning’ for the ultra-contemporary segment (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026) — a warning for the Boafo end of this list.
cases.money: Line by line at a £150,000 hammer at Bonhams London. (1) Buyer’s premium: Bonhams publishes a tiered premium on its site, highest on the lowest band; the page was not opened and the tiers are not carried here (U). For scale, Sotheby’s charges 28% and Christie’s 27% on the lowest band in London (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026), so budget about £40,000–42,000 of premium on £150,000 (computed at 27–28%, U for Bonhams). (2) UK VAT at 20% on the premium, not charged or refunded when the house exports the lot (from memory, U). (3) Export licence: Enwonwu’s Negritude is over 50 years old, so at a declared value of £180,000 or more an oil painting needs an individual Arts Council export licence, and other categories need one from £65,000 (Arts Council England, UK OGEL value limits); El Anatsui’s and Boafo’s recent works are under 50 years old and need none (same source, by the age limits). (4) Shipping London–Lagos: a museum crate, air freight and transit cover; an aggregator’s guide gives cover at 1–3% of declared value and advises booking 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S). (5) Nigerian or Ghanaian import duty and VAT on paintings: not established on any page opened in this session (U); the persona should get the shipper’s customs broker to quote the line in writing before bidding. (6) Insurance in Lagos: a fine-art policy quoted case by case; the transit insurer’s 1–3% is the benchmark (FreightAmigo, 2026, S). (7) A gallery alternative at Art X Lagos (held each November, from memory, U) carries no premium, no export licence and no international freight.

cases.task: I bought a €15,000 painting by an emerging artist from a gallery in 2023 and want to sell it in 2026 — what did I really pay, what does the artist get on resale, which house will take it, and what will the market give me now?
cases.sum: €15,000 gallery price in 2023; resale in 2026 at a fraction of it on current evidence
cases.reading: The secondary market for emerging work has turned. At Sotheby’s London Contemporary evening sale on 15 October 2026 works by Lynette Yiadom-Boakye and Jadé Fadojutimi went unsold, which The Art Newspaper called ‘concerning’ for the ultra-contemporary segment, reporting that buyers were no longer willing to pay inflated prices for young artists; the sale as a whole made £36.9m at hammer against a £39.5m low estimate with six of 34 lots unsold, and a 2021 Kusama hammered at a quarter of its £1m low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026). The dealer Thomas Stauffer told the paper that collectors ‘are not willing to take big risks’ and set limits conservatively (same source). In New York in May 2026 an adviser said buyers ‘are just not spending money in the middle’ (The Art Newspaper, 21 May 2026). For a €15,000 gallery purchase of 2023 the realistic 2026 outcome is a day-sale or online-sale estimate well below the gallery price unless the artist has since had institutional traction; the German side has one piece of good news — the VAT on art sales returned to the reduced 7% rate on 1 January 2025 after years at 19%, under the Jahressteuergesetz 2024 approved by the Bundesrat on 22 November 2024, which the Federal Government presented as support for galleries and artists (Bundesregierung press release 295, 22 November 2024).
cases.money: Line by line. (1) What was paid in 2023: €15,000 including German VAT at the 19% standard rate that applied to gallery sales until 31 December 2024 (the rate before 2025 is from memory, U; the change is on the Federal Government’s page) — about €2,395 of the price was VAT (computed). (2) The gallery’s terms: a typical primary-market split of 50/50 between gallery and artist and a request not to resell for a period (trade practice from memory, U; no gallery contract opened). (3) Selling in 2026 through a German dealer or house: 7% VAT applies to the supply of art objects from 1 January 2025 (Bundesregierung, 22 November 2024); a private seller is not a taxable person, so the VAT falls on the house’s commission and, where the house sells under the margin scheme, on its margin (from memory, U). (4) Folgerecht: the artist’s resale right under §26 UrhG applies when an art-market professional is involved; the rate is 4% of the price up to €50,000 on a sliding scale down to 0.25% above €500,000, with a minimum sale price of €400 and a cap of €12,500, collected through VG Bild-Kunst (all from memory, U; the statute was not opened). On a €6,000 hammer that is €240 (computed, U). (5) Seller’s commission at a German house: the houses that take a €6,000–15,000 lot — Grisebach in Berlin, Ketterer in Munich, Lempertz and Van Ham in Cologne — publish seller’s commissions and minimum lot values on their sites (names and the existence of minimums from memory, U; no house page opened), typically a seller’s commission of 10–20% plus catalogue and insurance charges (U). Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips do not take a lot at this value in their evening sales; Phillips charges buyers 29% on the lowest band and the others 27–28% (Grossman LLP, 14 May 2026; The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026), which the buyer prices in. (6) Income tax on the gain: a private sale of a movable asset held for more than one year is outside §23 EStG and tax-free; within one year the gain is taxable above the annual threshold (from memory, U) — three years after purchase there is no tax, but on current evidence there is no gain either. (7) Export: a sale outside the EU of a painting under 50 years old needs no export licence under the EU regulation or the Kulturgutschutzgesetz thresholds (from memory, U).

cases.persona: a family in Connecticut that has inherited a collection
cases.task: Our mother left us a collection appraised in the tens of millions — do we sell, give it to a museum, or keep it, and what does the IRS want from us first?
cases.sum: a collection above the 2026 federal estate-tax exclusion (US$15m per person in 2026, from memory, U); worked on a US$20m appraisal
cases.reading: The first reader of the family’s numbers is the IRS. Art Appraisal Services, a team of appraisers inside the IRS Independent Office of Appeals, reviews the fair market value claimed for art in federal income, estate and gift tax cases, advised by the Commissioner’s Art Advisory Panel of up to 25 unpaid art experts established in 1968 and chaired by the AAS Director; the Panel gives oral opinions and AAS makes the final determinations, and the works it looks at generally have individual values above US$150,000, at AAS’s discretion (IRS, Art Appraisal Services, last reviewed 28 June 2026). The market the appraisal is read against is cautious: Christie’s 21st Century evening sale in New York made US$136.8m on 20 May 2026 with 95% sold but a Richter trophy below estimate and an adviser saying buyers ‘are just not spending money in the middle’ (The Art Newspaper, 21 May 2026); Sotheby’s London Contemporary sale on 15 October 2026 fell short of its low estimate at hammer with six of 34 lots unsold (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026). The houses’ seller’s terms are bespoke since February 2025 (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024), and an estate of this size gets a proposal, often with a guarantee or a fee-free deal, that no page publishes. The federal estate-tax exclusion is US$15m per person for 2026 under the 2025 tax act, with a 40% rate above it, and Connecticut levies its own estate tax at a flat 12% with an exemption tied to the federal figure (all from memory, U; no IRS or Connecticut page on the exclusion was opened).
cases.money: Line by line on a US$20m collection. (1) The estate appraisal: a qualified appraisal for the estate-tax return, with the IRS citing 26 CFR §§20.2031-1 and 20.2031-6 for estate valuation (IRS, Art Appraisal Services); an appraiser’s fee quoted by the hour or the item (U). (2) Federal estate tax: on the value above the exclusion of US$15m (2026, from memory, U) at 40% (U) — US$2m on US$20m for a single decedent, computed on those figures (U); the heirs take a stepped-up basis to date-of-death value under IRC §1014 (from memory, U), which is what makes a sale soon after death nearly gain-free. (3) Connecticut estate tax: a flat 12% above the state exemption (from memory, U). (4) The Statement of Value option: a taxpayer can ask AAS to review an art valuation before filing, for items appraised at US$50,000 or more, at a fee of US$8,400 for one to three items and US$800 for each additional item under Internal Revenue Bulletin 2026-01, paid by direct debit through Pay.gov; AAS may decline a request (IRS, Art Appraisal Services). (5) Selling: seller’s commission by bespoke terms (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024); buyers pay 27–29% on the lowest band at the three houses (Grossman LLP, 14 May 2026), which sets the net the room can bear; capital gains on any rise above the stepped-up basis at the collectibles rate of 28% plus the 3.8% net investment income tax (from memory, U). (6) Giving: a charitable deduction at fair market value for a gift of art to a museum that will use it for its exempt purpose, limited to basis where the use is unrelated (IRC §170(e)(1)(B)(i), from memory, U); the deduction for appreciated property to a public charity is capped at 30% of adjusted gross income with a five-year carry-forward (from memory, U); a qualified appraisal is required where the deduction for an item exceeds US$5,000, signed and dated no earlier than 60 days before the gift and received by the return’s due date, with Form 8283 Section B for each item not part of a group (IRS, Art Appraisal Services); the appraisal is also the IRS’s own guide, Publication 561 (same source). (7) Fractional gifts: IRC §170(o) requires the gift to be completed within ten years or at death, values later fractions at no more than the initial appraisal, and recaptures the deduction if the museum does not take possession (from memory, U). (8) Keeping: insurance at a fine-art rate, storage, conservation and the next generation’s estate tax (quoted case by case).

cases.task: We have a £6m collection and we are divorcing — how will the court value it, who pays the expert, will it be sold, and what tax does moving pictures between us trigger?
cases.sum: £6m (the persona’s figure); the reported case below involved a personal collection the expert valued at £1,180,850 and an art business valued at £13m
cases.reading: English family courts value art through a single joint expert and then discount it hard for the sale the order implies. In GO v YA [2024] EWFC 411 the court first directed a full inventory to be valued by a single joint expert, but the expert’s fee of about £150,000 plus VAT was seen as too costly, so the parties moved to a sample: the wife chose up to 375 pieces, about 10% of the inventory, with costs capped at £70,000 plus VAT and the method of extrapolation left for later; the expert valued one painting at £550,000 where the husband had said £50,000 and the personal collection at £1,180,850 where the husband had said about £153,000; the expert advised a 70–75% discount for an immediate sale and 20–25% for a sale staggered over seven and a half years, which the judge accepted, and the judge applied the expert’s figures to the sampled items but refused to apply the same uplift to the roughly 90% not valued; because the husband did not put his challenge to the expert in cross-examination the court was bound to accept the evidence (Browne v Dunn [1893] 6 R 67); the business was valued at £13m on a seven-year staggered-sale assumption and the wife was awarded two lump sums, with the husband to sell his shares if the second was not paid (Forsters LLP, 4 August 2025, on GO v YA). The judgment cited Versteegh v Versteegh [2018] EWCA Civ 1050 and H v H [2008] EWHC 935 (Fam) on the fragility of private valuations (same source). The market the expert reads is soft in the middle: Sotheby’s London Contemporary sale of 15 October 2026 fell short of its low estimate at hammer with six of 34 lots unsold (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026).
cases.money: Line by line on a £6m collection. (1) The single joint expert: the fee in GO v YA was quoted at about £150,000 plus VAT for a full inventory and capped at £70,000 plus VAT for a 10% sample (Forsters, 2025); for a collection of a few dozen works the fee is a fraction of that (U). (2) The valuation basis and date: the expert values at open market value as at the hearing, net of the costs of sale the order implies, which is why the GO v YA discounts of 70–75% (immediate) and 20–25% (staggered) matter more than the headline figure (Forsters, 2025; the basis and date from memory of practice, U). (3) Costs of sale if the court orders one: seller’s commission by bespoke terms (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024) and the buyer’s premium of 27–28% on the lowest band that the room prices in (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026). (4) Capital gains tax on a transfer between spouses: a transfer is at no gain and no loss under s.58 TCGA 1992 while the couple live together, and since 6 April 2023 the no-gain-no-loss window runs for three tax years after the year of separation and without limit for transfers under a court order (Finance (No.2) Act 2023, from memory, U); a sale to a third party is chargeable at the CGT rate for chattels, with the £6,000 chattels exemption per item and the annual exempt amount (rates from memory, U). (5) Inheritance-tax and trust points if the collection is in a trust: outside this case (U). (6) Legal costs of the financial remedy proceedings: by the hour; the Family Procedure Rules Part 25 govern expert evidence (from memory, U).

cases.whispers: Forsters LLP (4 August 2025) drew the lessons of GO v YA: sample valuations, heavy discounts and the Browne v Dunn trap. The Art Newspaper (16 October 2026) reported a cautious London market with dealers saying collectors ‘are not willing to take big risks’. The Art Newspaper (19 December 2024) reported seller’s terms returning to bespoke at Sotheby’s. Spear’s and other wealth titles ran pieces on hidden chattels in divorce (headlines seen, not opened, U).
risks: The discount: 70–75% off for an immediate sale and 20–25% for a staggered one were accepted in GO v YA (Forsters, 2025); the £6m insurance figure is not what the court will use.
Not challenging the expert: the husband’s silence in cross-examination bound the court to the expert’s figures (Forsters, 2025).
The expert’s cost: £150,000 plus VAT was the quote for a full inventory in GO v YA (Forsters, 2025).
Missing the no-gain-no-loss window on transfers after separation (three tax years, from memory, U).
A forced sale into a soft market: six of 34 lots unsold at Sotheby’s London in October 2026 (The Art Newspaper).
cases.value_left: The houses value for insurance and for sale, not for the Family Court’s discounted basis; the law firms publish the cases but not a calculator; HMRC’s s.58 window is a date rule nobody runs for the parties. The persona cannot today see the collection at insurance value, at the expert’s open-market value, after the sale-timetable discount and after CGT on one sheet; the terminal can, with GO v YA as the worked precedent.

cases.task: I want to borrow against a US$10m collection without selling — who lends, at what advance and rate, where the pictures have to sit, and what the Swiss pledge rules do to that.
cases.sum: US$10m appraised value; a loan in the US$4–5m range at the advance rates the trade reports (from memory, U)
cases.reading: Art-secured lending is a house product and a private-bank product. Sotheby’s Financial Services describes loans ‘from US$1 million to over US$250 million’ secured by the appraised value of the collection, says that ‘in many cases, clients retain possession of their artworks throughout the life of the loan’ where insurance and security requirements are met, with in-residence possession available only in certain locations and approved storage vendors otherwise, and that ‘most loans close within approximately six weeks, depending on collateral and location’; it notes products may not be available in all locations and that terms depend on the jurisdiction (Sotheby’s, Art-Backed Lending 101, 2 December 2025, modified 15 October 2026). It does not publish the advance rate, the term or the rate basis. The trade press has reported Sotheby’s US$700m art-backed debt securitisation (The Art Newspaper headline, 23 May 2024, not opened, U) and in January 2026 Puck ran ‘the art-backed loan crisis that wasn’t’ (headline, not opened, U); Deloitte’s Art & Finance reports of 2025 and 2026 size the market (not opened, U). The collateral the lender reads is a cautious market: trophy lots hold and the middle is weak (The Art Newspaper, 21 May and 16 October 2026), and the lender’s appraisal will follow the low estimates, not the insurance schedule.
cases.money: Line by line on a US$10m collection. (1) Advance: the lenders’ advance rate is not on the Sotheby’s page; the trade convention is around 40–50% of the lender’s own low-estimate appraisal (from memory, U), so about US$4–5m here. (2) Rate: not published by Sotheby’s; bank art loans price off a reference rate plus a spread and specialist lenders higher, in the high single digits to low double digits in 2025–26 (from memory, U). (3) Appraisal: the lender’s own specialists appraise; a fee may apply (U). (4) Arrangement and legal fees: by the lender; not published (U). (5) Insurance: the borrower insures at agreed value with the lender named as loss payee (trade practice, U). (6) Possession: in-residence in certain locations or approved storage; in Switzerland a pledge of movables is a possessory pledge under Art. 884 of the Civil Code, so the lender or a third-party depositary must hold the works — the Geneva free port and bonded warehouses serve that role — whereas a US lender perfects a security interest by filing a UCC-1 financing statement under Article 9 and can leave the work on the wall (both from memory, U; the Civil Code was not opened). (7) Swiss import VAT if the works come into Switzerland from abroad: 8.1% since 1 January 2024, suspended in a bonded warehouse (from memory, U). (8) Storage at a Geneva bonded warehouse: per the operator’s tariff (not opened, U). (9) Time: about six weeks to close (Sotheby’s, 2025).

cases.task: A New York museum wants my painting for a year — what should the loan agreement say, what protects it from seizure, who insures it nail to nail, and what does the French side need before it leaves?
cases.category: Modern (a painting over 50 years old, so the French export rules bite)
cases.sum: an agreed insurance value set in the loan agreement (the persona’s figure); nothing changes hands
cases.reading: A museum loan is a contract, an insurance policy and two sets of law. On the United Kingdom model, Part 6 of the Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 gives objects lent from overseas for temporary public exhibition at an approved museum or gallery immunity from seizure ordered in civil or criminal proceedings and from seizure by law enforcement, for objects of any description owned by a non-resident, provided the import complies with the law on importing goods and the museum publishes information about the object as the Secretary of State’s regulations require (Explanatory Notes to the Act, summary of Part 6, legislation.gov.uk). The approved institutions are listed by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport and the publication must precede the object’s arrival (from memory, U; the DCMS list and the regulations, SI 2007/3613, were listed but not opened). In the United States the equivalent is the Immunity from Seizure Act, 22 U.S.C. §2459: the borrowing museum applies to the State Department before import and the determination is published in the Federal Register, after which the object is immune from judicial process while in the country for exhibition; the 2016 Foreign Cultural Exchange Jurisdictional Immunity Clarification Act narrowed the use of exhibition activity to found jurisdiction against foreign states (all from memory, U; no State Department page surfaced in the searches). The museum’s standard tools are the loan agreement, the general facility report, a courier, condition reports at each end and ‘nail to nail’ all-risks insurance in the lender’s agreed value, under the museum’s own policy or the US federal indemnity administered through the National Endowment for the Arts under the Arts and Artifacts Indemnity Act (from memory, U). The lender’s own market read matters for the agreed value: evening-sale results in 2026 show trophies holding and the middle soft (The Art Newspaper, 21 May and 16 October 2026).
cases.money: Line by line. (1) The lender pays nothing in a well-drafted museum loan: the borrower bears packing, crating, transport, courier, insurance and the facility report (museum practice, from memory, U). (2) Insurance: nail-to-nail all-risks cover in the agreed value under the museum’s fine-art policy or a federal indemnity certificate; a commercial transit policy benchmark is 1–3% of declared value with cover at 110% (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S), which the museum’s blanket policy undercuts. (3) The federal indemnity: covers loans from abroad to US exhibitions with a deductible borne by the museum and a programme ceiling set by Congress (from memory, U). (4) French export: a painting over 50 years old above the EU and French value thresholds needs a certificate for a permanent export and an authorisation for a temporary one, issued by the Ministry of Culture; a work under 50 years old needs neither (thresholds and procedure from memory, U — the Code du patrimoine was not opened). (5) US import: no duty on original works of art and no sales or use tax on a loan delivered outside New York or to an exempt museum (NY Advisory Opinion TSB-A-16(17)S found a loan to a New York museum was a licence for consideration but not taxable where delivery occurred outside the state and the museum held an exempt organisation certificate under Tax Law §1116(a)(4)). (6) Courier: the lender or the lender’s registrar travels with the work at the museum’s cost (practice, U). (7) Conservation: any treatment only with the lender’s written consent (practice, U).

cases.where: Tokyo, selling in Hong Kong or New York
cases.task: I own a Kusama and want to sell it at Sotheby’s in Hong Kong or New York — can it leave Japan, what tax does the sale carry, what does it cost to ship, and is this the right year?
cases.sum: a Kusama in the US$1–3m band (the persona’s figure); the 2026 comparables below are a warning on the estimate
cases.reading: The Kusama market has cooled in 2026. At Sotheby’s London Contemporary evening sale on 15 October 2026 her I Who Was Awestruck at the Shape of the Secret I Found in the Cosmos (2021) hammered at £250,000, a quarter of its £1m low estimate, selling for £320,000 with fees in a sale that made £36.9m at hammer against a £39.5m low estimate with 82% sold (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2026). A South China Morning Post headline seen on 13 November 2026 reports the Hong Kong autumn 2026 art auctions topping HK$2bn ‘as Kusama works get a cool reception’ (page refused to load; figures not carried, U). The wider read is the same: the trade told The Art Newspaper that collectors ‘are not willing to take big risks’ (16 October 2026) and that buyers ‘are just not spending money in the middle’ (21 May 2026). Hong Kong remains the deepest room for Asian post-war work — Sotheby’s spring 2026 evening sale there was 100% sold at HK$548.4m (US$70.3m), up more than 50% on 2025 (Sotheby’s, March 2026) — but the Kusama lots of autumn 2026 did not ride that. On the Japanese side the owner’s question is whether the work can leave: Japan prohibits in principle the export of designated National Treasures, Important Cultural Properties and certified Important Art Objects under the Act for the Protection of Cultural Properties, and the Agency for Cultural Affairs issues an export appraisal certificate for antiques confirming an item is none of these when customs asks for it (Agency for Cultural Affairs, 古美術品輸出鑑査証明 page). A work by a living artist is not a designated property; whether customs asks for the certificate for a modern painting is not stated on the page (U).
cases.money: Line by line on a US$2,000,000 hammer. (1) Seller’s commission: Sotheby’s terms are bespoke since 17 February 2025, with the 2% success fee above the high estimate retained (The Art Newspaper, 19 December 2024); for a lot of this size expect a negotiated low commission (U). (2) The buyer’s premium that sets the room’s all-in: 28% up to US$2m at Sotheby’s New York and 27% up to US$1.5m at Christie’s (The Art Newspaper, 17 February 2026). (3) Japanese consumption tax: 10% (rate from memory, U); it applies to supplies by taxable persons, so a private individual selling a personal asset does not charge it, while the house’s commission for services supplied in Japan carries it and a Hong Kong or New York sale is outside its scope (all from memory, U). (4) Japanese income tax on the gain: a resident individual’s gain on the sale of art is taxable as a capital gain, with works under ¥300,000 exempt and the taxable gain halved where the work was held more than five years (from memory, U). (5) Export paperwork: the Agency’s certificate, if customs requires it, is applied for by post with two copies of the form and photographs, takes about ten business days from a complete application, with delays warned at present, and no fee is stated on the page (Agency for Cultural Affairs). (6) Shipping Tokyo–Hong Kong or New York: crate, air freight and transit cover at 1–3% of declared value, booked 4–8 weeks ahead (FreightAmigo, updated 22 October 2026, S); the house may absorb the shipping for a lot of this size (U). (7) Hong Kong: no VAT or import duty (from memory, U); New York: none on import for sale (U).

kandinsky.summary: A designated Russian businessman cannot lawfully buy a Kandinsky at a New York sale or have it taken to Moscow, and no one in the chain can lawfully help. The United States blocks his property and bars every US person (the house, its bank, the shipper) from any dealing in it (EO 14024 s.1; 31 CFR 587.201, effective 1 March 2022); separately, Commerce requires a licence, reviewed under a policy of denial, for any export of a luxury good including works of art to Russia or to an SDN-listed oligarch anywhere in the world (15 CFR 746.10 and Supplement No. 5). The EU bans the sale, supply, transfer or export of works of art (Annex XVIII, ex chapter 97) to any person in Russia or for use in Russia (Regulation 833/2014 Article 3h, from 16 March 2022; the €300 general threshold carried as known), and freezes his assets under Regulation 269/2014. The United Kingdom prohibits the export of luxury goods to or for use in Russia and making them available to a person connected with Russia (regulation 46B, from 14 April 2022), and its Schedule 3A entry for works of art, collectors’ pieces and antiques states no sales-price threshold at all; since 14 May 2025 art market participants must report designated persons and breaches to OFSI, with civil penalties of up to £1m or 50 per cent of the breach and up to seven years on indictment. Switzerland adopted the EU luxury-goods ban on 18 March 2022. The record: the Senate PSI found over US$18m of art bought in 2014 for the Rotenbergs through an adviser the houses treated as the principal, with a German storage account’s whole contents shipped to Moscow in August 2019; a London dealer was jailed for two and a half years in June 2025 for selling ‘almost £140,000’ of art to a US- and UK-sanctioned Hezbollah financier without disclosing it; the first UK luxury-goods prosecution of a gallery and its shipper, charged in November 2025, was dismissed on 8 July 2026 because the Crown could not prove the buyer was ordinarily resident in Russia; Finnish customs detained €42m of museum loans in April 2022 and released them under the EU museum derogation; RFE/RL traced US$36m of Western art into Russia through Uzbekistan in 2022–24. The lawful course for the house on receiving the enquiry is to refuse the bid, freeze anything held, and report to OFSI or OFAC; for the shipper, to refuse the Russian destination; for a non-designated Russian national, the destination bans still apply and the house must establish residence and end-use before selling.

walls.n: US blocking sanctions: dealing in the blocked property of a designated person
walls.cite: Executive Order 14024 of 15 April 2021, section 1; 31 CFR Part 587 (Russian Harmful Foreign Activities Sanctions Regulations), § 587.201, 87 FR 11297, effective 1 March 2022
walls.authority: US Department of the Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
walls.threshold: None. Every dealing in blocked property is prohibited; OFAC’s 50 per cent rule extends the block to entities owned 50 per cent or more by one or more blocked persons (stated from OFAC practice, not read on the page)
walls.date: EO 14024 of 15 April 2021; regulations effective 1 March 2022; earlier Russia designations (the Rotenbergs) sit under EO 13661 of 16 March 2014
walls.what_it_does: Section 587.201(a) provides that all transactions prohibited pursuant to EO 14024 are prohibited pursuant to Part 587. Under section 1 of EO 14024 the property and interests in property of a designated person that are in the United States or in the possession or control of a US person are blocked and ‘may not be transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in’. A New York auction house, its bank and a US shipper are US persons: they may not accept a bid, a payment or a consignment from a designated person, or release a lot to him or to anyone acting for him, without an OFAC licence. Section 587.202 voids transfers made in breach.
walls.case: The Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (29 July 2020) traced over US$18m of art bought in the United States in 2014 to shell companies linked to Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, designated under EO 13661 on 20 March 2014; the purchases ran through a Moscow art adviser, and the houses treated the adviser as the principal. No house was charged; the houses stopped dealing with the adviser during the inquiry.
src: Federal Register, 87 FR 11297, Russian Harmful Foreign Activities Sanctions Regulations (1 March 2022)

walls.n: US export control: luxury goods, including works of art, to Russia and Belarus and to listed oligarchs anywhere
walls.cite: 15 CFR § 746.10 (Export Administration Regulations), with Supplement No. 5 to Part 746 (the luxury-goods list); rule of 11 March 2022 (87 FR 14785)
walls.authority: US Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
walls.threshold: Supplement No. 5 lists luxury goods by HTS heading; works of art, collectors’ pieces and antiques fall under chapter 97. The section text read in this session states no dollar threshold; the per-item wholesale-price thresholds that apply to many Supplement No. 5 entries could not be confirmed for chapter 97 in this session (see note).
walls.what_it_does: A licence is required for the export, re-export or in-country transfer to or within Russia or Belarus of any luxury good subject to the EAR listed in Supplement No. 5 (§ 746.10(a)(1)); and, wherever in the world the recipient is, for any luxury good to a Russian or Belarusian ‘oligarch or malign actor’, defined as a natural person designated on OFAC’s SDN List under the stated programmes (§ 746.10(a)(2)). Applications are reviewed under a policy of denial. No licence exception overrides the (a)(2) requirement; only BAG (personal baggage, excluding firearms) and a sliver of AVS override (a)(1). So the Kandinsky may not lawfully be exported from the United States to Moscow, and may not be exported from the United States to the designated buyer anywhere, without a BIS licence that policy says will be denied.

walls.n: The ‘agent as principal’ finding: houses treating an art adviser as the client
walls.cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, majority and minority staff report, The Art Industry and U.S. Policies that Undermine Sanctions, 29 July 2020, Findings 1, 4 and 14
walls.authority: US Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations
walls.threshold: Not a legal threshold; the report notes the EU then required AML checks on art transactions of €10,000 or more and the US Bank Secrecy Act did not cover art dealers or auction houses
walls.what_it_does: Finding 4: ‘The auction houses treated an art agent or dealer as the principal purchaser of art’, which the report calls a significant AML vulnerability. Finding 14: the houses ‘failed to ask basic questions of Mr. Baltser, including for whom he purchased art’. Finding 1: ‘The art market is the largest legal, unregulated market in the United States.’ The report recommends amending the Bank Secrecy Act to cover high-value art businesses, beneficial-ownership collection, concurrent sanctions on family members, and OFAC guidance for houses and dealers on identifying the principal. The compliance consequence for a New York house: the identity of the ultimate beneficial buyer must be established before a bid is accepted, because the sanctions prohibition attaches to the principal, not the agent.
walls.case: Christie’s signed a partnership with the Moscow agency BALTZER in February 2014; its chief AML officer gave one annual certification (December 2014) and then none for about three years. Sotheby’s declined the agency’s proposal but continued business with the adviser. Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips stopped transacting with him during the investigation. The report records that a Sotheby’s employee first said the adviser’s clients included the Rotenbergs and then told the Subcommittee she had fabricated this.

walls.n: US anti-money-laundering position on art: the Bank Secrecy Act does not yet cover art dealers or auction houses; the Art Market Integrity Act (2025) would
walls.cite: Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (extends the BSA to dealers in antiquities, not art); US Treasury, Study of the Facilitation of Money Laundering and Terror Finance Through the Trade in Works of Art (2022); Art Market Integrity Act, announced 23 July 2025 by Senators Grassley and Fetterman
walls.authority: US Congress; US Department of the Treasury, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)
walls.threshold: The bill as described would exempt persons with no single art transaction above US$10,000 or less than US$50,000 of art transactions in the prior year, and sellers of self-created works (threshold wording to be checked against the bill text)
walls.date: AMLA: 1 January 2021; Treasury study: 2022; AMIA announced 23 July 2025, not enacted as of the 21 August 2025 note; no later status opened in this session
walls.what_it_does: As of today the sanctions prohibitions bind a New York house, but the Bank Secrecy Act’s programme, reporting and customer-due-diligence duties do not. AMLA 2020 added antiquities dealers to the BSA; FinCEN’s antiquities rule had not been reported final in the note read. The Treasury’s 2022 study found the art market, ‘while not the highest area of risk’, susceptible to abuse. The AMIA would amend the BSA to cover ‘a person engaged in the trade in works of art’ (dealers, galleries, advisers, consultants, custodians, auction houses, museums), requiring AML programmes, customer identification, suspicious activity and currency transaction reporting, an AML officer, training and independent testing, and would direct FinCEN to build an examination regime. A similar bill, H.R. 5886 in the 115th Congress, did not leave committee.
walls.case: The Senate PSI report (2020) is the record on which the bill rests: over US$18m of art bought for the Rotenbergs after their designation, with no BSA duty on the houses.
