walls.n: EU trade sanction: luxury goods, including works of art, to Russia
walls.cite: Council Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, Article 3h and Annex XVIII (inserted by Regulation (EU) 2022/428 of 15 March 2022)
walls.authority: Council of the European Union; enforcement by the Member States’ customs and prosecutors
walls.threshold: Annex XVIII lists ‘ex 97 Works of art, collectors’ pieces and antiques’ (German text: Kunstgegenstände, Sammlungsstücke und Antiquitäten) with no item-specific threshold; the general threshold of Article 3h(2), €300 per item unless the Annex says otherwise, is carried from the regulation text as known and was not read on an official page in this session (see note)
walls.what_it_does: Article 3h prohibits selling, supplying, transferring or exporting the luxury goods in Annex XVIII, directly or indirectly, to any natural or legal person, entity or body in Russia or for use in Russia. Works of art are in the Annex at heading level (ex 97). The prohibition is destination-based: it applies to a sale to a non-designated Russian buyer for delivery to Russia as much as to a designated one.

walls.n: UK trade sanction: export of luxury goods, including works of art, to Russia
walls.cite: Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/855), regulation 46B and Schedule 3A, inserted by the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) (Amendment) (No. 8) Regulations 2022 (SI 2022/452)
walls.authority: Department for Business and Trade (trade sanctions licensing); HM Revenue & Customs (enforcement at the border); Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (the regulations)
walls.threshold: Schedule 3A item 21 reads: ‘Works of art, collectors’ pieces and antiques, meaning any thing which falls within chapter 97.’ The entry states no sales-price threshold. Other Schedule 3A entries carry thresholds (for example £250 per item for most goods, £630 and £840 for electronic and photographic goods, £42,000 per vehicle); the works of art entry does not.
walls.date: In force 5.00 p.m. on 14 April 2022; Schedule 3A Part 2 has since been amended by SI 2023/1364 (15 December 2023), SI 2025/504 (24 April 2025) and SI 2026/543 (20 May 2026); the works of art entry as currently printed was not re-read after those amendments (see note)
walls.what_it_does: Regulation 46B(1): ‘The export of luxury goods to, or for use in, Russia is prohibited.’ Regulation 46B(2): a person must not directly or indirectly supply luxury goods from a third country into Russia, make them available to a person connected with Russia, or make them available for use in Russia. The prohibition attaches to the destination and the connection with Russia, not to the buyer’s designation: a London house or shipper may not ship a painting to Moscow for any buyer. Breach is a criminal offence; it is a defence that the person did not know and had no reasonable cause to suspect the goods were destined for, connected with or for use in Russia.
walls.case: The Ojiri prosecution (2025) and the Hauser & Wirth and shipper charges (November 2025) are set out in the cases list.
src: Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) (Amendment) (No. 8) Regulations 2022, SI 2022/452, as made

The current revised Schedule 3A page confirms the structure, the per-entry thresholds and the amendment history but the extract read in this session was truncated before item 21; the 2025 and 2026 amendments are described on legislation.gov.uk as omitting words from Part 2, and whether they touched item 21 was not confirmed.

walls.n: UK financial sanctions: the asset freeze and the duty on art market participants to report to OFSI
walls.cite: Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018; Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019; OFSI, Financial sanctions guidance for high value dealers and art market participants (first published 14 November 2024, updated 12 May 2026); Policing and Crime Act 2017 (monetary penalties)
walls.authority: HM Treasury, Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI)
walls.threshold: The reporting duty covers an art market participant (a firm registered or required to register with HMRC as one) in respect of trading or intermediary transactions worth £10,000 or more, including linked transactions, and storage of art worth £10,000 or more for a person; a high value dealer is caught by cash payments of £10,000 or more in total. The asset freeze itself has no threshold.
walls.date: Reporting duty from 14 May 2025; guidance updated 12 May 2026
walls.what_it_does: From 14 May 2025 art market participants and high value dealers are ‘relevant firms’ and must tell OFSI as soon as practicable if they know or have reasonable cause to suspect that a person is a designated person or has breached the regulations, with the information behind the suspicion and, for a designated customer, the nature and amount of funds or economic resources held. On discovering that a counterparty is designated the firm must immediately stop dealing with them, freeze any assets held for them and inform OFSI. OFSI can impose civil monetary penalties of up to £1 million or 50 per cent of the breach, whichever is higher; breach is a criminal offence with up to seven years on indictment; failure to report is a separate summary offence (up to six months, a fine, or both). A licence is written permission for an otherwise prohibited act; trade licences come from the Department for Business and Trade, and one activity may need both.
walls.case: Ojiri (2025) is the first conviction under the UK Russia regulations of an art market participant; see the cases list.
src: OFSI, Financial sanctions guidance for high value dealers and art market participants (gov.uk)

walls.n: UK export licence for works of art leaving the United Kingdom (the Waverley system)
walls.cite: Export Control Act 2002, s.10(1)(a) (the annual report to Parliament); Export of Objects of Cultural Interest (Control) Order 2003 (not read); Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest, Annual Report 2024–25 (1 May 2024 to 30 April 2025)
walls.authority: Arts Council England (Export Licensing Unit) for the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport; the Reviewing Committee
walls.threshold: The value thresholds by category above which an object over 50 years old needs an individual licence were not printed in the report read; the report records 5,745 individual export licence applications in 2024–25 (5,035 the year before) and 28,307 items licensed after expert-adviser referral, worth £955,143,117
walls.date: Report period 1 May 2024 to 30 April 2025; published July 2025
walls.what_it_does: An object leaving the UK above the age and value thresholds needs an individual export licence; an expert adviser may refer it to the Reviewing Committee, which tests it against the three Waverley criteria (closely connected with our history and national life; outstanding aesthetic importance; outstanding significance for the study of some particular branch of art, learning or history) and may recommend deferral so a UK buyer can match the price. In 2024–25 the Committee considered 20 objects, found 18 met at least one criterion, and the Secretary of State deferred all 18 (aggregate £40,009,133); six were saved for £586,132 (1.5 per cent of deferred value), nine left after no offer (£16,969,020), and three were still under deferral at publication (a Hepworth, a Botticelli, a Rubens modello, together £22,453,981). For the Kandinsky case the licence is a separate control from sanctions: a licence to export does not license a sale to a designated person or a shipment to Russia, and the trade-sanctions prohibition bars the Russian destination whatever the licence says.
walls.case: Cases 11, 19 and 20 of the 2024–25 report (Hepworth, Botticelli, Rubens) were under deferral at publication; the report records the Hepworth Wakefield holding an option agreement on case 11.
src: Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art, Annual Report 2024–25 (gov.uk)
walls.note: The category value thresholds and the stated licence processing time were not in the report; the Arts Council’s guidance page was not opened.

walls.n: Switzerland: the luxury-goods export ban adopted from the EU
walls.cite: Ordinance on Measures connected with the Situation in Ukraine (SR 946.231.176.72); Federal Council decision of 18 March 2022 adopting the EU’s luxury-goods export ban
walls.authority: Swiss Federal Council; State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), sanctions enquiries
walls.threshold: The Federal Council release of 18 March 2022 gives no list of goods or threshold; the ordinance’s annex mirrors Annex XVIII (works of art ex 97) with a CHF 300 per item general threshold as known, not read in this session
walls.date: 18 March 2022 (adoption); in force in the following days per the release; the ordinance has been amended with each EU package since (the 16th to 19th packages in 2025–26 per law-firm trackers seen in search results, not opened)
walls.what_it_does: The Federal Council stated on 18 March 2022 that it adopted the EU’s further measures including ‘the ban on the export of luxury goods’, noting it ‘affects only a small portion of Switzerland’s global exports of such goods’. SECO is the contact for business enquiries. A Geneva free-port or a Basel dealer is therefore under the same destination-based ban on shipping a work of art to Russia as an EU house.
walls.case: None opened for art.
src: Swiss Federal Council / EAER, Ukraine: Adoption of further EU sanctions against Russia (18 March 2022)
walls.note: The ordinance article on luxury goods and the CHF threshold were not read; stated as known and flagged.

walls.n: Third-country routes: the re-export cases as the press reported them (Uzbekistan; the UAE, Hong Kong, Turkey, Kazakhstan and Armenia not opened)
walls.cite: RFE/RL (Systema) investigation of 6 September 2024
walls.authority: No authority: reporting. The EU rule at issue is the Annex XVIII luxury-goods ban (works of art above €300 as the article states it)
walls.threshold: €300 per item for works of art and antiques, as RFE/RL states the March 2022 EU, US and Swiss measures
walls.what_it_does: RFE/RL reported that an Uzbek logistics firm in Tashkent ‘helped import more than 200 works of art into Russia over the past two years’, estimated at over US$36m; customs data showed 1,962 shipments into Russia from Uzbekistan since the invasion with a declared value of US$41.6m, of which artworks were US$36.6m. In one case a Dutch art shipper unloaded 44 works (Dalí, Renoir, Matisse; US$4.6m) from a yacht at Vlissingen in January 2023 that went to Amsterdam, Tashkent and then Moscow; the shipper told RFE/RL it did not know the final destination; the yacht’s reported owner was sanctioned by the UK in February 2023. The article records no enforcement outcome against the logistics firm or the route. The compliance point is the one the article’s lawyer makes: liability turns on what the shipper knew or should have known about the final destination, which is why EU and UK shippers now demand end-use declarations and refuse Russian consignees. Positions of the UAE, Hong Kong, Turkey, Kazakhstan and Armenia on Russia sanctions were not opened in this session.
walls.case: As above; no prosecution reported. The same article records the UK seizure of a Fabergé egg of Viktor Vekselberg (May 2022) and the German police seizure of 30 paintings and four Fabergé eggs from Alisher Usmanov’s yacht (November 2022), as reported.
src: RFE/RL, 6 September 2024, investigation into art imports into Russia via Uzbekistan

cases.n: The Rotenberg purchases (Senate PSI report, 29 July 2020)
cases.what: The Subcommittee traced over US$18m of art bought in the United States in 2014 (the report gives the window as March to November 2014 in one place and May to November 2014 in another) to shell companies linked to Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, designated by OFAC on 20 March 2014 under EO 13661 (issued 16 March 2014). Rotenberg-linked companies moved over US$120m to Russia in the four days between the order and the designations, and were involved in over US$91m of transactions after the sanctions. The purchases ran through a Moscow-based art adviser (Gregory Baltser) who received US$1,116,000 in fees (US$9,500 a month, March 2010 to October 2018) from a company, Steamort, whose owner the Subcommittee could not identify. René Magritte’s La Poitrine was bought for US$7.5m in May 2014 through a private dealer; title went to Highland Ventures and the funds traced through Advantage Alliance to Senton Holdings, which a financial institution determined was owned by Arkady Rotenberg. Lyonel Feininger’s Brücke II, bought in February 2014 through the adviser, was withdrawn by Sotheby’s from a February 2019 sale (estimate £4m–6m) ‘due to a lack of interest’. Status: a staff report; it records no charge against any house or dealer. Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips stopped transacting with the adviser during the inquiry.

cases.n: The art shipped to Moscow in 2019 (Senate PSI report)
cases.what: The report records that art linked to the Rotenbergs was stored at the Hasenkamp facility in Germany; in August 2019 the storage account was closed and ‘all art stored under the account was shipped to Moscow’. The report does not state that La Poitrine specifically was among the works shipped. Status: as the report states it; no enforcement outcome is recorded against the storage firm.

cases.n: R v Hauser & Wirth Gallery Ltd and Artay Rauchwerger Solomons Ltd [2026] EWCR 7 (charged November 2025; charges dismissed July 2026)
cases.what: The Art Newspaper reported on 13 November 2025 that Hauser & Wirth’s UK gallery and the shipping company Artay Rauchwerger Solomons Ltd had been charged with two offences of making luxury goods available to a ‘person connected with Russia’, contrary to regulation 46B(2)(b) of the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019, over the sale of George Condo’s work on paper Escape from Humanity (2021) between 14 April and 31 December 2022 to the collector Alexander Popov, who The Art Newspaper states ‘is not under UK sanctions and was not accused of any wrongdoing’. The charges turned on whether the buyer was ordinarily resident in Russia. On 8 July 2026 (the day before The Art Newspaper’s 9 July report) HHJ Baumgartner at Southwark Crown Court dismissed both charges against both defendants under Schedule 3 paragraph 2 of the Crime and Disorder Act 1998, finding sufficient evidence that the work was made available to the buyer but not that he was ordinarily resident in Russia at the time of the sale. The gallery said it ‘strongly contested these proceedings and denied any wrongdoing’ and that the court ‘dismissed the case against our UK gallery in its entirety’. The prosecuting authority was not named in either report. Status: dismissed, July 2026; no appeal reported.
src: The Art Newspaper, 9 July 2026, Hauser & Wirth cleared of Russian sanction charges
Global Sanctions, 13 July 2026, UK Crown Court grants application to dismiss charges against London art gallery
cases.note: The brief described this matter as pending; as of 13 November 2026 the record shows the charges dismissed on 8 July 2026. The 13 November 2025 charge report was not opened separately; its date is taken from the July article’s link.

cases.n: R v Oghenochuko (Ochuko) Ojiri (Central Criminal Court, sentenced 6 June 2025)
cases.what: The Crown Prosecution Service states that the art dealer and television expert pleaded guilty on 9 May 2025 at Westminster Magistrates’ Court to eight offences of failing to disclose information in the regulated sector, contrary to section 21A of the Terrorism Act 2000, over eight sales of art worth ‘almost £140,000’ to Nazem Ahmad of Beirut, whom the CPS describes as sanctioned by the United States in 2019 and by the UK in 2023; the discussions ran from 24 October 2020 to 18 December 2021. On 6 June 2025 at the Central Criminal Court he was sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment with an extended 12 months on licence. The CPS says the prosecution is ‘believed to be the first of its kind’; the Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command called it ‘the first of its kind’. Status: convicted on his plea; sentenced 6 June 2025.
src: Crown Prosecution Service, statement on the sentencing of Ochuko Ojiri (6 June 2025)

cases.n: The Abramovich collection as ICIJ reported it (22 September 2023)
cases.what: ICIJ (with The Guardian, from the Cyprus Confidential leak) reported that a collection of more than 350 works ‘valued at almost $1 billion in 2018’ is owned by Seline-Invest, a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and later redomiciled to Jersey, controlled by the Ermis Trust Settlement set up in Cyprus in 2010 for Roman Abramovich’s sole benefit. In January 2021 Dasha Zhukova, his former spouse, was made an additional beneficiary with a 50 per cent interest each; on 4 February 2022, by a deed of amendment, the trustees made her ‘irrevocably entitled to 51%’ of distributions, and a later February 2022 deed barred Abramovich from increasing his stake; the UK sanctioned Abramovich in early March 2022 and the EU soon after the invasion began. ICIJ states that Zhukova ‘is not subject to sanctions in any jurisdiction and has publicly condemned the war’ and that ‘there is no suggestion that Zhukova, who is an advocate for the arts, has taken steps to undermine sanctions’; her link to the matter as reported is that of a former spouse and trust beneficiary. Works named include Monet, Degas, Matisse, Picasso, Magritte, Lucian Freud (Benefits Supervisor Sleeping, bought 2008 for US$33.6m), Francis Bacon and David Hockney. ICIJ states that ‘the collection is not subject to an asset freezing order’, that sanctions ‘may have blocked Ermis Trust’s ability to loan works’, and that the collection’s whereabouts are unknown. Abramovich declined to comment; Zhukova declined to comment on the record. Experts quoted by The Guardian linked the 51 per cent figure to the 50 per cent ownership rule under which assets more than half owned by a sanctioned person can be frozen. Status: reporting; no enforcement action against the collection is recorded in the article.
src: ICIJ, 22 September 2023, Leak reveals majority interest in Roman Abramovich’s nearly $1 billion art collection was transferred to his ex-wife ahead of sanctions
cases.note: The ‘frozen Freud and Bacon’ reports in the brief were not found in this article, which states the opposite (no freezing order); the Jersey freezing order of 2022 on Abramovich assets, if any covered art, was not opened. Carried as unconfirmed.

cases.n: The Finnish Customs detention at Vaalimaa (1–2 April 2022; released 9 April 2022)
cases.what: Finnish Customs states that on 1 and 2 April 2022 it detained at Vaalimaa three consignments of artworks bound for Russia, coming by truck from Italy and Japan through Finland, under the EU sanctions on goods traffic (Regulation 2022/428, the luxury-goods amendment). An EU amendment that took effect on 9 April 2022 allows such artworks to move between museums under an exceptional permit; Finland’s Ministry for Foreign Affairs granted the permit, Customs concluded the works were no longer needed as evidence in its preliminary investigation, and the shipments left Finland on 9 April 2022 at about 3 pm. The €42m (US$46m) valuation and the Hermitage as consignee are reported by the trade and general press, not in the Customs release. Status: released to Russia under the museum-loan derogation; outcome of the preliminary investigation not stated.
src: Finnish Customs (Tulli), Art shipments detained at Vaalimaa have continued on to Russia (9 April 2022)
cases.note: The €42m figure and the Hermitage are from press headlines seen in search results (The Art Newspaper, 7 April 2022; Bloomberg, 6 April 2022) that were not opened; flagged as such.

cases.n: United States v. Nazem Said Ahmad et al. (E.D.N.Y., unsealed 18 April 2023)
cases.what: The Department of Justice announced on 18 April 2023 a nine-count indictment in the Eastern District of New York against Nazem Said Ahmad, described as a Lebanese resident and dual Belgian-Lebanese citizen designated by OFAC on 13 December 2019 for financing Hezbollah, and eight co-defendants, charging conspiracy to defraud the United States and foreign governments, evasion of US sanctions and customs laws, and money laundering. The DOJ alleged that ‘approximately $160 million worth of artwork and diamond-grading services were transacted through the U.S. financial system’ after the designation; that entities linked to Ahmad moved more than US$400m (January 2020 to August 2022); that artwork obtained from the United States after December 2019 was valued at more than US$450,000 with a further US$780,000 from US persons abroad, including six paintings valued at US$199,800 exported through JFK to a Lebanese entity used by Ahmad. One defendant was arrested in the United Kingdom at the US request; the others, including Ahmad, were believed outside the United States. Seizure warrants covered assets including artwork. The DOJ release names no art dealer or gallery as a defendant. Status: indictment; allegations. The UK side is the Ojiri prosecution (above): the CPS states Ahmad was sanctioned by the UK in 2023.
src: US Department of Justice, press release 23-431 (18 April 2023)

cases.n: The re-export route through Uzbekistan (RFE/RL, 6 September 2024)
cases.what: As reported: an Uzbek logistics firm helped import more than 200 works (over US$36m) into Russia in two years; a Dutch shipper handled a 44-work, US$4.6m consignment from a yacht at Vlissingen in January 2023 that went via Amsterdam and Tashkent to Moscow, and said it did not know the final destination; the yacht’s reported owner was sanctioned by the UK in February 2023. No enforcement outcome reported.

cases.n: Seizures from sanctioned persons as RFE/RL relayed them (UK, May 2022; Germany, November 2022; 2023)
cases.what: RFE/RL (6 September 2024) records that Britain seized a Fabergé egg belonging to Viktor Vekselberg in May 2022, that German police seized 30 paintings and four Fabergé eggs from Alisher Usmanov’s yacht in November 2022, and that in 2023 authorities seized artworks from Farkhad Akhmedov’s yacht. Primary releases were not opened; the Dutch customs seizures and the Italian seizures named in the brief were not found within the budget.

lawful.course: Screen the bidder and any principal against the UK Sanctions List at the start of the relationship and at each new point in the transaction. On knowledge or reasonable suspicion that the bidder or principal is designated: stop dealing, freeze any assets held for them, and report to OFSI as soon as practicable with the information behind the suspicion (duty on art market participants from 14 May 2025). Do not ship a work of art to or for use in Russia for any buyer (regulation 46B, Schedule 3A item 21, no threshold). Any otherwise prohibited act needs an OFSI licence and, for the export, a Department for Business and Trade trade-sanctions licence; a licence is written permission, it compels nothing and transfers no risk to OFSI.
src: OFSI guidance for high value dealers and art market participants (gov.uk)

lawful.course: A US person may not accept a bid, a deposit, a payment or a consignment from a blocked person, or release property to one, because blocked property ‘may not be transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in’ (EO 14024 s.1; 31 CFR 587.201). The Senate PSI report’s lesson is that the principal behind an agent must be identified before the bid is accepted. Any dealing would need a specific OFAC licence; none is published for art purchases by designated persons. Export of the work to Russia or to a listed oligarch anywhere needs a BIS licence reviewed under a policy of denial (15 CFR 746.10).

As the authorities state it: a designated person’s property in the United States or in a US person’s control is blocked and ‘may not be transferred, paid, exported, withdrawn, or otherwise dealt in’ (EO 14024 s.1; 31 CFR 587.201); in the UK and the EU his funds and economic resources are frozen and nothing may be made available to him. The only lawful route is a licence: an OFAC specific licence applied for under 31 CFR 501.801 (no general licence covers art purchases by an SDN; OFAC’s published Russia general licences cover matters such as wind-downs, legal services and personal remittances, as known), an OFSI licence under the licensing grounds of the Russia Regulations (basic needs, legal fees, routine holding and maintenance, extraordinary expenses and the others, as known; OFSI states a licence is ‘written permission to permit an activity that would otherwise be prohibited’ and transfers no risk), or a Member-State derogation under Regulation 269/2014. None of those grounds, as published, covers buying a painting at auction. A purchase through an agent, a relative or a company he owns 50 per cent or more is the same prohibited dealing: that is what the PSI report, the Abramovich 51 per cent reporting and the Uzbek route are each evidence of, and each is why the houses now identify the principal.
src: OFSI guidance for high value dealers and art market participants (gov.uk)
lawful.note: OFAC and OFSI licensing grounds stated as known; the licensing pages were not opened.

lawful.course: A UK shipper may not export a work of art to or for use in Russia or make it available to a person connected with Russia (regulation 46B; Schedule 3A item 21, no threshold); the shipper charged beside Hauser & Wirth in November 2025 was discharged in July 2026 only because the prosecution could not prove the buyer was ordinarily resident in Russia. An EU shipper is under Article 3h (destination-based, ‘for use in Russia’); the Dutch shipper in the RFE/RL account said it did not know the final destination, and the lawyer quoted said liability turns on what the shipper knew or should have known. A US shipper needs a BIS licence under 15 CFR 746.10 for Russia and for any listed oligarch anywhere, reviewed under a policy of denial. The lawful course is an end-use and consignee declaration, screening of consignee and payer, refusal of a Russian destination, and, for a museum loan returning to Russia, the Member-State permit that Finland’s Foreign Ministry granted in April 2022.

A US bank may not process a payment that is the property of a blocked person or in which he has an interest (587.201; EO 14024); a UK bank is a relevant firm with the same reporting duty OFSI now imposes on art market participants and must freeze and report; the PSI report records that it was a financial institution that determined the owner of the company behind the Magritte payment, and that the houses had not asked. The bank’s lawful course is to reject or block the payment and file with OFAC or OFSI.
src: OFSI guidance for high value dealers and art market participants (gov.uk)

lawful.course: The trade sanctions attach to the destination and the connection with Russia, not to designation. UK: regulation 46B prohibits export to or for use in Russia and making luxury goods available to a ‘person connected with Russia’; the Hauser & Wirth ruling turned on whether the buyer was ordinarily resident in Russia, and the court found the evidence insufficient. EU: Article 3h prohibits supply to any person in Russia or for use in Russia. US: 15 CFR 746.10(a)(1) licenses by destination (Russia, Belarus) and (a)(2) by person (SDN-listed oligarchs anywhere). So a Russian national resident in Dubai buying for a Dubai home, or a Russian citizen resident in the EU buying for an EU home, is outside the destination bans as the texts read, and the house’s duty is the ordinary one: identify the principal, screen him, establish that he is not designated and not ordinarily resident in or located in Russia, and record the end-use; the house must not ship to Russia for him and must not accept payment from a sanctioned source. A buyer who later moves the work to Russia does so under the Russian import regime and his own exposure; the house’s file must show it did not know and had no reasonable cause to suspect (the regulation 46B defence).
lawful.note: Stated from the texts as read; the Commission FAQ on Article 3h (travellers, personal use) did not open.

russia_side.n: Russia’s import regime for cultural property (as the Ministry of Culture’s information note states it)
russia_side.what: The Ministry of Culture’s note on the package of federal laws on the import and export of cultural property (Federal Laws No. 435-FZ and No. 430-FZ, the latter amending part two of the Tax Code) states: the laws govern import into Russia and export to countries outside the EAEU; expert examination of imported cultural property ‘will be conducted at the applicants’ wish’ (экспертиза ввозимых культурных ценностей будет проводиться по желанию заявителей); import is simplified so as to free persons from customs payments (освобождение лиц от уплаты таможенных платежей), without specifics on the page; non-state organisations importing cultural property receive tax benefits if they hold an expert conclusion that the item is a cultural value; experts are certified and listed in a register; a new category of items of ‘special significance’ is barred from permanent export; and individuals need a Ministry permit to export cultural property for personal use. Movement within the EAEU is governed by EAEU law. The customs declaration, the import VAT rate and the EAEU duty rate for chapter 97 were not read in this session (carried as unconfirmed).
src: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation, information on the import and export of cultural property (reproduced by ConsultantPlus)
russia_side.note: Read on a legal database reproduction; the date of the note is not shown. The laws are those of 28 December 2017 as known. Import VAT and duty not confirmed.

Moscow auction houses, ‘parallel import’ and sales of Western art inside Russia were not researched within the budget.

files.n: The politically exposed person: a minister’s relative buys a US$5m work through a company
files.summary: A UK art market participant must find out whether the customer or the beneficial owner of the buying company is a politically exposed person, a family member or a known close associate (MLR 2017 regulation 35), must identify and verify the beneficial owner behind the company (regulation 28), and, where the answer is yes, must obtain senior-management approval, establish the source of wealth and the source of funds, and run enhanced ongoing monitoring, for at least 12 months after the PEP leaves office. A minister’s spouse, child, child’s spouse or parent is a ‘family member’ by definition. The record on which this rests is 1MDB (DOJ forfeitures of works by Van Gogh, Monet, Picasso, Basquiat and Arbus bought with misappropriated funds; over US$1.4bn returned to Malaysia by 2024) and the Obiang cases (carried from memory, flagged). The lawful course is the full enhanced check, documented, and a refusal where the source of wealth cannot be established; a report where there is suspicion.

walls.n: UK: enhanced due diligence on politically exposed persons
walls.cite: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (SI 2017/692), regulation 35, as amended by SI 2023/1371 (domestic PEPs, in force 10 January 2024)
walls.authority: HM Treasury; supervisor for art market participants: HM Revenue & Customs
walls.threshold: Applies to the business relationship or occasional transaction regardless of sum once the art market participant is in scope (the MLR scope for art market participants is €10,000 per transaction or linked transactions, stated from the regulations as known, not read on the page)
walls.what_it_does: A relevant person must have ‘appropriate risk-management systems and procedures to determine whether a customer or the beneficial owner of a customer is’ a PEP, a family member or a known close associate, and must manage the enhanced risks. Where one is identified the firm must have approval from senior management for establishing or continuing the business relationship, take adequate steps to establish the source of wealth and source of funds, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring. The measures continue ‘for a period of at least 12 months after the date on which that person ceased to be entrusted’ with the function (longer if the firm judges it necessary); for family members and close associates they end when the PEP leaves office. Family member means the spouse or civil partner, children and their spouses or civil partners, and parents. Known close associate means a person with joint beneficial ownership of an entity or arrangement with the PEP, other close business relations, or sole beneficial ownership of an entity known to have been set up for the PEP’s benefit. A domestic (UK) PEP is treated as presenting a lower level of risk than a non-domestic PEP absent enhanced risk factors. Prominent public functions include ministers, members of parliament, supreme and constitutional court judges, central bank boards, ambassadors and senior officers, and state-enterprise boards.
walls.case: No UK prosecution of an art market participant for a PEP failure was opened in this session.

walls.n: UK: customer due diligence on the company and its beneficial owner
walls.cite: MLR 2017, regulation 28
walls.authority: HM Treasury; HMRC as supervisor of art market participants
walls.threshold: As above
walls.what_it_does: The firm must identify the customer and verify identity from a reliable independent source; for a body corporate obtain and verify its name, registration number and registered office, and take reasonable measures to determine its law, constitution, board and senior managers; take reasonable measures to understand the ownership and control structure (28(3A)); identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify that identity (28(4)); not rely solely on the Companies House register (28(9)); where all means are exhausted, treat the senior managing official as the beneficial owner and keep written records of every step (28(6)–(8)); and ‘assess, and where appropriate obtain information on, the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship’. Ongoing monitoring includes scrutiny of transactions and, where necessary, the source of funds (28(11)).
walls.case: See the principal file (regulation 28(10) on agents).

walls.n: EU: the Anti-Money Laundering Directives and the 2024 AML Regulation (AMLR)
walls.cite: Directive (EU) 2015/849 as amended by Directive (EU) 2018/843 (5AMLD; art dealers and free-port operators in scope at €10,000; PEP enhanced due diligence in Articles 20–23; from memory, not read); Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), published in the Official Journal on 19 June 2024, applying from 10 July 2027
walls.authority: European Commission; Member-State supervisors; from 2025 the Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA, Frankfurt)
walls.threshold: €10,000 per transaction or linked transactions for persons trading in or acting as intermediaries for cultural goods, including art galleries and auction houses, and for those storing or trading cultural and high-value goods in free zones and customs warehouses; an EU-wide limit of €10,000 on cash payments accepted or made by persons trading in goods or services (Member States may set a lower limit); ‘high-value goods’ otherwise means jewellery, gold- or silversmith articles and watches above €10,000, motor vehicles above €250,000, aircraft or watercraft above €7,500,000
walls.date: 5AMLD transposition 10 January 2020 (from memory); AMLR applies from 10 July 2027 (football provisions 10 July 2029)
walls.what_it_does: The AMLR is the single rulebook that replaces the Directives’ national transpositions from 10 July 2027. It keeps traders in ‘cultural goods (like artworks)’ among the obliged entities, with the €10,000 transaction threshold and the free-zone storage rule; obliged entities must carry out customer due diligence on customers and counterparties; beneficial ownership ‘can be based on two components - ownership interest and control’, which ‘must be assessed independently and in parallel’; enhanced due diligence applies to ‘business relationships with very wealthy (high net-worth) individuals’; the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) ‘will identify ML/TF risks, trends and methods at global level’ and issue guidelines, and its draft technical standards on customer-due-diligence thresholds were submitted to the Commission on 1 October 2026. The PEP articles of the AMLR (senior-management approval, source of wealth and funds, enhanced monitoring, the period after leaving office) mirror the Directives and the UK regulation 35 as known; they were not on the pages read.
walls.case: None opened.
src: eucrim, The EU’s new AML single rulebook regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624)
HLC, Anti-money laundering rules and the luxury goods sector (14 October 2026)
walls.note: AMLR scope, thresholds and dates read on two secondary notes; the Regulation’s own text and its PEP articles were not opened.

walls.n: The US houses’ programmes: the conditions of business as published (Sotheby’s London edition read; the New York edition not read)
walls.cite: Sotheby’s Conditions of Business for Buyers (London, 2 July 2024), conditions 4(a)(v)–(viii), 6(a), 6(h), 8(a)(v), 16(a)–(b)
walls.authority: Sotheby’s (contract terms; the US Bank Secrecy Act does not yet bind art houses)
walls.threshold: None stated
walls.what_it_does: Sotheby’s may require ‘verification of identity and any additional information required to comply with our Know Your Client requirements’ and may ‘seek identification of the source of funds received’ (16(a)); a bidder for a principal ‘shall also disclose to us the identity of the principal’, whose identity Sotheby’s may verify, and may be prohibited from bidding if checks are incomplete (16(a)); the bidder warrants it is not ‘the subject of economic sanctions, embargoes or other trade restrictions in any jurisdiction’ (4(a)(vi)), that it has no reason to suspect the funds ‘are connected with the proceeds of criminal activity’ (4(a)(v)) and that the price will not be funded by anyone ‘the subject of Sanctions’ or located in a Sanctioned Jurisdiction (4(a)(viii)); Sotheby’s may ‘not complete, cancel or rescind the sale of any Lot, including refusing or returning any payment’ (16(a)); ‘We will not accept payment from a source other than the Buyer’ (8(a)(v)); the buyer ‘is solely responsible for identifying and obtaining any necessary export, import’ permits and ‘the denial of any permit or license will not justify cancellation or rescission of the sale’ (3(j)).
walls.case: See 1MDB.
src: Sotheby’s Conditions of Business for Buyers, London, 2 July 2024 (PDF)

cases.n: 1MDB: the DOJ civil forfeitures of art bought with misappropriated funds (Central District of California; release of 23 July 2024)
cases.what: The Department of Justice announced on 23 July 2024 an agreement with Loo Ai Swan (‘Jasmine’ Loo), a former general counsel of 1MDB, resolving a civil forfeiture action against a Picasso artwork and a Swiss financial account under her control worth ‘approximately $1.8 million’ combined; the agreement releases no criminal claims against her. The release records forfeiture orders against Low Taek Jho (Jho Low) covering diamond jewellery and artwork by Vincent van Gogh, Claude Monet, Pablo Picasso, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Diane Arbus, without titles or values; the three related civil forfeiture cases with the Loo assets are valued at ‘nearly $85 million’; before this settlement the United States had returned or assisted in returning ‘over $1.4 billion’ to Malaysia. Low faces separate criminal charges in the Eastern District of New York (money laundering and FCPA conspiracy) and the District of Columbia; the release states charges, not convictions. The actions were brought under the Kleptocracy Asset Recovery Initiative. Status: civil forfeitures and settlements; criminal charges against Low pending as the release states.
src: US Department of Justice, 23 July 2024, Justice Department to recover nearly $85M in additional funds linked to 1MDB scheme

cases.n: The Obiang cases: the US civil forfeiture settlement (10 October 2014); the French and Swiss proceedings (not opened)
cases.what: The Department of Justice announced on 10 October 2014 the settlement of its civil forfeiture cases in the Central District of California against US assets of Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, Second Vice President of Equatorial Guinea and son of its President. Under the Kleptocracy Asset Recovery Initiative the DOJ had alleged that he used his position to amass more than US$300m of assets through corruption and money laundering on an official salary under US$100,000; Assistant Attorney General Leslie R. Caldwell said: ‘Through relentless embezzlement and extortion, Vice President Nguema Obiang shamelessly looted his government’ and ‘This settlement forces Nguema Obiang to relinquish assets worth an estimated $30 million.’ He must sell the US$30m Malibu mansion, a Ferrari and Michael Jackson memorabilia bought with corruption proceeds; US$20m goes to a charity for the people of Equatorial Guinea, US$10.3m is forfeited to the United States for their benefit, he pays US$1m for memorabilia already removed from the country, and he must disclose and remove other US assets; a Gulfstream jet is subject to seizure if brought into the United States. The release does not say whether the settlement carries an admission. Status: civil settlement, 10 October 2014. The French conviction (reported as upheld by the Cour de cassation in 2021) and the Swiss closure of 2019 (reported as the auction of 25 cars for Equatorial Guinea’s benefit) were not opened and are carried from memory, unverified. The ‘Gulbenkian case’ named in the brief could not be identified and is not carried.
src: US Department of Justice, 10 October 2014, Second Vice President of Equatorial Guinea agrees to relinquish more than $30 million of assets purchased with corruption proceeds
cases.note: US case sourced on the DOJ release; French and Swiss cases from memory.

lawful.course: Run the PEP screen on the customer and on the beneficial owner of the buying company (regulation 35); identify and verify the beneficial owner and the ownership and control structure, and record every step (regulation 28); for a PEP or family member obtain senior-management approval, establish the source of wealth and the source of funds, and keep the relationship under enhanced monitoring for at least 12 months after the PEP leaves office. Refuse the transaction where the beneficial owner or the source of wealth cannot be established; where there is knowledge or suspicion of laundering, report to the National Crime Agency under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 (stated from the Act as known) and, if a sanctions link appears, to OFSI.

files.n: The unknown principal: an adviser bids for ‘a client’
files.summary: In the UK an art market participant that accepts an adviser’s bid must verify that the adviser is authorised to act, identify and verify the adviser, and identify and verify the principal as the customer and, where a company, its beneficial owner (MLR 2017 regulation 28(4) and (10)). Sotheby’s own conditions require the agent to disclose the principal and make agent and principal jointly and severally liable. In the United States no statute yet compels it, but the Senate PSI report (2020) found that treating the agent as the principal was the vulnerability through which over US$18m of art reached the Rotenbergs after their designation, and the sanctions prohibition attaches to the principal. The Rybolovlev–Bouvier litigation shows the other face of the problem: a jury in Manhattan found on 30 January 2024 that Sotheby’s had not aided a fraud, Bouvier ‘has never been convicted of any crime’, the parties settled everything in December 2023, and Monaco dismissed the proceedings against Rybolovlev in February 2025. The lawful course is to refuse the bid until the principal is identified and screened.

walls.n: UK: identifying the person who acts for the customer, and the beneficial owner
walls.authority: HM Treasury; HMRC (supervisor)
walls.threshold: Art market participants in scope at €10,000 per transaction or linked transactions (from the regulations as known)
walls.what_it_does: Where a person ‘A’ purports to act for the customer, the firm must verify that A is authorised to act, identify A and verify A’s identity from a source independent of both A and the customer (28(10)). Where the customer is beneficially owned by another person the firm must identify the beneficial owner and take reasonable measures to verify that identity and understand the ownership and control structure (28(4)); it may not rely solely on the Companies House register (28(9)); if every means is exhausted it may treat the senior managing official as the beneficial owner, keeping written records (28(6)–(8)). An adviser bidding ‘for a client’ is A; the client is the customer; the firm may not stop at A.
walls.case: Senate PSI (2020), Finding 4: ‘The auction houses treated an art agent or dealer as the principal purchaser of art’; Finding 14: the houses ‘failed to ask basic questions of Mr. Baltser, including for whom he purchased art’.

cases.n: Rybolovlev trusts v Sotheby’s (S.D.N.Y., Judge Jesse Furman; jury verdict 30 January 2024)
cases.what: As The Art Newspaper reported on 30 January 2024: Dmitry Rybolovlev’s trusts accused Sotheby’s of aiding and abetting fraud by the dealer Yves Bouvier, who was not a party, over four works (Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi, Klimt’s Wasserschlangen II, Magritte’s Le Domaine d’Arnheim, Modigliani’s Tête), seeking at least US$190m; after a trial of about three weeks the jury found for Sotheby’s on all counts in less than a day of deliberation. Sotheby’s said the verdict ‘totally vindicates Sotheby’s of any alleged misconduct’; Rybolovlev’s lawyer said the case ‘achieved our goal of shining a light on the lack of transparency that plagues the art market’. Rybolovlev had alleged that Bouvier overcharged him by more than US$1bn on 38 works sold to his trusts between 2003 and 2014; Bouvier maintained Rybolovlev knew he was a dealer free to set his own prices; The Art Newspaper states Bouvier ‘has never been convicted of any crime’. Rybolovlev had pursued civil and criminal cases in Switzerland, Monaco, Hong Kong and Singapore and settled all matters with Bouvier in all jurisdictions in December 2023; a later Art Newspaper report (3 March 2025) states that Bouvier was cleared across the proceedings, the last concluded by the Swiss authorities in December 2023. Status: verdict for Sotheby’s; whether Rybolovlev appealed was unclear at publication.

cases.n: The Monaco proceedings (Court of Appeal, 27 February 2025)
cases.what: As The Art Newspaper reported on 3 March 2025: the Monaco Court of Appeal formally dismissed the criminal proceedings against Dmitry Rybolovlev on 27 February 2025 and annulled the case against his lawyer Tetiana Bersheda, after the European Court of Human Rights found that the extraction and use of her telephone had violated Article 8 of the Convention; the ‘Monacogate’ investigation had begun in 2017. Her Monaco lawyer said ‘Monaco has finally recognised the illicit character of this case’. The article does not name the charges dismissed. Status: dismissed and annulled, February 2025.

files.n: The provenance gap: a work with a 1933–45 gap, or a 1970 gap for antiquities
files.summary: A gap in 1933–45 for a European work, or before 1970 for an antiquity, is the point at which the terminal stops being a price reading and becomes a claims reading. For Nazi-era losses the instruments are soft law made firmer by procedure: the Washington Principles (44 states, 3 December 1998) and their 2024 Best Practices (‘The primary just and fair solution is restitution’; forced sales and sales under duress count as confiscation; countries should consider exceptions to statutes of limitation), the UK Spoliation Advisory Panel (non-binding recommendations on objects in UK public collections, accepted as full and final settlement), and Germany’s new Court of Arbitration for Nazi-looted cultural property, which replaced the Advisory Commission and began work on 1 December 2025 with 36 arbitrators, unilateral access for claimants against public institutions, binding awards, and a reduced burden of proof with presumptive rules. For antiquities the law is hard: the UK Dealing in Cultural Objects (Offences) Act 2003 (dishonestly dealing in a tainted cultural object, up to seven years), the US CPIA (import of designated archaeological material from 32 countries barred without the source state’s documentation), and the Manhattan District Attorney’s Antiquities Trafficking Unit, whose Steinhardt resolution of December 2021 (180 objects, US$70m, lifetime ban) fed returns to Turkey (January 2022, 28 objects, US$4.6m) and Italy (July 2022, 142 objects, nearly US$14m). The lawful course is the same everywhere: search the registers, obtain the written provenance, stop where the chain breaks, and take a live claim to the panel or the court rather than the market.

walls.n: The Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art (1998) and the Best Practices (2024)
walls.cite: Washington Conference Principles, 3 December 1998, endorsed by 44 states; clarified by the Vilnius Forum Declaration (2000), the Terezín Declaration (2009) and the 2010 Terezín Guidelines; Best Practices for the Washington Conference Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art (text of 6 February 2024, released 5 March 2024)
walls.authority: Non-binding; convened by the US Department of State; the Best Practices text read lists 14 endorsing states (Austria, Canada, Croatia, Czech Republic, France, Germany, Greece, Israel, Luxembourg, Moldova, the Netherlands, Romania, the United Kingdom, the United States)
walls.threshold: None; applies to property looted, confiscated or spoliated by the Nazis, the Fascists and their collaborators in 1933–45, including ‘forced sales and sales under duress’
walls.what_it_does: The Best Practices state that ‘The primary just and fair solution is restitution’; that a sale by a persecuted person may, depending on the circumstances, be treated as an involuntary transfer; that ‘Provenance research carried out by public or private bodies should be made publicly available on the internet’ and ‘Provenance researchers should have access to all relevant archives and source documents’; that ‘Use of alternative resolution mechanisms is encouraged to avoid litigation’ and countries are encouraged to create independent expert bodies; that countries should ‘consider making exceptions to barriers such as’ statutes of limitations; and that claims bodies should publish their rules and decisions. For a house or a buyer, the practical rule is that a 1933–45 gap must be researched and published, not priced.
walls.case: See the German arbitration court and the UK Panel.

walls.n: Germany: from the Advisory Commission to the Court of Arbitration for Nazi-looted cultural property
walls.cite: Decision of the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media, the Länder and the municipal associations at the 21st Kulturpolitisches Spitzengespräch, 9 October 2024 (press release 249); administrative agreement, arbitration rules and binding evaluation framework; the court began work on 1 December 2025
walls.authority: Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media (funder); the Länder; the Deutsches Zentrum Kulturgutverluste (the Berlin service desk acting as secretariat)
walls.threshold: None; applies to cultural property taken through Nazi persecution, ‘in particular from Jewish ownership’
walls.date: Decision 9 October 2024; court in operation from 1 December 2025
walls.what_it_does: The court ‘replaces the former Advisory Commission on the return of cultural property’ (the Beratende Kommission, which could only act with both sides’ consent). Claimants may call it unilaterally where a bilateral preliminary procedure with the institution fails: it can be ‘einseitig, auf Basis von stehenden Angeboten der Träger von öffentlichen, Kulturgut bewahrenden Einrichtungen, angerufen werden’ (invoked unilaterally, on the basis of standing offers by the bodies responsible for public institutions holding cultural property). The panels ‘will issue binding arbitration awards’ on ‘an assessment framework’ that includes ‘a reduced burden of proof and presumptive rules’; 36 arbitrators are available; the executive committee is Dr Elisabeth Steiner, former judge of the European Court of Human Rights, and Peter Müller, former Minister-President and former judge of the Federal Constitutional Court. The 2024 decision rests on the Washington Principles and the March 2024 Best Practices; the chair of the Kulturministerkonferenz said ‘Kein öffentliches Haus soll sich künftig noch mit NS-Raubgut schmücken’ (no public institution should in future adorn itself with Nazi-looted property) and that the procedure will be independently evaluated after at most three years. Private holders are bound only by agreement (not stated on the pages read; carried as the structure implies).
walls.case: The court opened on 1 December 2025; no award was reported on the pages read.

walls.n: United Kingdom: the Spoliation Advisory Panel
walls.cite: Spoliation Advisory Panel (designated by the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport); Holocaust (Return of Cultural Objects) Act 2009 (not read; carried from memory as the power for national museums to transfer objects on the Panel’s recommendation)
walls.authority: Department for Culture, Media and Sport; chairs Rt Hon Sir Donnell Deeny and Rt Hon Sir Alan Moses
walls.threshold: None; objects lost between 1933 and 1945 now held in a UK national collection or another UK museum or gallery ‘established for the public benefit’; private collections only on the joint request of claimant and owner
walls.date: Established 2000 (from memory; not on the page read)
walls.what_it_does: The Panel ‘resolves claims from people, or their heirs, who lost possession of cultural property during the Nazi era’; its proceedings are an alternative to litigation and its recommendations are not legally binding; where a claimant accepts a recommendation and it is implemented, the claimant is expected to accept it as ‘full and final settlement of the claim’.

walls.n: United Kingdom: the Dealing in Cultural Objects (Offences) Act 2003
walls.cite: Dealing in Cultural Objects (Offences) Act 2003 (c. 27), ss. 1–4; passed 30 October 2003, in force two months later (30 December 2003)
walls.authority: Director of Public Prosecutions; HM Revenue & Customs where import or export is involved (s.4)
walls.threshold: None
walls.what_it_does: ‘A person is guilty of an offence if he dishonestly deals in a cultural object that is tainted’, knowing or believing it to be tainted (s.1(1)); it is immaterial whether he knows it is a cultural object (s.1(2)); on indictment up to seven years’ imprisonment, a fine, or both (s.1(3)). A cultural object is one of historical, architectural or archaeological interest; it is tainted if, after the Act’s commencement, it is excavated, or removed from a building, structure or monument of such interest, and the excavation or removal is an offence, whether in the UK or elsewhere and under UK or foreign law (s.2). ‘Deals in’ covers acquiring (buying, hiring, borrowing, accepting), disposing of (selling, letting, lending, giving), importing, exporting, and agreeing or arranging for another to do so (s.3). The 1970 cut-off of the UNESCO Convention is the market’s provenance convention; the UK statute’s own line is 30 December 2003.
walls.case: No prosecution under the Act was opened in this session.

walls.n: United States: the Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act (UNESCO 1970)
walls.cite: Convention on Cultural Property Implementation Act, 19 U.S.C. §§ 2601–2613; agreements under Article 9 of the 1970 UNESCO Convention (§ 2602); Designated Lists published in the Federal Register
walls.authority: US Department of State, Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs (Cultural Heritage Center); US Customs and Border Protection at the border
walls.threshold: Archaeological material must be of cultural significance and at least 250 years old and normally found through excavation or exploration; ethnological material must be the product of a tribal or non-industrial society and important to its cultural heritage (§ 2601)
walls.date: 1983; agreements and emergency actions continuously since
walls.what_it_does: The CPIA implements US obligations under the UNESCO 1970 Convention. On a State Party’s request under Article 9, the President may enter into bilateral agreements (‘typically framed as Memoranda of Understanding’) or take emergency action imposing import restrictions on designated archaeological and ethnological material; a Designated List is ‘a descriptive list of archaeological and/or ethnological materials subject to U.S. import restrictions’. The State Department’s archived page lists 32 countries with current agreements or emergency restrictions: Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Belize, Bolivia, Bulgaria, Cambodia, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cyprus, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, Greece, Guatemala, Honduras, Iraq, Italy, Jordan, Libya, Mali, Morocco, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, Syria, Tunisia, Turkey, Uzbekistan and Yemen (Canada and Nicaragua shown as expired). The documentation rule for import (the source state’s export certification or proof of departure before the restriction date, § 2606) and the museum-inventory rule (§ 2607) were not reached on the pages read and are carried from memory.
walls.case: See the Manhattan District Attorney’s returns (the DA acts under New York law, not the CPIA, but the countries overlap).

walls.n: The Manhattan District Attorney’s Antiquities Trafficking Unit
walls.cite: New York Penal Law (criminal possession of stolen property) applied by seizure warrant and by agreement; the Unit, under Assistant DA Matthew Bogdanos, was formed after the 2017 seizure of the Bull’s Head stolen from Lebanon
walls.authority: New York County District Attorney, with Homeland Security Investigations
walls.threshold: None
walls.date: Steinhardt resolution 6 December 2021; returns to Turkey 21 January 2022 and Italy 22 July 2022
walls.what_it_does: The Unit seizes antiquities in New York hands that it shows to be stolen under the law of the country of origin and returns them, and resolves cases by agreement with bans on collecting. The Antiquities Coalition records that before the Steinhardt seizure the Unit and HSI ‘had recovered several thousand stolen antiquities collectively valued at more than $200 million’. The DA’s release of 21 January 2022 returned 28 antiquities valued at about US$4.6m to Turkey, 14 of them from the Steinhardt collection including the Stag’s Head Rhyton (US$3.5m, sold to Steinhardt by the Merrin Gallery in 1991), and 12 coins forfeited by a collector who pleaded guilty in 2012 to attempted criminal possession of stolen property; DA Alvin Bragg said ‘stolen artifacts should not be collectible property for sale to the highest bidder’ and ‘Collectors and admirers must do their part to ensure items have been lawfully acquired’. On 22 July 2022 the DA returned 142 antiquities valued at nearly US$14m to Italy, 60 from Royal-Athena Galleries, 48 from Steinhardt and 34 from other investigations, including the Ercolano fresco of the infant Hercules (looted from Herculaneum in 1995, bought by Steinhardt that year for US$650,000, now valued at US$1m) and three Paestum tomb frescoes. The Unit’s 2024–26 returns were not opened (a September 2026 return of 36 Syrian objects appeared in search results but the page failed).
walls.case: Michael Steinhardt surrendered 180 antiquities valued at US$70m and accepted ‘the unprecedented lifetime ban’ on acquiring antiquities to avoid criminal prosecution (6 December 2021); the objects were to be returned to 11 countries (Bulgaria, Egypt, Greece, Iraq, Israel, Italy, Jordan, Lebanon, Libya, Syria, Turkey). Status: agreement; no prosecution.

lawful.who: the seller’s agent or the house
lawful.course: Search the Art Loss Register (its page could not be opened in this session) and the national lost-art databases; obtain the written chain of title with the gap stated; where a 1933–45 gap cannot be closed, research and publish the provenance as the Best Practices ask and refer a live claim to the Spoliation Advisory Panel (UK public collections) or the German Court of Arbitration rather than selling into it; for antiquities, require the source country’s export permit or proof of lawful export before its restriction date (the CPIA regime for 32 countries), and do not deal in an object known or believed to be tainted (UK 2003 Act, up to seven years). files.n: The protected material: ivory, rosewood, tortoiseshell, coral
files.summary: Two layers apply to any object with ivory, tortoiseshell, listed rosewood or coral: CITES at every border (Appendix I: commercial international trade prohibited, an import permit and an export permit for the exceptions; Appendix II: an export permit or re-export certificate; a pre-Convention certificate for specimens obtained before the species was listed), and the domestic trade bans. In the United Kingdom ‘Dealing in ivory is prohibited’ (Ivory Act 2018, s.1, in force generally from 6 June 2022; since 28 January 2025 also hippopotamus, killer whale, narwhal and sperm whale ivory) unless the item fits one of five exemptions and is registered (£20 an item, £50 for a group of 3–20) or certified (pre-1918 items of outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historical value: £250, about three months, assessed by one of 12 prescribed museums); the maximum penalty is £250,000 or five years. In the United States the 2016 African elephant rule (effective 6 July 2016) prohibits interstate and foreign commerce in African elephant ivory except ESA antiques (100 years, not repaired with listed material after 28 December 1973, entered through a designated port) and de minimis items (ivory a fixed component, not the primary source of value, under 200 grams). In the EU ‘the trade in elephant ivory is prohibited in general’; worked antiques need proof of acquisition before 3 March 1947 and a certificate from the national CITES authority before any sale, pre-1975 instruments likewise, raw ivory only for repairs, and certificates issued before the new rules lapsed 12 months after they took effect. The lawful course: classify the material, fit the exemption, register or certify before offering, and obtain the CITES document before any border.

walls.n: CITES: Appendix I and II, the permits and the pre-Convention certificate
walls.cite: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (1973), Articles III–IV (permits) and VII (exemptions); in the United States 50 CFR Part 23 (§ 23.4 defines the Appendices); in the EU Regulation (EC) No 338/97 (not read)
walls.authority: CITES Secretariat and the national Management Authorities: in the United States the Division of Management Authority of the US Fish and Wildlife Service; in the UK the Animal and Plant Health Agency (stated from memory); in the EU the Member States’ CITES authorities
walls.threshold: Appendix I ‘includes species threatened with extinction that are or may be affected by trade’ and ‘Trade in Appendix-I specimens may take place only in exceptional circumstances’; Appendix II ‘includes species that are not presently threatened with extinction’ but could become so without regulation, and look-alike species; Appendix III ‘includes species listed unilaterally by a range country’
walls.date: In force 1975 (from memory); the FWS factsheet is of 2024
walls.what_it_does: ‘CITES prohibits commercial international trade in specimens of these [Appendix I] species with limited exemptions’; an Appendix I import needs both a US import permit and an export permit from the exporting country; an Appendix II import needs an export permit from the exporting country and no import permit; ‘A re-export certificate is required for the re-export of CITES-listed specimens that were previously imported’; a pre-Convention certificate is issued ‘If a specimen was obtained prior to the CITES listing date of that species’, and for an Appendix I specimen a valid pre-Convention certificate means no import permit is required. The personal-effects exemption excludes Appendix I specimens (‘except certain African elephant ivory’) and applies to personal use only. The Parties regulate trade ‘through a system of permits and certificates’. Elephant (Appendix I save four southern African populations), hawksbill turtle (tortoiseshell, Appendix I), Dalbergia rosewoods (Appendix II since 2017, with the 2019 exemption for finished musical instruments) and the listed corals are carried from memory.
walls.case: None opened.

walls.n: United Kingdom: the Ivory Act 2018, the exemptions, the registration and the certificate
walls.cite: Ivory Act 2018 (c. 30), ss. 1, 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 37; SI 2022/94 (commencement); SI 2024/664 (power to extend species, 21 May 2024); SI 2025/9 (hippopotamus, killer whale, narwhal, sperm whale, 28 January 2025); gov.uk guidance ‘Declare ivory you intend to sell or hire out’ (updated 24 July 2026) and ‘Ivory: apply for an exemption certificate’ (updated 15 May 2025)
walls.authority: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA) runs registration and certificates and refers certificate applications to an expert at one of 12 prescribed institutions; police and courts for enforcement
walls.threshold: Exemptions: (s.2) pre-1918 items of ‘outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historic value’ with an exemption certificate, £250 per item or set, about three months; (s.6) ‘a portrait miniature made before 1918 with a total surface area of no more than 320 square centimetres’; (s.7) items ‘made before 3 March 1947 with less than 10% ivory by volume, where all the ivory is integral’; (s.8) ‘a musical instrument made before 1975 with less than 20% ivory by volume’; (s.9) sale or hire to a qualifying museum. Registration under s.10 costs £20 an item or £50 for a group of 3 to 20 items that are not a set (by application to APHA, not online)
walls.date: Royal Assent 20 December 2018; s.1 in force in part from 1 February 2022 and generally from 6 June 2022; species extended 28 January 2025
walls.what_it_does: ‘Dealing in ivory is prohibited.’ Dealing covers buying, selling, hiring, offering, keeping for sale or hire, and importing or exporting for sale or hire; the offence requires that the person knows or suspects, or ought to know or suspect, that the item contains ivory, with a defence of all reasonable precautions and due diligence; on indictment ‘imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years or a fine (or both)’, which the guidance states as a maximum fine of £250,000 or up to 5 years. The certificate exemption sets ‘a very high threshold’: the applicant must show the item is rare or an important example of its type (artistic quality, craftsmanship, condition, provenance, historical context), APHA refers it to an expert assessor, ‘Assessments take approximately 3 months’, the item ‘can only be legally sold or hired out once it has been awarded an exemption certificate’, and ‘When you sell the item, you must give the exemption certificate to the new owner.’ Dealing between two qualifying museums needs no registration.
walls.case: No prosecution under the Act was opened in this session.
src: gov.uk, Declare ivory you intend to sell or hire out (updated 24 July 2026)
gov.uk, Ivory: apply for an exemption certificate to deal in pre-1918 outstandingly high artistic, cultural or historical value items (updated 15 May 2025)

walls.n: United States: the Endangered Species Act and the 2016 African elephant ivory rule
walls.cite: Endangered Species Act, s.10(h) (antiques); 50 CFR 17.40(e), final rule of 6 June 2016 (81 FR 36388), effective 6 July 2016
walls.authority: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Department of the Interior
walls.threshold: Antique: ‘Is not less than 100 years of age’, ‘has not been repaired or modified with any part of any such species on or after December 28, 1973’, and ‘is entered at a port designated for the import of ESA antiques’. De minimis: the ivory is a ‘fixed component or components of a larger manufactured item’, is not the ‘primary source of the value of the item’, and ‘the total weight of the ivory component or components in the item must be less than 200 grams’. Sport-hunted trophies: ‘two per hunter per year’
walls.date: Announced 2 June 2016; published 6 June 2016; effective 6 July 2016
walls.what_it_does: The Service ‘completed a rulemaking process under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) to institute a near-total ban on the domestic commercial trade of African elephant ivory’; ‘Interstate and foreign commerce in African elephant ivory is prohibited by the final rule’ with exceptions for ESA antiques and the de minimis items (‘such as musical instruments, furniture pieces and firearms’); antiques ‘are not subject to the provisions of this rule’. State laws (New York, California) add their own bans; the rule’s preamble notes, in answer to New York, that the revised rule ‘would likely require that the State of New York allow sale’ of certain items (the pre-emption question is not resolved on the pages read).
walls.case: None opened.

Federal Register final rule 2016-13173, African elephant 4(d) rule (FWS policy library)

walls.n: European Union: the 2022 ivory rules
walls.cite: European Commission factsheet on the EU ivory rules (January 2022); Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/2280 amending Regulations (EC) 338/97 and 865/2006, and the Commission guidance on the EU ivory regime, applying from 19 January 2022 (instrument numbers and date from memory; not on the factsheet page read)
walls.authority: European Commission (DG Environment); the Member States’ CITES management authorities issue the certificates
walls.threshold: Worked antiques: ‘proof that the ivory item was acquired before 3 March 1947’ and that it has been ‘clearly altered from its natural state to create the object’; musical instruments: ‘The ivory was acquired before 1975’ and the instrument is, or until recently was, ‘used by a performing artist’
walls.what_it_does: ‘the trade in elephant ivory is prohibited in general.’ Raw ivory can only be sold to repair pre-1947 antiques (where a public cultural heritage authority supports the transaction) or pre-1975 musical instruments; ‘Commercial trade in elephant trophies consisting of raw ivory is prohibited within the EU; they can only be imported for personal use.’ To sell a qualifying item: verify the evidence, apply to the national CITES authority for a certificate, and trade only once ‘a valid certificate is issued’; certificates issued before the amended regulation took effect ‘will cease to be valid 12 months after this date’. The Commission’s guidance document redirected to a general page and was not read; China’s 2017 ban was not sourced.
walls.case: None opened.
src: European Commission, factsheet on the EU ivory rules (January 2022)
walls.note: The regulation number and the 19 January 2022 date are from memory; the factsheet page read gave the rules without them.

lawful.course: Identify the material and the species; in the UK fit the item to an exemption (ss. 2, 6, 7, 8 or 9 of the Ivory Act 2018), register it (£20) or obtain the certificate (£250, about three months) before offering it, and hand the certificate to the buyer; in the EU obtain the national CITES authority’s certificate on proof of pre-3 March 1947 acquisition before any sale; in the United States sell only ESA antiques or de minimis items across state lines; for any export obtain the CITES export permit, re-export certificate or pre-Convention certificate from the management authority; where no exemption fits, do not deal.
