files.n: The tax wall: VAT on import, the margin scheme, sales tax and the cases
files.summary: From 1 January 2025 EU Member States may apply a reduced VAT rate to works of art under Directive (EU) 2022/542, on condition that the reduced rate is not combined with the dealers’ margin scheme; Italy went to 5 per cent on all supplies and imports from 1 July 2025 (Decree-Law 95 of 30 June 2025, Article 9), replacing 22 per cent on dealer sales and 10 per cent on imports; the trade press states France at 5.5 per cent and Germany at 7 per cent (one source states France’s 5 per cent for imports and authors’ sales only; the French and German texts were not opened). The United Kingdom’s 5 per cent effective import rate and 20 per cent standard rate are carried from memory. On sales tax, the New York Attorney General and the Department of Taxation and Finance secured US$6.25m from Sotheby’s on 14 November 2024 for accepting resale certificates from clients it knew were not buying for resale (a collector who bought US$27m of art in 2010–15; at least seven other clients 2012–20), after the collector’s company paid over US$10m in 2018 under the New York False Claims Act. The Wildenstein and Mary Boone cases and the Swiss and free-port positions are from memory and flagged. The lawful course: charge and declare the tax at the rate of the place of supply or import; use the margin scheme or the reduced rate, not both; accept a resale certificate only where resale is real.

walls.n: EU: reduced VAT rates on works of art from 1 January 2025 and the bar on combining them with the margin scheme
walls.cite: Council Directive (EU) 2022/542 of 5 April 2022 amending Directive 2006/112/EC (works of art added to Annex III; Member States to apply by 1 January 2025); Italy: Decree-Law No. 95 of 30 June 2025 (Official Gazette No. 149), Article 9
walls.authority: Council of the European Union; Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance and Agenzia delle Entrate; the French and German finance ministries for their rates
walls.threshold: Italy 5 per cent on ‘the generality of supplies of art, antiques or collectibles’ including imports and intra-Community acquisitions, from 1 July 2025 (previously 10 per cent for imports and authors’ supplies, 22 per cent for other supplies); France 5.5 per cent and Germany 7 per cent as The Art Newspaper states (finestresullarte states France 5 per cent for imports and authors’ supplies and Germany 7 per cent on the same basis); Cyprus and Malta 5 per cent on imports only; Spain 21 per cent, Netherlands 9 per cent, Austria 20 per cent (finestresullarte, 29 July 2025)
walls.date: Directive 5 April 2022, applicable 1 January 2025; Italy 1 July 2025 (cabinet approval 20 June 2025; to be confirmed by parliament within 60 days)
walls.what_it_does: ‘The application of the new 5 percent VAT rate is incompatible with the so-called margin scheme’: a dealer may use the margin scheme only for goods not bought or imported at the reduced rate, and may charge the reduced rate only for goods not bought under the margin scheme. The Art Newspaper (23 June 2025) reported the Italian cut from 22 per cent, ‘the highest rate in Europe’, to 5 per cent, ‘its lowest’, after a letter from 500 art-world figures and a campaign led by the dealers’ association ANGAMC; a Nomisma and Intesa Sanpaolo study cited by the proponent estimated €1.5bn of annual turnover within three years.
walls.case: None (a rate change, not an enforcement).
src: Finestre sull’Arte, 29 July 2025, The VAT revolution in the Italian art market
The Art Newspaper, 23 June 2025, Italy to slash art VAT to 5%
walls.note: The Directive and the French and German implementing texts were not opened; the two secondary sources differ on France’s rate and scope.

walls.n: United Kingdom: import VAT on works of art at an effective 5 per cent; 20 per cent standard rate; the margin scheme
walls.cite: Value Added Tax Act 1994, s.21(4)–(6) (reduced value for import of works of art, antiques and collectors’ items, giving an effective 5 per cent); VAT Notice 718 (margin scheme) and Notice 702 (imports)
walls.authority: HM Revenue & Customs
walls.threshold: Effective 5 per cent on import of qualifying works of art, antiques over 100 years old and collectors’ items; 20 per cent on domestic sales outside the margin scheme; the margin scheme taxes the dealer’s margin at 20 per cent
walls.date: Long-standing; the UK left the EU VAT area on 1 January 2021
walls.what_it_does: Carried from memory, unverified; not opened in this session.
walls.case: None opened.

walls.n: New York: sales tax and the resale certificate
walls.cite: New York Tax Law (sales and use tax; resale certificates); New York False Claims Act (the 2018 Porsal Equities settlement); the Attorney General’s 2020 action against Sotheby’s, settled 14 November 2024
walls.authority: New York State Attorney General; New York State Department of Taxation and Finance
walls.threshold: None; the tax is due on every taxable retail sale delivered in New York unless a valid resale certificate or an out-of-state delivery applies
walls.what_it_does: The Attorney General alleged that Sotheby’s helped clients avoid sales tax on tens of millions of dollars of purchases from 2010 to 2020 by encouraging them to claim they were buying for resale; a collector bought US$27m of art between 2010 and 2015 using resale certificates that Sotheby’s accepted ‘even though it knew that the Collector was not buying art for resale’, some of it installed in the collector’s home; from 2012 to 2020 Sotheby’s improperly accepted resale certificates from at least seven other clients and in several cases provided or filled in the forms. Sotheby’s paid US$6.25m to the State and must train employees in New York tax law and review whether a client intends to resell. Attorney General James: ‘Sotheby’s intentionally broke the law to help its clients dodge millions of dollars in taxes’. The collector’s company, Porsal Equities, had agreed in 2018 to pay ‘over $10 million in taxes, penalties, and damages’ and admitted improperly using resale certificates for personal purchases in violation of the tax laws and the New York False Claims Act.
walls.case: As above. The Christie’s and dealers’ sales-tax cases named in the brief were not opened (carried as unconfirmed).
src: New York Attorney General, 14 November 2024, Attorney General James and Acting DTF Commissioner Hiller secure more than $6 million from Sotheby’s for tax fraud

walls.n: Switzerland: import VAT and the free port; the tax point
walls.cite: Swiss VAT Act (standard rate 8.1 per cent from 1 January 2024); the Geneva Free Port and the Swiss customs rules on bonded storage (goods under customs control are not imported and no VAT is due until release into free circulation); the 2016 Swiss customs tightening on free-port inventories and the six-month limit on goods held for export
walls.authority: Swiss Federal Office for Customs and Border Security; Federal Tax Administration
walls.threshold: 8.1 per cent on import (from memory)
walls.what_it_does: Carried from memory, unverified: VAT falls due at the tax point of release into free circulation, not on entry into bonded storage; a sale inside the free port of goods still under customs control is outside Swiss VAT, but the buyer pays the import VAT of whichever country the work is released into. Not opened.
walls.case: None opened.

cases.n: People of the State of New York v Sotheby’s (settled 14 November 2024)
cases.what: US$6.25m paid to New York State; conduct 2010–2020; reforms on training and resale-intent review; see the wall entry. Status: settled; no admission is recorded on the page read.

cases.n: Porsal Equities (settled 2018)
cases.what: The collector’s company paid ‘over $10 million in taxes, penalties, and damages’ and admitted improperly using resale certificates for personal art purchases in violation of the tax laws and the New York False Claims Act (as the 2024 release states it; the 2018 release itself was not opened).

cases.n: The Wildenstein judgment (Paris, 2024) and the Mary Boone case (New York, 2019) — carried from memory
cases.what: Not opened. From memory, unverified: after acquittals in 2017 and 2018 and a Cour de cassation ruling of January 2021 ordering a retrial, the Paris Court of Appeal in 2024 convicted Guy Wildenstein of tax fraud and laundering over the family trusts that held the art collection; the sentence and fine as reported should be verified before use. The dealer Mary Boone pleaded guilty in 2018 to filing false tax returns and was sentenced in January 2019 to 30 months’ imprisonment.

lawful.course: Charge VAT at the rate and place that apply (the reduced rate or the margin scheme, never both on the same goods); declare import VAT at release into free circulation; accept a resale certificate only from a registered reseller buying for resale, and keep the evidence; where the client installs the work at home, the sale is retail and the tax is due.

files.note: UK rates, Swiss VAT, the free-port tax point, Wildenstein, Boone and the Christie’s and dealers’ cases from memory and flagged.

files.n: The export wall: a national treasure
files.summary: The United Kingdom defers, it does not refuse: in 2024–25 the Reviewing Committee considered 20 objects, found 18 met a Waverley criterion, the Secretary of State deferred all 18 (£40,009,133 in aggregate), six were saved for £586,132 and nine left for £16,969,020 after no offer, with a Hepworth, a Botticelli and a Rubens modello (together £22,453,981) still under deferral at publication. Italy moved the other way on 4 May 2026: works over 70 years old valued under €50,000 (previously €13,500) no longer need the attestato di libera circolazione but a self-declaration (DVAL 50_MILA) valid five years, as the conservation blog art-test reports it; the EU threshold for paintings under Regulation 116/2009 is €150,000 and France’s and Germany’s national thresholds for paintings are €300,000 as the same source states. France’s trésor national refusal (30 months for the State to buy), Germany’s Kulturgutschutzgesetz 2016, Spain’s inexportable, Russia’s ‘special significance’ category, China’s pre-1911 ban, Egypt’s and Greece’s state ownership and India’s 100-year rule are from memory or thin sources and flagged. The lawful course is the licence application with the object described at its true value, and acceptance of the deferral or the refusal.

walls.n: United Kingdom: the Waverley criteria and the Reviewing Committee
walls.cite: Export Control Act 2002, s.10(1)(a); Export of Objects of Cultural Interest (Control) Order 2003 (not read); Reviewing Committee Annual Report 2024–25
walls.authority: Arts Council England for the Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport; the Reviewing Committee
walls.threshold: Objects over 50 years old above category value thresholds need an individual licence (thresholds not printed in the report read); 5,745 individual licence applications in 2024–25; 28,307 items licensed after expert-adviser referral worth £955,143,117
walls.what_it_does: Three criteria: ‘Is it closely connected with our history and national life?’, ‘Is it of outstanding aesthetic importance?’, ‘Is it of outstanding significance for the study of some particular branch of art, learning or history?’ A deferral gives a UK buyer time to match the price; if no offer comes the licence issues. In 2024–25: 20 objects considered, 18 deferred (£40,009,133), six saved (£586,132: Dresser’s Birds of Europe £127,000 to Manchester; an Iron Age coin £20,040 to the British Museum; Alan Turing’s Delilah papers £397,680 to King’s College Cambridge; a Menai Bridge sampler £14,564 to Storiel; the Sutton Scotney brooch donated; an Anglo-Saxon cloisonné panel £3,968), nine left (£16,969,020), three still deferred (Hepworth, Botticelli, Rubens modello; £22,453,981). Two objects (the Piprahwa stupa gems; a Zoffany) met no criterion.
walls.case: The 2024–25 cases as listed; the Hepworth’s second deferral ended 27 August 2025, the Botticelli’s first on 8 August 2025, the Rubens’s on 15 September 2025 (outcomes after the report not opened).
src: Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art, Annual Report 2024–25

walls.n: Italy: the 2026 threshold change for works over 70 years old
walls.cite: Law on the ‘Valorizzazione sussidiaria dei beni culturali’ (number and date not given by the source), in force 4 May 2026; Codice dei beni culturali (D.Lgs. 42/2004), Articles 65–68 (notifica, attestato di libera circolazione) as known; Regulation (EC) No 116/2009 (EU export licence, €150,000 for paintings)
walls.authority: Ministero della Cultura, Uffici Esportazione (SUE portal)
walls.threshold: Works created over 70 years ago and valued under €50,000 (previously €13,500) no longer need the attestato di libera circolazione; a self-declaration form, DVAL 50_MILA, filed on the SUE portal and valid five years (previously six months) replaces it, as art-test reports
walls.what_it_does: As the source states it: the new law removes the export-office attestation for works over 70 years old under €50,000 and extends the declaration’s validity from six months to five years; the author, writing against the change, says it ‘treats heritage as an economic opportunity’ and warns that works previously kept in Italy could now be exported. The notifica (declaration of cultural interest) and the thresholds for it are not changed by the source’s account. The same source gives the EU licence threshold for paintings as €150,000 and France’s and Germany’s national thresholds for paintings as €300,000.
walls.case: None opened.
src: art-test, 29 April 2026, Italy for sale: the new law is much more laissez-faire
walls.note: A conservation firm’s blog, partisan; the law’s number and the Gazzetta Ufficiale text were not opened.

walls.n: France: the trésor national and the 30-month refusal
walls.cite: Code du patrimoine, Articles L111-1 to L111-7 and L121-1 (certificat d’exportation; refusal for a trésor national; 30 months for the State to make an offer; the 2003 tax incentive for corporate purchase of trésors nationaux); thresholds per décret 93-124 as amended (€300,000 for paintings over 50 years as art-test states)
walls.authority: Ministère de la Culture, Service des musées de France; Commission consultative des trésors nationaux
walls.threshold: €300,000 for paintings (as art-test states); other categories not confirmed
walls.what_it_does: Carried from memory, unverified: refusal of the export certificate classifies the work as a trésor national for 30 months, during which the State may make an offer at international market value; if none is made the certificate cannot be refused again on the same grounds. The 2024–26 cases named in the brief (the Louvre’s acquisitions after refusal) were not opened.
walls.case: None opened.

walls.n: Germany: the Kulturgutschutzgesetz 2016
walls.cite: Gesetz zum Schutz von Kulturgut (KGSG) of 31 July 2016, in force 6 August 2016; § 24 (export licence thresholds within the EU, e.g. paintings over 75 years and €300,000); §§ 41–44 (due-diligence duties of the trade); the register of national cultural property
walls.authority: Beauftragte der Bundesregierung für Kultur und Medien; the Länder
walls.threshold: Paintings €300,000 (as art-test states for Germany); age 75 years for intra-EU licences (from memory)
walls.what_it_does: Carried from memory, unverified: export licence required above the thresholds even within the EU; entry in the register of national cultural property bars permanent export; the trade must record provenance and check the registers before dealing. Not opened.
walls.case: None opened.

walls.n: Spain, Russia, China, Egypt, Greece, India
walls.cite: Spain: Ley 16/1985 del Patrimonio Histórico Español (Bienes de Interés Cultural inexportable; export permit for objects over 100 years; the declared value as an irrevocable offer of sale to the State). Russia: Law 4804-1 of 15 April 1993 as amended by Federal Law 435-FZ (28 December 2017): a category of cultural property of ‘special significance’ barred from permanent export; individuals need a Ministry of Culture permit to export cultural property for personal use (the Ministry’s note, read). China: Law on the Protection of Cultural Relics and the 2007 export standard (ban on export of cultural relics made before 1911; restrictions on 1911–1949 works and works of listed deceased artists). Egypt: Law 117 of 1983 (antiquities are state property; export banned). Greece: Law 3028/2002 (antiquities before 1453 belong to the State; export of monuments prohibited save temporary loans). India: Antiquities and Art Treasures Act 1972 (an antiquity is an object at least 100 years old, a manuscript 75; export only by the Central Government)
walls.authority: The ministries of culture of each state
walls.threshold: As stated in the citation
walls.what_it_does: Carried from memory except the Russian item, which the Ministry of Culture’s information note states; none of the other texts was opened.
walls.case: None opened.

cases.n: The 2024–25 Reviewing Committee cases (United Kingdom)
cases.what: See the wall entry: 20 considered, 18 deferred, six saved for £586,132, nine exported after no offer (£16,969,020), three pending at publication (£22,453,981).

lawful.course: Apply for the export licence with the object described at the price agreed; if an expert adviser objects, answer the Waverley case before the Committee; accept the deferral and, if a matching offer comes at the fair market price, sell to the UK institution; in France, Italy, Germany and Spain, apply for the certificate before the sale is contracted for export and treat a refusal as a classification, not a negotiation; in Russia, China, Egypt, Greece and India, assume that antiquities and listed works cannot leave and seek the ministry’s written ruling before offering abroad.

regulation.n: UK: anti-money-laundering registration for art market participants
regulation.what: A business that trades in, or acts as an intermediary in, works of art where a transaction or linked series is €10,000 or more must register with HMRC; so must a freeport operator storing art above that value. Negotiating prices or acting on a customer’s behalf counts as intermediation. Giving art advice, charging for research or provenance checks, or introducing customers does NOT by itself require registration. Registration and annual fees are payable per premises (amounts not on the page); HMRC may cancel a registration for non-payment. Page first published 7 Feb 2020, last updated 6 Aug 2024.
regulation.authority: HM Revenue & Customs (gov.uk guidance), under the money laundering regulations
src: GOV.UK, Money laundering supervision for art market participants

regulation.n: US: Bank Secrecy Act and the art trade
regulation.what: The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 added antiquities dealers to the BSA but not art dealers, auction houses or advisers; Treasury’s 2022 study found the art market susceptible but not the highest-risk area. The Art Market Integrity Act, announced 23 Jul 2025 by Senators Grassley and Fetterman, would add ‘a person engaged in the trade in works of art’ (dealers, galleries, advisers, consultants, custodians, auction houses, museums) to the BSA definition of financial institution, with AML programmes, CTRs, SARs and customer identification, exempting persons with no single art transaction above US$10,000 or under US$50,000 of art transactions in the prior year, and sellers of their own work. It is a bill, not law, on the page opened (21 Aug 2025).

runs.what: Digital bidding. CEO Charles Stewart told Spear’s that digital accounted for about 40% of bidding in 2019 and ‘around 93%’ by October 2024; bidders came from 125 countries in 2023; app-based bidding and online brochures are the stated tools. He said that when he arrived there was ‘a notable absence, or underinvestment, in a lot of the digital tools’ the business should have had, and that back-end investment in ‘better analysis of client and object data’ is ‘a huge competitive advantage’. Sotheby’s has also invested in blockchain to authenticate certain works (no cost given). The article does not name the app or mention artificial intelligence.
Sotheby’s Metaverse, the first on-chain auction platform at a major house, launched October 2021. Its current status is not stated in the source.

Sotheby’s Mei Moses indices: repeat-sale indices (an All Art index and category indices) drawing on about 200 years of auction history from Sotheby’s, Christie’s and Phillips, per Masterworks Research (July 2026), which lists them as still published.
runs.note: Sotheby’s own indices page could not be opened (client error), so the current publication cadence is unconfirmed.

bought.what: Mei Moses Art Indices, acquired and renamed Sotheby’s Mei Moses on 26 October 2016: a database of 45,000 repeat sales across eight collecting categories, about 4,000 changing hands each year. Adam Chinn, Executive Vice President, said the indices give ‘objective and verifiable information’ to support specialists and that Sotheby’s would give collectors ‘proprietary information tailored to their needs’. Price not stated; the indices were presented as proprietary, for clients, not as a public data product.

Thread Genius, acquired 25 January 2018: a two-person image-recognition and recommendation start-up (TechStars NY 2017; founders ex-Spotify). Price undisclosed, called non-material. Sotheby’s said it had ‘united all of our data-related activities under one umbrella’; the team (three people with a data scientist already hired) was to build a recommendation engine on the Mei Moses image database of about 50,000 images.

ai.what: No disclosed use of AI in estimates, cataloguing or client matching was found on an opened page. Sotheby’s did not feature in The Art Newspaper’s November 2024 survey of AI at auction houses, and its CEO’s October 2024 interview on technology does not mention AI. Bloomberg’s February 2026 report on AI valuation quoted no auction-house executive.

failures.what: The cost base behind the technology (FT, from the Luxembourg accounts filed July 2025): 2024 pretax loss US$248m (2023: US$106m); commissions and fees down 18% to US$813m; headcount down 24 to 2,218; severance costs US$29.2m (2023: US$11.4m); long-term net debt down from US$3.55bn to US$2.76bn after US$794m repaid; ADQ invested US$909m in August 2024 for a 24% stake in Sotheby’s Holdings UK within a US$1bn injection with Patrick Drahi’s BidFair (US$85m).
src: FT via The Irish Times, 11 Sep 2025

cannot.what: The repeat-sale index is proprietary: Sotheby’s 2016 announcement offered ‘proprietary information tailored to their needs’ to clients through a mailbox, not a public feed. A client of Sotheby’s cannot get a cross-house index from Christie’s, nor the reverse.

The underbidder: no house publishes it. The Baer Faxt sells it (buyers’ and underbidders’ identities from 1996, identified in the saleroom by Josh Baer and informants), priced in October 2021 at US$200 a month for an individual and US$500 a month for a large company, and made free with log-in from February 2025.

runs.what: Christie’s LIVE online bidding. The online terms of use (as published on Christie’s China site) apply ‘in addition to Christie’s Conditions of Sale’, state that ‘Live internet bidding may be recorded’, that Christie’s does not hold card data (a third-party payment provider does) and that conversion rates are ‘updated daily’. The page contains no clause on copyright of results, scraping or automated access, and no date or governing law.
src: Christie’s LIVE online terms of use (christies.com.cn)
runs.note: The main christies.com terms of use and the launch date of Christie’s LIVE (2006, from memory) were not opened.

runs.what: Christie’s 3.0, the house’s own blockchain-based NFT sales platform, launched 2022 alongside a digital art department. The Art Newspaper reported in September 2025 that the platform remains live while the department closed; none of its 11 auctions (about 17 lots each) exceeded US$400,000.

The King Street archive, which Christie’s describes as the largest and most complete auction archive in the world (annotated catalogues back to its first sale in 1766, every buyer and price paid). External access was withdrawn in February 2021 after staff cuts: ‘the archives team has had to be reduced and can now only serve the needs of our own specialist teams’. Agnew’s called it ‘rather mean spirited’; the Soane Museum ‘a great blow to scholarship’ and suggested charging instead. No reopening reported.

Collectrium Market Data Beta, a subscription database run by Christie’s subsidiary Collectrium, held over 11 million item descriptions by December 2016 (per Heritage Auctions’ complaint), of which Heritage alleged more than 2.7 million had been copied from its own site.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 20 Dec 2016

bought.what: Collectrium, a collection-management software company, acquired by Christie’s in 2015 (per Grossman LLP; an Artnet headline seen but not opened gave a US$16m price). Its fate: Heritage Auctions sued Christie’s and Collectrium in December 2016 for scraping about five million pages of ha.com; the court sent the case to arbitration under the website’s terms (2017); in January 2019 a retired federal judge as arbitrator awarded nearly US$1.8m against Collectrium alone (DMCA anti-circumvention US$1,755,000, being US$1,000 for each of at least 1,755 wilful accesses; CFAA US$5,000, the statutory minimum; breach of the website terms US$1 nominal), held Collectrium’s use of the listings to be fair use with ‘thin’ copyright, and rejected a US$38bn copyright-management-information claim. Confirmed by the Northern District of Texas in June 2019. An Artnet headline (not opened) reported Christie’s ‘scales back Collectrium’.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 20 Dec 2016
Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019
bought.note: Acquisition year differs between sources (Grossman: 2015; Artnet headline: 2016 purchase story). Price and scaling-back are from unopened Artnet headlines.

bought.what: Christie’s Ventures, an in-house investment arm announced 19 July 2022 at the Art+Tech Summit in New York. Stated focus: Web 3.0 (NFTs, cryptocurrencies, blockchains), art-related financial products and technologies that make art easy to consume. First investment: LayerZero Labs, a cross-chain infrastructure firm (its own round was US$135m; the fund’s size was not stated).

Christie’s Ventures invested (terms undisclosed) in Artsignal, an ‘agentic AI’ art-market research platform launched September 2025; Devang Thakkar, global head of Christie’s Ventures, endorsed it at launch; vice president Ryan Ludgate led the deal and reportedly noted that market data and graphs ‘only tell so much’ because each work is unique.

ai.what: ‘Augmented Intelligence’, Christie’s first sale devoted to AI-generated art, February 2025; it drew protests and, per The Art Newspaper, did not reach seven figures. This is a sale of AI art, not a disclosed use of AI in the house’s own estimates or cataloguing. Christie’s did not feature in The Art Newspaper’s November 2024 survey of AI use at houses; its AI position is expressed through Christie’s Ventures’ investment in Artsignal.

failures.what: May 2024 cyber incident attributed to RansomHub. The class action In re Christie’s Data Breach Litigation (SDNY, Judge Jesse M. Furman) alleged that data of more than 500,000 customers was exposed (names, passport and driving-licence details, government ID data). Christie’s paid US$990,000 to settle; class counsel fees US$324,907; final approval reported 29 July 2025. Christie’s agreed to enhanced data-security measures.
failures.note: The Bloomberg Law page does not give the exact May 2024 date or the days of downtime; those are carried from memory (site down about ten days before the May marquee sales).

failures.what: Digital art: the Beeple sale of March 2021 hammered at US$69.3m with no estimate; NFT sales totalled only US$4.8m in the first half of 2022; the crypto lead Noah Davis left in June 2022; the digital art department (founded 2022) was closed in September 2025, with the vice president and director of digital art sales let go in August 2025. Christie’s said it had ‘made a strategic decision to reformat digital art sales’ within its 20th/21st Century category. Whether the Art+Tech Summit (held since 2018) continues was not stated.

Collectrium’s data strategy ended in an arbitration award of nearly US$1.8m against it (January 2019, confirmed June 2019) for circumventing Heritage’s access controls; Christie’s itself was not held liable and said the award was ‘a small fraction’ of what Heritage sought.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019

failures.what: Christie’s International’s own profit before tax rose 18% to £85m in 2024 (FT), against Sotheby’s pretax loss of US$248m; Christie’s sales fell 6% to US$5.7bn.

ai.what: The Art Newspaper’s November 2024 survey of AI at auction houses found the disclosed uses were translation of lot details (Kunst-Auktionshaus Wendl), translation and automatic categorisation of partner vendors’ lots (Drouot.com, about 3 million items a year from 790 houses with non-standardised data) and personalisation of e-commerce (Forum Auctions). No vendor, headcount or spend figure was given; Roseberys said AI’s ‘lack of nuance’ keeps humans on high-stakes communication.

Heritage Auctions (ha.com) publishes descriptions, images and past prices to registered users under its website terms: about five million pages and over eight million images of items sold since 1993 (per its 2016 complaint). It defended that data with copyright, CFAA, DMCA, Texas computer-access, trespass and contract claims.

attempts.n: Artnet (Artnet AG) — and the 2026 Artnet–Artsy combination
attempts.backers: Public company (Frankfurt) until 2025; taken private by Leonardo Art Holdings GmbH, a vehicle advised by Beowolff Capital Management Ltd (London; founder/CEO Andrew Wolff, a former Goldman Sachs trader; CIO Jan Petzel). The Neuendorf family and both boards supported the offer. Beowolff already held a majority stake in Artsy.
attempts.raised: Take-private at €11.25 a share in cash (acceptance period 8 July–5 August 2025): about 97% above the XETRA close of 3 March 2025, the day before Weng Fine Art AG’s notice of a potential €11.00 offer; about 56% above the three-month VWAP of €7.20; about 88% of the shares secured by 8 July 2025 and about 98.93% at completion.
attempts.built: The Artnet Price Database (Bloomberg: ‘the art market’s most influential auction price database’; Masterworks: more than 1,800 auction houses with data back to 1985, indices built on a median price per artist, equally weighted), Artnet News, Artnet Auctions and a gallery network.
attempts.charged: Price Database subscription tiers not opened in this session (artnet.com refuses fetches).
attempts.state: Delisted from the Frankfurt regulated market at the end of 22 August 2025; completion announced 27 August 2025; squeeze-out of the minority requested 19 August 2025. Artnet reported a loss of just over US$1m in its Q1 2025 income statement. In mid-April 2026 Artnet and Artsy were merged under Beowolff, with Artsy’s CEO Jeffrey Yin leading both and Wolff as chairman; dozens were laid off (at least seven Artnet News staff); Artnet’s Berlin office closed. The Deloitte/ArtTactic 2025 report cites the Artnet Fine Art Top 100 index at 3.2% annualised over 20 years and minus 2.9% over 10 years, against the S&P 500’s 10.4% and 13.3%.
attempts.why: Wolff says he will ‘develop additional data and information services’ and financial services alongside the media business, which Georgina Adam summarised as ‘a sort of Bloomberg for the arts’. Her doubts (23 April 2026): cutting editorial hurts the advertising it is sold against; software and AI can scrape prices from the internet, often free; financial institutions may not pay Bloomberg-style prices of about US$27,000–30,000 a year; the art market is small, elite and ‘not infinitely scalable’. Bloomberg (February 2026) reported Wolff’s plan for AI analytics combining Artnet auction data with Artsy primary-market sales and user behaviour, plus exhibition histories, scholarly citations, news and search trends; details ‘still to be determined’ and no product launched.
attempts.note: Offer terms are from the EQS newswire (company announcement); the merger, losses and layoffs are trade-press reports (S). Total equity value not stated on the opened pages.

attempts.backers: Venture-backed; majority-owned by Beowolff Capital by May 2025; merged with Artnet in April 2026 under CEO Jeffrey Yin.
attempts.raised: Over US$130m since 2009 (The Art Newspaper); ‘it is unclear whether Artsy ever turned a profit’.
attempts.built: A gallery marketplace and online auctions; primary-market sales and user-behaviour data that Beowolff plans to combine with Artnet’s auction data.
attempts.state: Merged with Artnet in April 2026; layoffs at both companies (‘dozens’, Hyperallergic, 16 April 2026).
attempts.why: See Artnet entry: the data and media businesses are to be run together as a ‘Bloomberg for the arts’; the trade’s doubts are the scrapability of prices, the terminal price point and the market’s size.

attempts.backers: Listed on Euronext Paris (ISIN FR0000074783); founder-CEO Thierry Ehrmann; Groupe Serveur.
attempts.built: Databanks the company says hold over 30 million indices and auction results, 901,000+ artists, about 7,200 auction houses, 181 million images and 180 proprietary databases; the annual Art Market report (free; 2025 global auction turnover US$11.1bn, up 12%); the Artprice100 index (Masterworks: about 0.88 correlation with the S&P 500 since 2000, as Artprice reports it); the vertical AIs it calls Intuitive Artmarket and Blind Spot; a Perplexity AI partnership; a planned 2026 ‘DIGITS’ NVIDIA build-out with 20 specialised AIs.
attempts.charged: Subscription prices not on the opened pages (the release links to a general subscription page).
attempts.state: FY2025 revenue €8,497K (2024: €8,359K); net income €1K (2024: €654K), which the company attributes to restructuring (absorption of The European Judicial Server; write-off of Artprice Inc.); the company says the recurring result would have been €143K. It claims 9.3 million members and about 270 million monthly visitors.
attempts.why: Revenue has been flat at about €8.4–8.5m for two years with the largest database in the trade, which shows the ceiling of a data-only subscription in this market; the company now presents itself as an AI business.
src: Idéal Investisseur on Artmarket FY2025 results, 29 Apr 2026
Artmarket.com press release via AAP, 10 Mar 2026

attempts.backers: Founder Anders Petterson (from memory, not on the opened page).
attempts.built: Reports across categories, auction analysis, ‘market signals’; co-author of the Deloitte Private Art & Finance Report (first edition December 2011; 8th edition February 2024 on 2023, 438 pages, 435+ stakeholders surveyed; 2025 edition reported November 2026).
attempts.charged: Analyst Pro monthly membership £195 a month ex VAT, cancel any time; Analyst Pro+ £1,195 a year on sale (list £2,340 a year).
attempts.state: Live.
attempts.note: The confidence index is not described on the opened page.

attempts.backers: Josh Baer; financial backing in 2020 from LionTree and the family office of Glenn Fuhrman (The Art Newspaper).
attempts.built: A newsletter of buyers, underbidders and gossip, faxed from 1994 and now e-mailed; from October 2021 the Baer Faxt Auction Database of buyers’ and underbidders’ identities from 1996, compiled in the saleroom by Baer and informants (for some lots a buyer or an underbidder but not both); Baer claimed five to ten name corrections since 1996 out of over 10,800 names; the trade’s nickname ‘The Barely Factual’ refers to variable spelling (The Art Newspaper). By February 2025 the database covered over 10,000 artworks and was integrated into Arthur Analytics’ research platform.
attempts.charged: October 2021: US$200 a month individual, US$500 a month for a large company. From February 2025: free, unlimited searches with an e-mail log-in (earlier day passes, monthly and annual bundles withdrawn).
attempts.state: Live; the database became a free funnel in 2025.
attempts.why: The one product that sells what the houses do not publish (who bought, who underbid) could not hold a US$2,400–6,000 a year price for the data alone and reverted to free access in 2025.
attempts.note: The newsletter’s own subscription price was not on the opened pages.

attempts.backers: Founded by Jianping Mei and Michael Moses; sold to Sotheby’s on 26 October 2016.
attempts.built: Repeat-sale art price indices from 45,000 repeat sales in eight categories (Sotheby’s, 2016); the Thread Genius team was assigned to its image database in 2018. Mei and Moses (2002) found masterpieces underperformed the broad art index by roughly 1–2 points a year (Masterworks).
attempts.state: Published as Sotheby’s Mei Moses (All Art and category indices), per Masterworks Research, July 2026.
attempts.why: The only independent repeat-sale index was taken inside a house, so the market lost its neutral benchmark.

attempts.backers: Acquired by Christie’s (2015 per Grossman LLP).
attempts.built: Collection-management software and ‘Collectrium Market Data Beta’, a subscription database of over 11 million item descriptions (December 2016).
attempts.state: Held liable in arbitration (award January 2019, confirmed June 2019, N.D. Texas, No. 3:16-cv-03404-D) for nearly US$1.8m to Heritage Auctions for DMCA anti-circumvention (US$1,755,000), CFAA (US$5,000) and breach of website terms (US$1); the copyright claim failed on fair use. Later scaled back (Artnet headline, not opened).
attempts.why: It built its database by scraping a competitor through rotating accounts and IP addresses; the data itself was held to be fair use with thin copyright, but the circumvention of access controls was not.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 20 Dec 2016
Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019

attempts.built: Fractional ownership of works; Masterworks Research publishes an All Art index and a Post-War and Contemporary index by repeat-sales methodology and a research blog; a teaser describes ‘Building a Usable Art Transaction Database: Lessons From 50M+ Records’ aggregated across 6,000+ houses with currency normalisation, artist entity resolution and human review. Its July 2026 note lists the limitations of every art index: selection and survivorship bias (a Sharpe ratio falling from about 0.24 to 0.04 after selection correction, Korteweg, Kräussl and Verwijmeren 2016), infrequent trading, appraisal smoothing (true volatility 1.5–3 times higher in de-smoothed studies), heterogeneity, and returns gross of insurance, storage, shipping, conservation and commissions ‘well into double digits’.
attempts.charged: Not on the opened page (fees and SEC filings not opened).
attempts.state: Live.
attempts.note: Masterworks’ fees, AUM and SEC filings were not opened; its data arm is described only by the teaser.

attempts.built: A mobile app that scans a work and estimates a price from auction results, curatorial interest, social media and press, over data on 700,000 artists from 1863, compiled from over 1,000,000 exhibitions and 45,000 institutions.
attempts.state: At Art Basel 2021 it valued a Conny Maier painting at €4,500 in Johann König’s booth, where it was offered at more than three times that; König said he had ‘more buyers than I can handle’. The Art Newspaper compared it to Magnus (2016), which ‘quietly folded’. Current status not confirmed.
attempts.why: The gallery price and the model price diverged by a factor of three on the first public test; dealers other than König did not admit the app.
attempts.note: The brief’s ‘closure’ is not confirmed by an opened page.

attempts.built: Two products. (1) Indices: an All Art Index (market-cap weighted, artists with 5+ sales, monthly, back-tested to 1986), segment indices, a Top 100 Market Cap index and an ‘AI Valuation Index’ built on its LiveArt Estimate (‘No other provider can calculate this’), with 5–10 page methodologies ‘required by Bloomberg, LSEG, and ICE’, co-brandable with ICE or S&P DJI as calculation agent for structured notes, ETPs and annuities. (2) For auction houses: the LiveArt Estimate (min/mid/max with a confidence interval; the example shows US$3.2M ±11% for a Richter), 8–10 ranked comparables, AI-assisted cataloguing, pre-sale estimates, live sale intelligence and post-sale analytics; XGBoost pricing ‘on 100+ features’, image recognition and vector search, ‘< 3 seconds’ a lot; 10M+ auction records from 1986 across 1,400+ houses, which it calls ‘the largest structured auction dataset in the market’.
attempts.charged: No prices published; records, analytics and rankings free without an account; enterprise agreements with onboarding and quarterly reviews.
attempts.state: Live; no house clients or partners named on either page; no accuracy or back-test results published.
attempts.note: Founders, funding and any ‘Bloomberg of art’ phrase were not on the opened pages.

attempts.backers: MCH Group (Art Basel’s parent) provides financing and strategic expertise; LUMA Foundation (Maja Hoffmann) advises; BCG X built the network.
attempts.built: A blockchain platform for ‘secure, seamless transactions for artists, galleries, fairs, and collectors’; a Stripe integration; it powers Art Basel’s online ‘art discovery experience’. Offices in Zurich, Berlin and London; CEO Rodrigo Esmela, CFO Chris Jukes, about 20 further staff.
attempts.state: Site copyright 2025; press room dated to 2023 events.

attempts.backers: Founder Nanne Dekking (then chairman of TEFAF); US$7.3m Series A, April 2019, from 2020 Ventures (a Spotify backer) and Hasso Plattner Capital.
attempts.built: A blockchain registry of vetted provenance, title and sales records; recorded Christie’s Ebsworth sale (November 2018); acquired Auction Club (March 2019), a subscription database of sales from about 4,000 houses with records since the 1970s. Dekking: the product is data integrity rather than the platform.
attempts.state: The Winston Art Group vetting tie (November 2019) appears only as a link on the page; current status not confirmed.

attempts.backers: Co-CEOs Sarah Wendell Sherrill and Lori Hotz (ex-Christie’s and Sotheby’s); US$6m round (April 2021) from Upside Partnership, 8VC, Franklin Templeton, Dream Machine, Weekend Fund, BoostVC and angels.
attempts.built: An art asset-management platform combining ownership proofs with a CRM, analytics and pricing tools; about 45,000 objects and an estimated US$5.4bn in asset value; about 300 artists; the stated model was a ‘Carta for art’.
attempts.state: Not confirmed in this session.

attempts.backers: Co-founders Sam Glatman (CEO) and Ivan Bestvina (CTO); investment from Christie’s Ventures (terms undisclosed).
attempts.built: An ‘agentic AI’ research platform producing artist and artwork reports (biography with source links, auction results, public presence, ‘market outlook’, similar artists, image search) from open-source data: auction results, exhibition announcements and news. Glatman’s claim: ‘dominant intelligence layer for the art world’.
attempts.charged: Credits: 35 free at sign-up; an artist report 10 credits, an artwork report 3 more, an artist search 1; the auction database free; 50 credits from US$35 plus taxes.
attempts.state: Launched September 2025; no independent criticism in the source.

attempts.backers: Artscapy: CEO Alessandro De Stasio. MyArtBroker: managing director Charlotte Stewart.
attempts.built: Artscapy: free AI price estimates and a £59.99 appraisal report (value, liquidity, volatility) from a ChatGPT-based model trained about three and a half years on auction, platform and verified private sales; the same model underpins its loans and insurance. MyArtBroker: a free instant valuation for prints and editions from predictive machine learning over 400 auction houses, private sales and platform demand, 40 factors, with human audit.
attempts.charged: Artscapy £59.99 per appraisal; MyArtBroker free instant valuation.
attempts.state: Live (Bloomberg, February 2026). Limits the trade named: more than 60% of sales are private; dirty data (thousands of Warhol Marilyn iterations); condition, provenance and rarity unmodelled; an estimate is not a buyer (‘theoretical values’); no interviewee thought AI replaces the specialist.

attempts.backers: Art Basel (MCH Group), built with the design firm Fantasy; Chief Digital Officer Craig Hepburn; Global Head of Digital Products Alain Brusch.
attempts.built: An app with an ‘AI Liaison’ concierge recommending galleries, artists and works and building itineraries; over 75,000 users and a 4.5-star App Store rating at launch (Art Basel Miami Beach, December 2024); 5,000+ artists; no data or sales features described.
attempts.state: Live; the 2026 data ambitions were not found on an opened page (search results pointed to ‘Zero 10’, a digital-art platform launched at Miami Beach 2025, not opened).

attempts.n: Deloitte Private / ArtTactic Art & Finance Report
attempts.built: A free biennial report. 8th edition (February 2024, on 2023): UHNWI art and collectible wealth US$2.174trn in 2022; art-secured lending US$29–34.1bn at end-2023; 81% of wealth managers, 79% of collectors and 83% of art professionals say technology could increase transparency; 50% of art professionals (a record) see regulation as a way to rebuild trust; 76% of wealth managers, 70% of collectors and 82% of art professionals call for modernised business practices. 2025 edition (as Paperjam reports it): UHNWI art wealth US$2.56trn in 2024, projected US$3.47trn by 2030; art-secured lending US$33.9–40bn in 2025; only 38% of collectors and 27% of wealth managers report high trust in art market data; wealth managers offering art services fell from 63% (2023) to 51% (2025); Bloomberg reports more than half of collectors in it named lack of transparent pricing as a major barrier.
attempts.state: Live.
attempts.note: The 2025 report itself (PDF) was not opened; figures are as relayed by Paperjam and Bloomberg. No compliance-cost figure was found.

attempts.built: An art-app that identified works and showed prices (2016).
attempts.state: ‘Quietly folded’, per The Art Newspaper (2021).

attempts.n: Pi-eX, Wondeur AI, Tagsmart, Vastari, Fairchain, MutualArt, Arthena
attempts.built: From memory only: Pi-eX (London) sells auction analytics and ‘MESO’ reports on the three houses’ evening sales; Wondeur AI (Toronto) sells artist-trajectory scores from museum and exhibition data; Tagsmart (London) sells DNA tagging and certificates; Vastari (London) matches collectors and museums for loans and sells exhibition data; Fairchain (New York) issues title and royalty certificates; MutualArt sells a price database and artist pages by subscription; Arthena ran a data-driven art fund. edge.n: The structured database is a commodity; the record of what is not in the results is not
edge.what: Every vendor rebuilds the same auction results: Artprice (30m results, 7,200 houses), Artnet (1,800+ houses from 1985), LiveArt (10M+ records, 1,400+ houses), Masterworks (50M+ records, 6,000+ houses), Artory/Auction Club (4,000 houses since the 1970s), Collectrium (11m descriptions by 2016). The trade’s own verdict (Georgina Adam, April 2026) is that software and AI can scrape prices ‘often for free’. The arbitrator in Heritage v Collectrium found the copyright in auction listings ‘thin’ and the use fair. So the price alone cannot carry a subscription: Artprice’s revenue has sat at about €8.5m, the Baer Faxt gave its database away in 2025. What no vendor structures is the condition, the underbidder, the private price, the export and tax position and the house’s own conduct, which the houses either do not publish or have closed (Christie’s archive, 2021; Sotheby’s proprietary index, 2016).
edge.evidence: Artmarket FY2025 revenue €8,497K; Adam’s comment; the 2019 award; the Baer Faxt’s February 2025 change; Christie’s archive closure; Sotheby’s Mei Moses statement.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019

edge.n: The regulatory map nobody sells, and a terminal can give it without becoming a regulated party
edge.what: HMRC’s guidance draws the line: a business that only gives art advice, charges for research or provenance checks without taking part in the transaction, or introduces customers to a participant, does not need to register as an art market participant; one that negotiates prices or acts for a customer in a sale or purchase at €10,000 or more does. A research terminal that never transacts sits on the lawful side of that line and can map the AML, export, VAT and sanctions position for the people who are inside it. The Deloitte/ArtTactic surveys show the demand: 50% of art professionals (a record) see regulation as a way to rebuild trust; 81% of wealth managers, 79% of collectors and 83% of art professionals say technology could increase transparency.
edge.evidence: gov.uk guidance (first published 7 Feb 2020, updated 6 Aug 2024); Deloitte 8th edition.
src: HMRC, Money laundering supervision for art market participants
edge.note: No compliance-cost figure for the trade was found on an opened page. The FCA and SEC positions on advice about art as an investment were not opened (see unconfirmed).

edge.n: The trust gap is measured and large
edge.what: Only 38% of collectors and 27% of wealth managers report high trust in art market data (Deloitte/ArtTactic 2025, as Paperjam reports it); more than half of collectors in the same report named lack of transparent pricing as a major barrier (Bloomberg); the market’s own benchmark index sits inside a house; the one vendor of underbidders is nicknamed ‘The Barely Factual’ in the trade for its spelling while claiming five to ten corrections in 10,800 names; LiveArt claims ‘no other provider’ can do what it does and publishes no accuracy figure; Limna’s first public test missed the asking price by a factor of three; Artprice’s audience figures are its own. A terminal that cites every figure and scores its own calls has no incumbent to displace on that ground.
edge.evidence: Paperjam; Bloomberg via The Star; The Art Newspaper 2021 (Baer Faxt; Limna); LiveArt pages; Artmarket release.

edge.n: The AI position in 2026: the models price prints and translate lots; they cannot see condition, provenance or the private sale, and they invent paperwork
edge.what: What is disclosed: the houses in The Art Newspaper’s 2024 survey use AI for translation, categorisation and personalisation; LiveArt sells an XGBoost estimate with a ±11% band in its example; Artscapy’s appraisal is a fine-tuned ChatGPT at £59.99; MyArtBroker prices prints over 40 features with human audit; Artsignal sells reports for credits; Artprice re-labels its databases as vertical AIs while revenue is flat. What the trade reports as the limits: more than 60% of sales are private; many versions of one image; condition, rarity and provenance unmodelled; an estimate is not a buyer. What the FT reported in December 2025 (via Futurism): chatbots ‘are helping fraudsters convincingly forge sales invoices’ (a Marsh fine-art broker), an adjuster received dozens of convincing certificates for a collection found to be fake, and collectors using AI tools to find provenance received hallucinated results. The houses’ caution is visible in what they do not say: no major house has disclosed an AI estimate.
edge.evidence: TAN 5 Nov 2024; LiveArt; Bloomberg Feb 2026; TAN 20 Nov 2025; Futurism/FT Dec 2025; Artmarket FY2025.
src: Artmarket.com press release via AAP, 10 Mar 2026
edge.note: The FT’s original article was not opened; no named case with a court or authority was found for a hallucinated-provenance loss.

edge.n: Cost structure: the houses carry thousands of staff and a loss; the data vendors carry debt or venture money; a desk of three can run on a fraction
edge.what: Sotheby’s: 2,218 staff, commissions and fees US$813m, pretax loss US$248m, severance US$29.2m, net debt US$2.76bn (2024). Christie’s International: pretax profit £85m (2024). Artnet: a Q1 2025 loss of just over US$1m before its take-private at €11.25 a share; dozens laid off in 2026. Artsy: over US$130m raised, profit unclear. Artmarket: €8.5m revenue, 180 databases, net income €1K. The vendors that survive on their own cash are the small desks: ArtTactic at £195 a month and the Baer Faxt, which runs on a saleroom network rather than a database build.
edge.evidence: FT via Irish Times; TAN 23 Apr 2026; EQS; Idéal Investisseur; ArtTactic store; TAN 7 Oct 2021.
src: FT via The Irish Times, 11 Sep 2025
edge.note: No source for research-analyst salaries was opened; the desk cost in the plan is an assumption.

edge.n: Two-sided data: the trade enters what it sees, and that is the only data the houses cannot copy
edge.what: The Baer Faxt’s thirty years of buyer and underbidder identities come from Josh Baer and informants in the saleroom, not from a database licence; by 2025 that record covered over 10,000 artworks and was licensed into Arthur Analytics. Beowolff’s stated plan for Artnet–Artsy is the same idea at scale: combine auction results with Artsy’s primary-market sales and user behaviour. The houses’ own data advantage, per Sotheby’s CEO, is ‘better analysis of client and object data’, which they will never share. A terminal whose users log the condition they saw, the price they were quoted and the licence they waited for builds the only record the houses cannot reproduce.
edge.evidence: TAN 7 Oct 2021; the Baer Faxt Feb 2025; Bloomberg Feb 2026; Spear’s Oct 2024.

edge.n: The price point the trade already pays, and the one it will not
edge.what: The record gives the band: ArtTactic £195 a month (list £2,340 a year); the Baer Faxt database US$200 a month individual and US$500 a month corporate in 2021 (now free); Artsignal US$35 per 50 credits; Artscapy £59.99 an appraisal; Bloomberg’s terminal about US$27,000–30,000 a year, which Georgina Adam doubts financial institutions will pay for art. A seat priced between ArtTactic and the old corporate Baer Faxt, with the house editions above it, is the only price range the comparables support.
edge.evidence: ArtTactic store; TAN 7 Oct 2021; TAN 20 Nov 2025; Bloomberg Feb 2026; TAN 23 Apr 2026.

risks.n: The houses’ terms of use and the DMCA: the facts are free, the login is not
risks.what: Heritage v Christie’s and Collectrium is the control that caught someone. Heritage alleged a spider copied about five million pages through more than two dozen accounts, some under false names, rotating IP addresses to defeat its security. The court held the website’s arbitration clause binding (2017). The arbitrator (January 2019) found the listings’ copyright ‘thin’ and Collectrium’s use fair, but awarded US$1,755,000 for DMCA anti-circumvention (US$1,000 per wilful access, at least 1,755), US$5,000 under the CFAA and US$1 for breach of the terms; the Northern District of Texas confirmed it in June 2019. The lawful course: take results only from pages open to the public without circumventing a login, a rate limit or a robots rule; license what sits behind a login; keep a record of every page’s source. Christie’s LIVE online terms (as published on its China site) contain no scraping clause; Sotheby’s and christies.com main terms were not opened.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 20 Dec 2016
Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019
Christie’s LIVE online terms of use (christies.com.cn)

risks.n: Copyright in catalogue text and images
risks.what: The arbitrator treated the copyright in auction listings as ‘thin’ and the reuse as fair use, and rejected a US$38bn DMCA copyright-management claim because the notice did not specify the protected parts of each page; but Heritage had sought up to US$150,000 per work for wilful infringement of over eight million images. Images and catalogue essays remain protected works; a terminal should store the fact (lot, price, date, condition as reported) and link to the image rather than copy it.
src: Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 20 Dec 2016
Grossman LLP Art Law Blog, 19 Aug 2019
risks.note: US arbitration, one case; UK copyright and database-right positions were not opened.

risks.what: Defamation Act 2013, section 1 (valid from 1 January 2014): ‘A statement is not defamatory unless its publication has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to the reputation of the claimant’; for a body that trades for profit, harm is not serious harm ‘unless it has caused or is likely to cause the body serious financial loss’. A terminal that prints whispers about collectors, dealers and houses publishes in England; the people rules in BRIEF_COMMON (attribution, dated authority, acquittals in the same line, rumours labelled) are the pre-publication control.
risks.note: The US position (public figures, actual malice under New York Times v Sullivan) and the trade lawyers’ commentary were not opened; carried from memory as U.

risks.n: Data protection on named individuals (GDPR / UK GDPR)
risks.what: Not opened in this session. From memory: naming private collectors as buyers or underbidders is processing of personal data that needs a lawful basis (legitimate interests or the journalism exemption) and a response to access and erasure requests; the Baer Faxt has done it since 1994 without a reported challenge in the pages opened.

Beowolff now owns the Artnet Price Database, Artnet News and Artsy together and plans its own AI analytics on the combined data; Artprice has a Perplexity AI partnership and plans a 2026 NVIDIA build-out. A terminal that depends on either feed can be cut off or repriced; the record supports building on the houses’ public results and the trade’s own entries instead.
src: Artmarket.com press release via AAP, 10 Mar 2026

risks.what: Christie’s US$990,000 settlement (final approval July 2025) followed the exposure of more than 500,000 customers’ names, passport and driving-licence data in the May 2024 RansomHub incident. A terminal that stores KYC documents for its compliance readings carries the same exposure; the lawful course is to record the check’s outcome and date, not the document.

risks.n: Being treated as an art market participant or an investment adviser
risks.what: HMRC: a business that negotiates prices or acts for a customer in a sale or purchase at €10,000 or more must register; one that only advises, researches or introduces need not. The FCA and SEC positions on advice about art as an investment were not opened; from memory, art is not a specified investment under the UK Regulated Activities Order and the SEC’s reach runs to securities (fractional interests such as Masterworks’ offerings), so a terminal must avoid personal investment recommendations on securitised art and must keep clear of brokering.
src: HMRC, Money laundering supervision for art market participants
risks.note: The FCA/SEC part is from memory (U).

plan.breakeven: Cost base about £260,000–270,000 a year on the assumptions above (desk £216,000; data £12,000; hosting £9,000; legal £20,000; registration £0). kills.n: The houses’ terms of use and the DMCA
kills.what: A terminal that takes results from behind a login, rotates accounts or defeats a rate limit faces the Collectrium outcome: US$1,000 per wilful access under the DMCA (US$1,755,000 on 1,755 accesses), the CFAA, and the house’s arbitration clause. tools.what: Phillips’ early-bidding structure (September 2025) rewards a binding written bid at or above the low estimate placed at least 48 hours before the sale with a lower premium; the house’s April 2026 release restates its premium for all salerooms.
Sotheby’s Financial Services’ US$900m ArtFi Master Trust Series 2026-1 (closed 3 February 2026) turns art-loan cash flows into upfront capital; a US$700m offering was first announced in 2024.

tools.n: Sanctions screening and the KYC file
tools.what: OFSI expects a relevant firm to know when a customer is a designated person and to report the nature and amount of funds or economic resources held for them; HMRC’s sector guidance for AMPs is awaiting ministerial sign-off (October 2026), so AMPs follow the British Art Market Federation guidance meanwhile.

A database of over 700,000 items including Interpol’s; auction houses pay per lot (UK £3.66, US $4.95, DACH €5.60, rest of Europe €5.10) with a minimum annual fee of £800 / €900 / $1,000 excluding VAT, searches usually applying to lots over £1,500 / €1,500 / $2,000; a single trade search £85 / €100 / $110 plus VAT, urgent £300 / €350 / $400 with a one-working-day answer; an ALR Certificate adds archive checks for 1933–45 provenance gaps; auction-house vetting checks the database only and issues no per-item confirmation; more than 130 auction houses and fairs subscribe.

Sotheby’s Fiduciary Client Group: a dedicated team for executors, trustees and advisers, with in-house lawyers and a worldwide team, offering appraisals and sale and disposition strategies, linked to Valuations, Sotheby’s Financial Services, Collection Sale Management, Restitution, Tax, Heritage & UK Museums; no fees or timelines on the page.

failures.n: Beneficial owners not asked for (Senate PSI, 2020)
failures.what: The Subcommittee traced over US$18m of art bought in the US between May and November 2014, after the March 2014 sanctions, to shell companies linked to Arkady and Boris Rotenberg; a Moscow-based adviser bought through a Belize company and later his own firm; Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips and Bonhams treated the adviser as the principal and never asked whom he was buying for; Christie’s accepted a verbal claim about the Belize company’s owner without documentation; the houses said they relied on banks to vet the source of funds; the report recommends extending the Bank Secrecy Act to high-value art.

failures.what: Sotheby’s paid US$6.25m to New York State to settle a suit alleging it helped clients avoid sales tax with resale certificates for art bought for personal use, 2010–2020; one client’s company bought US$27m of art on resale certificates in 2010–15 and staff helped install the works at home; seven other clients 2012–20; in several cases the house gave clients the forms or filled in parts of them; it agreed to train staff in the tax rules and to review whether a client intends to resell.

failures.n: The first corporate sanctions prosecution of a gallery (2025–26), dismissed
failures.what: Hauser & Wirth Gallery Limited and the shipper Artay Rauchwerger Solomons Limited were charged under regulation 46B of the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 with making a George Condo painting (Escape from Humanity, 2021) available to a collector alleged to be connected with Russia, sold July 2021 and invoiced October 2021; Border Force seized the work on 8 September 2022; both companies appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 12 November 2025 and denied the charges. On 9 July 2026 HHJ Baumgartner dismissed all charges against both defendants: the work had been ‘made available’, but the buyer was found not to be ordinarily resident in Russia. Mishcon de Reya calls the outcome a significant setback for HMRC’s enforcement objectives.

failures.what: Chardin’s Cut Melon (1760) sold for €26.7m against an €8–12m estimate at Christie’s in June 2024; the invoice was due in full one week after the sale; The Art Newspaper reported, citing legal documents, that the final bidder was an Italian investor new to the Old Masters market, that Christie’s spent six months seeking payment, added a €195,000 penalty in September and sued in Paris for €27.4m with a hearing listed for 16 December 2024. The outcome was not confirmed in this session.

desk.day: The published accounts are thin and dated, and the houses’ careers pages could not be read in this session, so the day is drawn from one specialist’s own description (Mr Porter, 2018), the houses’ sale reports and the trade press. The morning goes to overnight e-mail from the other time zones, then to whatever is most pressing: a client bringing a work in for inspection, a valuation, catalogue research and writing, the press, and the planning of exhibitions and fairs. In the weeks before a sale the specialist briefs senior management, designs the hang with the house’s software, sits with the Private Client Group over the list of interested collectors and works with the media team; the preview is long days on the gallery floor (the March 2026 London preview drew more than 6,000 visitors and bidding from 40 countries) with breakfasts and lunches for collectors, museum directors and dealers. The consignment side is less visible: Apollo describes the business-getter building a package of seller’s and buyer’s premium, guarantee and reinsurance acceptable to seller, guarantor and house, and the Senate PSI record shows the compliance desk opening a file on who the buyer really is. On the night the bid department runs the room under the auctioneer with a row of telephones; afterwards Post-Sales Service invoices the buyer and the seller is paid within 45 days if the buyer has paid.

cases.task: ‘The executors want a proposal by Friday for the family’s Impressionist landscape — they think £3–5m — and the other two houses are pitching too.’
cases.sum: £3–5m, the family’s expectation; the estimate is the house’s to set against the comparables below (Sotheby’s London, March 2026; Christie’s and Sotheby’s New York, 2025–26)
cases.reading: London’s spring evening sale sold every lot: Sotheby’s Modern & Contemporary Evening Auction of 4 March 2026 was the first fully sold-through various-owner sale in decades, the various-owner sales totalled £154m and the Lewis Collection £35.8m of that; a Monet, Maison du Jardinier, once John Singer Sargent’s, made £8.2m, a Giacometti Femme debout £5.1m against £2.2–2.8m, a Brancusi Une Muse £3.6m against £2–3m and a Hepworth £3.5m against £3.5–4.5m (Sotheby’s, March 2026). In New York the Lauder sale of 18 November 2025 sold all 24 lots for US$527.5m against US$379.2–412.5m, 83% above high estimate, with a Matisse Figure décorative at US$16.71m (est. US$12–18m) and a Van Gogh reed-pen drawing at US$11.2m (est. US$8–10m) (Sotheby’s press release). At Christie’s on 19 May 2026 a Renoir, La femme aux lilas (1876–77), hammered at US$24m (US$28.2m with fees) (The Art Newspaper). The autumn was weaker: Sotheby’s London contemporary evening sale of 15 October 2026 hammered £36.9m against a £39.5m low estimate with six of 34 lots unsold, though the house said its London sales in 2026 had passed US$1bn, with £598m from modern and contemporary auctions, the highest year-to-date since 2015 (The Art Newspaper, 16 Oct 2026). Guarantees now cover most of the value: 72% of Impressionist and modern evening-sale value by hammer was guaranteed in the first half of 2025 (Apollo, 7 Oct 2025). The next public test is this week: Sotheby’s Modern Evening Auction in New York on 18 November 2026 carries Monet’s La Barque bleue at US$20–30m, a Cézanne still life at US$20–30m, Signac’s Collioure at US$12–18m, a Degas pastel at US$10–15m and a Pissarro and a Renoir from the Armand Hammer Collection, with sections from three further private collections (Sotheby’s catalogue, opened 16 Nov 2026).
cases.money: Seller’s side, on Sotheby’s published terms: seller’s commission standard 10% of hammer, negotiable on a lot of this size; a success fee of 2% of hammer if the lot sells above the high estimate; packing, shipping and insurance for the consignor’s account; settlement within 45 days of the sale if the buyer has paid (Sotheby’s fee structure, 2026). Buyer’s side, which sets what the room will bid: Sotheby’s buyer’s premium in London 28% of hammer to £1.5m and 22% from £1.5m to £6m since 13 February 2026 (The Art Newspaper, 17 Feb 2026) — on a £4m hammer that is £970,000 on the published bands (my arithmetic), plus the overhead premium (rate not published on the fee page) and VAT at the standard rate on the premium under the auctioneers’ scheme (GOV.UK, VAT margin schemes). No VAT on the hammer for a UK private seller’s work under the margin scheme (from memory, unconfirmed). Artist’s Resale Right: none for an artist dead more than 70 years (Monet d. 1926, Pissarro d. 1903, Sisley d. 1899); for a later artist the royalty is 4% to £50,000 then 3%, 1%, 0.5% and 0.25%, capped at £12,500 (GOV.UK, ARR). Inheritance tax: 40% above the nil-rate band (from memory); an Acceptance in Lieu offer remits 25% of the tax that would have been payable to the estate — on a £100,000 object at 40% the estate nets £60,000 from an open-market sale but £70,000 as a tax settlement value, about 17% more (Arts Council England leaflet). Conditional Exemption (IHTA 1984 ss.30–35) exempts a transfer of pre-eminent objects on a claim within two years against undertakings to preserve the object, allow reasonable public access and keep it in the UK, with a tax charge normally arising if the undertakings are broken or the object is sold or given away (HMRC IHTM11260); on an open-market sale the exemption is lost and capital gains tax may apply (Withers, 28 Sep 2020). The stolen-art check costs the house £3.66 a lot in the UK on its Art Loss Register subscription, or £85 plus VAT for a single trade search (ALR FAQ).

walls.n: Acceptance in Lieu / inheritance tax
walls.cite: Inheritance Tax Act 1984 (section not cited by the leaflet)
walls.authority: HMRC; the AIL Panel (Arts Council England); DCMS Secretary of State
walls.threshold: pre-eminent objects; acceptance depends on available funds
walls.what_it_does: Settles tax with the object; 25% of the tax that would have been payable is remitted to the estate (the douceur); HMRC cannot ‘give change’, so a public body may fund the difference in a hybrid offer; a private treaty sale to a museum at a special price works on a similar calculation; the Cultural Gifts Scheme gives individuals up to a 30% reduction in income or capital gains tax on a lifetime gift.
walls.case: The leaflet’s own example: £100,000 object, 40% tax, £70,000 settlement value against £60,000 net from sale.

walls.n: Conditional Exemption
walls.cite: Inheritance Tax Act 1984 ss.30–35; HMRC IHTM11260
walls.authority: HMRC Heritage Team
walls.threshold: pre-eminent national, scientific, historic or artistic interest; claim within two years of the transfer
walls.what_it_does: Exempts the transfer against undertakings to preserve the object, allow reasonable public access (in situ or by loan to a public museum) and keep it in the UK; a tax charge normally arises on breach, sale or gift; an open-market sale loses the exemption and may attract capital gains tax.

risks: The lot fails: six of 34 lots unsold at Sotheby’s London on 15 October 2026 and the sale under its low estimate (The Art Newspaper).
A guarantee set at or below the low estimate hands the guarantor 15–20% of any upside (Apollo, 7 Oct 2025).
A title claim after cataloguing: the Schiele turnover order of 23 April 2025 came decades after purchase (The Art Newspaper).
The executors sign before probate or before the tax route is chosen; an AIL offer and a sale are alternatives (Arts Council England).

cases.value_left: The house’s fee page gives the standard seller’s terms but not the overhead premium rate; the premium bands sit in a PDF chart; nothing public shows the net-to-seller on a given hammer under each house’s terms side by side, nor the estate’s AIL or Conditional Exemption outcome against a sale — the Arts Council leaflet’s own example shows the offer in lieu worth about 17% more than a sale on a 40% liability, and no house page opened does that sum for an executor. Consignment deadlines are not published. Comparables are scattered across sale reports; no page opened lists Impressionist results in the £3–5m band for the last three years in one place.

cases.persona: a head of sale at Sotheby’s in New York, with the business-getter and the finance desk
cases.task: ‘The consignor wants a guarantee on the US$20m picture or she goes across the street. Do we write it, lay it off, or walk?’
cases.sum: US$20m (the guarantee level sought; the trade sets guarantees at or somewhat below the low estimate — Apollo, 7 Oct 2025)
cases.reading: Guarantees have become the market’s floor. In the first half of 2025 nearly 73% of post-war and contemporary evening-sale value at Christie’s, Sotheby’s and Phillips was guaranteed, a record and a US$400m outlay, and 72% of Impressionist and modern value; Christie’s says about 1.5% of its lots carry guarantees, far more by value (Apollo, 7 Oct 2025, citing the houses and ArtTactic-type data). Guaranteed post-war and contemporary sales ran US$1.46bn in 2022, US$858m in 2024 and US$392m in H1 2025 (Apollo). Christie’s S.I. Newhouse sale of 18 May 2026 was reported as entirely backed by third-party guarantees and made US$540.5m hammer (US$630.8m with fees) against US$462–595m, with a Pollock at US$157m hammer and a Brancusi at US$93m (The Art Newspaper, 19 May 2026). Sotheby’s Mnuchin sale of 14 May 2026 had all 11 works guaranteed; a Rothko made US$85.8m with fees (HENI, 1 Jun 2026). In London on 15 October 2026 the guaranteed de Kooning opened at £7m against an £8m low estimate and hammered at £8.2m; the guaranteed Rothko, Hockney and Baselitz are named but not priced (The Art Newspaper, 16 Oct 2026). HENI’s index for May 2026 found ‘weak guarantees’ (lots selling near or below the low estimate) 2.4 points above the norm (HENI, 1 Jun 2026).
cases.money: The guarantee: a secret agreed price, usually at or somewhat below the low estimate, at which the house (or its reinsurer) buys the lot if bidding fails (Apollo). The third-party guarantor’s reward: insiders say 15–20% of any amount bid above the guaranteed price; Christie’s pioneered giving guarantors a discount whether they took a flat fee or an upside share, and Sotheby’s later changed its approach to attract guarantors (Apollo). What the house earns if the lot sells at US$20m: the buyer’s premium on Sotheby’s bands since 13 February 2026 is 28% to US$2m, 22% to US$8m and 15% above — US$3.68m on a US$20m hammer on the published bands (my arithmetic; The Art Newspaper, 17 Feb 2026) — against a seller’s commission that on a guaranteed trophy is negotiated and often small (standard 10%, Sotheby’s fee page; the discount is from memory). What the house risks: Sotheby’s reportedly committed US$902m of guarantees in 2007; by end-2008 the two houses held an estimated US$63m of art they were obliged to buy; Phillips under Bernard Arnault reportedly ran up about US$400m of losses in 1999–2002, the 2001 Smooke sale making US$85m against a rumoured US$170m guarantee (Apollo, citing the Wall Street Journal and Philip Hook). Insiders put top-end margins as low as 2% (Apollo). The Taubman case is the modern benchmark: Sotheby’s guaranteed US$515m to win the A. Alfred Taubman collection in 2015, expected a shortfall of about US$6m (1%) in sale proceeds and, with about US$6m of sale expenses, reported a US$12m loss, with a fourth-quarter 2015 loss of US$10–19m expected partly on Taubman charges and US$24m of unsold inventory at low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 22 Jan 2016). The 2022–23 losses are not quantified in any page opened. The buyer’s premium bands are confirmed on Sotheby’s own help page, updated 9 September 2026: 28% to US$2m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above, with the same shape in sterling, euros, Hong Kong dollars and francs.

road.doc: irrevocable bid agreement

road.doc: KYC file; sanctions screening

walls.n: Disclosure of guarantees in New York
walls.cite: New York City’s auction regulations of about thirty years’ standing, repealed with effect from 15 June 2022 (authorised in 2021); auctioneers no longer need a licence
walls.authority: New York City (the article does not name the agency)
