The houses still mark guaranteed lots with symbols; Apollo notes the diamond for a third-party guarantee.

walls.n: Know the guarantor: sanctions and AML
walls.cite: US: no Bank Secrecy Act duty on art dealers (Senate PSI, 2020); OFAC sanctions apply. UK: MLR 2017 as amended, AMP threshold £10,000; OFSI reporting since 14 May 2025
walls.authority: OFAC; HMRC; OFSI
walls.what_it_does: A guarantor who may end up owning the lot is a buyer; the file must show who stands behind the money.
walls.case: Senate PSI (2020): the houses treated an adviser as the principal and never asked whom he bought for; the funds traced to shell companies linked to sanctioned individuals.

walls.n: The house’s own balance sheet
walls.cite: Sotheby’s Financial Services securitisation: US$900m ArtFi Master Trust 2026-1, closed 3 February 2026
walls.authority: Morningstar DBRS ratings (as reported)
walls.what_it_does: Gives the house upfront capital against loan cash flows; the guarantee book is separate and not disclosed on any page opened.

cases.people: The house’s finance committee and the chairman who writes guarantees; the third-party guarantors the business-getters know (collectors and dealers; none named by a source opened for this work); Christie’s Ben Gore and Mari-Claudia Jiménez are quoted by Apollo on the mechanics; compliance for the guarantor’s file; outside counsel for the irrevocable bid agreement.
cases.calendar: New York marquee weeks: May (14–19 May 2026) and November (the Lauder sale was 18 November 2025; the November 2026 dates were not confirmed); London March, June and October (4 March, 24 June, 15 October 2026). The guarantee and its lay-off must be in place before the catalogue is published, since the symbol goes in the catalogue.
cases.whispers: Apollo (7 Oct 2025): a record 72–73% of evening-sale value guaranteed in H1 2025; margins at the top ‘as low as 2 per cent’; Fisher Landau (Nov 2023) all 31 lots guaranteed, 13 sold at or below the low estimate, very likely to guarantors. The Art Newspaper (19 May 2026): Newhouse ‘entirely backed by third-party guarantees’ and a US$1.1bn two-night total at Christie’s. HENI (1 Jun 2026): strong and weak guarantees both 2.4 points above the norm in May 2026; the index grade B. The Art Newspaper (16 Oct 2026): guaranteed lots in London opened below their low estimates and the sale missed its low estimate.
risks: The lot sells to the guarantor at the guarantee: 13 of 31 Fisher Landau lots sold at or below the low estimate (Apollo).

The house keeps the risk and the market turns: an estimated US$63m of art the houses were obliged to buy at end-2008 (Apollo, citing the WSJ); a US$12m loss on the US$515m Taubman guarantee (The Art Newspaper, 22 Jan 2016).
The guarantor is outbid by a whisker and takes 15–20% of a thin upside (Apollo).
The guarantor’s money is somebody else’s: the Senate PSI record of undisclosed principals (2020).
A guaranteed lot opening below the low estimate signals weakness to the room, as with the de Kooning at £7m against £8m (The Art Newspaper, 16 Oct 2026).
cases.value_left: No house publishes its guarantee book, its loss history or the fee it pays guarantors; the Apollo figures come from insiders and the losses from the WSJ and memoirs. The disclosure is a symbol, not a number. A specialist cannot today see, for one artist, how guaranteed lots performed against unguaranteed ones over the last three years, nor what the lay-off cost on comparable lots — the kind of ledger the terminal could keep from the catalogues and results.
next: Set the guarantee no higher than the low estimate and write down the house’s loss at each hammer from zero to the guarantee.
Ask the business-getters for two third-party guarantors and price the lay-off at the 15–20% upside share the trade quotes.
Open a KYC file on each guarantor and its beneficial owner before any term sheet.
Put the symbol in the catalogue and the online listing.
Check the sale’s total guaranteed value against the house’s appetite for the week before adding this lot.

cases.persona: a Sotheby’s specialist in London, with the compliance officer
cases.task: ‘A new client I have never met wants to bid £1.2m through an agent; the paperwork names a company with no beneficial owner on the form; and the deposit has arrived from an account in a third party’s name. Can I take the bid, and if not, how do I say no?’
cases.sum: £1.2m (the bid sought; the UK AMP threshold is £10,000 per transaction or linked series — SI 2026/621)
cases.reading: Three flags at once, each on the record as a failure point. The Senate PSI found in 2020 that Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips and Bonhams treated a Moscow-based adviser as the principal and never asked whom he was buying for, while over US$18m of purchases after the March 2014 sanctions traced to shell companies linked to Arkady and Boris Rotenberg; Christie’s accepted a verbal claim about a Belize company’s owner with no documentation; the houses said they relied on banks to vet the source of funds (PSI report, 29 Jul 2020). In the UK the house is an art market participant supervised by HMRC, and since 14 May 2025 a ‘relevant firm’ that must report to OFSI as soon as practicable where it knows or suspects a customer is a designated person, with penalties of up to £1m or 50% of the breach and a criminal offence for failing to report (OFSI guidance, updated 12 May 2026). The 2026 Regulations set the AMP threshold at £10,000 and widen enhanced due diligence to any transaction that is unusually complex or unusually large (SI 2026/621; HMRC AMLG2100). Enforcement cuts both ways: the first corporate prosecution of a gallery under the Russia sanctions, over a George Condo painting made available to a collector with Russian connections, ended on 9 July 2026 with all charges against Hauser & Wirth and its shipper dismissed, the judge finding the buyer not ordinarily resident in Russia; counsel on both sides say expectations on client checks are rising (Mishcon de Reya, 29 Jul 2026; CMS, 14 Nov 2025). In New York, Sotheby’s paid US$6.25m in November 2024 over resale certificates it knew were false (NY Attorney General).
cases.money: The cost of saying no is the lost premium: 28% of hammer to £1.5m on Sotheby’s London bands (The Art Newspaper, 17 Feb 2026), about £336,000 on a £1.2m hammer on the published bands (my arithmetic). The cost of saying yes wrongly: OFSI monetary penalties up to £1m or 50% of the breach value, whichever is higher; up to six months’ imprisonment for failing to report; up to seven years on indictment for a sanctions breach (OFSI guidance). HMRC supervises AMPs and can penalise registration and due-diligence failures (HMRC AMLG2100; penalty figures not on the page opened). The 2024 New York settlement cost Sotheby’s US$6.25m plus new training and review duties (NY AG, 14 Nov 2024). The Hauser & Wirth defence ran from a November 2025 charge to a July 2026 dismissal (CMS; Mishcon de Reya).

road.n: Identify the customer and, where an agent bids, the principal: the agent is not the client
road.who: compliance; the specialist supplies the facts
road.doc: customer due diligence file under regulation 27 (trigger £10,000); for a company, the beneficial owner

road.n: Apply enhanced due diligence: a first-time client, an agent in front, a company with no owner on the form and a third-party payment make the transaction unusually complex

road.doc: EDD record; source-of-funds evidence; mandatory EDD for FATF call-for-action countries (Iran, DPRK, Myanmar)

road.doc: OFSI report as soon as practicable, stating the nature and amount of funds held; OFSI licence application if a prohibited act is to be done lawfully

road.who: post-sales and finance
road.doc: returned-payment record

road.n: Decline lawfully: if due diligence cannot be completed, do not transact, keep the record; the MLRO reports suspicion to the National Crime Agency before the transaction proceeds and without informing the client; the house’s conditions let it refuse the bid or rescind the sale when checks are unsatisfactory

road.doc: SAR; file note; Condition 16(a) refusal

walls.n: Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017, as amended
walls.cite: SI 2017/692; art market participants in scope from 10 January 2020 under the UK’s transposition of the EU’s fifth directive (SI 2019/1511, number from memory), with HMRC registration required by 10 January 2021; amended by SI 2026/621 (made 9 June 2026, in force 21 days later)
walls.authority: HMRC
walls.threshold: £10,000 per transaction or series of linked transactions (regulation 14; regulation 27 triggers); €10,000 from 2020 to June 2026
walls.what_it_does: Registration, customer due diligence (identity and address for individuals; beneficial owner, purpose and source of funds for companies and trusts; an agent’s authority to act; sanctions and PEP screening), enhanced due diligence for unusually complex or large transactions, an MLRO who reports suspicions to the National Crime Agency before the transaction proceeds and without telling the client, record-keeping; HMRC’s sector guidance awaits ministerial sign-off (October 2026) and AMPs follow the British Art Market Federation guidance meanwhile. Sotheby’s London conditions make the same demands contractual: identity and source-of-funds information on demand, bids refused and sales rescinded if checks are unsatisfactory, agents to keep due-diligence records for five years.
walls.case: No UK AMP penalty case was opened in this session; the Senate PSI (2020) is the record of what unasked questions cost.

walls.authority: OFSI (HM Treasury)

walls.what_it_does: Report knowledge or suspicion that a customer is a designated person as soon as practicable; penalties up to £1m or 50% of the breach; licences available for otherwise prohibited acts.

walls.authority: HMRC (enforcement); CPS (prosecution)
walls.what_it_does: Prohibits making luxury goods available to a person connected with Russia; up to six months’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine on the charge brought.

walls.authority: Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations; OFAC; FinCEN
walls.threshold: the report cites the EU’s €10,000 rule as the model
walls.what_it_does: The US houses run voluntary AML controls; sanctions apply regardless.

walls.authority: New York Attorney General; Department of Taxation and Finance
walls.what_it_does: A resale certificate is for dealers buying to resell; a house that knows the buyer is collecting cannot accept it.
walls.case: Sotheby’s paid US$6.25m; conduct 2010–2020; eight clients.

cases.people: The house’s money-laundering reporting officer and compliance team; OFSI for reports and licences; HMRC as supervisor; sanctions counsel (the Hauser & Wirth case was analysed publicly by Mishcon de Reya and CMS); the British Art Market Federation for the interim sector guidance; the bank that received the third-party payment.
cases.calendar: SI 2026/621 in force 21 days after 9 June 2026; HMRC’s updated AMP guidance due after ministerial sign-off (pending at 13 October 2026); OFSI reports ‘as soon as practicable’; the £1.2m bid cannot wait for any of it — the file must close before the sale.
cases.whispers: Mishcon de Reya (29 Jul 2026): the dismissal is ‘a significant setback for HMRC’s enforcement objectives’ and the judgment heavily fact-specific. CMS (14 Nov 2025): the first prosecution signalled a new enforcement focus on arts and luxury goods. The Art Newspaper (17 Feb 2026): Sotheby’s Financial Services securitised US$900m of art loans, so the house also lends to the clients it screens. The Art Newspaper (17 Dec 2025): spend from Asia-Pacific buyers at Christie’s down 3% in 2025.
risks: Taking the agent as the client: the PSI record of US$18m bought for undisclosed principals (2020).
A verbal assurance about a company’s owner, as Christie’s accepted for the Belize company (PSI, 2020).
A third-party payment that cannot be traced to the buyer.
Missing an OFSI report: offence and penalty up to £1m or 50% (OFSI guidance).
Over-refusing on nationality alone: the July 2026 judgment turned on ordinary residence, not citizenship (Mishcon de Reya).
cases.value_left: The houses’ compliance is a cost centre that never reaches the specialist’s desk as a tool: no public page shows the specialist what the file needs before a bid is registered, which jurisdictions trigger enhanced due diligence this month, or how the ‘ordinarily resident’ test was applied. HMRC’s sector guidance is still unsigned in October 2026 and AMPs are told to use the BAMF guidance meanwhile. A terminal that turned the regulations, the OFSI guidance and the one decided case into a checklist with dates would fill the gap.
next: Tell the agent the house needs the principal’s identity and the company’s beneficial owner before any bid is registered.
Return the third-party deposit to the originating account and ask for payment from the invoiced buyer only.
Run sanctions screening on the client, the agent, the company and its owner; if any hit or suspicion, report to OFSI as soon as practicable.
Record the enhanced due diligence and the decision; if the file cannot be completed, decline in writing without giving the reason that would tip off.
Brief the head of sale that the lot may need another underbidder.
cases.note: The SI number for the 2019 amendment and the POCA section numbers are from memory; the 10 January 2020 start, the 10 January 2021 registration deadline and the MLRO reporting duty are as a law firm stated them the day before commencement. The third-party-payment practice is from memory. The brief described the Hauser & Wirth matter as a money-laundering charge; the record shows a sanctions charge, dismissed.

cases.persona: a head of sale at a London house, with post-sales and the legal desk
cases.where: London (with the Paris and New York cases as the record)
cases.task: ‘The buyer of the £2m lot has not paid and the seller is asking where her money is. What do the conditions let us do, and what do we actually get back?’
cases.sum: £2m hammer (illustrative); the record case is Chardin’s Cut Melon at €26.7m, Christie’s, June 2024, unpaid
cases.reading: The seller is paid only when the buyer pays: Sotheby’s pays the seller within 45 days of the sale date ‘provided the buyer’s payment has been received’ (Sotheby’s fee structure, 2026). The record case is at Christie’s: Chardin’s Cut Melon (1760) sold for €26.7m against an €8–12m estimate in June 2024; the invoice was due in full one week after the sale; The Art Newspaper reported on 13 December 2024, citing legal documents, that the final bidder was an Italian investor previously unknown in the Old Masters market, that Christie’s spent about six months seeking payment, demanded it in full in August and September, added a €195,000 penalty in September and sued in Paris for €27.4m including interest and penalties, with a hearing listed for 16 December 2024; the buyer’s lawyer had offered in July to deposit the sum in escrow with a notary; Christie’s declined to comment. The outcome of that hearing was not confirmed in this session. Earlier Sotheby’s non-payment suits in New York (a Keith Haring bid of US$6.5m in 2017–19) were seen only as headlines in this session and are not relied on. A house that has guaranteed the lot carries the loss itself if the buyer defaults (Apollo, 7 Oct 2025, on the mechanics).
cases.money: What the house is owed: hammer plus buyer’s premium (28% to £1.5m, 22% to £6m, 15% above at Sotheby’s London — Sotheby’s help centre, 9 Sep 2026), plus VAT on the premium at the standard rate (GOV.UK). What the conditions add on default at Sotheby’s London (Conditions of Business for Buyers, 2 July 2024, Condition 9(a)): payment is due immediately on conclusion of the auction and the buyer is in default after five days without cleared funds; then interest at 6% above HSBC Bank plc base rate (capped at the legal maximum), storage at the buyer’s risk and expense, cancellation of the sale, set-off against sums any Sotheby’s Group company owes the buyer, application of the buyer’s deposits to this lot, another lot, a resale shortfall or damages, rejection of future bids or a deposit demand, a lien over the buyer’s property held by any Sotheby’s Group company, resale at the buyer’s expense with the buyer liable for any shortfall and the costs of resale, proceedings for the price, damages, interest and costs, and release of the buyer’s name and address to the seller. At Christie’s Paris a penalty (€195,000 on €26.7m) and interest, as the claim of €27.4m shows (The Art Newspaper, 13 Dec 2024); Christie’s own conditions could not be read (bot challenge). What the seller gets: nothing until the buyer pays (Sotheby’s fee structure: payment within 45 days ‘provided the buyer’s payment has been received’). What the house loses: the premium on a cancelled sale and, on a guaranteed lot, the difference between the guarantee and the eventual price (Apollo).

cases.calendar: Invoice due within days of the sale (one week at Christie’s Paris); seller’s settlement at 45 days conditional on payment (Sotheby’s); the Chardin claim reached a Paris hearing six months after the June 2024 sale; a re-offer waits for the next sale of the category (Old Masters in London in July and December, from memory).

Apollo (7 Oct 2025): the trade’s margins at the top ‘as low as 2 per cent’, which a single default erases. The Art Newspaper (16 Oct 2026): a cautious London market with unsold and withdrawn lots.

The seller is unpaid at 45 days and the house holds the lot (Sotheby’s fee structure).
A resale in a weaker market fixes the shortfall at the house’s or the seller’s cost (from memory of the conditions).

A specialist today cannot show a consignor, before signing, what happens to her settlement if the buyer defaults, nor compare the houses’ remedies. The terminal could carry each house’s conditions (payment period, interest, cancellation, resale, costs) as a table with the cases where they were tested.

cases.persona: a Sotheby’s specialist in London, with the legal desk
cases.where: London (the decided cases are in New York and Germany)
cases.task: ‘A letter from a claimant’s lawyer says our lot 12 was sold under duress in Vienna in 1938. The catalogue is printed. What do we do, and whose procedure governs?’
cases.sum: The Schiele drawing at the centre of the New York turnover order was valued at about US$1.25m at seizure (The Art Newspaper, 25 Apr 2025)
cases.reading: The record has moved against the holder. In New York the Manhattan DA’s Art Trafficking Unit obtained a warrant on 12 September 2023 and seized Schiele’s Russian War Prisoner (1916) ‘in place’ at the Art Institute of Chicago, filed a turnover application on 23 February 2024, and on 23 April 2025 Justice Althea Drysdale of the New York Supreme Court ordered the drawing turned over to the heirs of Fritz Grünbaum under Penal Law §450.10, finding it stolen, the museum presumed to know so when it bought it in 1966, New York jurisdiction made out because the work passed through a Manhattan gallery, no limitation period and no laches; the museum had argued a civil court had already dismissed the heirs’ replevin claims and said it would look at options for appeal (ABA Year in Review 2025; The Art Newspaper, 25 Apr 2025). MoMA, the Carnegie Museum and private collectors had already returned or agreed to return other Grünbaum Schieles (The Art Newspaper). A July 2026 practitioner note describes a September 2025 order to surrender the drawing and warns that art with ‘a tenuous New York connection’ can face seizure wherever it is held (Shook Hardy & Bacon, July 2026); the present status was not confirmed. For the Pissarro at the Thyssen-Bornemisza, the US Supreme Court on 10 March 2025 sent the Cassirer case back to the Ninth Circuit in a brief order in the light of a new California law requiring California law to apply to Holocaust-era claims, after the Ninth Circuit had applied Spanish law in the museum’s favour (The Algemeiner, 11 Mar 2025); the later Ninth Circuit ruling was not confirmed. Germany’s Court of Arbitration for Nazi-looted Cultural Property began work on 1 December 2025, replacing the Advisory Commission: claimants may file unilaterally, 36 arbitrators are available, and panels issue binding awards on a framework with a reduced burden of proof and presumptive rules (German Lost Art Foundation, 1 Dec 2025). In the UK the Spoliation Advisory Panel hears claims to objects in national and public collections and, by joint request, in private collections; its recommendations are not binding (GOV.UK, updated 23 Oct 2026).
cases.money: A withdrawn lot earns nothing and the catalogue cost is sunk (from memory; no house page opened states a withdrawal fee). A title claim that succeeds after sale returns the price: the Schiele was ordered turned over without compensation to the museum that paid for it in 1966 (ABA). A Spoliation Advisory Panel recommendation, if accepted, is treated as full and final settlement (GOV.UK). The stolen-art check is cheap and the house already pays for it: the Art Loss Register charges auction houses £3.66 a lot in the UK (US $4.95) on a subscription with an £800 minimum, a single trade search £85 plus VAT, an urgent one £300 with an answer within a working day; a registrant pays the ALR a 5% location fee and a further 5% on recovery or settlement, or 20% if the ALR is appointed to recover (ALR FAQ). Legal costs are the house’s and the consignor’s; the Cassirer litigation has run since 2005 (The Algemeiner).

cases.persona: a private-sales director at a New York house, with the post-war specialist
cases.task: ‘The client will sell her Rothko, about US$15m, but not at auction: no catalogue, no price in the papers, done by spring. What can we offer, at what fee, and how long will it take?’
cases.sum: about US$15m (the client’s figure); the auction record is US$98.39m, Christie’s New York, 18 May 2026 (HENI)
cases.reading: Rothko’s public market reset in May 2026: No. 15 (Two Greens and Red Stripe) (1964), acquired directly from the artist by Agnes Gund, sold at Christie’s New York on 18 May 2026 for US$98.39m (US$85m hammer, from the Gund estate), above the 2012 record of US$86.88m for Orange Red Yellow; Sotheby’s sold Brown and Blacks in Reds (1957) from Robert Mnuchin for US$85.8m with fees on 14 May 2026 and a second Mnuchin Rothko for US$20.8m, all 11 Mnuchin lots guaranteed; Rothko’s combined May total was US$232m, more than Pollock (HENI, 18 May and 1 Jun 2026; The Art Newspaper, 19 May 2026). In London on 15 October 2026 a guaranteed Rothko Untitled (1969) was in a sale that missed its low estimate (The Art Newspaper, 16 Oct 2026). The private desks are large and opaque: Christie’s 2025 private sales were about US$1.5bn, 24% of revenue, and its top three sales of the year were private; Sotheby’s about US$1.2bn, 17%; both ‘gently declined or held steady’ against 2024 (The Art Newspaper, 17 Dec 2025). In 2016 Christie’s private sales were US$935.5m (16.2% of its total) and Sotheby’s US$583m (about 12%), and Phillips’ then CEO put the chief benefit as ‘People don’t know the price, there’s no risk of a public failure’ (The Art Newspaper, 8 Mar 2017). No private Rothko sale with a price was found on any page opened; the houses do not publish them.
cases.money: The fee: the houses do not publish private-sale commissions on any page opened; Sotheby’s own consigning roadmap (2024) names the private treaty sale as an option and gives seller’s commissions at auction of 0% to 10% or more, with guarantees or a give-back of part of the buyer’s premium for major collections; the trade commonly describes a negotiated private-sale commission of a few per cent to about 10% with a buyer’s fee on top (from memory, unconfirmed). The comparison the client will make: at auction a US$15m hammer carries a buyer’s premium of about US$2.93m on Sotheby’s bands (28% to US$2m, 22% to US$8m, 15% above — Sotheby’s help centre, updated 9 Sep 2026; my arithmetic) plus the seller’s commission (standard 10%, negotiable) and a 2% success fee above the high estimate (Sotheby’s fee structure). The tax: a New York buyer pays sales tax unless the work ships out of state or is bought for resale by a dealer; Sotheby’s paid US$6.25m in November 2024 for accepting resale certificates it knew were false (NY Attorney General). Shipping, insurance and storage are for the parties’ account (Sotheby’s fee structure, for auction consignments). Legal: a private-sale agreement and, if the buyer is abroad, export papers (see the cross-border case).

HENI (18 May 2026): the Rothko record moved 13% to US$98.39m. HENI (1 Jun 2026): US$232m of Rothko in one May week, every Mnuchin lot guaranteed. The Art Newspaper (16 Oct 2026): a guaranteed Rothko in a London sale that missed its estimate. The Art Newspaper (8 Mar 2017): discretion is the chief benefit, ‘no risk of a public failure’.

A buyer whose money is not his own: the PSI’s private-dealer Magritte (2020).

Exclusivity that outlasts the client’s patience while the house shows the work to a short list.
A leak: the whole point of the route is that nobody knows the price (Phillips’ CEO, 2017).
cases.value_left: Nothing public prices a private sale: no fee schedule, no time to sale, no record of what private Rothkos made. The houses publish annual private-sales totals and nothing else. A specialist cannot show the client, on paper, the net from a private sale against an auction with a guarantee, because one side of the comparison is unpublished; the terminal can at least set out the public side (premium bands, commission, success fee, tax) and the dated record.

cases.persona: a Sotheby’s specialist in London, with Paris colleagues and the shipping desk
cases.where: Paris to London, or Paris to New York
cases.task: ‘A Paris owner will consign a 1890s painting worth about €2m. She wants London in March or New York in May. What papers, what tax at each border, how long, and what can stop it?’
cases.sum: about €2m (the owner’s figure); the French certificate threshold for paintings over 50 years old is €300,000 (Ministère de la Culture, 2021)
cases.reading: The French side is the slow part. A painting more than 50 years old and worth €300,000 or more needs a certificat d’exportation before it leaves France, the threshold having been doubled from €150,000 by décret 2020-1718 of 28 December 2020 with effect from 1 January 2021 (watercolours and pastels €50,000, drawings €30,000, prints €20,000, sculptures €100,000, photographs €25,000); an EU export licence is now required for exits to the United Kingdom and its thresholds were not changed (Ministère de la Culture note, 13 Jan 2021). The Minister has four months to decide (Code du patrimoine R.111-6) and the Conseil d’État held on 13 February 2026 (no. 497557) that silence for four months on a complete application is in principle a tacit certificate, but not where the Minister has suspended review under L.111-3-1 and asked for proof of the object’s status that the applicant does not supply — in that case, two Renaissance sculptures the court found to be in the public domain since 1789, applied for through an auction house as agent (Conseil d’État; CMS, 19 Mar 2026). A refusal is possible only for a national treasure, no new application for 30 months, during which the State may offer to buy at an expert price; a certificate for an object under 100 years old runs for a renewable 20 years (CMS). On the UK side works of art imported into Great Britain carry import VAT at a reduced rate of 5%; a lot is commonly entered under Temporary Admission to be sold at auction, then re-exported, declared to another procedure or finally imported, and VAT on the buyer’s premium is at the standard rate, zero-rated if the lot is re-exported directly from Temporary Admission (GOV.UK, updated 30 Sep 2026). On the US side the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs by six to three in February 2026; the Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on about 80 countries announced in July 2026 largely exempt works of art, antiques and collectors’ items under USTR’s fact sheet of 23 July 2026, while Canada’s separate 50% tariffs of 20 July 2026 apply to art, antiques and collectibles (The Art Newspaper, 28 Jul 2026). The May 2026 Section 122 surcharge of up to 15% is mentioned only in that article’s summary of an earlier piece.
cases.money: France: the certificate is free of charge (from memory, unconfirmed); the cost is time, four months unless the file is complete and no question is raised. UK: import VAT at 5% of the customs value on final import; none if the lot is re-exported from Temporary Admission after the sale; VAT at the standard rate on the buyer’s premium, zero-rated on direct re-export (GOV.UK). US: works of art under HTS Chapter 97 duty-free (from memory); the 2026 Section 301 tariffs largely exempt art (The Art Newspaper, 28 Jul 2026); state sales or use tax on delivery in the US is the buyer’s matter (see the NY resale-certificate settlement). Shipping, packing and insurance are for the consignor’s account at Sotheby’s (fee structure); crate, courier and transit-insurance quotes are not published on any page opened. The sale itself: seller’s commission standard 10% and success fee 2%, buyer’s premium 28%/22%/15% at Sotheby’s since 13 February 2026 (fee structure; The Art Newspaper, 17 Feb 2026). Artist’s Resale Right in the UK on a sale of £1,000 or more where the artist died within the last 70 years (GOV.UK).

cases.calendar: Four months for the French decision, so a certificate applied for now reaches March 2027 only if the file is complete and no question is raised; the London sales are in March (4 March 2026 this year), June and October; New York’s May week (14–19 May 2026 this year); the 2026 French thresholds have applied since 1 January 2021; the UK VAT guidance was updated 30 September 2026; the US Section 301 regime dates from July 2026.
cases.whispers: CMS (19 Mar 2026): the certificate’s ‘apparent guarantee of free circulation’ can overstate the protection, and the procedure can be suspended on serious indications of public-domain status, illicit import, forgery or criminal origin. The Art Newspaper (28 Jul 2026): Cinoa welcomed the exemption of works of art, antiques and collectors’ items from the new US duties. The Art Newspaper (17 Feb 2026): the premium rises at the lower tiers make the London sale dearer for the buyer than a year ago. GOV.UK (30 Sep 2026): the import-VAT guidance was updated this autumn.

Final import into the UK at 5% when the buyer meant to re-export: the premium then carries standard-rate VAT too (GOV.UK).
A tariff change on the US route: the regime changed twice in 2026 (The Art Newspaper).
cases.value_left: The houses do not publish a route sheet: which threshold applies, how long the certificate takes, what the UK and US entries cost, and what the net is under each. The French thresholds doubled in 2021 and the trade press still quotes the old €150,000; the Conseil d’État settled the four-month silence point only in February 2026. A terminal that carried the thresholds by category, the decision clock and the two 2026 rulings would save the Paris owner a season.

cases.persona: an executor of a Connecticut estate, across the table from the house’s fiduciary client group in New York
cases.task: ‘I have forty works, an estate-tax return due in nine months and three houses offering to appraise and to sell. What does the IRS need, what do the houses offer an estate, and what did the big estates of the last year actually get?’
cases.sum: Forty works, value to be fixed at date of death; the 2026 federal basic exclusion is US$15,000,000 per decedent (IRS, updated 3 Nov 2026)
cases.reading: The benchmarks are the best single-owner results on record. Sotheby’s sold the Leonard A. Lauder collection on 18 November 2025, its first sale in the Breuer building: 24 lots, all sold, 83% above high estimate, US$527.5m against US$379.2–412.5m, led by Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer at US$236.4m against expectations of US$150m, with Blumenwiese at US$86m and a Munch at US$35.1m (Sotheby’s press release). Christie’s sold the S.I. Newhouse collection on 18 May 2026 for US$540.5m hammer (US$630.8m with fees) against US$462–595m, every lot sold, reported as entirely backed by third-party guarantees, with Pollock’s Number 7A at US$157m hammer and Brancusi’s Danaïde at US$93m; the Newhouse estate’s Christie’s sales since 2018 total US$1.05bn with fees; the Agnes Gund estate’s Rothko made US$85m hammer (US$98.3m) in the same week (The Art Newspaper, 19 May 2026). Sotheby’s Mnuchin sale of 14 May 2026 was white-glove with all 11 works guaranteed, led by a Rothko at US$85.8m (HENI, 1 Jun 2026). The Lewis Collection (Joe Lewis) took the other route: four School of London works made £35.8m with fees in March 2026, and the June 2026 standalone sale was estimated at £150–200m with no guarantee, the owners choosing to let the market set the result; Sotheby’s London’s 24 June 2026 evening, combining the Lewis sale and the various-owner sale, made £393.4m (US$520.7m), the highest for a single night in Europe (The Art Newspaper, 30 Apr 2026; HENI, 24 Jun 2026). Sotheby’s New York’s Modern Evening Auction of 18 November 2026 carries single-owner sections including works from the Armand Hammer Collection sold to benefit the foundation (Sotheby’s catalogue). The IRS side is fixed by regulation: items of artistic value worth more than US$3,000 in total need an expert appraisal under oath filed with the return (26 CFR 20.2031-6).
cases.money: Federal estate tax: Form 706 is due nine months after death, with an automatic six-month extension to file on Form 4768 but not to pay; the gross estate is valued at fair market value at death; copies of appraisals go with the return (IRS FAQ, updated 23 Jul 2026). The basic exclusion is US$15,000,000 for 2026 decedents (US$13,990,000 for 2025) under Public Law 119-21 of 4 July 2025 (IRS, updated 3 Nov 2026); the top rate of 40% is from memory. Connecticut: for decedents dying in 2026 the exemption is US$15 million, the tax is 12% of the excess over the federal basic exclusion amount, the combined gift and estate tax payable is capped at US$15 million, and Form CT-706/709 is due six months after death (extension on CT-706/709 EXT); a taxable estate over US$15 million files with the Probate Court and DRS, one at or below it files CT-706 NT with the Probate Court only (Connecticut DRS, updated 30 Jun 2026). The appraisal: an expert under oath for articles of artistic or intrinsic value above US$3,000 (26 CFR 20.2031-6); IRS Art Appraisal Services must be referred any single item claimed at US$50,000 or more and the Art Advisory Panel sees items above US$150,000; a Statement of Value under Rev. Proc. 96-15 is available for items appraised at US$50,000 or more, with a fee paid through Pay.gov that the IRS updates biannually, issued by 31 December for requests received by 15 July and by 30 June for requests received by 15 January (IRS, reviewed 30 Apr 2026). The house’s terms: seller’s commission from 0% to 10% or more; for major collections guarantees or a ‘give-back’ of part of the buyer’s premium; costs that may fall to the estate — insurance, marketing, shipping, restoration, framing, storage, catalogue rights; buyers have about five business days to pay and the seller is paid around 30 to 45 days after the sale (Sotheby’s, Roadmap for consigning, 2024; Sotheby’s fee structure: standard 10%, 2% success fee, 45 days). The cases: in Newberger (Tax Court, 2015) a US$5m appraisal was rejected after the work sold for nearly US$13m seven months later and the court set US$10m; in Kollsman the Ninth Circuit found a conflict of interest where the auction house appraised a collection while offering to sell it (Sotheby’s, Navigating the estate administration of art collections, 2023).

cases.people: The estate’s probate counsel and tax adviser; an independent qualified appraiser (or the house’s valuation department with the Kollsman conflict managed); the houses’ fiduciary or trusts-and-estates groups (Sotheby’s Fiduciary Client Group, with contacts in New York and London; Phillips and Bonhams publish trusts-and-estates pages, not opened); IRS Art Appraisal Services for a Statement of Value; a fine-art shipper and storage for the works during administration; the house’s financial services arm if the estate needs liquidity before the sale (Sotheby’s names it among FCG’s related services).
cases.calendar: Connecticut CT-706/709 six months after death; federal Form 706 nine months after death (extension to file six months); Statement of Value windows: requests by 15 July answered by 31 December, by 15 January answered by 30 June; the marquee weeks: New York 16–20 November 2026 (Sotheby’s Modern Evening Auction 18 November 2026) and May 2027; London March, June and October; Lauder sold 18 November 2025, Newhouse 18 May 2026, Mnuchin 14 May 2026, Lewis 4 March and 24 June 2026; settlement 30–45 days after the sale.
cases.whispers: The Art Newspaper (30 Apr 2026): the Lewises declined a guarantee on a £150–200m sale, the most valuable single-owner collection offered in the UK; the same piece recalls a 2016 Guardian report, citing Panama Papers documents, of a 1997 profit-sharing arrangement with Christie’s as an early form of guarantee. The Art Newspaper (19 May 2026): Newhouse entirely third-party guaranteed; the estate’s Christie’s total US$1.05bn since 2018. HENI (1 Jun 2026): every Mnuchin lot guaranteed; strong and weak guarantees both above the norm. Sotheby’s (Nov 2025): 83% of Lauder lots above high estimate. Sotheby’s (2023): the Tax Court says no evidence is more probative of value than the direct sale price.
risks: An appraisal the IRS rejects after the sale shows the real price: Newberger, US$5m against a US$13m sale (Sotheby’s, 2023).
The selling house as appraiser: Kollsman (Ninth Circuit).
Selling before probate steps are complete: a custodian may refuse release (Sotheby’s, 2023).
A guaranteed single-owner sale that sells to the guarantors at the low estimate (Apollo, 7 Oct 2025, on Fisher Landau).
Ivory, rhino horn or other restricted materials in the forty works (Sotheby’s, 2023).
cases.value_left: The houses offer the executor a proposal and an appraisal from the same desk; the Ninth Circuit called that a conflict. No house page opened shows the estate’s net under each house’s terms, what the premium give-back is worth, or how the great estates’ terms compared. The IRS pages give the thresholds and the clock; the houses give the sale dates; nobody puts the nine-month return, the Statement of Value windows and the marquee weeks on one calendar for the executor.
next: Inventory and secure the forty works and check for any in another state or abroad.
Appoint an independent appraiser now for the date-of-death values; manage any conflict if a house also values.

Take written proposals from three houses on one template: estimate, venue, date, commission, costs, guarantee or give-back, settlement.
Decide guaranteed or unguaranteed for the top lots with the Lauder, Newhouse, Mnuchin and Lewis results in front of the beneficiaries.

sources.record: 27 Oct 2026: the Art Basel Qatar 2027 list with the 35 non-returning galleries named. 20 Oct 2025: Bonhams’ sale to Pemberton and the leadership overhaul.
sources.how_to_read: Fair and corporate structure first; quotes the organisers and lets the list speak.

sources.n: HENI News and the HENI Auction Index (an Art Market Monitor successor in spirit)
sources.who: HENI, the London art-services and publishing group (from memory, Joe Hage’s firm); articles unsigned.
sources.cadence: Before and after every marquee sale; season grades.
sources.good_for: A letter grade per sale and per week ‘based on 10+ metrics’: bidders per lot, share above estimates, bought-ins, strong versus weak guarantees, records.
sources.record: 5 Nov 2025: ‘even a modest rebound would lift the HENI Auction Index this November’; 25 Nov 2025: graded the week A (Sotheby’s A+, Christie’s B, Phillips B-), the best since spring 2022. 29 Sep 2025: Christie’s Hong Kong B-.
sources.how_to_read: Useful standardisation; the metrics are HENI’s own and the grade is a composite, so cite the underlying number where it gives one. HENI also sells art, so keep that in view.

sources.who: A subscription art-market newsletter (editors not verified this session).
sources.good_for: Short items on gallery moves, hires and consignments; interviews with dealers.
sources.price: Not verified; from memory a paid annual subscription.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Trade-facing and quick; attribute and verify before use.

sources.who: London; ‘News Desk’ bylines.
sources.good_for: Fast relays of reports and London results; free.
sources.record: 12 Mar 2026: relayed the Art Basel and UBS report figures accurately (US$59.6bn, up 4%; auctions US$20.7bn, up 9%).
sources.how_to_read: A relay, not a source of record; go to the report or house it cites.

sources.who: Not verified this session.
sources.good_for: Short daily market items (from memory).
sources.record: None checked.
sources.how_to_read: Carry nothing from it until opened.

sources.n: The Fiduciary Eye (Withers Art and Advisory)
sources.who: Mari-Claudia Jiménez (partner, co-head of art law, New York; former chairman and president of Sotheby’s) and Frank K. Lord IV (senior counsel).
sources.cadence: Twice a year, after the New York seasons.
sources.good_for: The fiduciary’s reading of a season: guarantees, estimate-setting, blockage discounts, when an estate should sell privately.
sources.record: November 2025: 16 works above US$20m and six above US$50m; warned that single-bid sales to third-party guarantors mean lots were ‘effectively presold’.
sources.how_to_read: A law firm’s marketing, but expert; no tax figures in the edition read.

sources.who: New York non-profit (501(c)(3)); student and practitioner authors; a Case Law Database; the Art in Brief podcast.
sources.cadence: Rolling case reviews and a newsletter.
sources.good_for: Case numbers, parties and claims as filed (Cahn v. Sotheby’s, No. 659868/2025), summaries of art-law decisions.
sources.price: Some content free; membership US$70–150 a year for the archive and database.
sources.record: 13 Jan 2026 review of Cahn v. Sotheby’s noted the complaint offered no evidence for its central claim.
sources.how_to_read: Reliable for the docket; always cite the court and number it gives.

sources.who: Artnet News editors and reporters.
sources.good_for: Sale previews and post-mortems in the reporters’ own voices.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Artnet’s frame in audio; no new facts beyond its reporting.

sources.who: Benjamin Godsill and Nate Freeman (from memory).
sources.good_for: Gossip and reading of the week from an adviser and a reporter.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Opinion and rumour; attribute.

sources.who: Russell Tovey and Robert Diament (from memory).
sources.good_for: Artists and collectors in conversation; taste, not prices.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Not a market source.

sources.n: The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report (Clare McAndrew, Arts Economics)
sources.who: Dr Clare McAndrew, Arts Economics; co-published by Art Basel and UBS.
sources.cadence: Annual, March (2026 edition released 12 March 2026); a mid-year survey of collectors in the autumn.
sources.good_for: The market’s size and shares: 2025 global sales US$59.6bn (up 4%), 41.5m transactions; dealers US$34.8bn, auctions US$20.7bn, private sales just under US$4.2bn; US 44%, UK 18%, China 14%, France 8%; fine-art lots over US$1m up 21% in value, over US$10m up 30%; online US$9.2bn, lowest since 2019; Post-war US$3.1bn (31%), Modern US$2.4bn, Impressionist up 47%, Old Masters up 30%.
sources.price: Free download (the page opened offers press releases in four languages; the full PDF has historically been free).
sources.record: The dealer-side figures are survey extrapolations; the auction figures reconcile broadly with Artprice’s US$11.1bn fine-art count once decorative and collectibles are added.
sources.how_to_read: The benchmark everyone quotes; its dealer sales are estimates from surveys, its auction figures include the houses’ own disclosures; sponsored by a fair and a bank.
src: Art Basel, Global Art Market Report 2026

sources.who: Anders Petterson (founder and chief executive); analysts Lindsay Dewar Leite and James Cocksey on the Hong Kong report; partners Deloitte, Mishcon de Reya (China Market Report), Affordable Art Fair.
sources.cadence: After every marquee week; half-year and annual auction reviews; the biennial Deloitte report; a confidence survey.
sources.good_for: Evening-sale comparisons with guarantee analysis, ten-year trends, sell-through, the single-owner share (15.6% of value over a decade, 31.3% in 2022, 18.5% in the first ten months of 2025, per Observer), H1 2026 totals (US$6.8bn, up 70%).
sources.price: Single auction report £195; Analyst Pro membership £1,195 a year (report page, March 2026).
sources.record: H1 2026 (10 Jul 2026): the recovery ‘proving to be far broader than the headline-grabbing results at the very top end’. January 2026: Petterson expected the US$1m-plus ‘flow again’; London’s H1 then ran at US$1.42bn, up 131%.
sources.how_to_read: The trade’s statistician; sells to the houses and advisers; methodology consistent year to year, which makes it the best comparator even where its totals differ from the houses’.
src: ArtTactic report page, Hong Kong March 2026
October Gallery relaying The Art Newspaper, 14 Jul 2026
Ocula on the ArtTactic/Mishcon China Market Report 2026

sources.who: Artmarket.com (Euronext: PRC), Thierry Ehrmann; the annual report ‘The Art Market in 2025’ (32nd edition, 10 March 2026) and the annual Contemporary Art Market Report (October).
sources.cadence: Annual reports in March and October; database continuous; weekly indices.
sources.good_for: Fine-art auction turnover with lots and unsold rates: 2025 US$11.1bn (up 12%), 867,000 lots sold, 32% unsold, average US$12,820, median about US$600; US 42%, China 16%, UK 13%, France 8.5%; Klimt US$397m the year’s top artist; the record US$236.36m.
sources.price: Reports free in three languages (the release); database subscriptions not priced in the release (from memory, tiered from a few hundred euros a year; unverified).
sources.record: Its releases carry internal inconsistencies (country shares stated two ways; a 2024/2025 mix-up in the US$1m-plus lot count) and promotional projections from the chief executive.
sources.how_to_read: The widest auction coverage, including Chinese houses via its AMMA partnership; fine art only; French framing (Paris ranked third among cities at US$844m); separate the data from the marketing.

sources.n: Deloitte Private and ArtTactic Art & Finance Report
sources.who: Deloitte Luxembourg (Adriano Picinati di Torcello, global art and finance coordinator) with ArtTactic; 57 experts and nearly 500 survey responses in the 9th edition (2025); 30 contributed articles.
sources.good_for: Wealth managers’ art services (51% offer them, up from about a quarter in 2011), art-secured lending, the wealth-transfer estimate (about US$992bn of art and collectibles to change hands over the next decade), surveys of collectors and advisers.
sources.price: Download via a form; the page does not state a price (historically free).
sources.record: Not checked against outcomes; its projections are survey-based.
sources.how_to_read: Written for private banks and family offices; strong on lending and services, weak on prices; treat the trillion-dollar figures as modelled.

sources.n: Hiscox Online Art Trade Report (with ArtTactic)
sources.who: Hiscox (insurer) with ArtTactic.
sources.good_for: Online sales share, platform rankings, buyer surveys on trust and shipping.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: An insurer’s survey; sample skews to online buyers.

sources.who: The European Fine Art Foundation (Maastricht); earlier editions by Clare McAndrew (to 2016) and Rachel Pownall (2017); later themed reports (from memory).
sources.good_for: Art finance and the dealer sector in earlier editions.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Historic series; check which edition and author before citing.

sources.who: MutualArt (London); artist pages with results and exhibitions.
sources.good_for: Artist-level price histories and upcoming lots; alerts.
sources.price: Not verified (from memory: tiered monthly subscriptions).
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Aggregated; check the house’s page for the fee basis.

sources.who: Invaluable (Boston); live-bidding platform with a price archive.
sources.good_for: Regional and mid-market houses, an auction calendar, price archive for decorative arts.
sources.price: Bidding free to register; archive subscription not verified.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.

sources.good_for: Mid-market and regional houses in the US, past prices with images, the calendar.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.

sources.good_for: Cross-house search of upcoming lots and past results; alerts.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Aggregator; the source house’s page governs.

sources.who: Barnebys (Stockholm); aggregator with a magazine (Giulia Zileri Dal Verme, global senior editor) and a price bank.
sources.good_for: Cross-house search of lots in Europe and the US; readable season previews.
sources.price: Search free; price-bank subscription not verified.
sources.record: 10 Oct 2025 preview: ‘understood’ Sotheby’s had guaranteed the Lauder collection, Klimt above US$150m; the Klimt made US$236.4m.
sources.how_to_read: An aggregator’s magazine; attribute its ‘understood’ items.

sources.who: askART (US); artist dictionary with auction records, strong on American art.
sources.good_for: American artists’ biographies, signatures and past prices.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: US regional bias; dated interface; verify prices elsewhere.

sources.who: Louise Blouin Media’s index (BASI), descended from Hislop’s Art Sales Index; status after the group’s 2020 troubles not verified.
sources.good_for: Historic results back to the 1920s where still accessible.
sources.record: Not checked; no page opened.
sources.how_to_read: Treat as an archive; confirm it is live before relying on it.

sources.n: The houses’ own catalogues and result pages (Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips, Bonhams)
sources.who: The houses.
sources.cadence: Catalogues from about four weeks before a sale; results within hours; press releases the same night.
sources.good_for: The estimates as published, lot order, guarantee and irrevocable-bid symbols (in the printed catalogue and lot pages), prices with premium, the house’s own totals.
sources.record: This session: Sotheby’s catalogue pages read cleanly (Blaquier 12 lots; The Now 53 lots; Modern 26 lots) but showed no guarantee symbols in the text returned; Phillips’ release and sale page disagree on its evening sale’s day and hour; Christie’s pages return a bot-check script; Bonhams’ release page carries no date.
sources.how_to_read: Primary for estimates and prices; the symbols for guarantees are in the lot notes and conditions, not the headline pages; totals are quoted with premium unless stated.

sources.who: Private company, London, founded 1990; also runs The Watch Register, recovery, mediation and Nazi-era research services.
sources.cadence: Continuous; ‘more than 400,000 checks a year’ (its own figure).
sources.good_for: Due-diligence searches before purchase or consignment against ‘over 700,000 items’ of stolen, looted, missing and disputed property, including the Interpol database and six external 1933–45 databases.
sources.price: Single search £85 / €100 / US$110 plus VAT; urgent £300 / €350 / US$400 (reply within one working day where possible); subscriptions of 10 searches £700 / €800 / US$850 a year or 25 searches £1,500 / €1,750 / US$2,000; auction-house rates per lot UK £3.66, US US$4.95, DACH €5.60, rest of Europe €5.10, annual minimum £800 / €900 / US$1,000; registering a loss £15 / €17.50 / US$20, plus a 5% location fee and a 20% recovery fee of the net benefit (FAQ page, read 13 Nov 2026).
sources.record: A clean ALR certificate is what the houses and fairs ask for; it is not proof of title.
sources.how_to_read: Commercial and incentive-driven (the fees on recovery); a search covers what has been registered, not every claim; keep the certificate on file.

sources.n: Interpol Stolen Works of Art database and the ID-Art app
sources.who: Interpol (Lyon); funded for the app by the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World.
sources.cadence: Continuous; entries come from member countries’ police.
sources.good_for: Checking an object against ‘almost 57,000 objects’ reported stolen by police worldwide, from a phone, with no account.
sources.price: Free; the app (Apple and Android, in Arabic, English, French and Spanish) needs no username or password; a separate application form exists for direct database access.
sources.record: Only what police have entered; many losses never reach it.
sources.how_to_read: Necessary, not sufficient; pair with the ALR and the Nazi-era registries.

sources.n: Lost Art database (Deutsches Zentrum Kulturgutverluste, Magdeburg)
sources.who: German Lost Art Foundation, founded 1 January 2015 by the federal government, the states and the municipal associations; about €12.4m federal funding in 2023.
sources.cadence: Continuous; search and found reports from about 1,400 institutions and individuals.
sources.good_for: Nazi-era losses (almost 180,000 detailed object entries plus several million summarised), war losses, Soviet-zone and GDR losses, colonial contexts; the German provenance-research funding record (435 Nazi-era projects, about €48.8m, 2008–June 2023).
sources.price: Publicly accessible (‘öffentlich zugänglich’); no charge stated.
sources.record: Entries are claims and reports, not adjudications.
sources.how_to_read: German-centred; a hit is a reason to stop and research, not a finding of title.

sources.n: Commission for Looted Art in Europe and its Central Registry (lootedart.com)
sources.who: London-based non-profit; the Central Registry of Information on Looted Cultural Property 1933–1945 covers about 49 countries.
sources.good_for: Country-by-country laws, claims bodies, restitution decisions (Spoliation Advisory Panel reports), research resources.
sources.price: Free (the page read is a navigation index; no fee shown).
sources.record: Not checked beyond the index.
sources.how_to_read: A reference library rather than a searchable object database; use with Lost Art and the French repertory (MNR).
src: Commission for Looted Art in Europe

sources.who: Office of Foreign Assets Control, US Treasury.
sources.cadence: SDN list last updated 13 November 2026 11:32; Non-SDN consolidated list 4 November 2026 (as shown on the tool).
sources.good_for: Screening counterparties against the SDN list, the Foreign Sanctions Evaders list, the Sectoral Sanctions Identifications list and other OFAC lists, with fuzzy matching and a confidence slider.
sources.record: The tool itself warns that its use ‘is not a substitute for undertaking appropriate due diligence’ and does not limit liability; it does not apply the 50% ownership rule for you.
sources.how_to_read: Names only; ownership chains and the 50% rule must be read from OFAC’s own guidance, not inferred from a no-hit; the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 extended the Bank Secrecy Act to antiquities dealers, with FinCEN’s implementing rules still pending as far as this session could tell (from memory, unverified).

sources.n: OFSI consolidated list (UK) and the EU Sanctions Map
sources.who: HM Treasury’s Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation; the European Commission and EEAS for the EU map.
sources.good_for: UK and EU designations, which differ from OFAC’s; the EU’s art-specific prohibitions (the luxury-goods ban on works of art above €300 to Russia under Regulation 833/2014 as amended, from memory).
sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: Three lists, three regimes; a hit on any one blocks the trade in that jurisdiction; from memory, unverified.

sources.n: Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art (Arts Council England / DCMS)
sources.who: DCMS and Arts Council England; the committee’s 70th annual report (2024–25) published 21 July 2025.
sources.cadence: Annual report each summer; deferral decisions announced case by case.
sources.good_for: Which objects were deferred as ‘national treasures’, bought by UK institutions or exported: 2024–25 (1 May 2024–30 April 2025): 20 cases, 18 deferred, 2 not meeting the criteria, 6 bought in the UK, 9 exported or exportable, 3 still under deferral.
sources.record: The report lists every deferred case with its recommended price.
sources.how_to_read: Only the cases referred to the committee; routine licences do not appear; the lead time for a deferral runs months.

sources.who: Free Law Project, a US non-profit.
sources.cadence: Continuous; RECAP mirrors PACER filings as users fetch them.
sources.good_for: Free access to US federal dockets and opinions and many state opinions; the first stop for a lawsuit named in the press.
sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: Coverage depends on what users have uploaded; state-court suits such as Cahn v. Sotheby’s (New York Supreme Court) are on the state’s own e-filing system. From memory.

sources.who: Art Basel (MCH Group); Noah Horowitz, chief executive; Vincenzo De Bellis, global director of fairs; Bridget Finn, director, Miami Beach.
sources.cadence: Exhibitor lists months ahead; sales reports at each fair’s close; the March report with UBS.
sources.good_for: Exhibitor lists and sector changes (Miami Beach 2026: 272 exhibitors, Galleries 204; Qatar 2027: 82), the fairs’ own dealer-reported sales.
sources.price: Free; ticket prices not read this session.
sources.record: The exhibitor numbers reported by The Art Newspaper matched the fair’s framing; Art Basel’s own stories page returned a server error on fetch.
sources.how_to_read: Sales reports are dealer-declared and unaudited; withdrawals are never explained by the fair.

sources.who: Frieze (Endeavor until its 2025 sale; owners not verified this session).
sources.cadence: Exhibitor lists and sales reports per fair; Frieze Abu Dhabi launches in November 2026 (per Reyburn, January 2026).
sources.good_for: London, Los Angeles, New York, Seoul and now Abu Dhabi exhibitor lists; dealer-reported sales.
sources.record: No Frieze page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: As Art Basel: declared sales, no reasons for absences.

sources.who: The European Fine Art Foundation.
sources.cadence: March (Maastricht) and May (New York); vetting reports.
sources.good_for: Old Masters, antiques and jewellery dealers’ offerings; the strictest vetting in the fair world.
sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: Vetting committees’ decisions are not published lot by lot. From memory.

sources.n: The houses’ and fairs’ social accounts
sources.who: Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips, Bonhams, Art Basel, Frieze on Instagram and X (official accounts).
sources.good_for: First notice of a withdrawn lot, a record, a sale total; auctioneer clips.
sources.record: Not sampled this session.
sources.how_to_read: Marketing; totals are with premium; nothing on guarantees.

sources.who: Instagram account run, as the press has described it, by the artist Hilde Lynn Helphenstein (from memory).
sources.good_for: What the trade is laughing at; a mood indicator for fairs and sales.
sources.record: Not sampled this session.
sources.how_to_read: Satire; never a source of fact.

sources.who: UK weekly trade paper (Auction Technology Group); the recruitment column records hires and departures.
sources.good_for: Appointments (22 May 2026: François Henri Pinault named Christie’s chairman, Guillaume Cerutti departs; 25 Nov 2025: Henry House to Dreweatts as chief executive from Sotheby’s), the UK regional houses, ownership changes (Pierre Bergé & Associés, April 2026).
sources.price: Not shown on the page read.
sources.record: Its recruitment page carried nothing dated after 26 May 2026 at the time of reading.
sources.how_to_read: UK trade first; the big-four moves appear, but New York hires are thin.

sources.n: The Art Newspaper China (艺术新闻/中文版)
sources.who: The Chinese-language edition published under licence in Shanghai (Modern Media, from memory).
sources.good_for: Mainland museum and gallery news, Shanghai and Beijing fairs, Chinese collectors’ moves.
sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: Reads the market from the mainland; auction coverage lighter than Hong Kong’s outlets.

sources.n: Artron (雅昌) and the AMMA index
sources.who: Artron Art Group (Shenzhen); AMMA (Art Market Monitor of Artron) supplies Chinese auction data to Artprice.
sources.good_for: Mainland auction results (Poly, China Guardian and the regional houses), Chinese painting and calligraphy indices.
sources.record: No page opened; Artprice’s China figures rest on it (China US$1.76bn in 2025, down 5.4%).
sources.how_to_read: Chinese-language; mainland totals include unpaid lots, a known gap between ‘sold’ and ‘settled’.

sources.who: TheValue.com Ltd, Hong Kong; English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese.
sources.cadence: Daily; every Hong Kong sale reported with hammer and premium.
sources.good_for: Hong Kong results lot by lot (Phillips autumn 2025: HK$160m, 100% sold, Nara’s Pinky HK$56.6m after a day-of estimate cut), the houses’ mechanics (Phillips’ Priority Bidding), Chinese works of art.
sources.price: Free; apps for iOS and Android.
sources.record: 30 Sep 2025: documented that Phillips lowered Pinky’s estimate from HK$60m–80m to HK$35m–55m on the day and withdrew seven lots inside the 48-hour window.
sources.how_to_read: The best free record of the Hong Kong rooms; trilingual; strong on Chinese ceramics and jewellery as well.

sources.who: Tokyo art portal and magazine run by Culture Convenience Club; market reports by its editorial department.
sources.cadence: Daily online; paid membership for premium content and the print magazine.
sources.good_for: Japanese reading of Hong Kong and New York sales with yen conversions; Kusama, Nara and Foujita markets; the Christie’s Hong Kong autumn 2026 result (HK$726.4m, 100% sold).
sources.price: Paid memberships (amount not read); articles read free.
sources.record: 30 Sep 2026: carried Arkou Yu’s pre-sale view that Kusama prices were ‘fairly stable’ after her death; her A-Pumpkin then hammered just under its low estimate.
sources.how_to_read: Japanese-language; precise on premiums and comparisons; the source for the Japanese artists’ markets.

sources.n: South China Morning Post (arts and luxury)
sources.who: Hong Kong daily (Alibaba-owned).
sources.cadence: Daily; season wraps after each Hong Kong week.
sources.good_for: Cross-house Hong Kong totals (its autumn 2026 wrap: ‘top HK$2 billion as Kusama works get a cool reception’), jewellery and watches, the Van Gogh’s Hong Kong showing ahead of New York.
sources.price: Subscription; the site refused both fetches this session.
sources.record: Headlines seen only; contents not carried.
sources.how_to_read: English-language record of the Hong Kong market; paywalled and bot-protected, so take it as relayed.

sources.who: Saffronart, Mumbai (Dinesh and Minal Vazirani); online and live auctions of Indian art.

sources.good_for: Indian modern and contemporary prices, the Husain, Gaitonde and Raza markets; its results are the comparables for Indian art.
sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: A house reporting its own sales; pair with Pundole’s and AstaGuru (which opened in London in March 2026, per ATG).

sources.record: No page opened this session.

sources.record: No page opened this session.

sources.record: No page opened this session.

sources.good_for: Gulf museums and fairs (Abu Dhabi Art, Art Dubai, Art Basel Qatar, Frieze Abu Dhabi), Sotheby’s Abu Dhabi weeks (US$1bn in December 2025 per Reyburn), regional collectors.

sources.who: Latin American art magazine (English and Spanish; copyright 2003–2026); partner of the Pinta fairs (Lima, BAphoto, Miami, Panamá, Asunción); María Sancho-Arroyo writes market pieces.
sources.good_for: Latin American galleries and collectors, the Pinta fairs, regional readings of global fairs (its February 2026 Art Basel Qatar report: modest reported sales, low booth prices, Art Mill Museum c. 2030).

sources.cadence: Journal issues through the year; biennial congress.
sources.good_for: Conservation science and treatment literature; finding a conservator by specialism.
sources.record: No page opened this session.

sources.record: No page opened this session.
sources.how_to_read: Professional body; the directory does not rate members.

sources.good_for: Peer-reviewed work on auction returns, guarantees, the death effect, buyer’s premium incidence, art as an asset.
sources.price: Institutional and personal subscriptions; article pay-per-view (not verified).
